en: Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.1 1. Ānisaṁsavagga Kimatthiyasutta (The Discourse on What Purpose) “Monks, what purpose does the cultivation of loving-kindness serve? “It serves the purpose of non-ill will, venerable sir. “But, monks, what purpose does the cultivation of non-ill will serve? “It serves the purpose of a pleasant abiding here and now, venerable sir. “But, monks, what purpose does the cultivation of a pleasant abiding here and now serve? “It serves the purpose of rapture, venerable sir. “But, monks, what purpose does the cultivation of rapture serve? “It serves the purpose of joy, venerable sir. “But, monks, what purpose does the cultivation of joy serve?

“It serves the purpose of tranquility, venerable sir. “But, monks, what purpose does the cultivation of tranquility serve? “It serves the purpose of happiness, venerable sir. “But, monks, what purpose does the cultivation of happiness serve? “It serves the purpose of concentration, venerable sir. “But, monks, what purpose does the cultivation of concentration serve? “It serves the purpose of knowing and seeing things as they really are, venerable sir. “But, monks, what purpose does the cultivation of knowing and seeing things as they really are serve? “It serves the purpose of disenchantment, venerable sir. “But, monks, what purpose does the cultivation of disenchantment serve? “It serves the purpose of dispassion, venerable sir. “But, monks, what purpose does the cultivation of dispassion serve? “It serves the purpose of liberation, venerable sir. “But, monks, what purpose does the cultivation of liberation serve? “It serves the purpose of the knowledge and vision of liberation, venerable sir. “But, monks, what purpose does the cultivation of the knowledge and vision of liberation serve? “It serves the purpose of final Nibbāna without clinging, venerable sir. “Monks, when one has cultivated loving-kindness, non-ill will is cultivated; when one has cultivated non-ill will, a pleasant abiding here and now is cultivated; when one has cultivated a pleasant abiding here and now, rapture is cultivated; when one has cultivated rapture, joy is cultivated; when one has cultivated joy, tranquility is cultivated; when one has cultivated tranquility, happiness is cultivated; when one has cultivated happiness, concentration is cultivated; when one has cultivated concentration, knowing and seeing things as they really are are cultivated; when one has cultivated knowing and seeing things as they really are, disenchantment is cultivated; when one has cultivated disenchantment, dispassion is cultivated; when one has cultivated dispassion, liberation is cultivated; when one has cultivated liberation, the knowledge and vision of liberation are cultivated; when one has cultivated the knowledge and vision of liberation, final Nibbāna without clinging is cultivated. Thus, monks, the cultivation of final Nibbāna without clinging is for the purpose of the cultivation of the knowledge and vision of liberation; the cultivation of the knowledge and vision of liberation is for the purpose of the cultivation of liberation; the cultivation of liberation is for the purpose of the cultivation of dispassion; the cultivation of dispassion is for the purpose of the cultivation of disenchantment; the cultivation of disenchantment is for the purpose of the cultivation of knowing and seeing things as they really are; the cultivation of knowing and seeing things as they really are is for the purpose of the cultivation of concentration; the cultivation of concentration is for the purpose of the cultivation of happiness; the cultivation of happiness is for the purpose of the cultivation of tranquility; the cultivation of tranquility is for the purpose of the cultivation of joy; the cultivation of joy is for the purpose of the cultivation of rapture; the cultivation of rapture is for the purpose of the cultivation of a pleasant abiding here and now; the cultivation of a pleasant abiding here and now is for the purpose of the cultivation of non-ill will; the cultivation of non-ill will is for the purpose of the cultivation of loving-kindness.”
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"For what purpose, Bhante, are wholesome virtues (sīla), and what is their benefit?
"Wholesome virtues, Ānanda, have non-regret as their purpose and non-regret as their benefit."
“But, Bhante, what is the purpose of freedom from remorse, and what is its benefit?
“Freedom from remorse, Ānanda, has gladness as its purpose;
it has gladness as its benefit. “But, Bhante, what is the purpose of gladness, and what is its benefit?”
“Joy, Ānanda, has rapture as its purpose and rapture as its benefit.
“But what, Bhante, is the purpose and what is the benefit of rapture?
“Rapture, Ānanda, has tranquility as its purpose and tranquility as its benefit.”
“But, Bhante, what is the purpose of tranquility, and what is its benefit?
“Tranquility, Ānanda, has happiness as its purpose and happiness as its benefit.
“But, Bhante, what is the purpose of happiness, and what is its benefit?”
“Happiness, Ānanda, has concentration as its purpose and concentration as its benefit.
“But what, Bhante, is the purpose and benefit of concentration?
“Concentration, Ānanda, has the knowledge and vision of things as they really are as its purpose and the knowledge and vision of things as they really are as its benefit.”
“But, venerable sir, what is the purpose and what is the benefit of knowing and seeing things as they really are?
“Knowing and seeing things as they really are, Ānanda, has disenchantment and dispassion as its purpose and disenchantment and dispassion as its benefit.
“But, venerable sir, what is the purpose and what is the benefit of disenchantment and dispassion?”
“Disenchantment and dispassion, Ānanda, have the knowledge and vision of liberation as their purpose and the knowledge and vision of liberation as their benefit.
Thus, Ānanda, wholesome virtues have non-regret as their purpose and non-regret as their benefit;
non-regret has gladness as its purpose and gladness as its benefit.”
Gladness has rapture as its purpose and rapture as its benefit;
rapture has tranquility as its purpose and tranquility as its benefit; tranquility has happiness as its purpose and happiness as its benefit.
Happiness has concentration as its purpose and concentration as its benefit;
concentration has knowledge and vision of things as they really are as its purpose and knowledge and vision of things as they really are as its benefit;
knowledge and vision of things as they really are has disenchantment and dispassion as its purpose and disenchantment and dispassion as its benefit.
Disenchantment and dispassion have the knowledge and vision of liberation as their purpose and the knowledge and vision of liberation as their benefit.
Thus, Ānanda, wholesome virtues lead gradually to the highest state. Thus ends the first [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.2 1. Ānisaṁsavagga Cetanākaraṇīyasutta “Monks, there are these ten things that should be done with volition by one who has gone forth out of faith from the household life into homelessness. What ten? One should dwell with a mind full of loving-kindness, without hostility and without ill will. One should purify the mind of the taint of ill will. One should dwell observing the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. One should purify the mind of the taint of sensual desire. One should dwell observing feelings in feelings... One should dwell observing the mind in the mind... One should dwell observing phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. One should purify the mind of the taint of ignorance. One should train in the higher virtuous behavior, the higher mind, and the higher wisdom. One should purify the mind of the taints through the higher training in virtuous behavior, the higher training in mind, and the higher training in wisdom. One should be one who gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life. One should purify the mind of the taints through the higher mind. One should gain at will, without trouble or difficulty, the knowledge and vision of the recollection of past lives, with their modes and details. One should purify the mind of the taints through the knowledge and vision of the recollection of past lives. One should gain at will, without trouble or difficulty, the divine eye, the purified superknowledge, seeing beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and understand how beings fare according to their kamma. One should purify the mind of the taints through the divine eye. One should gain at will, without trouble or difficulty, the destruction of the taints, and having realized for oneself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, enter therein and dwell. One should purify the mind of the taints through the destruction of the taints. These, monks, are the ten things that should be done with volition by one who has gone forth out of faith from the household life into homelessness.”
“Monks, for one who is virtuous, endowed with virtue, there is no need for a volitional effort:
‘May non-remorse arise in me.’”
This is the natural law, monks: that non-regret arises in one who is virtuous and endowed with virtue.
For one who has no regret, monks, there is no need for a volitional effort to think, "May joy arise in me."
It is the natural law, monks, that joy arises in one who is without remorse.
For one who is joyful, monks, no effort need be made [to think]:
“May rapture arise in me.”
It is the natural law, monks, that rapture arises in one who is gladdened.
For one whose mind is filled with rapture, monks, no volitional effort is required to think:
"May my body become tranquil."
It is the natural law, monks, that for one whose mind is filled with rapture, the body becomes tranquil.
For one whose body is tranquil, monks, there is no need for volition to think:
"I am experiencing pleasure."
This is the natural law, monks: one whose body is tranquil experiences happiness.
For one who is happy, monks, no volitional effort need be made to think, "May my mind become concentrated."
This is the natural law, monks: the mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated.
For one who is concentrated, monks, there is no need for volition, thinking:
"May I know and see things as they truly are."
This is the natural law, monks: one who is concentrated knows and sees things as they truly are.
For one who knows and sees things as they truly are, monks, there is no need for a volitional effort to think, "I am becoming disenchanted;
I am becoming dispassionate."
It is the nature of things, monks, that one who knows and sees according to reality becomes disenchanted and dispassionate.
For one who is disenchanted and dispassionate, monks, there is no need for a volitional effort to think:
"I shall realize the knowledge and vision of liberation."
It is the natural law, monks, that one who is disenchanted and dispassionate realizes the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Thus, monks, disenchantment and dispassion have the knowledge and vision of liberation as their purpose and the knowledge and vision of liberation as their benefit;
the knowledge and vision of things as they really are has disenchantment and dispassion as its purpose and disenchantment and dispassion as its benefit.
Concentration has the purpose of knowing and seeing things as they truly are, and its benefit is knowing and seeing things as they truly are;
happiness has concentration as its purpose and concentration as its benefit; tranquility has happiness as its purpose and happiness as its benefit.
Rapture has tranquility as its purpose and tranquility as its benefit;
gladness has rapture as its purpose and rapture as its benefit;
freedom from remorse has gladness as its purpose and gladness as its benefit.
Wholesome virtues have non-remorse as their purpose and non-remorse as their benefit.
Thus, monks, phenomena flow into phenomena, and phenomena fulfill phenomena, for the sake of going from the near shore to the far shore. Thus ends the second [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.3 1. Ānisaṁsavagga First Discourse on the Underlying Conditions “Monks, there are these ten underlying conditions for the arising of the unarisen Noble Eightfold Path, and for the fulfillment and completion of the arisen Noble Eightfold Path. What ten? (1) Here, monks, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.

This is the first underlying condition for the arising of the unarisen Noble Eightfold Path, and for the fulfillment and completion of the arisen Noble Eightfold Path. (2) Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. This is the second underlying condition... (3) Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this is the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples, worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. This is the third underlying condition... (4) Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—virtues that are untorn, unbroken, unspotted, unsplattered, liberating, praised by the wise, not clung to, leading to concentration. This is the fourth underlying condition... (5) Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple hears at times a talk connected with the wholesome, connected with the Dhamma, connected with the training, such as a talk on generosity, talk on virtue, talk on heaven, talk on the danger, degradation, and defilement of sensual pleasures; talk on the benefit of renunciation; talk on seclusion, dispassion, cessation, and Nibbāna; talk on the qualities of a Buddha, a Dhamma, and a Saṅgha. This is the fifth underlying condition... (6) Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple has heard much, remembers what he has heard, and retains it in mind; what he has heard and learned, he accumulates through his mental attention. This is the sixth underlying condition... (7) Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple is endowed with wisdom—wisdom that is noble and penetrative, leading to the destruction of suffering. This is the seventh underlying condition... (8) Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple is supported by these seven factors, and he gains the four factors of stream-entry. What seven? Here, monks, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha... confirmed confidence in the Dhamma... confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha... possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones... hears at times a talk connected with the wholesome... has heard much... is endowed with wisdom... He gains the four factors of stream-entry: the factor of stream-entry that is confirmed confidence in the Buddha, the factor of stream-entry that is confirmed confidence in the Dhamma, the factor of stream-entry that is confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha, and the factor of stream-entry that is the virtues dear to the noble ones. This is the eighth underlying condition... (9) Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple is supported by these eight factors, and he gains the four factors of stream-entry. What eight? Here, monks, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha... confirmed confidence in the Dhamma... confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha... possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones... hears at times a talk connected with the wholesome... has heard much... is endowed with wisdom... is supported by these seven factors and gains the four factors of stream-entry. This is the ninth underlying condition... (10) Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple is supported by these nine factors, and he gains the four factors of stream-entry. What nine? Here, monks, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha... confirmed confidence in the Dhamma... confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha... possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones... hears at times a talk connected with the wholesome... has heard much... is endowed with wisdom... is supported by these eight factors and gains
“Bhikkhus, for one who is immoral,
for one deficient in virtue, the proximate cause for non-regret is destroyed.
When there is no non-regret, for one deficient in non-regret, the proximate cause for gladness is destroyed.”
When there is no gladness, for one devoid of gladness, rapture has its proximate cause destroyed.
When there is no rapture, for one devoid of rapture, tranquility has its proximate cause destroyed.
When there is no tranquility, for one devoid of tranquility, happiness has its proximate cause destroyed.
When there is no happiness, for one devoid of happiness, right concentration lacks its proximate cause.
When there is no right concentration, for one devoid of right concentration, knowledge and vision of things as they really are lacks its proximate cause.
When there is no knowledge and vision of things as they really are, for one devoid of knowledge and vision of things as they really are, disenchantment and dispassion lack their proximate cause.
When there is no disenchantment and dispassion, for one deficient in disenchantment and dispassion, the knowledge and vision of liberation lacks its proximate cause.

Just as, monks, when a tree is deficient in branches and foliage, its shoots do not reach full development, nor its bark, nor its inner bark, nor its softwood, nor its heartwood reaches full development;
even so, monks, for an immoral person deficient in virtue, non-remorse lacks its proximate cause.
When there is no freedom from remorse, for one who has failed in freedom from remorse, the necessary condition for non-regret is destroyed...
[and so on] ...up to the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Monks, for one who is virtuous and endowed with virtue, freedom from remorse is possessed of its necessary condition.
When there is non-regret, for one endowed with non-regret, joy is fulfilled through its proximate cause.
When there is joy, for one endowed with joy, rapture is fulfilled through its proximate cause.
When there is rapture, for one endowed with rapture, tranquility is fulfilled through its proximate cause.
When there is tranquility, for one possessed of tranquility, happiness possesses its proximate cause.
When there is happiness, for one possessed of happiness, right concentration possesses its proximate cause.
When there is right concentration, for one possessed of right concentration, the knowledge and vision of things as they truly are possesses its proximate cause.

When there is knowledge and vision of things as they really are, for one endowed with knowledge and vision of things as they really are, disenchantment and dispassion are fully supported by that condition.
When there is disenchantment and dispassion, for one endowed with disenchantment and dispassion, the knowledge and vision of liberation is fully supported by that condition.
Just as, monks, when a tree is endowed with branches and foliage, its bark reaches full development, its inner bark... its softwood... and its heartwood also reach full development.
"In the same way, monks, for one who is virtuous and perfected in virtue, non-regret is supported by that foundation.
When there is non-regret, for one perfected in non-regret, [the subsequent stages] are supported by that foundation...
[and so on] ...up to the knowledge and vision of liberation."
The Third [Discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.4.
1. The Chapter on Benefits (Ānisaṁsavagga).
The Second Discourse on the Underlying Conditions (Dutiyaupanisasutta).
There, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus: “… [as before] …”
“Friend, for one who is immoral, for one deficient in virtue, non-regret lacks its proximate cause.
When there is no non-regret, for one deficient in non-regret, [non-remorse] lacks its proximate cause... and so on, up to...
knowledge and vision of liberation.”
"Friend, just as when a tree is deprived of its branches and foliage, its bark does not reach full development, nor its inner bark, nor its softwood, nor its heartwood reaches full development;
even so, friend, for one who is immoral and deficient in virtue, the proximate cause for non-regret is destroyed.
When non-regret is absent, for one who is deficient in non-regret, the proximate cause for joy is destroyed... [and so on]."
the knowledge and vision of liberation.
For one who is virtuous, friend, for one perfected in virtue, non-regret is a supporting condition;
when there is non-regret, for one perfected in non-regret, [non-remorse] is a supporting condition... (and so on).
and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Just as, friend, there might be a tree endowed with branches and foliage: its outer bark reaches full development, its inner bark... its softwood... and its heartwood reaches full development;
even so, friend, for one who is virtuous and perfected in virtue, non-regret is fully supported by its proximate cause.
"When there is freedom from remorse, for one endowed with freedom from remorse, the proximate cause is fulfilled … [and so on] … down to … knowledge and vision of liberation.
This is the fourth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.5 1. Ānisaṁsavagga Tatiyaupanisasutta (The Third Discourse on Conditions) “Monks, there are these ten conditions for the arising of the Dhamma-vinaya. What ten? (1) Here, monks, a bhikkhu possesses faith; he places confidence in the Tathāgata’s enlightenment thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.

This, monks, is the first condition for the arising of the Dhamma-vinaya. (2) He is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults; having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. This, monks, is the second condition for the arising of the Dhamma-vinaya. (3) He has heard much, has retained what he has heard, and has stored up what he has heard. Whatever teachings are lovely at the beginning, lovely in the middle, and lovely at the end, in their meaning and expression, which proclaim the holy life that is utterly perfect and pure—such teachings he has heard much of, retained, recited verbally, mentally examined, and penetrated well by view. This, monks, is the third condition for the arising of the Dhamma-vinaya. (4) He is one who gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life. This, monks, is the fourth condition for the arising of the Dhamma-vinaya. (5) With the destruction of the taints, he has realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, he dwells therein. This, monks, is the fifth condition for the arising of the Dhamma-vinaya. (6) He is a speaker of what is true, a speaker of what is factual, a speaker of what is meaningful, a speaker of the Dhamma, a speaker of the Vinaya; at the proper time, he speaks what is beneficial, speaks according to the Dhamma, speaks according to the Vinaya. This, monks, is the sixth condition for the arising of the Dhamma-vinaya. (7) He is one who, when questioned, answers without evasion, and when asked about a matter, explains it thoroughly. This, monks, is the seventh condition for the arising of the Dhamma-vinaya. (8) He does not live off the gains of others, nor does he seek gain through gain; he is content with what he receives. This, monks, is the eighth condition for the arising of the Dhamma-vinaya. (9) He is easy to correct and possesses qualities that make him easy to correct; he is patient with his teacher’s instructions. This, monks, is the ninth condition for the arising of the Dhamma-vinaya. (10) He is endowed with wisdom; he possesses the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. This, monks, is the tenth condition for the arising of the Dhamma-vinaya. These, monks, are the ten conditions for the arising of the Dhamma-vinaya.”
There, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the bhikkhus: “… Friends, for one who is immoral,
for one deficient in virtue, the proximate cause for freedom from remorse is destroyed.”
When there is no freedom from remorse, for one who has failed in freedom from remorse, the necessary condition for joy is destroyed.
When there is no joy, for one who has failed in joy, the necessary condition for rapture is destroyed.
When there is no rapture, for one who has failed in rapture, the necessary condition for tranquility is destroyed.
When there is no tranquility, for one deficient in tranquility, the necessary condition for pleasure is destroyed.
When there is no pleasure, for one deficient in pleasure, the necessary condition for right concentration is destroyed.
When there is no right concentration, for one deficient in right concentration, the necessary condition for the knowledge and vision of things as they truly are is destroyed.

When there is no knowledge and vision of things as they really are, for one who has failed in knowledge and vision of things as they really are, the proximate cause for disenchantment and dispassion is destroyed.
When there is no disenchantment and dispassion, for one who has failed in disenchantment and dispassion, the proximate cause for the knowledge and vision of liberation is destroyed.
Just as, friends, a tree that has failed in its branches and foliage: its bark does not reach full development, nor its inner bark, nor its softwood, nor its heartwood reaches full development.
In the same way, friends, for one who is immoral and deficient in virtue, the proximate cause for non-regret is destroyed.
When there is no non-regret, for one who is deficient in non-regret, the proximate cause for [the knowledge and vision of] liberation is destroyed... [and so on].
For one who is virtuous, friends, for one endowed with virtue, non-regret is a proximate cause.
When there is non-regret, for one endowed with non-regret, joy is a proximate cause.
When there is joy, for one endowed with joy, rapture is a proximate cause.
When there is rapture, for one possessed of rapture, tranquility is possessed of its proximate cause.
When there is tranquility, for one possessed of tranquility, happiness is possessed of its proximate cause.
When there is happiness, for one possessed of happiness, right concentration is possessed of its proximate cause.
When right concentration exists, for one endowed with right concentration, the knowledge and vision of things as they really are is possessed of its proximate cause.

When the knowledge and vision of things as they really are exists, for one endowed with the knowledge and vision of things as they really are, disenchantment and dispassion are possessed of their proximate cause.
When disenchantment and dispassion exist, for one endowed with disenchantment and dispassion, the knowledge and vision of liberation is possessed of its proximate cause.

"Friend, just as a tree endowed with branches and foliage has its outer bark reach full development, its inner bark reach full development, its softwood reach full development, and its heartwood reach full development;
even so, friend, for one who is virtuous and perfected in virtue, non-regret is a proximate cause.
When there is non-regret, for one who possesses non-regret, [confidence] is a proximate cause... [and so on]."
“...the knowledge and vision of liberation.
The fifth. *Aṅguttara Nikāya* 10.6.

1. Ānisaṁsavagga Samādhisutta (AN 10.6, PTS AN v 7) “Monks, there are these five benefits of concentration. What five? One attains concentration; one gains a pleasant abiding here and now; one gains a pleasant death; after the breakup of the body, after death, one is reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world; and, with the destruction of the taints, one realizes for oneself in this very life, by direct knowledge, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, dwells therein. These, monks, are the five benefits of concentration.”
Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One... [as before] ...and sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"Could it be, Bhante, that a bhikkhu might attain such a state of concentration that he would not perceive earth as earth, nor water as water, nor fire as fire, nor air as air?"

He would perceive air, but he would not perceive the base of infinite space as the base of infinite space; he would not perceive the base of infinite consciousness as the base of infinite consciousness;
he would not perceive the base of nothingness as the base of nothingness; he would not perceive the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
he would not perceive this world as this world, nor the other world as the other world.
“...and yet he would still be percipient?
“It is possible, Ānanda, that a bhikkhu might attain such a state of concentration that he would have no perception of earth in earth,
no perception of water in water, no perception of fire in fire, and no perception of air in air.”

He would not have the perception of the base of infinite space in the base of infinite space; he would not have the perception of the base of infinite consciousness in the base of infinite consciousness;

he would not have the perception of the base of nothingness in the base of nothingness; he would not have the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
he would not have the perception of this world in this world; he would not have the perception of the other world in the other world; yet he would still be percipient.”
“But how, venerable sir, might a bhikkhu attain such a state of concentration that he would not perceive earth as earth, nor water as water, nor fire as fire, nor air as air,
nor the base of infinite space as the base of infinite space, nor the base of infinite consciousness as the base of infinite consciousness?”

“Would he be percipient of the base of infinite consciousness, but not percipient of the base of nothingness; would he be percipient of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, but not percipient of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
would he be percipient of this world, but not percipient of this world; would he be percipient of the other world, but not percipient of the other world;
and yet he would still be percipient?”
“Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu perceives thus:
‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna.
It is in this way, Ānanda, that a bhikkhu might attain such a state of concentration that he does not [perceive] the earth.”
He would have the perception of earth; he would not have the perception of water in water, he would not have the perception of fire in fire, he would not have the perception of air in air;

he would not have the perception of the base of infinite space in the base of infinite space, he would not have the perception of the base of infinite consciousness in the base of infinite consciousness, he would not have the perception of the base of nothingness in the base of nothingness, nor the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

“He would have the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he would not have the perception of this world as this world, nor would he have the perception of the other world as the other world;
yet he would still be percipient.
This is the sixth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.7 1. Ānisaṁsavagga Sāriputtasutta “Bhikkhus, there are these ten qualities of one who has entered the stream, which are the factors of stream-entry. What ten? (1) Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One. (2) He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. (3) He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. (4) He possesses the virtue that is cherished by the noble ones, unbroken, flawless, unblemished, unblotched, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. (5) He possesses a mind that has been cultivated by much hearing, endowed with faith, trust, and confidence in the Dhamma of the noble ones. (6) He possesses a mind that has been cultivated by much hearing, endowed with faith, trust, and confidence in the Saṅgha of the noble ones. (7) He possesses a mind that has been cultivated by much hearing, endowed with faith, trust, and confidence in the path. (8) He possesses a mind that has been cultivated by much hearing, endowed with faith, trust, and confidence in the way. (9) He possesses a mind that has been cultivated by much hearing, endowed with faith, trust, and confidence in the Dhamma as a raft, as something to be used for crossing over, not for grasping. (10) He possesses a mind that has been cultivated by much hearing, endowed with faith, trust, and confidence in the Dhamma as a light, as something to be looked upon, not for grasping. These, bhikkhus, are the ten qualities of one who has entered the stream, which are the factors of stream-entry.”
Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Venerable Sāriputta; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Sāriputta.
When they had concluded their polite and friendly conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Venerable Sāriputta:
“Could it be, friend Sāriputta, that a bhikkhu might attain such a state of concentration that he would not perceive earth as earth,
nor water as water, nor fire as fire, nor air as air,
nor the base of infinite space as the base of infinite space, nor the base of infinite consciousness?”

“Would he perceive the base of infinite consciousness, yet not perceive the base of nothingness as the base of nothingness; would he not perceive the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
would he not perceive this world as this world, nor perceive the other world as the other world;
and yet, would he still be percipient?”

“It may be, friend Ānanda, that a bhikkhu attains such a state of concentration that he is neither percipient of earth in earth … nor percipient of the world beyond in the world beyond, yet he is still percipient.
“But how, friend Sāriputta, might a bhikkhu attain such a state of concentration that he is neither percipient of earth in earth … yet he is still percipient?
“Once, friend Ānanda, I was staying right here in Sāvatthī, in the Blind Men’s Grove.”
Therein, I entered into such a state of concentration that I was not percipient of earth in earth,
not percipient of water in water, not percipient of fire in fire, not percipient of air in air,
not percipient of the base of infinite space in the base of infinite space, and not percipient of the base of infinite consciousness in the base of infinite consciousness.

"I existed, yet I did not perceive the sphere of nothingness as the sphere of nothingness; I did not perceive the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
I did not perceive this world as this world, nor did I perceive the other world as the other world;
nevertheless, I was percipient."
“But what was the perception, friend Sāriputta, that you had at that time?
“Friend, the thought ‘the cessation of existence is Nibbāna, the cessation of existence is Nibbāna’ arose in me as one perception and ceased as another perception.
It was just as when a firebrand is burning at its tip: one flame arises and another flame ceases.”
"In the same way, friend, regarding 'the cessation of existence is Nibbāna, the cessation of existence is Nibbāna,' one perception arises and another perception ceases.
Yet at that time, friend, I was one who perceived: 'The cessation of existence is Nibbāna.
This is the seventh [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.8 1. Ānisaṁsavagga Jhānasutta “Monks, there are these ten benefits of jhāna. What ten? One attains the destruction of the taints with the destruction of the five lower fetters; one attains non-returning with the destruction of three fetters and the weakening of greed, hatred, and delusion; one attains once-returning with the destruction of three fetters; one attains stream-entry with the complete destruction of three fetters; one attains the state of a non-returner with the complete destruction of the five lower fetters; one attains the state of a once-returner with the complete destruction of the five lower fetters; one attains the state of a stream-enterer with the complete destruction of three fetters; one attains the attainment of the fruit of arahantship with the complete destruction of all taints; one attains the attainment of the fruit of non-returning with the complete destruction of the five lower fetters; and one attains the attainment of the fruit of once-returning with the complete destruction of the five lower fetters. These, monks, are the ten benefits of jhāna.”
“Monks, a monk may be endowed with faith, yet not be virtuous;
thus, he is incomplete in that respect.”
"Therefore, that factor should be fulfilled by him:
'How may I be endowed with faith and possessed of virtue?
But when, monks, a monk is both endowed with faith and possessed of virtue, then he is complete in that factor."
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu may be endowed with faith and virtuous, yet not be learned; ...
he may be learned, yet not be an expounder of the Dhamma; ...
he may be an expounder of the Dhamma, yet not be one who frequents assemblies; ...”
He frequents assemblies, yet he does not teach the Dhamma in an assembly with confidence;
he teaches the Dhamma in an assembly with confidence, yet he is not a master of the Vinaya;
he is a master of the Vinaya, yet he is not a forest-dweller who uses remote lodgings.

One who dwells in the forest and frequents remote lodgings, yet does not gain at will, without difficulty, and without trouble, the four jhānas that are higher mental states providing a pleasant dwelling in this very life;
and one who gains at will, without difficulty, and without trouble, the four jhānas that are higher mental states providing a pleasant dwelling in this very life,
yet does not, through the destruction of the taints, realize for oneself in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom.
He dwells having realized it for himself through direct knowledge and having attained it.
In this way, he is incomplete in that factor.
Therefore, that factor must be fulfilled:
‘But what if I were to be endowed with faith, virtuous, learned, a speaker on the Dhamma, one who frequents assemblies,
and confident in teaching the Dhamma to an assembly; and if I were to be a master of the Vinaya, a forest-dweller living in remote lodgings,
and one who gains at will the four jhānas that are higher mental states and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life?’

‘May I obtain without difficulty, may I obtain without hardship, and having realized for myself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom through the destruction of the taints, may I enter and dwell therein.
But when, monks, a monk is endowed with faith, virtuous, learned, and a speaker on the Dhamma—
He frequents assemblies and teaches the Dhamma to the assembly with confidence;

he is a master of the Vinaya, a forest-dweller who uses remote lodgings, and he attains at will, without difficulty or hardship, the four jhānas that are higher mental states providing a pleasant dwelling in this very life;
and through the destruction of the taints, he attains the taintless liberation of mind...
Having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life, he enters and dwells in liberation through wisdom;
in this way, he is complete in that respect.
“Monks, a monk endowed with these ten qualities is one who is serene on all sides and complete in every aspect.”
The Eighth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.9 1.
Ānisaṁsavagga (The Chapter on Benefits)
The Discourse on Peaceful Liberation (Santavimokkhasutta; AN 10.9, PTS AN v 11):
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu may be endowed with faith, yet not virtuous... [as in the full text] ...”
One who is virtuous but not learned;
one who is learned but not a speaker of the Dhamma;
and one who is a speaker of the Dhamma but does not frequent assemblies.
One who frequents assemblies but does not fearlessly teach the Dhamma in the assembly;
one who fearlessly teaches the Dhamma in the assembly but is not a bearer of the Vinaya;
and one who is a bearer of the Vinaya but is not a forest-dweller who uses remote lodgings.

He is a forest-dweller who frequents remote lodgings, yet he does not dwell having personally touched with the body those peaceful liberations that transcend the realm of form— the formless attainments— and he does not,
through the destruction of the taints, realize for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom.
Having realized it and attained it, he dwells therein.
In this way, he is incomplete in that factor.
Therefore, that factor must be fulfilled:
‘But what if I were to be endowed with faith, virtuous, learned, a speaker on the Dhamma, one who frequents assemblies,
and confident that I might teach the Dhamma to an assembly; and being a master of the Vinaya, a forest-dweller, and one who stays in remote lodgings,
may I dwell having personally realized those peaceful liberations that are formless and transcend the realm of form, and [attain] the destruction of the taints?’
‘By means of destruction, may I, in this very life, through my own direct knowledge, realize and enter into the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom.
But when, monks, a monk is endowed with faith, virtuous, learned, and a preacher of the Dhamma...
He frequents assemblies, teaches the Dhamma to the assembly with confidence, is a master of the Vinaya,
is a forest-dweller who lives in remote lodgings, dwells having personally realized with his own body those peaceful liberations that transcend the realm of form—
the formless attainments— and, through the destruction of the taints, realizes for himself in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom.
Having realized the higher knowledges (abhiññā) and having attained them, he dwells therein;
thus he is complete in that respect.
Monks, a monk endowed with these ten qualities is one who is serene on all sides and complete in every way.”
The Ninth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.10 1.
Ānisaṁsavagga (The Chapter on Benefits)
Vijjāsutta (AN 10.10, PTS AN v 12):
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu may be endowed with faith, but not possessed of virtue.”
In this way, he is incomplete with respect to that factor.
Therefore, that factor must be fulfilled by him, thinking:
"How can I be both endowed with faith and possessed of virtue?"
But when, monks, a monk is both endowed with faith and possessed of virtue, he is thus complete in that respect.
Monks, a monk may be endowed with faith and possessed of virtue, yet not be learned;
or he may be learned, yet not be a preacher of the Dhamma... [and so on].
He is a preacher of the Dhamma but not one who frequents assemblies;

he is one who frequents assemblies but not one who teaches the Dhamma in an assembly with confidence; he is one who teaches the Dhamma in an assembly with confidence but not one who is an expert in the Vinaya;
he is an expert in the Vinaya... [and so on].
And he does not recollect his manifold past abodes, that is to say, one birth,

two births … [as detailed] … thus with their aspects and particulars he recollects his manifold past abodes. And he recollects his manifold past abodes … [as detailed] … with their aspects and particulars.
He does not, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, ... [as before] ... know beings passing away and being reborn according to their karma;
nor does he, through the destruction of the taints, ... [as before] ... enter and dwell in the realization of liberation.
Thus, in that respect, he is incomplete.
Therefore, that factor should be fulfilled:
"How may I be endowed with faith, virtuous, learned, a speaker of the Dhamma, one who frequents assemblies, and confidently teach the Dhamma in assemblies;
and be a bearer of the Vinaya, and [recall] manifold former abodes?"
‘May I recollect my manifold past abodes, that is, one birth, two births... [and so on]... thus may I recollect my manifold past abodes with their modes and details;
and with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human... may I see beings passing away and being reborn according to their kamma;
and, through the destruction of the taints, may I realize for myself, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, may I dwell therein.’”
But when, monks, a monk is endowed with faith, virtuous, learned, a speaker on the Dhamma, one who frequents assemblies,
and teaches the Dhamma in assemblies with confidence; when he is a bearer of the Vinaya and recollects his manifold past abodes,
such as one birth, two births … [and so on] … thus with their aspects and particulars;
He recollects his manifold past lives; and with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn according to their kamma...
having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, he dwells having attained it through the destruction of the taints.
"In this way, he is complete in that respect.
Monks, a monk endowed with these ten qualities is one who is serene on all sides and complete in every aspect. Thus ends the tenth [discourse].
The first chapter on Benefits.
Its summary verse:
"What is the purpose? and "volition," and so forth.
And the three proximate causes;
concentration, Sāriputta,
and jhāna— these are found by one who is at peace.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.11 2. Nāthavagga Senāsanasutta (The Discourse on Lodgings) "Bhikkhus, there are these ten kinds of lodgings that are praised by the Noble Ones, not censured by the wise, and if cultivated and made much of, lead to the destruction of the taints.

What ten? (1) A lodging that is secluded, remote, free from crowds, devoid of people, and suitable for retreat; (2) a lodging where one can easily obtain robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick; (3) a lodging where there are many elders who are learned, heirs to the Dhamma, experts in the Dhamma, experts in the Vinaya, and who have mastered the Agamas; (4) a lodging where there are many middle-aged monks who are learned... [as above]; (5) a lodging where there are many newly ordained monks who are learned... [as above]; (6) a lodging where one dwells with a teacher or a preceptor who is learned, an heir to the Dhamma, an expert in the Dhamma, an expert in the Vinaya, and who has mastered the Agamas; (7) a lodging where one dwells with companions in the holy life who are learned, heirs to the Dhamma, experts in the Dhamma, experts in the Vinaya, and who have mastered the Agamas; (8) a lodging where one dwells having obtained a superior dwelling place that is empty, quiet, and free from noise; (9) a lodging where one dwells having obtained a superior seat that is empty, quiet, and free from noise; (10) a lodging where one dwells having obtained a superior bed and chair that are empty, quiet, and free from noise. Bhikkhus, these are the ten kinds of lodgings that are praised by the Noble Ones, not censured by the wise, and if cultivated and made much of, lead to the destruction of the taints."
“Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu endowed with five factors dwells in and frequents a lodging endowed with five factors,
before long, through the destruction of the taints, he realizes for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom.
Having realized the Dhamma for himself through direct knowledge, he would enter upon and abide in it.
And how, monks, is a monk possessed of five factors?
Here, monks, a monk has faith; he has faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata:
‘Such indeed is the Blessed One … [as above] … the Blessed One’;
he is free from illness and affliction, possessing a digestive system that is well-balanced—neither too cold nor too hot, but moderate and capable of bearing the strain of striving;
he is not fraudulent nor deceitful, revealing himself as he truly is to the Teacher or to wise companions in the holy life.

He dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the attainment of wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in his exertion, and does not lay down the burden regarding wholesome states.
He is wise, endowed with the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away—noble, penetrative, and leading to the complete destruction of suffering.
In this way, monks, a monk is possessed of five factors.
And how, monks, is a lodging endowed with five factors? Here, monks,
a lodging is not too far and not too near, is well-suited for coming and going,
has little crowding by day, and little noise and few sounds at night.
It is free from the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, heat, and creeping reptiles;
moreover, while dwelling in that lodging, the requisites of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal provisions for the sick arise with little difficulty;
furthermore, in that lodging there dwell elder bhikkhus who are learned, of inherited tradition, bearers of the Dhamma, bearers of the Vinaya, and bearers of the Mātikā.
From time to time, they approach them and inquire and question them, saying:
"Venerable sirs, what is this? What is the meaning of this?
Those venerable ones reveal to him what has not been revealed, clarify what has not been made clear, and dispel his doubt regarding various matters that are grounds for uncertainty.
“In this way, monks, a lodging possesses five factors.

A monk who possesses these five factors, while frequenting and resorting to a lodging that possesses these five factors, will before long—through the destruction of the taints—abide in the realization of the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having personally realized it through direct knowledge.
Thus was the first [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.12 2. Nāthavagga Pañcaṅgasutta (The Discourse on the Five Factors) "Bhikkhus, there are these five factors that lead to the decline of a lay follower who has gone for refuge. What five? Here, bhikkhus, a lay follower dwells with a mind obsessed by sensual lust, without having fully understood it; he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen sensual lust. He dwells with a mind obsessed by ill will... obsessed by sloth and torpor... obsessed by restlessness and remorse... obsessed by doubt, without having fully understood it; he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen doubt. These, bhikkhus, are the five factors that lead to the decline of a lay follower who has gone for refuge. There are, bhikkhus, these five factors that lead to the non-decline of a lay follower who has gone for refuge. What five? Here, bhikkhus, a lay follower dwells with a mind devoid of sensual lust, having fully understood it; he understands as it really is the escape from the arisen sensual lust. He dwells with a mind devoid of ill will... devoid of sloth and torpor... devoid of restlessness and remorse... devoid of doubt, having fully understood it; he understands as it really is the escape from the arisen doubt. These, bhikkhus, are the five factors that lead to the non-decline of a lay follower who has gone for refuge."
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who has abandoned five factors and possesses five factors is called, in this Dhamma and Discipline, ‘one who is complete, one who has lived the holy life,
the supreme person. And how, bhikkhus, has a bhikkhu abandoned five factors?
“Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has abandoned sensual desire, he has abandoned ill will, he has abandoned sloth and torpor, he has abandoned restlessness and remorse, and he has abandoned doubt.
It is in this way, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu has abandoned five factors.
And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu possessed of five factors?”
In this case, monks, a bhikkhu is endowed with the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training, he is endowed with the aggregate of concentration of one beyond training,
he is endowed with the aggregate of wisdom of one beyond training, he is endowed with the aggregate of liberation of one beyond training,
and he is endowed with the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation of one beyond training.
In this way, monks, a monk is endowed with five factors.

Monks, a monk who has abandoned five factors and is endowed with these five factors is called in this Dhamma and Discipline “one who is complete, one who has lived the holy life, a supreme person. [The five factors he has abandoned are:
sensual desire and ill will...
For that bhikkhu, sloth and torpor,
restlessness and doubt,
do not exist at all.
Endowed with the virtue of one beyond training,
with the concentration of one beyond training,
and with liberation, he is perfected.
And through such knowledge,
he indeed becomes one endowed with five factors,
having abandoned the five factors.
In this Dhamma and Discipline,
one is called "complete. Thus ends the second [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.13 2.

Nāthavagga Saṁyojanasutta (The Fetter) “Monks, there are these ten fetters. What ten? The fetter of attachment, the fetter of aversion, the fetter of views, the fetter of doubt, the fetter of conceit, the fetter of adherence to rules and observances, the fetter of envy, the fetter of stinginess, the fetter of ignorance, and the fetter of agitation. These, monks, are the ten fetters.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these ten fetters. What are the ten? [The Buddha said:]”
There are five lower fetters and five higher fetters. What are the five lower fetters?
Identity view, doubt, adherence to rules and observances, sensual desire, and ill will.
These are the five lower fetters.
What are the five higher fetters?
Lust for the form realm, lust for the formless realm, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance.
These are the five higher fetters.
These, monks, are the ten fetters. Thus [ends] the third.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.14 2. Nāthavagga Cetokhilasutta: The Discourse on the Barrenness of Mind “Monks, there are these five kinds of barrenness of mind. What five? Here, monks, a monk harbors resentment toward his teacher. This is the first kind of barrenness of mind. Furthermore, monks, a monk harbors resentment toward his companions in the holy life. This is the second kind of barrenness of mind. Furthermore, monks, a monk harbors resentment toward the teachings he has learned. This is the third kind of barrenness of mind. Furthermore, monks, a monk harbors resentment toward the teachings he has mastered. This is the fourth kind of barrenness of mind. Furthermore, monks, a monk harbors resentment toward his fellow monks who are of similar status, whether they be elders, those of middle standing, or juniors. This is the fifth kind of barrenness of mind. These, monks, are the five kinds of barrenness of mind. Monks, there are these five kinds of non-barrenness of mind. What five? Here, monks, a monk does not harbor resentment toward his teacher. This is the first kind of non-barrenness of mind. Furthermore, monks, a monk does not harbor resentment toward his companions in the holy life. This is the second kind of non-barrenness of mind. Furthermore, monks, a monk does not harbor resentment toward the teachings he has learned. This is the third kind of non-barrenness of mind. Furthermore, monks, a monk does not harbor resentment toward the teachings he has mastered. This is the fourth kind of non-barrenness of mind. Furthermore, monks, a monk does not harbor resentment toward his fellow monks who are of similar status, whether they be elders, those of middle standing, or juniors. This is the fifth kind of non-barrenness of mind. These, monks, are the five kinds of non-barrenness of mind.”
“Bhikkhus, for any bhikkhu or bhikkhunī who has not abandoned the five kinds of mental barrenness and has not severed the five fetters of the mind, whether night or day comes, there is only decline.”
One may expect no growth in wholesome states.
For whom are the five mental barrennesses (*cetokhila*) unabandoned?
Here, monks, a monk is doubtful, uncertain, undecided, and lacks confidence regarding the Teacher.
“Monks, when a monk is doubtful, uncertain, undecided, and lacks confidence in the Teacher, his mind does not incline toward ardor, commitment, perseverance, and striving.
When the mind does not incline toward ardor, commitment, perseverance, and striving, this first wilderness of the mind remains unabandoned by him.
Furthermore, monks, when a monk is doubtful, uncertain, undecided, and lacks confidence in the Dhamma … [and so on] …”
He doubts the Saṅgha...
he doubts the training...
he is angry with his fellow practitioners of the holy life, displeased, with a resentful mind, harboring a thicket of ill will.

“Monks, when a monk is angry with his fellow celibates, displeased, with a resentful mind, and harboring a thicket of ill will, his mind does not incline toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving.
For one whose mind does not incline toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving, this fifth mental thicket remains unabandoned.
Thus, these five mental thickets remain unabandoned by him.”
For whom are the five mental fetters not severed?

Here, monks, a monk is not free from lust for sensual pleasures; he has not departed from desire, not departed from affection, not departed from thirst, not departed from fever, and not departed from craving.
That monk, monks, who is not free from lust for sensual pleasures, who has not departed from desire...
“With fever unabated and craving unabated, his mind does not incline toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving.
For one whose mind does not incline toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving, this first mental bond remains unsevered.
Furthermore, monks, a monk is not free from lust for the body … [as before] …”
He is not free from lust for forms...
having eaten as much as he wants until his belly is full, he dwells devoted to the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of reclining, and the pleasure of drowsiness...
or he leads the holy life aspiring to a certain class of devas, thinking: "By this virtue, or vow, or austerity, or holy life, may I become a deva or one among the devas."
“Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu leads the holy life aspiring for some order of devas,
thinking: ‘By this virtue, or observance, or austerity, or holy life, may I become a deva or some other kind of deva,’ his mind does not incline toward ardor, commitment, perseverance, and striving.”
For one whose mind does not incline toward ardor, devotion, persistence, and striving, this fifth mental shackle remains unsevered.
Thus, these five mental shackles remain unsevered for such a person.
Monks, for any monk or nun who has not abandoned these five wildernesses of the heart...
As long as these five mental fetters are not severed, whatever night or day comes for him,
only decline in wholesome qualities is to be expected,
not growth. Just as, monks, during the dark fortnight of the moon, whatever night or day comes, it wanes in beauty, wanes in its orb, wanes in radiance, and wanes in height and circumference;
In the same way, monks, for any bhikkhu or bhikkhunī who has not abandoned these five mental barrennesses and has not severed these five mental shackles, whether night or day comes,
only decline is to be expected in wholesome qualities, not growth.
“Bhikkhus, for any bhikkhu or bhikkhunī who has abandoned the five kinds of mental barrenness and thoroughly cut off the five fetters of the mind, whether night or day comes,
only growth in wholesome qualities is to be expected, not decline.”
For whom have the five mental barrennesses been abandoned?
Here, monks, a monk does not doubt, does not waver, is resolved, and has full confidence in the Teacher.
For that monk, monks, who does not doubt, does not waver, is resolved, and has full confidence in the Teacher, his mind inclines toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving.
When one’s mind inclines toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving, then this first mental barrenness has been abandoned by him.
Furthermore, monks, a monk does not doubt the Dhamma … nor does he doubt the Saṅgha … [and so on].
He has no doubt regarding the training… he is not angry with his fellow celibates, but is well-disposed, with a mind that is not struck down and free from barrenness.

Monks, for that monk who is not angry with his fellow celibates, but is well-disposed, with a mind that is not struck down and free from barrenness, his mind inclines toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving.
For one whose mind inclines toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving, this fifth mental barrenness is abandoned.
These five mental barrennesses are abandoned by him.
For whom are the five mental shackles completely severed?
"Here, monks, a monk is free from lust for sensual pleasures; he is devoid of desire, devoid of affection, devoid of thirst, devoid of fever, and devoid of craving for them.

Monks, when a monk is free from lust for sensual pleasures—devoid of desire, devoid of affection, devoid of thirst, devoid of fever, and devoid of craving—his mind inclines toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving.
When his mind inclines toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving, then this first mental bond of his is completely severed."
Furthermore, monks, a monk is free from lust for the body … [as before] … he is free from lust for forms … [as before] … he does not eat as much as he needs until his belly is full,
and then remain devoted to the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of reclining, and the pleasure of drowsiness.

He does not lead the holy life aspiring for any particular class of devas, thinking: “By this virtue, or by this vow, or by this austerity, or by this holy life, may I become a deva or some other kind of deva.
Monks, when a monk does not aspire for any particular class of devas... nor for some other kind of deva, his mind inclines toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving.
When one’s mind inclines toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving, then this fifth mental fetter is thoroughly severed for them.
Thus these five mental fetters are thoroughly severed.
Monks, for any monk or nun who has abandoned these five wildernesses of the heart...
These five mental bondages have been completely severed. For him, whether night or day comes, only growth in wholesome qualities is to be expected, not decline.

Just as, monks, in the bright fortnight, for the moon, whether night or day comes, it increases in beauty, it increases in its orb, it increases in radiance, and it increases in height and circumference; so too for him.
"In the same way, monks, for any bhikkhu or bhikkhunī who has abandoned these five mental barrennesses and has completely cut off these five mental shackles, whether night or day comes,
only growth in wholesome qualities is to be expected, not decline."
The Fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.15.
2. The Chapter on the Protector (Nāthavagga).
Appamādasutta (AN 10.15, PTS AN v 21):
“To whatever extent, bhikkhus, there are beings—whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed; whether possessing form, or...”

Whether they be formless, percipient, non-percipient, or neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient, the Tathāgata—the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One—is declared to be the foremost among them.
Even so, monks, whatever wholesome states there may be, they all have heedfulness as their root and converge upon heedfulness. Heedfulness is declared to be the foremost among them.

“Just as, monks, whatever footprints of terrestrial creatures there may be, they all fit within the footprint of an elephant, and the elephant’s footprint is declared the foremost among them by reason of its size;
even so, monks, whatever wholesome states there may be, they all have heedfulness as their root and converge upon heedfulness. Heedfulness is declared the foremost among them.”
“Just as, monks, whatever rafters there are in a peaked house, they all go toward the peak, incline toward the peak, converge at the peak, and the peak is declared to be their chief;
even so, monks, whatever wholesome states there are, they all have heedfulness as their root, converge upon heedfulness, and heedfulness is declared to be their chief.
Just as, monks, among all fragrant roots, black orris root is declared to be the chief;”
In the same way, monks … [as before] … Just as,
monks, among all fragrant heartwoods, red sandalwood is declared to be the foremost;
even so, monks … [as before] …
“Just as, monks, of all flower fragrances, the jasmine is declared to be the foremost;
even so, monks, … [as above] … Just as, monks,
whatever minor kings there may be, they all become followers of the Wheel-turning King (cakkavatti-rāja), and the Wheel-turning King is declared to be the foremost among them.”

"In the same way, monks … [as before] … Just as, monks, whatever light there is from the stars, all that does not equal even a sixteenth part of the moon’s radiance; the moon’s radiance is declared to be the foremost among them;
even so, monks … [as before] …"
“Just as, monks, in the autumn season, when the sky is clear and free from clouds, the sun, rising into the heavens, dispels all darkness that has gathered in the air and shines,
blazes, and radiates; even so, monks … [as above] … Just as, monks,
whatever great rivers there are, such as the Ganges, the Yamunā, the Aciravatī, …”
“Bhikkhus, just as the rivers— the Sarabhū, the Mahī, and all others— flow toward the ocean, incline toward the ocean, slope toward the ocean, and tend toward the ocean,

and the great ocean is declared to be their chief; even so, bhikkhus, whatever wholesome states there are, they are all rooted in heedfulness, converge in heedfulness, and heedfulness is declared to be their chief.”
The Fifth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.16. 2.
The Chapter on the Protector (Nāthavagga).
“Bhikkhus, these ten persons are worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation; they are an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.”
Which ten?

The Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One; the Paccekabuddha; one liberated both ways; one liberated by wisdom; a body-witness; one attained to view; one liberated by faith; a follower by faith; a follower by Dhamma;
and one of the lineage—these, monks, are the ten persons worthy of gifts … the unsurpassed field of merit for the world.”
The Sixth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.17 2.
Nāthavagga (The Chapter on the Protector)
The First Discourse on Having a Protector (Paṭhamanāthasutta):
“Monks, dwell with a protector; do not dwell without a protector.”
"Bhikkhus, it is suffering for one who dwells without a protector.
Bhikkhus, there are these ten qualities that constitute a protector.
What are the ten?"

"Here, monks, a monk is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains himself in the rules of training.
That, monks, a monk is virtuous... and having undertaken them, he trains himself in the rules of training—this too is a quality that acts as a protector."
Furthermore, monks, a monk is learned, one who has retained what he has heard, and one who has accumulated what he has heard;
those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, which proclaim the holy life in its spirit and its letter,
entirely complete and pure— such teachings as these are well-learned by him, remembered, and mastered through speech.
“Investigated with the mind and well-penetrated by view.
Monks, that a monk is learned … [and so on] … and has well-penetrated [the Dhamma] by view—
this too is a quality that provides a protector.
Furthermore, monks, a monk has good friends, good companions, and good associates.
That a monk has good friends, good companions, and good associates—
this too is a quality that provides a protector.
Furthermore, monks, a monk is easy to speak to and possesses the qualities that make one easy to speak to; he is patient, receptive to instruction, and accepts it respectfully.
Insofar as a monk is easy to speak to... and accepts instruction respectfully, this too is a quality that makes one a protector.

Furthermore, monks, whatever various duties there may be for his fellow celibates, a monk is skillful therein, diligent, endowed with the investigation of appropriate means, and capable of acting and capable of organizing. That a monk is skillful, diligent,
endowed with the investigation of appropriate means, and capable of acting and capable of organizing regarding those various duties for his fellow celibates—
this too is a quality that provides a protector.
Furthermore, monks, a monk is one who loves the Dhamma, delights in its proclamation, and finds great joy in the higher Dhamma and the higher Vinaya.
That a monk loves the Dhamma, delights in its proclamation, and finds great joy in the higher Dhamma and the higher Vinaya—
this too is a quality that acts as a protector.

Furthermore, monks, a monk dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the acquisition of wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in effort, and does not relinquish his burden regarding wholesome states.

That, monks, a monk dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the acquisition of wholesome states—being steadfast, firm in effort, and not relinquishing his burden regarding wholesome states—is also a quality that provides a protector.
Furthermore, monks, a monk is content with any kind of robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
That a monk is content with any kind of robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick—
this too is a quality that makes one a protector.
Furthermore, monks, a monk is mindful, endowed with supreme mindfulness and circumspection; he remembers and recollects what was done long ago and what was said long ago.

That a monk is mindful, endowed with supreme mindfulness and circumspection, remembering and recollecting what was done long ago and what was said long ago—this, too, is a quality that provides a protector.
Furthermore, monks, a monk is wise; he is endowed with the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away—noble, penetrative, and leading rightly to the destruction of suffering.

That a monk is wise, endowed with the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away—noble, penetrative, and leading rightly to the destruction of suffering—this too is a quality that makes him a protector.
“Monks, dwell with a protector, not without a protector.
Monks, it is suffering to dwell without a protector.
These, monks, are the ten qualities that provide protection.”
Seventh. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.18. 2.
The Chapter on the Protector (Nāthavagga).
The Second Discourse on the Protector (Dutiyanāthasutta).
Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, dwell with a protector; do not dwell without a protector.”
Monks, one who is without a protector dwells in suffering.
Monks, there are these ten qualities that constitute a protector.
What are the ten?
"Here, monks, a monk is virtuous... he trains himself by undertaking the training precepts.

Thinking, ‘This monk is indeed virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and trains himself by undertaking the training precepts,’ even the elder monks should speak of him thus."
They think he should be instructed; even the middle-ranking monks... and even the newly ordained monks think he should be spoken to and instructed.
For one who is thus favored by the elders, favored by the middle-ranking monks, and favored by the newly ordained monks, only growth in wholesome qualities is to be expected, not decline.
This, too, is a quality that provides a protector.
Furthermore, monks, a monk is learned... [and so on] ...one who has well-penetrated right view.
"This monk is indeed learned, a retainer of what he has heard, an accumulator of what he has heard;

those teachings which are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure holy life—[he possesses them]."
They speak in praise of him, saying: ‘Such qualities have been well-heard by him, retained, mastered by word, examined by mind, and well-penetrated by view.
Thus, the elder monks think he should be spoken to and instructed; the middle-ranking monks...
and the junior monks also think he should be spoken to and instructed.
For one who is thus favored by the elders, favored by those of middle standing, and favored by the juniors, only growth in wholesome qualities is to be expected, not decline.
This too is a quality that provides a protector.
Furthermore, monks, a monk has good friends, good companions, and good associates.
‘This bhikkhu indeed has good friends, good companions, and good associates,’ so the elder bhikkhus think that he should be instructed and exhorted;
the middle-ranking bhikkhus... and the junior bhikkhus also think that he should be instructed and exhorted.
For one who is thus favored by the elders, favored by the middle-ranking, and favored by the juniors, growth alone in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline.
This too is a quality that makes one a protector.
Furthermore, monks, a monk is easy to speak to; he possesses the qualities that make him easy to speak to, being patient and receptive to instruction.
"Truly, this monk is easy to speak to; he possesses the qualities that make him easy to speak to, being patient and receptive to instruction."
"One who is to be instructed" means that the elder monks think he should be exhorted and instructed; the middle-ranking monks...
and the junior monks also think he should be exhorted and instructed.
For one who is thus favored by the elders, favored by the middle-ranking monks, and favored by the juniors, only growth in wholesome qualities is to be expected, not decline.
This too is a quality that makes one a protector.

Furthermore, monks, a monk is skillful and diligent regarding those various services for his fellow celibates; he possesses the means and the investigative wisdom to be able to perform and arrange them.
"This monk is indeed skillful regarding those various services for his fellow celibates."
If he is not lazy, possesses the means for that purpose, and is endowed with investigation, thinking, "He is capable of acting;
he is capable of making arrangements," then the elder bhikkhus also consider him one who should be spoken to and instructed, as do the middle-ranking bhikkhus and the junior bhikkhus.
For one who is thus favored by the elders, favored by those of middle standing, and favored by the novices, only growth in wholesome qualities is to be expected, not decline.
This, too, is a quality that provides a protector.
Furthermore, monks, a monk is a lover of the Dhamma, delights in its proclamation, and finds great joy in the higher Dhamma and the higher Vinaya.
‘This bhikkhu is truly one who loves the Dhamma, whose speech is pleasing, and who finds great joy in the higher Dhamma and the higher Vinaya.
Thus, the elder bhikkhus think that he should be instructed and exhorted; the middle-ranking bhikkhus think so too;
and even the junior bhikkhus think that he should be instructed and exhorted.
For one who is thus favored by the elders, favored by those of middle standing, and favored by the juniors, only growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline.
This too is a quality that provides a protector.
Furthermore, monks, a monk dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states.
For the attainment of wholesome states, he is steadfast, firm in effort, and does not lay down his burden regarding wholesome states:
“This bhikkhu indeed dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the attainment of wholesome states;
he is steadfast, firm in effort, and does not lay down his burden regarding wholesome states.”
The elder bhikkhus also think that he should be exhorted and instructed; the middle-ranking bhikkhus...
and the junior bhikkhus also think that he should be exhorted and instructed.
For one who is thus favored by the elders, favored by the middle-ranking, and favored by the juniors, only growth in wholesome qualities is to be expected, not decline.
This, too, is a quality that makes one a protector.
Furthermore, monks, a monk is content with whatever robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick he may receive. [People think:
