"Truly, this monk is content with whatever robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick he may receive."
The elder bhikkhus also think that he should be instructed and exhorted; the middle-ranking bhikkhus...
and the junior bhikkhus also think that he should be instructed and exhorted.
For one who is thus favored by the elders, favored by the middle-ranking, and favored by the juniors, only growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline.
This too is a quality that makes one a protector.
Furthermore, monks, a monk is mindful, endowed with supreme mindfulness and circumspection; he remembers and recollects what was done long ago and what was said long ago.

"Truly, this monk is mindful, endowed with supreme mindfulness and circumspection; he remembers and recollects what was done long ago and what was said long ago. This too is a quality that makes one a protector.
Thinking, ‘She has been remembered, she has been recollected,’ the elder bhikkhus think that she should be instructed and exhorted; the middle-ranking bhikkhus...
and the junior bhikkhus also think that she should be instructed and exhorted.
For her, who is thus favored by the elders, favored by the middle-ranking, and favored by the juniors, only growth in wholesome qualities is to be expected, not decline.
This too is a quality that makes one a protector.
Furthermore, monks, a monk is wise; he possesses the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble, penetrative, and leads to the complete destruction of suffering.
"Truly, this monk is wise; he possesses the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative."
‘leading to the complete destruction of suffering’—the elder bhikkhus think that he should be exhorted and instructed;
the middle-ranking bhikkhus... and the junior bhikkhus also think that he should be exhorted and instructed.
When he is thus shown compassion by the elders... there is no decline.
This too is a quality that provides a protector.
Monks, dwell with a protector; do not dwell without a protector.
Monks, it is suffering to dwell without a protector.
“Monks, these are the ten qualities that provide protection.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
The monks, being uplifted, rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Eighth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.19 2.
Nāthavagga (The Chapter on the Protector)
The First Discourse on the Noble Abodes (Paṭhamaariyāvāsasutta): “Bhikkhus,
there are these ten noble abodes which the noble ones have dwelt in, do dwell in, or will dwell in.”
What are the ten? Here, monks,
a bhikkhu has abandoned five factors, is endowed with six factors, has a single guard, has four supports,
has shaken off individual dogmatic views, has thoroughly given up searching, has untroubled intentions, and has tranquilized bodily formations.
“With mind well-liberated and wisdom well-liberated.
These, monks, are the ten abodes of the noble ones, which the noble ones have dwelt in, do dwell in, or will dwell in. Thus ends the ninth [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.20 2. Nāthavagga Dutiyaariyāvāsasutta (The Second Discourse on the Noble Abodes) "Bhikkhus, there are these ten noble abodes. What ten? (1) Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: 'The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.

This is the first noble abode. (2) He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: 'The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally realized by the wise. This is the second noble abode. (3) He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: 'The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. This is the third noble abode. (4) He possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones, unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. This is the fourth noble abode. (5) He dwells with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, suffusing one quarter, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; so above, below, across, and everywhere, to all as to himself, he dwells suffusing the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility, and without ill will. This is the fifth noble abode. (6) He dwells with a mind imbued with compassion... without ill will. This is the sixth noble abode. (7) He dwells with a mind imbued with altruistic joy... without ill will. This is the seventh noble abode. (8) He dwells with a mind imbued with equanimity, suffusing one quarter, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; so above, below, across, and everywhere, to all as to himself, he dwells suffusing the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity—abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility, and without ill will. This is the eighth noble abode. (9) He is a forest-dweller. This is the ninth noble abode. (10) He is a wearer of rag-robes. This is the tenth noble abode. These, bhikkhus, are the ten noble abodes."
(AN 10.20, PTS AN v 29) On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kurus at a town of the Kurus named Kammāsadhamma.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus... [as above] ...pe... [as above].
“Monks, there are these ten abodes of the noble ones, which the noble ones have dwelt in, do dwell in, or will dwell in.
What are the ten?
Here, monks, a monk has abandoned five factors, is endowed with six factors, and has a single guard.”
One who has the four supports, who has dispelled individual dogmatic views, who has thoroughly exhausted all quests, whose intentions are undisturbed, whose bodily formations are tranquil,
and who is well-liberated in mind and well-liberated in wisdom.
And how, monks, is a monk one who has abandoned five factors?
“Here, monks, a monk has abandoned sensual desire, he has abandoned ill will, he has abandoned sloth and torpor, he has abandoned restlessness and remorse, and he has abandoned doubt.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk has abandoned five factors.
And how, monks, is a monk possessed of six factors?
"Here, monks, having seen a form with the eye, a monk is neither glad nor sad; he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending.
Having heard a sound with the ear...
having smelled an odor with the nose..."
Having tasted a flavor with the tongue...
having touched a tangible object with the body...
having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one is neither glad nor sad; one dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending.
"In this way, monks, a monk is endowed with six factors.
And how, monks, is a monk one who has a single guard?
Here, monks, a monk is endowed with a mind guarded by mindfulness."
In this way, monks, a monk has a single guard.
And how, monks, does a monk have four supports?
Here, monks, a monk, having reflected, pursues one thing; having reflected, he endures one thing; having reflected, he avoids one thing; having reflected, he dispels one thing.
"In this way, monks, a monk has four supports.
And how, monks, does a monk have shaken off his private truths?
Here, monks, whatever various private truths there are among the various recluses and brahmins—namely:"

‘The world is eternal,’ or ‘the world is not eternal,’ or ‘the world is finite,’ or ‘the world is infinite,’ or ‘the soul and the body are the same,’ or ‘the soul is one thing and the body another,’ or ‘a Tathāgata exists after death,’ or ‘a Tathāgata does not exist after death,’ or ‘a Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death’—

Or that "the Tathāgata exists after death," or "the Tathāgata does not exist after death," or "the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death," or "the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death"—
all these are pushed away, cast off, abandoned, vomited out, released, relinquished, and discarded.
In this way, monks, a monk has shaken off individual dogmatic assertions.
And how, monks, is a monk one who has completely renounced seeking?
Here, monks, a monk’s seeking for sense-pleasures is abandoned, his seeking for existence is abandoned, and his seeking for the holy life has subsided.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk is one who has completely renounced seeking.
And how, monks, is a monk one whose intentions are untroubled?
Here, monks, a monk has abandoned the intention of sensual desire, abandoned the intention of ill will, and abandoned the intention of cruelty.
It is in this way, monks, that a monk is one whose intentions are untroubled.
And how, monks, is a monk one whose bodily formations have become tranquil? Here, monks,
with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief,
a monk enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
In this way, monks, a monk has tranquilized the bodily formations.
And how, monks, is a monk well-liberated in mind?
Here, monks, a monk’s mind is liberated from lust, his mind is liberated from hatred, and his mind is liberated from delusion.
In this way, monks, a monk is one whose mind is well-liberated.
And how, monks, is a monk one whose wisdom is well-liberated? Here, monks, a monk thinks:
"Lust has been abandoned by me; it is cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent."
He understands: ‘In the future, it is subject to non-arising. He understands: ‘Hatred has been abandoned by me... ... ‘Delusion has been abandoned by me;
it is cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and is subject to non-arising in the future.
In this way, monks, a monk is one whose wisdom is well-liberated.
"Monks, whatever noble ones in the past dwelt in noble dwellings, all of them dwelt in these very ten noble dwellings.
Monks, whatever noble ones in the future will dwell in noble dwellings, all of them will dwell in these very ten noble dwellings.
Monks, whatever noble ones at present dwell in noble dwellings, all of them dwell in these very ten noble dwellings."
“Monks, these are the ten abodes of the noble ones, which the noble ones have dwelt in, do dwell in, or will dwell in.
The tenth.
The second chapter on the Protector is finished.
Its summary verse:
The lodging, the five factors,
and the fetter along with the thorn.
Heedfulness is worthy of offerings;
the two protectors and the two noble abodes.
(Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.21)

3. Mahāvagga Sīhanādasutta (AN 10.21, PTS AN v 32) At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, there are these four Tathāgata’s powers that the Tathāgata has, possessing which he claims the place of the chief bull, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets rolling the Wheel of Brahmā. “What four? Here, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering. He understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering. He understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering. He understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. These, bhikkhus, are the four Tathāgata’s powers that the Tathāgata has, possessing which he claims the place of the chief bull, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets rolling the Wheel of Brahmā.”
“Bhikkhus, in the evening time, Sīha, the lion-king, emerges from his lair.
Having emerged from his lair, he stretches.
Having stretched, he surveys the four quarters all around.”
Having surveyed the four directions all around, he roars his lion’s roar three times.
Having roared his lion’s roar three times, he sets out for his range.
For what reason?
‘May I not bring about the destruction of small creatures that have come into my path.
Monks, “lion” is a designation for the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
When the Tathāgata teaches the Dhamma to an assembly, monks, this constitutes his lion’s roar.
“Monks, there are these ten powers of a Tathāgata, endowed with which the Tathāgata claims his place as a leader, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
What are the ten?
Here, monks, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible.”
Furthermore, monks, in that the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible—
this too, monks, is a power of the Tathāgata, by virtue of which power the Tathāgata claims his place of leadership,
roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
Furthermore, monks, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the result of the undertaking of kamma in the past, future, and present, according to its basis and according to its cause.

That the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the result of the undertaking of kamma in the past, future, and present, according to its basis and according to its cause— this too, monks, is a power of the Tathāgata.
Relying on which power the Tathāgata claims his place as the leader, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies,
and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
Furthermore, monks, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the practice leading everywhere.
Moreover, monks, that the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the practice leading to all destinations—
this too, monks, is a power of the Tathāgata, by virtue of which power the Tathāgata claims his place of leadership,
roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
Furthermore, monks, the Tathāgata understands the world with its many and diverse elements as it really is.
That the Tathāgata understands the world with its many and diverse elements as it really is, this too, monks, is a power of the Tathāgata... [as before] ...he sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
Furthermore, monks, the Tathāgata understands the diversity of the inclinations of beings as it really is.

Furthermore, monks, in that the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the diversity of inclinations among beings, this too, monks, is a power of the Tathāgata... [as before] ...he sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
Furthermore, monks, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the degrees of the faculties of other beings and other individuals.

Furthermore, monks, when the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the degrees of development of the faculties of other beings and other individuals, this too, monks, is a power of the Tathāgata... [as before] ...he sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
Furthermore, monks, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the defilement, the cleansing, and the emergence from the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments.
When he understands this... [as before] ...this too, monks, is a power of the Tathāgata... [as before] ...he sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
Furthermore, monks, the Tathāgata recollects his manifold past abodes,
that is to say: one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births,
twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births...
Even for a hundred thousand births, or for many aeons of world-contraction, many aeons of world-expansion, and many aeons of both contraction and expansion, [he recollects:
"In that place I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan;
passing away from there, I arose in another place; there too I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, and such experience of pleasure and pain."
‘Having had such a lifespan, having passed away from there, I have reappeared here,’ thus he recollects his manifold past abodes with their modes and details.
And, monks, that the Tathāgata recollects his manifold past abodes, namely— even one...
He recollects two births... [and so on] ...thus he recollects his manifold past lives with their modes and details.
This, monks, is a Tathāgata’s power of a Tathāgata, by virtue of which power the Tathāgata claims his place as a leader, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
Furthermore, monks, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans,
the Tathāgata sees beings passing away and being reborn— lowly and exalted, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—
and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma, [knowing]: "These worthy beings, indeed, were possessed of misconduct of body..."
Possessed of misconduct in speech, possessed of misconduct in mind, revilers of the noble ones, holding wrong views, and undertaking actions based on wrong views—
these beings, with the breakup of the body after death, have been reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell. But these worthy beings,
possessed of good conduct in body and good conduct in speech...
‘...endowed with good conduct of mind, not revilers of the noble ones, possessing right view, and undertaking actions based on right view;
they, with the breakup of the body, after death, have been reborn in a happy destination, a heavenly world.
Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—lowly and exalted, beautiful and ugly.
He understands beings who are ugly or beautiful, those who are well-faring or ill-faring, as they pass on according to their karma.
Monks, that the Tathāgata, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans,
understands beings as they pass on according to their karma— this too, monks, is a power of the Tathāgata.
Relying upon which power the Tathāgata claims his place as a leader, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies,
and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel. Furthermore, monks,

through the destruction of the taints, the Tathāgata dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having entered upon it.
Furthermore, monks, that the Tathāgata, through the destruction of the taints,
dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having attained it— this too, monks,
is a power of the Tathāgata, by virtue of which power the Tathāgata claims his place as a leader among the assemblies.
He roars his lion’s roar; he sets in motion the sublime wheel.
These, monks, are the ten powers of a Tathāgata, endowed with which the Tathāgata claims his place as the leader, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the sublime wheel.
Thus was the first [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.22 3. Mahāvagga Adhivuttipadasutta “Monks, there are these ten designations for the Tathāgata that are true, real, and factual; they are not false, not otherwise, and are so stated by the Tathāgata. What ten? ‘The Tathāgata is an Arhat’—this is a designation for the Tathāgata that is true, real, and factual; it is not false, not otherwise, and is so stated by the Tathāgata. ‘The Tathāgata is fully awakened’—this is a designation for the Tathāgata that is true, real, and factual; it is not false, not otherwise, and is so stated by the Tathāgata. ‘The Tathāgata has destroyed the āsavas’—this is a designation for the Tathāgata that is true, real, and factual; it is not false, not otherwise, and is so stated by the Tathāgata. ‘The Tathāgata has lived the holy life’—this is a designation for the Tathāgata that is true, real, and factual; it is not false, not otherwise, and is so stated by the Tathāgata. ‘The Tathāgata has done what was to be done’—this is a designation for the Tathāgata that is true, real, and factual; it is not false, not otherwise, and is so stated by the Tathāgata. ‘The Tathāgata has laid down the burden’—this is a designation for the Tathāgata that is true, real, and factual; it is not false, not otherwise, and is so stated by the Tathāgata. ‘The Tathāgata has lived out the holy life’—this is a designation for the Tathāgata that is true, real, and factual; it is not false, not otherwise, and is so stated by the Tathāgata. ‘The Tathāgata has reached the ultimate goal’—this is a designation for the Tathāgata that is true, real, and factual; it is not false, not otherwise, and is so stated by the Tathāgata. ‘The Tathāgata is the supreme being among all beings’—this is a designation for the Tathāgata that is true, real, and factual; it is not false, not otherwise, and is so stated by the Tathāgata. ‘The Tathāgata is the unsurpassed teacher of those who deserve instruction’—this is a designation for the Tathāgata that is true, real, and factual; it is not false, not otherwise, and is so stated by the Tathāgata. These, monks, are the ten designations for the Tathāgata that are true, real, and factual; they are not false, not otherwise, and are so stated by the Tathāgata.”

Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As the Venerable Ānanda was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Ānanda, regarding those teachings that lead to the direct knowledge and realization of various designations, I claim to be confident therein.”
‘In such and such a way he teaches the Dhamma to various persons so that, practicing accordingly, they will know what exists as “it exists,” what does not exist as “it does not exist”;
they will know what is inferior as “inferior,” what is superior as “superior”;
they will know what is surpassable as “surpassable,” and what is unsurpassable as “unsurpassable.”’
‘In whatever way that which is to be known, seen, or realized may be, in that very way one will know, see, or realize it’—this is possible.
This, Ānanda, is the unsurpassed excellence among forms of knowledge, namely, knowledge of things as they truly are in each particular case.
And, Ānanda, I declare that there is no other knowledge higher or more sublime than this knowledge.
"Ānanda, there are these ten powers of a Tathāgata, endowed with which the Tathāgata claims his place as a leader, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
What are the ten?
Here, Ānanda, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible."
Furthermore, Ānanda, that the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible—
this, Ānanda, is a power of the Tathāgata, by virtue of which power the Tathāgata claims his place of leadership,
roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
Furthermore, Ānanda, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the result of the undertaking of kamma—past, future, and present—in terms of its basis and its cause.
That which, Ānanda... [as before] ...this too, Ānanda...
Furthermore, Ānanda, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the path leading everywhere.

And furthermore, Ānanda, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the world with its many and diverse elements. That which, Ānanda... [as before] ...that too, Ānanda... [as before]. Furthermore, Ānanda, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the world with its manifold elements and various elements.
That which, Ānanda... [as before] ...that too, Ānanda... [as before].
Furthermore, Ānanda, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the diversity of inclinations among beings.
That too, Ānanda... [as before] ...this too, Ānanda...
Furthermore, Ānanda, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the degrees of the faculties of other beings and other individuals.

And furthermore, Ānanda, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the defilement, the purification, and the emergence regarding the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments. That which, Ānanda... [as before] ...this too, Ānanda... [as before]. Furthermore, Ānanda, the Tathāgata understands, as it really is, the defilement, the purification, and the emergence regarding the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments.
That which, Ānanda... [as before] ...this too, Ānanda... [as before].

Furthermore, Ānanda, the Tathāgata recollects his manifold past abodes, that is to say: one birth, two births... [as before] ...thus with their aspects and particulars he recollects his manifold past abodes.
That too, Ānanda... [as before] ...this too, Ānanda...
Furthermore, Ānanda, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human... [as before] ...he understands beings as faring according to their deeds.

And furthermore, Ānanda, the Tathāgata, through the destruction of the taints, dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having attained it...

And furthermore, Ānanda, that the Tathāgata, through the destruction of the taints, [dwells] having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind... and having attained it.

He dwells [thus]. This, Ānanda, is a Tathāgata’s power of a Tathāgata, by virtue of which power the Tathāgata claims his place as the leader, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.
These, Ānanda, are the ten powers of a Tathāgata, endowed with which the Tathāgata claims his place as the leader, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Brahma-wheel.”
The Second.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.23 3. Mahāvagga
Kāyasutta: “Bhikkhus,
there are things to be abandoned by means of the body, not by speech.”
“Monks, there are phenomena to be abandoned by speech, not by body.
There are, monks, phenomena that are neither to be abandoned by body nor by speech, but are to be abandoned by seeing with wisdom.
And what, monks, are the phenomena to be abandoned by body, not by speech?”
In this case, monks, a bhikkhu has committed some unwholesome act with his body.
Wise fellow practitioners of the holy life, having investigated the matter, say to him:
"Venerable sir, you have indeed committed some unwholesome act with your body."
“It would be well indeed if the venerable one, having abandoned bodily misconduct, were to develop bodily good conduct.
Being thus addressed by wise fellow-celibates after they have investigated him, he abandons bodily misconduct and develops bodily good conduct.
These, monks, are called the things that are to be abandoned by means of the body, not by speech.
"And what, bhikkhus, are the things that should be abandoned by speech, not by body?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has committed some unwholesome act by way of speech in a certain matter.
Wise fellow-celibates, having investigated him, say this to him:"
‘The venerable one has indeed fallen into unwholesome conduct in some respect by way of speech.
It would be well if the venerable one were to abandon verbal misconduct and cultivate verbal good conduct.
Being thus addressed by wise fellow-celibates who have investigated the matter, he abandons verbal misconduct and cultivates verbal good conduct.
“Monks, these are called the qualities that are to be abandoned by speech, not by body.
And what, monks, are the qualities that are to be abandoned neither by body nor by speech, but are to be abandoned by seeing with wisdom?
Greed, monks, is to be abandoned neither by body nor by speech, but is to be abandoned by seeing with wisdom.”
Aversion, monks … delusion … anger … [and so on] …"
Enmity … hypocrisy … spite …
“Monks, stinginess is to be abandoned neither by body nor by speech; it is to be abandoned by seeing with wisdom.
Monks, wicked envy is to be abandoned neither by body nor by speech; it is to be abandoned by seeing with wisdom.
And what, monks, is wicked envy?”
In this case, monks, a householder or a householder’s son succeeds in wealth, grain, silver, or gold.
Then, a certain slave or laborer thinks:
“Oh, that this householder or householder’s son might not succeed in wealth, grain, silver, or gold!”
Now, suppose a certain ascetic or brahmin is a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
Then, it occurs to another ascetic or brahmin:
“Oh, may this venerable one not be a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick!”
This, monks, is called evil envy.
Evil desire, monks, is to be abandoned neither by body nor by speech, but is to be abandoned by seeing with wisdom.
And what, monks, is evil desire?
In this case, monks, someone who is faithless desires, ‘May they know me as faithful’;
being immoral, he desires, ‘May they know me as virtuous’;
being of little learning, he desires, ‘May they know me as learned.’
Being fond of company, he desires: "May they know me as one who is secluded.
Being lazy, he desires: "May they know me as one whose energy is aroused.
Being muddle-minded, he desires: "May they know me as one whose mindfulness is established."
Being unconcentrated, he desires: "May they know me as one who is concentrated.
Being lacking in wisdom, he desires: "May they know me as one possessed of wisdom.
Being one whose taints are not destroyed, he desires: "May they know me as one whose taints are destroyed."
This, monks, is called evil desire.
These, monks, are called states that are to be abandoned neither by body nor by speech, but by seeing with wisdom they are to be abandoned.
And if, monks, greed overcomes that bhikkhu and persists, [he is overcome].
hatred … delusion … anger …
Resentment … hypocrisy … spite …
Having overcome stinginess,
evil envy,
and evil longing, he conducts himself.
Thus he should be understood in this way:
‘This venerable one does not understand in such a way that greed would not exist for one who understands thus; rather, greed overcomes this venerable one and persists.
This venerable one does not understand in such a way that hatred would not exist for one who understands thus…’
Delusion … anger … resentment …
Deceit … hypocrisy … stinginess …
“Evil envy… evil desire does not exist; rather, it is this evil desire that, having overcome this venerable one, continues to course through him.
If, monks, greed does not continue to course by overcoming that bhikkhu, [then he is well-established].
Hatred … delusion … anger …
Enmity … hypocrisy … spite …
When stinginess,
evil envy,
and evil desire do not overcome and persistently dwell within one, [the mind becomes pliable].
He should be understood in this way:
‘This venerable one understands in such a way that, for one who understands thus, greed does not exist; therefore, greed does not overcome this venerable one as it persists.
This venerable one understands in such a way that, for one who understands thus, hatred does not exist…’
delusion … anger … hostility …
Deceit … hypocrisy … stinginess …
“Evil envy does not exist in him, nor does evil desire; for indeed, evil desire does not overcome this venerable one as it courses through him.
The third.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.24 3. Mahāvagga Mahācundasutta Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Venerable Mahācunda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “Cunda, there are these ten qualities of a true man. What ten? Here, Cunda, a true man is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in minute faults. Having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. He has learned much, remembers what he has learned, and accumulates what he has learned. These teachings, which are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, and which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure spiritual life—such teachings as these he has learned much of, retained in mind, recited verbally, mentally investigated, and penetrated well by view.

He is a speaker on the Dhamma, one who speaks at the right time, speaks what is factual, speaks what is beneficial, speaks on the Dhamma and the Discipline; at the right time he speaks such words as are worth recording, reasonable, succinct, and definitive. He is easy to correct and possesses qualities that make him easy to correct; he is patient and receives instruction respectfully. He does not harbor resentment toward his fellow monks for their faults or lapses; he does not speak of them, nor does he harbor such thoughts. He is content with any kind of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. He dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in exertion, not shirking the burden of wholesome qualities. He is wise; he possesses the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, which is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. These, Cunda, are the ten qualities of a true man. Possessing these ten qualities of a true man, one is called a true man who is accomplished in both ways. When this was said, the Venerable Mahācunda said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! Just as if one were to set upright what had been overturned, or to reveal what was hidden, or to show the way to one who was lost, or to bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, in the same way the Blessed One has explained the Dhamma in many ways. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May I receive the going forth under the Blessed One, may I receive the full admission. “Cunda, one who has previously belonged to another sect cannot be given the going forth or the full admission on the same day. After waiting four months, when it is known that one’s mind is settled and one’s character is stable, then one may be given the going forth and the full admission to the bhikkhu’s state. “But, venerable sir, if one who has previously belonged to another sect were to receive the going forth and the full admission after four months, then people would say: ‘The Sakyan son of the Sakyans has become a money-changer for the sake of gain. “In that case, Cunda, I shall grant you an exception. From today onward, Cunda, one who has previously belonged to another sect may receive the going forth and the full admission after waiting three months, when it is known that one’s mind is settled and one’s character is stable. Then the Venerable Mahācunda received the going forth under the Blessed One, and he received the full admission. Not long after his full admission, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, the Venerable Mahācunda, by realizing it for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life entered and dwelt in that unsurpassed goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness. He directly knew: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being. And the Venerable Mahācunda became one of the arahants. Deceit … hypocrisy … stinginess …
When evil envy… evil desire does not remain overwhelming him, he should be understood thus:
"This venerable one understands in such a way that greed does not arise for one who understands; therefore, greed does not remain overwhelming this venerable one."
In the same way, this venerable one understands such that, for one who understands thus, there is no hatred,
no delusion,
and no anger.
Enmity … hypocrisy … spite …
‘There is no stinginess… no evil envy… no evil desire in me;
thus, evil desire does not remain overwhelming this venerable one.’”
And when, friend, a bhikkhu speaks of knowledge and speaks of development, saying:

"I know this Dhamma, I see this Dhamma; I am one whose body is developed, whose virtue is developed, whose mind is developed, and whose wisdom is developed"—if, friend, greed does not persist by overpowering that bhikkhu, [then he is truly so].
Hatred … delusion … anger …
Enmity … hypocrisy … spite …
If stinginess,
evil envy,
or evil desire does not remain unovercome, he should be understood thus:
‘In such a way this venerable one understands that for one who understands thus, greed does not exist; thus greed does not remain having overcome this venerable one.
In such a way this venerable one understands that for one who understands thus, hatred does not exist… delusion does not exist…’
Anger … resentment … hypocrisy …
... malice ...
stinginess ...
evil envy ...
‘There is no evil desire in me; for this reason, evil desire does not remain overwhelming this venerable one.

It is just as if, friends, a man who is actually wealthy were to speak words of wealth, a man who is actually affluent were to speak words of affluence, and a man who is actually possessed of riches were to speak words of riches.
Then, when some financial obligation arises, he would be able to bring forth wealth, grain, silver, or gold.
They would know him thus:

“This venerable one, being himself wealthy, speaks as one who is wealthy; this venerable one, being himself possessed of riches, speaks as one who possesses riches; this venerable one, being himself possessed of enjoyments, speaks as one who possesses enjoyments.
For what reason?”
"For just as this venerable one, when some financial obligation arises, is able to produce wealth, grain, silver, or gold;
even so, friend, a bhikkhu who speaks of knowledge and speaks of development says:
'I know this Dhamma, I see this Dhamma; I am one whose body is developed, whose virtue is developed, whose mind is developed, and whose wisdom is developed.'"
If, friends, greed does not overcome that bhikkhu and persist, nor hatred … nor delusion … [then he is well-established].
Anger … resentment … hypocrisy …
... spite ...
avarice ...
evil envy ...
Evil desire does not remain overwhelming him; this should be understood of him thus:
"This venerable one understands in such a way that greed does not arise in one who understands thus; therefore, greed does not remain overwhelming this venerable one.
This venerable one understands in such a way that hatred does not arise in one who understands thus..."
Delusion … anger … malice …
Deceit … hypocrisy … stinginess …
“Evil envy does not exist in him… evil desire does not exist; for thus evil desire does not remain overwhelming this venerable one.
The fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.25 3.

Mahāvagga Kasiṇasutta “Monks, there are these ten kasiṇa-spheres. What ten? The earth-kasiṇa, the water-kasiṇa, the fire-kasiṇa, the air-kasiṇa, the blue-kasiṇa, the yellow-kasiṇa, the red-kasiṇa, the white-kasiṇa, the space-kasiṇa, and the consciousness-kasiṇa. These, monks, are the ten kasiṇa-spheres.”
“Monks, there are these ten kasiṇa bases. Which ten? [The list follows].”
One person perceives the earth-kasina above, below, and across, non-dual and immeasurable;
one person perceives the water-kasina … [and so on] … one person perceives the fire-kasina …
One person perceives the air-kasina;
one person perceives the blue-kasina;
one person perceives the yellow-kasina.
One person perceives the red kasiṇa...
one person perceives the white kasiṇa...
one person perceives the space kasiṇa...
“One person perceives the consciousness-kasina above, below, and across, undivided and immeasurable.
These, monks, are the ten kasina-bases. Thus ends the fifth [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.26 3. Mahāvagga Kāḷīsutta At Sāvatthī. Then the wanderer Kāḷī approached the Blessed One and, having approached, exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their courteous and amiable conversation, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the wanderer Kāḷī said to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama, I have heard this: ‘The ascetic Gotama knows the path to the company of the devas. Now, Master Gotama, does the ascetic Gotama know the path to the company of the devas? “I know the path to the company of the devas, Kāḷī,” the Blessed One replied. “But, Master Gotama, what is that path to the company of the devas? “There is the case, Kāḷī, where a bhikkhu dwells restrained in body, speech, and mind, established in the practice of virtue, consummate in his behavior, seeing danger in the slightest fault. He trains himself, having undertaken the training rules, seeing them as a treasure. This is the first factor of the path to the company of the devas. “Again, Kāḷī, a bhikkhu dwells with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, vast, exalted, measureless, without enmity, without ill will toward all living beings. This is the second factor of the path to the company of the devas. “Again, Kāḷī, a bhikkhu dwells with a mind imbued with compassion... with a mind imbued with altruistic joy... with a mind imbued with equanimity, vast, exalted, measureless, without enmity, without ill will toward all living beings. This is the fourth factor of the path to the company of the devas. “Again, Kāḷī, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having put aside hankering and fretting for the world. This is the fifth factor of the path to the company of the devas. “Again, Kāḷī, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... mind in mind... phenomena in phenomena—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having put aside hankering and fretting for the world. This is the sixth factor of the path to the company of the devas. “Again, Kāḷī, a bhikkhu dwells having abandoned covetousness and dejection regarding the world; he dwells with a mind free from covetousness and dejection, purified and bright. This is the seventh factor of the path to the company of the devas. “Again, Kāḷī, a bhikkhu dwells having abandoned ill will and anger regarding the world; he dwells with a mind free from ill will and anger, compassionate and kind toward all living beings. This is the eighth factor of the path to the company of the devas. “Again, Kāḷī, a bhikkhu dwells having abandoned sloth and torpor regarding the world; he dwells with a mind free from sloth and torpor, percipient of light, mindful, and clearly comprehending. This is the ninth factor of the path to the company of the devas. “Again, Kāḷī, a bhikkhu dwells having abandoned restlessness and remorse regarding the world; he dwells with a mind free from restlessness and remorse, inwardly stilled. This is the tenth factor of the path to the company of the devas. “Again, Kāḷī, a bhikkhu dwells having abandoned doubt regarding the world; he dwells with a mind free from doubt, not perplexed about wholesome qualities. This is the eleventh factor of the path to the company of the devas. “When, Kāḷī, a bhikkhu dwells possessing these eleven factors of the path to the company of the devas, he is capable of shaking off the human state and reappearing in the company of the devas. When this was said, the wanderer Kāḷī said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama! Just as if one were to set upright what had been overturned, or to reveal what was hidden, or to point out the way to one who was lost, or to bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, in the same way has Master Gotama—through many lines of reasoning—made the Dhamma clear. I go to Master Gotama for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. From this day forth, may Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”
(AN 10.26, PTS AN v 46) On one occasion the Venerable Mahākaccāna was dwelling among the Avantīs at Kuraraghara on Mount Pavatta.
Then the female lay follower Kāḷī of Kuraraghara approached the Venerable Mahākaccāna; having approached, she...
Having paid homage to the Venerable Mahākaccāna, she sat down to one side.
As she was sitting there, the female lay follower Kālī of Kuraraghara said this to the Venerable Mahākaccāna:
"Bhante, this was said by the Blessed One in the *Kumāripañha*: [The text continues with the verses of the *Kumāripañha*.]"
"Having conquered the army of forms that are dear and pleasant, I have attained the goal and peace of heart;
meditating alone, I have awakened to bliss."
"Therefore, I do not make a witness of people;
no witness is established for me by anyone.
"Venerable sir, how is the meaning of this statement, which was spoken in brief by the Blessed One, to be understood in detail?"
“Sister, some recluses and brahmins have generated the notion that ‘this is the goal,’ making the attainment of the earth-kasiṇa their limit.
To whatever extent there is the limit of the attainment of the earth-kasiṇa, the Blessed One has directly known it.
Having directly known it, the Blessed One saw the gratification, saw the danger, and saw the escape; he saw the knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path.”

Because of seeing its gratification, because of seeing its danger, because of seeing the escape, and because of seeing the knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path, the attainment of the goal and the peace of the heart are known to him.
Sister, the highest attainment regarding the water-kasiṇa...
[and so on] ...the highest attainment regarding the fire-kasiṇa, sister... is indeed this.
"O Sister, [the attainment] culminates in the air-kasiṇa attainment...
O Sister, it culminates in the blue-kasiṇa attainment...
O Sister, it culminates in the yellow-kasiṇa attainment..."
"Indeed, sister, the limit is the attainment of the red-kasiṇa...
indeed, sister, the limit is the attainment of the white-kasiṇa...
indeed, sister, the limit is the attainment of the space-kasiṇa..."
“Sister, some recluses and brahmins have generated the view that ‘this is the goal,’ making the attainment of the consciousness-kasiṇa their limit.
To whatever extent there is the attainment of the consciousness-kasiṇa as its limit, the Blessed One has directly known it.

Having directly known it, the Blessed One saw the gratification in it, he saw the danger in it, he saw the escape from it, and he saw the knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path.”

Through seeing the gratification, through seeing the danger, through seeing the escape, and through seeing the knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path, the attainment of the goal and the peace of the heart are known.
Thus indeed, sister, as it was said by the Blessed One in the *Kumāripañha*:
“The attainment of the goal, the peace of the heart...”
Having conquered the army of pleasant and agreeable forms,
I meditated alone and awakened to bliss;
therefore, I do not associate with the crowd.
“No witness can be found for me by anyone.
Sister, this is how the meaning of what was spoken in brief by the Blessed One should be understood in detail.
The sixth [discourse].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.27 3.
Mahāvagga Paṭhamamahāpañhāsutta (The First Discourse on the Great Questions)
(AN 10.27, PTS AN v 48) On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Then, in the morning,
a number of bhikkhus dressed, took their bowls and robes, and entered Sāvatthī for alms.
Then it occurred to those bhikkhus:
“It is still too early to wander for alms in Sāvatthī;
what if we were to go to the park of the wanderers of other sects?”
Then those bhikkhus went to the park of the wanderers of other sects. Having approached, they exchanged greetings with those wanderers of other sects.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, they sat down to one side. As they were sitting there, those wanderers of other sects said this to the bhikkhus:
"Friends, the ascetic Gotama teaches the Dhamma to his disciples thus:"
‘Come, monks, directly know all phenomena; having directly known all phenomena, dwell [in that state].
Friends, we too teach the Dhamma to our disciples in this way:
‘Come, friends, directly know all phenomena; having directly known all phenomena, dwell [in that state].’
"Friends, what is the distinction here, what is the difference, what is the disparity between the ascetic Gotama and us—namely, in the teaching of the Dhamma or in the instruction?
Then those bhikkhus neither rejoiced in nor rejected the words of those wanderers of other sects.
Without rejoicing and without rejecting, they rose from their seats and departed.
“We shall learn the meaning of this statement in the presence of the Blessed One.
Then those bhikkhus, having walked for alms in Sāvatthī, returned from their almsround after the meal and approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
As they were sitting to one side, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:
"Here, Bhante, having dressed in the morning and taken our bowls and robes, we entered Sāvatthī for alms.
Then, Bhante, this thought occurred to us:"
“It is still too early to wander for alms in Sāvatthī;
what if we were to go to the park where the wanderers of other sects reside?
Then, venerable sir, we went to the park where the wanderers of other sects reside, and having arrived, we exchanged greetings with those wanderers of other sects.
Having exchanged polite and courteous greetings, we sat down to one side. As we were sitting there, Bhante, the wanderers of other sects said this to us:
“Friends, the ascetic Gotama teaches the Dhamma to his disciples thus:
‘Come, monks, directly realize the whole of the Dhamma; having directly realized the whole of the Dhamma, dwell therein.’”
“Friends, we too teach the Dhamma to our disciples in this way:
‘Come, friends, directly know all phenomena; having directly known all phenomena, dwell therein.

In this regard, friends, what is the distinction, what is the specific intention, and what is the difference between the ascetic Gotama and us, namely, in the teaching of the Dhamma or in the instruction?”
“Then, venerable sir, we neither rejoiced in the words of those wanderers of other sects nor did we reject them.
Without rejoicing and without rejecting, we rose from our seats and departed, thinking:
‘We shall learn the meaning of these words in the presence of the Blessed One.’”
“Bhikkhus, when wanderers of other sects speak thus, they should be addressed as follows:
‘Friends, one question, one summary, and one exposition; two questions, two summaries, and two expositions;
three questions, three summaries, and three expositions; four questions, four summaries, and four expositions.’”
‘Five questions, five expositions, five explanations; six questions, six expositions, six explanations;
seven questions, seven expositions, seven explanations; eight questions, eight expositions, eight explanations;
nine questions, nine expositions, nine explanations; ten questions, ten expositions, ten explanations.’”
When questioned thus, monks, the wanderers of other sects will not be able to answer, and they will fall into further distress.
Why is that? Because, monks, it is outside their domain.
“Bhikkhus, I do not see anyone in the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its ascetics and brahmins,
its devas and humans, who could satisfy the mind with an answer to these questions,
except for the Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata, or one who has heard it from them.”
‘One question, one summary, and one answer’—thus it was said.
With reference to what was this said?

Monks, when a monk is completely disenchanted with one thing, completely dispassionate toward it, completely liberated from it, completely seeing its limit, and having fully realized its meaning, he makes an end of suffering in this very life.
"In what single dharma?
In this single dharma, monks: 'All beings subsist by nutriment'—a bhikkhu who becomes completely disenchanted with this, completely dispassionate toward this, completely..."
Being liberated, seeing the limit correctly, and having fully realized the goal, one makes an end of suffering in this very life.
"One question, one summary, one exposition"—
this was said with reference to this.
‘Two questions, two indications, two explanations’—this is what was said.
With reference to what was this said?

Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu becomes completely disenchanted with two things, completely dispassionate toward them, completely liberated from them, seeing their limits, and having fully realized their meaning, he makes an end of suffering in this very life.
In which two?
In name and form.
It is in these two things, monks, that a bhikkhu, becoming completely disenchanted and completely dispassionate, [should train].
Being rightly liberated, seeing rightly the limits, and having fully realized the goal,
one makes an end of suffering in this very life.
"Two questions, two summaries, two explanations"— this is what was said, and it was said with reference to this.
‘Three questions, three summaries, and three explanations’—thus it was said.
With reference to what was this said?

Monks, when a monk becomes completely disenchanted with three things, completely dispassionate toward them, completely liberated from them, and completely sees their limits, he fully realizes the goal and makes an end of suffering in this very life.
In which three?
In the three feelings.
It is, monks, by becoming completely disenchanted with these three things and completely dispassionate toward them that a monk [attains liberation].
Being rightly liberated, seeing rightly the limit, and having fully realized the goal,
one makes an end of suffering in this very life.
"Three questions, three summaries, and three explanations"— it was with reference to this that it was said.
‘Four questions, four summaries, four explanations’—thus it was said.
With reference to what was this said?

Monks, when a monk becomes completely disenchanted with four things, completely dispassionate toward them, completely liberated from them, completely sees their limit, and completely realizes their meaning, he makes an end of suffering in this very life.
In which four?
In the four nutriments.
It is in these four things, monks, that a bhikkhu, becoming completely disenchanted and completely dispassionate, [should train].
Being rightly liberated, seeing the limit rightly, and having fully realized the goal rightly, one makes an end of suffering in this very life.
It was with reference to this that it was said: "Four questions, four summaries, and four explanations. This is what was meant by those words.
‘Five questions, five expositions, and five answers’—thus it was said.
With reference to what was this said?

Monks, when a monk becomes completely disenchanted with five things, completely dispassionate toward them, completely liberated from them, completely sees their limits, and fully realizes their meaning, he makes an end of suffering in this very life.
In which five?
In the five aggregates of clinging—
in these five things, monks, a bhikkhu becoming completely disenchanted and becoming completely dispassionate...
Being rightly liberated, seeing the limit rightly, and having fully realized the goal rightly,
one makes an end of suffering in this very life.
"Five questions, five expositions, and five explanations"— this is what was said, and it was said with reference to this.
‘Six questions, six indications, and six explanations’—thus it was said.
With reference to what was this said?

Monks, when a monk becomes completely disenchanted with six things, completely dispassionate toward them, completely liberated from them, completely sees their limit, and completely realizes their meaning, he makes an end of suffering in this very life.
In which six?
In the six internal sense bases.
It is, monks, in these six things that a bhikkhu, becoming completely disenchanted and completely dispassionate, [should train].
Being rightly liberated, seeing rightly the limit, and having fully realized the goal, one makes an end of suffering in this very life.
It was with reference to this that it was said: "Six questions, six summaries, and six explanations. This is what was meant by that statement.
‘Seven questions, seven indications, and seven explanations’—thus it was said.
With reference to what was this said?

Monks, when a monk becomes completely disenchanted with seven things, completely dispassionate toward them, completely liberated from them, completely sees their limit, and completely realizes their meaning, he makes an end of suffering in this very life.
In which seven?
In the seven stations of consciousness.
It is, monks, in these seven things that a bhikkhu, becoming completely disenchanted and completely dispassionate, [should train].
Being rightly liberated, rightly seeing the limit, and having fully realized the goal,
one makes an end of suffering in this very life.
“Seven questions, seven indications, and seven explanations”— it was with reference to this that it was said.
‘Eight questions, eight demonstrations, and eight explanations’—thus it was said.
With reference to what was this said?

Monks, when a monk becomes completely disenchanted with eight things, completely dispassionate toward them, completely liberated from them, and seeing their limit, he realizes the goal correctly and makes an end of suffering in this very life.
In which eight?
In the eight worldly conditions.
It is, monks, by becoming completely disenchanted with these eight things... [as before] ...that a monk becomes an ender of suffering.
‘Eight questions, eight expositions, eight explanations’—this is what was said; it was said with reference to this.
‘Nine questions, nine expositions, nine explanations’—this, too, has been said.
With reference to what was this said?

“Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is completely disenchanted with nine things, completely dispassionate toward them, completely liberated from them, completely sees their limit, and has fully realized their meaning, he makes an end of suffering in this very life.
What are the nine?
The nine abodes of beings.”
Monks, when a monk is completely disenchanted with these nine things, completely dispassionate toward them,
completely liberated from them, seeing their complete limit, and having fully realized the goal,
he makes an end of suffering in this very life.
‘Nine questions, nine summaries, and nine explanations’—this is what was said; it was said with reference to this.
‘Ten questions, ten summaries, and ten explanations’—this too has been said.
With reference to what was this said?

“Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu becomes completely disenchanted with ten things, completely dispassionate toward them, completely liberated from them, completely sees their limit, and fully realizes their meaning, he makes an end of suffering in this very life.
What are the ten?
The ten unwholesome courses of action.”
Monks, when a monk is completely disenchanted with these ten things, completely dispassionate toward them,
completely liberated from them, completely seeing their limits, and having fully realized the goal,
he makes an end of suffering in this very life.
‘Ten questions, ten topics, ten explanations’—
it was with reference to this that it was said.
The seventh.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.28 3.
Mahāvagga Dutiyamahāpañhāsutta (The Second Discourse on the Great Question)
(AN 10.28, PTS AN v 54) On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Kajaṅgalā in the Bamboo Grove.
Then a number of lay followers from Kajaṅgalā approached the bhikkhunī of Kajaṅgalā.
Having approached and paid homage to the bhikkhunī of Kajaṅgalā, they sat down to one side.
Sitting there, the lay followers of Kajaṅgalā said this to the bhikkhunī of Kajaṅgalā:
“This was said, noble lady, by the Blessed One in the Mahāpañha:”
‘One question, one summary, one answer; two questions, two summaries, two answers;
three questions, three summaries, three answers; four questions, four summaries, four answers;
five questions, five summaries, five answers; six questions, six summaries, six answers.’
“Seven questions, seven expositions, and seven answers; eight questions, eight expositions, and eight answers;
nine questions, nine expositions, and nine answers; ten questions, ten expositions, and ten answers.
Now, Noble Lady, how should the meaning of this brief statement by the Blessed One be understood in detail?”
“However, friends, this was not heard by me in the presence of the Blessed One, nor was it received directly from the presence of the venerable bhikkhus;
nevertheless, listen to how it appears to me and attend closely, and I shall speak.”
“Yes, Venerable Madam,” the lay followers of Kajaṅgalā replied to the bhikkhunī of Kajaṅgalā.
The bhikkhunī of Kajaṅgalā said this:
“‘One question, one summary, one exposition’—thus indeed was it said by the Blessed One.”
And with reference to what was this said?

Friends, when a bhikkhu becomes completely disenchanted with one thing, completely dispassionate toward it, completely liberated from it, completely sees its limit, and completely realizes its meaning, he makes an end of suffering in this very life. With which one thing? With the mind. For the mind, friends, is the root of suffering; the mind is the source of suffering; the mind is the origin of suffering; the mind is the cause of suffering. When a bhikkhu becomes completely disenchanted with the mind, completely dispassionate toward it, completely liberated from it, completely sees its limit, and completely realizes its meaning, he makes an end of suffering in this very life. This is what was said, and with reference to this it was said.

"All beings subsist on nutriment"— it is with reference to this one thing, friends, that when a bhikkhu becomes completely disenchanted, completely dispassionate, completely liberated, and completely sees the limit, and having fully realized the goal, he makes an end of suffering in this very life.
"One question, one summary, one answer"— this is what was said by the Blessed One, and it is in reference to this that it was said.
‘Two questions, two topics, two explanations,’ so it was said by the Blessed One.
With reference to what was this said?

Friends, when a bhikkhu becomes completely disenchanted with two things, completely dispassionate toward them, completely liberated from them, seeing their limit, and having fully realized their meaning, he makes an end of suffering in this very life.
In which two? In name and form...
In which three?
Regarding the three feelings: "In these three things, friends, a bhikkhu who becomes completely disenchanted, completely dispassionate, completely liberated,
and completely sees their limit, having fully realized the goal, makes an end of suffering here and now."
‘Three questions, three summaries, and three explanations’—this is what was said by the Blessed One; with reference to what was this said?
‘Four questions, four summaries, and four explanations’—this too was said by the Blessed One.
With reference to what was this said?
"Friends, when a bhikkhu has rightly developed his mind regarding four things, rightly seen their limits, and rightly realized their meaning, he makes an end of suffering in this very life.
Which four? The four foundations of mindfulness."
"Friends, when a bhikkhu has rightly cultivated his mind regarding these four things, rightly seen their limits, and rightly realized their meaning, he makes an end of suffering in this very life.
'Four questions, four summaries, four explanations'—this is what was said by the Blessed One, and it is in reference to this that it was said.
Furthermore, 'Five questions, five summaries, five explanations'—this too was said by the Blessed One."
And with reference to what was this said?
Friends, when a bhikkhu has well cultivated his mind regarding five things, seeing their limits correctly and having fully realized their meaning, he makes an end of suffering in this very life.
Which five?
In the five faculties ...
[as before] ... in which six?
In the six elements leading to deliverance ... [as before] ...
In which seven?
In the seven factors of enlightenment...
In which eight?
Regarding the eight factors of the Noble Eightfold Path:
"In these eight things, friends, a bhikkhu whose mind is rightly well-developed, who rightly sees the limit, and who has fully realized the goal, makes an end of suffering in this very life.
This is what was said by the Blessed One when he spoke those words: "Eight questions, eight expositions, eight explanations. It is with reference to this that it was said.
‘Nine questions, nine statements, and nine explanations’—this was said by the Blessed One.
With reference to what was this said?

Friends, when a bhikkhu becomes completely disenchanted with nine things, completely dispassionate toward them, completely liberated from them, and completely sees their limit, he realizes the goal correctly and makes an end of suffering in this very life.
In which nine? In the nine abodes of beings—
in these nine things, friends, a bhikkhu becoming completely disenchanted, becoming completely dispassionate...
Being liberated, seeing the limit rightly, and having fully realized the goal, he makes an end of suffering in this very life.
"Nine questions, nine expositions, nine explanations"—this is what was said by the Blessed One, and it was said with reference to this.
"Ten questions, ten expositions, ten explanations"—this, too, was said by the Blessed One.
And with reference to what was this said?
Friends, when a bhikkhu has well cultivated his mind regarding ten things, seeing their limits correctly and having fully realized their meaning, he makes an end of suffering in this very life.
What are the ten?
Regarding the ten courses of wholesome action:
"In these ten things, friend, a bhikkhu whose mind is well-developed, who sees the limit correctly, and who has fully realized the goal, makes an end of suffering in this very life.
This is what was said by the Blessed One when he spoke the words, "Ten questions, ten expositions, ten explanations," and it is with reference to this that he spoke.
"Thus, friend, regarding that which was spoken in brief by the Blessed One in the *Mahāpañhā*—
'one question, one summary, one exposition...
ten questions, ten summaries, ten expositions'— it is in this way, friend, that I understand the meaning of what was spoken in brief by the Blessed One in detail."
"But if you wish, friends, you should approach the Blessed One himself and ask him about this matter.
You should remember it exactly as the Blessed One explains it to you.
"Very well, noble lady," the lay followers of Kajaṅgalā replied, rejoicing in what the bhikkhunī of Kajaṅgalā had said.
Having rejoiced, they rose from their seats, paid homage to the bhikkhunī of Kajaṅgalā, and keeping her to their right, they approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the lay followers of Kajaṅgalā reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation that had taken place with the bhikkhunī of Kajaṅgalā.
“Excellent, excellent, householders!
Wise, householders, is the bhikkhunī of Kañjanga; the bhikkhunī of Kañjanga has great wisdom, householders.
If you had approached me and asked me about this matter, I too would have answered exactly as the bhikkhunī of Kañjanga has answered.”
This is precisely its meaning. And you should remember it thus.
The eighth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.29

3. Mahāvagga: The First Discourse to Kosala (AN 10.29, PTS AN v 59) At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, King Pasenadi of Kosala said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how many things does a noble disciple possess that make him a stream-enterer, no longer subject to perdition, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination? “A noble disciple, great king, possesses four things that make him a stream-enterer, no longer subject to perdition, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. What four? Here, great king, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One. “He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. “He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. “He possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—untorn, unbroken, unspotted, unsplattered, liberating, praised by the wise, untarnished, leading to concentration. “A noble disciple, great king, who possesses these four things is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to perdition, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. When this was said, King Pasenadi of Kosala said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir!... From today let the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Not long after King Pasenadi of Kosala had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, do you see that King Pasenadi of Kosala has departed? “Yes, venerable sir. “That King Pasenadi of Kosala, bhikkhus, is a person of little faith, little affection, and little conviction. Yet even so, when he hears my teaching, he gains confirmed confidence in the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, and he acquires the virtues dear to the noble ones. It is enough, bhikkhus, for a noble disciple to possess these four things to be a stream-enterer, no longer subject to perdition, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination.”
“Bhikkhus, as far as Kāsī and Kosala extend, as far as King Pasenadi of Kosala’s realm reaches, there King Pasenadi of Kosala is declared to be the foremost.
Yet, bhikkhus, even for King Pasenadi of Kosala there is alteration, there is change.
Seeing this, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with that as well.”
Becoming disenchanted with that, one becomes detached from the highest; how much more so from what is inferior.
Monks, as far as the moon and sun revolve, illuminating and shining forth in all directions, so vast is the world-system of a thousand worlds.
In that world-system of a thousand worlds, there are a thousand moons, a thousand suns, and a thousand Sineru kings of mountains.
A thousand Jambudīpas, a thousand Aparagoyānas, a thousand Uttarakurus, a thousand Pubbavidehas,
four thousand great oceans, four thousand [realms of] the Four Great Kings, a thousand [realms] of the Cātumahārājikas,
a thousand [realms] of the Tāvatiṃsas, a thousand [realms] of the Yāmas, and a thousand [realms] of the Tusitas; a thousand [realms] of the Nimmānaratis.
A thousand [worlds] of the Paranimmitavasavatti devas, and a thousand Brahma-worlds.
Monks, as far as a thousandfold world-system extends, the Great Brahmā is declared to be the foremost therein.
Yet, monks, even for the Great Brahmā there is indeed alteration; there is indeed change.
Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with that as well.
Becoming disenchanted with that, he becomes dispassionate toward the highest, let alone the inferior.
There comes a time, bhikkhus, when this world contracts.
“Bhikkhus, when the world is contracting, beings for the most part are reborn in the Ābhassara realm.
There they are mind-made, feeding on rapture, self-luminous, moving through the air, and established in beauty; they remain for a long, vast period of time.
When the world is contracting, bhikkhus, the Ābhassara devas are said to be the foremost.”
“Bhikkhus, even for the Ābhassara devas there is indeed alteration, there is change.
Seeing this, bhikkhus, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with that as well.
Becoming disenchanted with that, he becomes dispassionate toward the highest, let alone toward what is inferior.”
"Bhikkhus, there are these ten kasiṇa bases.
What are the ten?
One perceives the earth-kasiṇa above, below, and across, undivided and immeasurable."
One person perceives the water-kasiṇa … one person perceives the fire-kasiṇa … one person perceives the air-kasiṇa …
One person perceives the blue kasiṇa;
one person perceives the yellow kasiṇa;
one person perceives the red kasiṇa.
One perceives the white kasiṇa;
one perceives the space kasiṇa;
one perceives the consciousness kasiṇa—above, below, across, non-dual and immeasurable.
“Monks, these are the ten kasiṇa bases.
Of these ten kasiṇa bases, monks, the foremost is this: that one perceives the consciousness-kasiṇa above, below, across, non-dual, and immeasurable.
There are, monks, beings who possess such a perception.”
“Monks, even for beings who have such a perception, there is indeed change and there is transformation.
Seeing this, monks, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with that as well.
Becoming disenchanted with that, he becomes detached from the highest, let alone from what is inferior.”
“Monks, there are these eight bases of mastery.
What are the eight?
One who is percipient of forms internally sees forms externally as limited, beautiful or ugly;”
Having mastered them, one perceives: "I know, I see. Such is his perception.
This is the first base of mastery (*abhibhāyatana*).
One who is percipient of forms internally sees external forms that are immeasurable, both beautiful and ugly.
"Having mastered them, I know and see," thus he perceives.
This is the second base of mastery.
Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are limited, beautiful or ugly.
Having mastered them, one perceives thus: "I know, I see.
This is the third base of mastery.
Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms, immeasurable, beautiful and ugly.
Having mastered them, one perceives: "I know, I see.
This is the fourth base of mastery.
Not perceiving form internally, one sees forms externally that are blue, blue in color, blue in appearance, and blue in luster.
Just as an umā flower is blue, blue in color, blue in appearance,
and blue in luster; or just as Benares cloth, smooth on both sides, might be blue, blue in color, blue in appearance, and blue in luster— even so,
one who is percipient of the formless internally sees forms externally that are blue, blue in color, blue in appearance, and blue in luster.
Having mastered them, one perceives thus: "I know, I see.
This is the fifth base of mastery.
Not perceiving form internally, one sees forms externally that are yellow, yellow in color, yellow in appearance, and yellow in luster.
Just as a *kaṇikāra* flower is yellow, yellow-colored, yellow in appearance,
and yellow in luster; or just as Benares cloth, smooth on both sides, is yellow, yellow-colored, yellow in appearance, and yellow in luster— even so,
one who is percipient of the formless internally sees forms externally that are yellow, yellow-colored, yellow in appearance, and yellow in luster.
Having mastered them, one perceives: "I know, I see.
This is the sixth base of mastery.
Not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are red, red in color, red in appearance, and red in luster.
Just as a bandhujīvaka flower is red, red-colored, red in appearance, and red in luster;
or just as a Benares cloth, smooth on both sides, is red, red-colored,
red in appearance, and red in luster.
In the same way, not perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are red, red in color, red in appearance, and red in luster;
having mastered them, one perceives: "I know, I see.
This is the seventh base of mastery.
Not perceiving form internally, one sees forms externally that are white, white in color, white in appearance, and white in luster.
Just as, for example, the morning star is white, white in color, white in appearance, and white in luster;
or just as, for example, a Benares cloth, smooth on both sides, is white, white in color, white in appearance, and white in luster.
In the same way, not perceiving forms internally, one sees forms externally that are white, white in color, white in appearance, and white in luster;
having mastered them, one perceives: "I know, I see.
This is the eighth base of mastery.
"These, monks, are the eight bases of mastery. Of these eight bases of mastery, monks, the foremost is this:
one who is percipient of the formless internally sees forms externally that are white, of white color, with white appearance, and white luster;
having mastered them, one is percipient thus: 'I know, I see.'"
“Monks, there are beings who have such a perception.
Even for those beings who have such a perception, there is indeed change and there is transformation.
Seeing this, monks, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with that as well.”
Becoming disenchanted with that, one becomes detached from the highest; how much more so from the inferior.
Monks, there are these four ways of practice. Which four?
The painful practice with slow direct knowledge,
the painful practice with quick direct knowledge,
and the pleasant practice with slow direct knowledge.
The pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge—these, monks, are the four practices.
Of these four practices, monks, the foremost is this: the pleasant practice with quick direct knowledge.
"Monks, there are beings who practice in this way.
Even for those beings who practice in this way, there is indeed change; there is indeed alteration.
Seeing this, monks, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with that as well."
Becoming disenchanted with that, one becomes detached from the highest, let alone from what is inferior.
Monks, there are these four perceptions.
What are the four?
One perceives the limited,
another perceives the exalted,
and another perceives the immeasurable.
‘There is nothing at all,’ one perceives the base of nothingness—these, monks, are the four perceptions.
Among these four perceptions, monks, the foremost is this: that one perceives the base of nothingness, thinking, ‘There is nothing at all.’
“Monks, there are beings who have such a perception.
Even for those beings who have such a perception, there is indeed alteration; there is indeed change.
