Seeing this, monks, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with that as well.”
Becoming disenchanted with that, one becomes detached from the highest, let alone from what is inferior.
Monks, this is the foremost among the external speculative views, namely: "May I not be, and may nothing be mine; may I not come to be, and may nothing be mine in the future.
For one who holds such a view, monks, this is to be expected:
‘There will be no lack of repulsion toward existence for him,
nor will there be any repulsion toward the cessation of existence. Such, monks, are beings who hold such a view.
“Bhikkhus, even for beings with such views, there is indeed alteration and there is change.
Seeing this, bhikkhus, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with that as well.
Becoming disenchanted with that, he becomes dispassionate toward the highest, let alone what is inferior.”
“Bhikkhus, there are some recluses and brahmins who proclaim the purification of the ultimate goal.

Of those who proclaim the purification of the ultimate goal, this is the foremost: namely, having completely transcended the base of nothingness, one enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Having directly known that, they teach the Dhamma for its realization.”
“Monks, there are beings who speak thus.
Even for those beings who speak thus, there is indeed change; there is indeed alteration.
Seeing this, monks, the well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with that as well.”
Becoming disenchanted with that, one becomes dispassionate toward the foremost, let alone the inferior.
There are, monks, some recluses and brahmins who proclaim a supreme Nibbāna in this very life.
Of those who proclaim a supreme Nibbāna in this very life, monks, this is the foremost: namely, [the cessation] of the six bases of contact.
"Having understood, as they really are, the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding these things, there is liberation through non-clinging.
Yet, monks, some ascetics and brahmins, being insincere, hollow, false, and untruthful, misrepresent me—who speak thus and declare this—saying:
'The ascetic Gotama does not prescribe the full understanding of sensual pleasures, nor does he prescribe the full understanding of forms, nor does he prescribe the full understanding of feelings.'"
“Monks, I prescribe the full understanding of sensual pleasures; I prescribe the full understanding of forms; I prescribe the full understanding of feelings.
In this very life, I prescribe the state of being free from hunger, extinguished, cooled, and attained final Nibbāna through non-clinging.
Thus ends the ninth [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.30 3. Mahāvagga Dutiyakosalasutta (The Second Discourse to the King of Kosala) Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, King Pasenadi of Kosala said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘the world, the world. In what way, venerable sir, is it said, ‘the world’?

“It is, great king, because it disintegrates that it is called ‘the world. For whatever, great king, disintegrates, that is called ‘the world. “But what, venerable sir, disintegrates? “The eye, great king, disintegrates; forms disintegrate; eye-consciousness disintegrates; eye-contact disintegrates; and whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as its condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too disintegrates. “The ear disintegrates... The nose disintegrates... The tongue disintegrates... The body disintegrates... The mind disintegrates; mental phenomena disintegrate; mind-consciousness disintegrates; mind-contact disintegrates; and whatever feeling arises with mind-contact as its condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too disintegrates. “It is, great king, because these things disintegrate that it is said, ‘the world. When this was said, King Pasenadi of Kosala said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! Just as if one were to set upright what had been overturned, or to reveal what was hidden, or to show the way to one who was lost, or to bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has the Dhamma been made clear by the Blessed One in many ways. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last. “Great king, it is not easy to find a person who has not previously been your mother, or your father, or your brother, or your sister, or your son, or your daughter in the course of this beginningless saṃsāra. Therefore, great king, you should train yourself thus: ‘Even toward those who have done me no service, I will act with kindness; how much more so toward those who have done me a service? It is in such a way, great king, that you should train yourself. When this was said, King Pasenadi of Kosala said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! Just as if one were to set upright what had been overturned, or to reveal what was hidden, or to show the way to one who was lost, or to bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has the Dhamma been made clear by the Blessed One in many ways. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, King Pasenadi of Kosala delighted in the Blessed One’s words. (This concludes the second discourse to the King of Kosala.)
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now on that occasion King Pasenadi of Kosala had returned from a military expedition, victorious in battle and having achieved his purpose.
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala set out for the monastery.
Having gone by carriage as far as the ground would allow for a vehicle, he alighted from the carriage and entered the monastery on foot.
Now at that time, a number of bhikkhus were walking back and forth in the open air.
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala approached those bhikkhus; having approached, he said this to them:
"Venerable sirs, where does the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, dwell at present?
For we, venerable sirs, desire to see that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One."
“Great King, that dwelling has its door closed. Approach it quietly and without haste; enter the porch, cough, and knock on the bolt, and the Blessed One will open the door for you.
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala approached that dwelling with its door closed; he entered the porch quietly and without haste, coughed, and knocked on the bolt. The Blessed One opened the door.

Then King Pasenadi of Kosala entered the monastery, prostrated with his head at the Blessed One’s feet, kissed the Blessed One’s feet with his mouth, stroked them with his hands, and announced his name:
"I am King Pasenadi of Kosala, venerable sir;
I am King Pasenadi of Kosala, venerable sir."
“But for what purpose, Great King, do you regard this body with such supreme devotion, performing such an act of self-surrender and offering this gift of loving-kindness?
“For the sake of gratitude and thankfulness, venerable sir, I perform such supreme devotion toward the Blessed One and offer this gift of loving-kindness.

For the Blessed One, venerable sir, has practiced for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many; he has established many people in the noble method, namely, in the state of wholesome qualities and skillful qualities.”
Furthermore, Bhante, because the Blessed One has practiced for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many,
and has established many people in the noble way— namely, in the state of wholesome qualities and skillful qualities— it is with this purpose in view, Bhante,
that I perform such supreme service toward the Blessed One and offer this tribute of loving-kindness.
Furthermore, Bhante, the Blessed One is virtuous, possessed of the virtue of the elders, possessed of noble virtue, possessed of wholesome virtue, and endowed with wholesome virtue.
Seeing this benefit, Bhante, I perform such supreme acts of self-surrender toward the Blessed One.
I offer it; I present this offering of loving-kindness.
Furthermore, Bhante, for a long time the Blessed One has been a forest-dweller, frequenting remote lodgings in forest and jungle thickets.
That the Blessed One, Bhante, for a long time has been a forest-dweller, frequenting remote lodgings in forest and jungle thickets—
“Furthermore, venerable sir, seeing this purpose as well, I perform such supreme acts of service toward the Blessed One and offer him an offering of loving-kindness.
Moreover, venerable sir, the Blessed One is content with whatever robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick he may receive.”
“Venerable sir, since the Blessed One is content with whatever robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick he may receive,
it is because I see this benefit, venerable sir, that I perform such supreme acts of reverence toward the Blessed One and offer him my loving-kindness.”
Furthermore, venerable sir, the Blessed One is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
Venerable sir, seeing this benefit as well, I perform such supreme acts of homage toward the Blessed One.
I offer it; I present this offering of loving-kindness.

Furthermore, Bhante, the Blessed One [delivers] whatever discourse is conducive to effacement and favorable for the opening of the mind—namely, a discourse on fewness of desires, a discourse on contentment, a discourse on seclusion, a discourse on non-association, a discourse on the arousal of energy, a discourse on virtue, and a discourse on concentration.
discourse on wisdom, discourse on liberation, and discourse on the knowledge and vision of liberation—he is one who gains such talk at will, without difficulty, and without trouble.
Furthermore, Bhante, as for that talk which is conducive to effacement and favorable to the opening of the mind—namely, discourse on fewness of desires ...
[and so on] ... up to discourse on the knowledge and vision of liberation—he is one who gains such talk at will, without difficulty, and without trouble.
"Furthermore, venerable sir, seeing this purpose, I perform such supreme acts of self-surrender toward the Blessed One and offer him my loving-kindness. Moreover, venerable sir,
the Blessed One is one who gains at will, without difficulty, and without trouble, the four jhānas that belong to the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life."

Furthermore, venerable sir, since the Blessed One is one who gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas— states of higher mind that provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life— I too, venerable sir, seeing this benefit,
perform such supreme service toward the Blessed One and offer him my loving-kindness.
Furthermore, Bhante, the Blessed One recollects his manifold past lives,
that is to say: one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births,
twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births...
Even for a hundred thousand births, or for many aeons of world-contraction, many aeons of world-expansion, and many aeons of both contraction and expansion, [he recollects:
“In that place I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a lifespan;
passing away from there, I reappeared elsewhere; and there too I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, and such experience of pleasure and pain.”
‘Having had such a lifespan, having passed away from there, I was reborn here. Thus he recollects his manifold past lives in their modes and details.
And, Bhante, that the Blessed One recollects his manifold past lives, namely: one birth... [and so forth].
"I recall two births... [and so on] ...thus I recollect my manifold past lives with their modes and details.
Venerable sir, seeing this benefit, I perform such supreme service toward the Blessed One and offer this tribute of loving-kindness."
Furthermore, Bhante, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans,
the Blessed One sees beings passing away and being reborn— low and high, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate— and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma:
"These worthy beings, indeed, were possessed of misconduct of body and misconduct of speech..."
...endowed with misconduct of mind, revilers of the noble ones, holding wrong views, and undertaking actions based on wrong views,
they— upon the breakup of the body, after death— were reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
But these worthy beings were endowed with good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind...

‘...endowed with these qualities, not reviling the noble ones, possessing right view, and undertaking actions based on right view, they—upon the breakup of the body, after death—have been reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.
Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings... [as before] ...he understands beings according to their kamma.
“Furthermore, venerable sir, when the Blessed One, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, perceives beings passing away and being reborn according to their kamma—
this too, venerable sir, is a reason I see for performing such supreme acts of homage toward the Blessed One and offering him my loving-kindness.”

"Furthermore, Bhante, the Blessed One, through the destruction of the taints, has realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, he dwells therein. Bhante,
seeing this reason for its benefit, I perform such supreme acts of reverence toward the Blessed One."
“I offer this, I present this gift of loving-kindness.
Now, venerable sir, let us depart;
we have many duties and much to do.”
“Now, Great King, you may go at whatever time you deem appropriate.
Then King Pasenadi of Kosala rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed.
The tenth [sutta].
The Third Chapter: The Mahāvagga.
Its summary (uddāna) is:
The lion’s response with the body;
Cunda and Kasiṇa;
Kāḷī and two great questions—
these two others are from the Kosala people.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.31 4. Upālivagga Upāli Sutta [The Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Then the Venerable Upāli approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how many qualities does a bhikkhu possess to be dear, agreeable, and pleasing to his fellow monks? “A bhikkhu, Upāli, possesses ten qualities to be dear, agreeable, and pleasing to his fellow monks. What ten? Here, Upāli, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in minute transgressions; having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. He has learned much, remembers what he has learned, and accumulates what he has learned.

These teachings, which are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, and which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure spiritual life—such teachings as these he has learned much of, retained in mind, recited verbally, investigated with the mind, and penetrated well through view. He is a speaker on the Dhamma, one who speaks at the right time, speaks what is factual, speaks on the goal, speaks on the Dhamma and the Vinaya; at the proper time, he speaks such words as are beneficial, reasonable, and connected to the goal. He is one who gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life. He possesses the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing that of humans; he hears both kinds of sounds, the divine and the human, those that are far as well as near. He understands with his mind the minds of other beings and persons, having encompassed them with his own mind; he understands a mind affected by lust as affected by lust, and a mind free from lust as free from lust; he understands a mind affected by hate as affected by hate, and a mind free from hate as free from hate; he understands a mind affected by delusion as affected by delusion, and a mind free from delusion as free from delusion; he understands a contracted mind as contracted, and a distracted mind as distracted; he understands an exalted mind as exalted, and an unexalted mind as unexalted; he understands a surpassed mind as surpassed, and an unsurpassed mind as unsurpassed; he understands a concentrated mind as concentrated, and an unconcentrated mind as unconcentrated; he understands a liberated mind as liberated, and an unliberated mind as unliberated. He recollects his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many eons of world-dissolution, many eons of world-evolution, and many eons of world-dissolution and evolution: ‘There I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a lifespan; passing away from there, I reappeared elsewhere; and there too I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a lifespan. Thus he recollects his manifold past lives in their modes and details. With the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, he sees beings passing away and reappearing—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma: ‘These beings who engaged in misconduct by body, speech, and mind, who reviled the noble ones, held wrong views, and undertook actions based on wrong views, with the breakup of the body, after death, have reappeared in a state of deprivation, in a bad destination, in perdition, even in hell; but these beings who engaged in good conduct by body, speech, and mind, who did not revile the noble ones, who held right views, and undertook actions based on right views, with the breakup of the body, after death, have reappeared in a good destination, in a heavenly world. Thus, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, he sees beings passing away and reappearing, and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma. He realizes for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, he dwells therein. “A bhikkhu, Upāli, possesses these ten qualities to be dear, agreeable, and pleasing to his fellow monks. When this was said, the Venerable Upāli said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir!... From today let the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”
(AN 10.31, PTS AN v 70) Then the Venerable Upāli approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Upāli said this to the Blessed One:
“For how many reasons, Bhante, has the Tathāgata laid down the training rules for his disciples and recited the Pātimokkha?”
“Upāli, it was for ten reasons that the Tathāgata prescribed the training rules and recited the Pātimokkha for his disciples.
What are the ten?
For the well-being of the Saṅgha, for the comfort of the Saṅgha, for the restraint of individuals who are difficult to manage, for the support of well-behaved bhikkhus...”
“For the sake of living in comfort, for the restraint of the taints pertaining to the present life, for the warding off of the taints pertaining to future lives,
for inspiring confidence in those without confidence, for increasing the confidence of those already confident, for the endurance of the true Dhamma,
and for supporting the discipline— it is for these ten reasons, Upāli, that the Tathāgata has prescribed the training rules for his disciples and recited the Pātimokkha.”
First.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.32.
4. Upālivagga.
The Discourse on the Suspension of the Pātimokkha (AN 10.32, PTS AN v 70):
“Venerable sir, how many grounds for the suspension of the Pātimokkha are there?”
“There are, Upāli, ten grounds for the suspension of the Pātimokkha.
Which ten?
A person who has committed a *pārājika* offense is sitting in that assembly; a discussion concerning a *pārājika* offense is underway; one who is not fully ordained is sitting in that assembly...”
He is sitting in that assembly; a discussion concerning those not yet ordained is underway and remains unfinished; a person who has renounced the training is sitting in that assembly;

a discussion concerning one who has renounced the training is underway and remains unfinished; a paṇḍaka is sitting in that assembly; a discussion concerning a paṇḍaka is underway and remains unfinished; a defiler of bhikkhunīs is sitting in that assembly...
He is seated in the assembly, and a discussion concerning a violator of nuns has been left unfinished—
Upāli, these are the ten grounds for the suspension of the Pātimokkha. This is the second [section].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.33 4.
Upālivagga Ubbāhikāsutta (The Discussion on Arbitration)
“Bhante, with how many qualities should a bhikkhu be endowed to be appointed to a committee?
“Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with ten qualities should be appointed to a committee.”
By which ten?

Here, Upāli, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains himself in the rules of training.
He is learned, a bearer of the Dhamma, a storehouse of what has been heard; those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end—
They proclaim the holy life in its entirety, perfect and pure, with its meaning and its phrasing.
Such teachings as these have been heard much by him, retained in mind, mastered verbally, examined with the mind, and well-penetrated through right view.
Furthermore, both Pātimokkhas have been properly received by him in detail, well-analyzed, well-mastered, and well-determined, both as to the rules and their specific phrasing.
Furthermore, he stands firm in the Vinaya and is unshakable;
he is capable of persuading, instructing, convincing, inspiring, and gladdening both those who support his cause and those who oppose it;
and he is skilled in the arising and the settling of legal issues.
He knows the legal issue;
he knows the origin of the legal issue;
he knows the cessation of the legal issue.
He knows the practice that leads to the cessation of legal issues.
Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with these ten qualities may be appointed to a committee.
The third [section].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.34 4.
Upālivagga Upasampadāsutta (The Discourse on Ordination)
“Venerable sir, with how many qualities should a bhikkhu be endowed to grant full ordination?
“Upāli, a bhikkhu should grant full ordination when endowed with ten qualities.”
By which ten?

Here, Upāli, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains in the rules of training.
He is learned, one who has retained what he has heard and accumulated what he has heard—those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end.
They proclaim the holy life in its entirety, perfect and pure, with its meaning and its phrasing.
Such teachings as these are well-learned by him, retained, mastered verbally, examined by the mind, and thoroughly penetrated by view.
Furthermore, the Pātimokkha has been properly received by him in detail, well-analyzed, well-proclaimed, and well-determined, both in its rules and its sub-phrasings.
He is capable of attending to the sick or having them attended to;
he is capable of dispelling dissatisfaction or having it dispelled; he is capable of removing, in accordance with the Dhamma, any remorse that has arisen.
He is capable of detaching one from a arisen speculative view by means of the Dhamma;
he is capable of exhorting one toward higher virtue;
he is capable of exhorting one toward higher mind.
“He is capable of exhorting others in higher wisdom.
Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with these ten qualities may grant full ordination.
The fourth [section].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.35 4.

Upālivagga Nissayasutta (The Discourse on Reliance) “Bhikkhus, there are these ten kinds of reliance. What ten? Reliance on the Teacher, reliance on the Dhamma, reliance on the Saṅgha, reliance on the training, reliance on concentration, reliance on energy, reliance on heedfulness, reliance on the forest, reliance on solitude, and reliance on non-contentment with regard to wholesome qualities. These, bhikkhus, are the ten kinds of reliance.”
“Venerable sir, with how many qualities should a bhikkhu be endowed to give formal support?
“Upāli, a bhikkhu should be endowed with ten qualities to give formal support.”
By which ten?
Here, Upāli, a bhikkhu is virtuous … [as above] … he trains himself in the training precepts after having undertaken them;
he is learned … [as above] … his view is well-penetrated.
Furthermore, the Pātimokkha is well-expounded to him in detail, well-analyzed, well-proclaimed, and well-determined, both in its rules and its phrasing;
he is capable of attending to the sick or having them attended to;
he is capable of dispelling dissatisfaction or having it dispelled.
He is capable of removing arisen remorse in accordance with the Dhamma;
he is capable of disentangling arisen views in accordance with the Dhamma;
he is capable [of training] in higher virtue... [and so forth].
“...to exhort [others] in higher mind ... and in higher wisdom.
Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with these ten qualities may grant formal support (nissaya).”
The Fifth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.36.
Chapter 4: The Section on Upāli.
The Discourse on the Novice (Sāmaṇerasutta):
“Venerable sir, with how many qualities should a bhikkhu be endowed to have a novice attend upon him?”
“Upāli, a monk endowed with ten qualities may have a novice attend upon him.
What are the ten?
Here, Upāli, a monk is virtuous … [as above] … having undertaken them, he trains in the rules of training.”
He is learned … [as above] … his view is well-penetrated;
moreover, the Pātimokkha has been well-learned by him in detail, well-analyzed, well-recited, and well-judged, both in terms of the rules and their specific phrasing;
he is capable of attending to the sick or of having them attended to.
He is capable of dispelling or causing the dispelling of discontent;
he is capable of removing, in accordance with the Dhamma, arisen remorse;
he is capable of disentangling, in accordance with the Dhamma, arisen views.
He is capable of exhorting others in regard to higher virtue;
he is capable of exhorting others in regard to higher mind;
he is capable of exhorting others in regard to higher wisdom.
“Upāli, a novice should be attended upon by a bhikkhu who is endowed with these ten qualities.
The sixth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.37
4. Upāli Chapter:
The Discourse on Schism in the Sangha (AN 10.37, PTS AN v 73)
“‘Schism in the Saṅgha, schism in the Saṅgha,’ it is said, Bhante.
To what extent, Bhante, is the Saṅgha split?
“In this case, Upāli, monks represent what is not Dhamma as Dhamma, and they represent what is Dhamma as not Dhamma; they represent what is not Vinaya as...”

They proclaim what is discipline as non-discipline; they proclaim non-discipline as discipline; they proclaim what was not spoken nor uttered by the Tathāgata as having been spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata;
they proclaim what was spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata as not having been spoken nor uttered by the Tathāgata;
they proclaim what was not practiced by the Tathāgata as having been practiced by the Tathāgata; [and] what was practiced by the Tathāgata...
They proclaim what has not been practiced by the Tathāgata as having been practiced by him; they proclaim what was not laid down by the Tathāgata as having been laid down by him;
and they proclaim what was laid down by the Tathāgata as not having been laid down by him.
On account of these ten grounds, they exclude one another, they alienate one another, they perform formal acts separately, and they recite the Pātimokkha separately.
"To this extent, Upāli, the Saṅgha is split.
(The seventh. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.38
4. Upāli Chapter:
Discourse on Concord in the Sangha (Saṅghasāmaggīsutta) (AN 10.38, PTS AN v 74)
“Venerable sir, it is said: ‘Harmony in the Saṅgha, harmony in the Saṅgha.
To what extent, venerable sir, is the Saṅgha harmonious?

“Here, Upāli, monks point out what is non-Dhamma as non-Dhamma, and they point out what is Dhamma as Dhamma; they point out what is non-Vinaya as non-Vinaya, and they point out what is Vinaya as Vinaya.”
They proclaim what is non-discipline as discipline; they proclaim discipline as non-discipline;

they proclaim what was not spoken nor uttered by the Tathāgata as "not spoken nor uttered by the Tathāgata"; they proclaim what was spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata as "spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata";
they proclaim what was not practiced by the Tathāgata as "not practiced by the Tathāgata"; [and they proclaim] what was practiced by the Tathāgata...
They proclaim what has been practiced by the Tathāgata as such; they proclaim what was not laid down by the Tathāgata as "not laid down by the Tathāgata";
and they proclaim what was laid down by the Tathāgata as "laid down by the Tathāgata.
On account of these ten grounds, they do not withdraw, they do not depart, they do not perform formal acts separately, and they do not recite the Pātimokkha separately.
"To this extent, Upāli, the Saṅgha is harmonious.
(The eighth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.39
4. Upāli Chapter First Discourse to Ānanda (AN 10.39, PTS AN v 75)

Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“‘Schism in the Saṅgha, schism in the Saṅgha,’ it is said, Bhante.
To what extent, Bhante, is the Saṅgha considered split?”
“Here, Ānanda, monks represent what is non-Dhamma as Dhamma, and what is Dhamma as non-Dhamma; they represent what is non-Vinaya as Vinaya, and what is Vinaya as non-Vinaya...
they represent what was laid down by the Tathāgata as not laid down by the Tathāgata.
On these ten grounds, they draw away and pull apart, performing legal acts separately and reciting the Pātimokkha separately.”
"To this extent, Ānanda, the Saṅgha is split.
"But, Bhante, having split a harmonious Saṅgha, what does he produce?
"He produces an evil that lasts for an eon, Ānanda."
“But what, Bhante, is a transgression that lasts for an eon?
“Ānanda, it is one that ‘cooks in hell for an eon’—
one who is bound for the state of loss, bound for hell.”
One who causes a schism in the Saṅgha remains in the world for an eon;
delighting in factions and established in what is not Dhamma,
he falls away from security from bondage.
Having split a harmonious Saṅgha,
one roasts in hell for an eon.
Thus ends the ninth [verse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.40 4. Upālivagga Dutiya-Ānandasutta (The Second Discourse to Ānanda) At Sāvatthī. There, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these ten qualities of one who has entered the stream, who is no longer subject to perdition, who is firmly established, and who has gained assurance in regard to enlightenment. What ten? (1) Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One. (2) He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. (3) He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. (4) He possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones, unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. (5) He is devoid of anger and resentment; he is devoid of denigration and insolence; he is devoid of envy and avarice; he is devoid of deceit and fraud; he is devoid of hypocrisy and stubbornness; he is devoid of evil desire and wrong view. (6) He is one who has abandoned the five lower fetters.

(7) He is one who has abandoned the five hindrances, those corruptions of the mind that weaken wisdom. (8) He is one who dwells with a mind that has transcended the world. (9) He is one who has understood the nature of things as they really are. (10) He is one who has attained the destruction of the taints. These, bhikkhus, are the ten qualities of one who has entered the stream, who is no longer subject to perdition, who is firmly established, and who has gained assurance in regard to enlightenment. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s words. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “Ānanda, if you were to abandon these ten states, it would lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time. What ten? (1) Abandon covetousness. (2) Abandon ill will. (3) Abandon sloth and torpor. (4) Abandon restlessness and remorse. (5) Abandon doubt. (6) Abandon anger and resentment. (7) Abandon denigration and insolence. (8) Abandon envy and avarice. (9) Abandon deceit and fraud. (10) Abandon hypocrisy and stubbornness. If you were to abandon these ten states, Ānanda, it would lead to your welfare and happiness for a long time. “But, venerable sir, how should I act when I encounter people who are hostile and unfriendly? “Ānanda, when you encounter people who are hostile and unfriendly, you should act with loving-kindness through body, speech, and mind. This is how you should act when you encounter people who are hostile and unfriendly. “But, venerable sir, how should I act when I encounter people who are friendly and helpful? “Ānanda, when you encounter people who are friendly and helpful, you should act with compassion through body, speech, and mind. This is how you should act when you encounter people who are friendly and helpful. “But, venerable sir, how should I act when I encounter people who are both hostile and unfriendly, yet also friendly and helpful? “Ānanda, when you encounter people who are both hostile and unfriendly, yet also friendly and helpful, you should examine them carefully. Having examined them carefully, you should act with equanimity through body, speech, and mind. This is how you should act when you encounter people who are both hostile and unfriendly, yet also friendly and helpful. “But, venerable sir, how should I act when I encounter people who are neither hostile and unfriendly nor friendly and helpful? “Ānanda, when you encounter people who are neither hostile and unfriendly nor friendly and helpful, you should act with mindfulness and clear comprehension. This is how you should act when you encounter people who are neither hostile and unfriendly nor friendly and helpful. “But, venerable sir, how should I act when I encounter people who are heedless? “Ānanda, when you encounter people who are heedless, you should act with heedfulness through body, speech, and mind. This is how you should act when you encounter people who are heedless. “But, venerable sir, how should I act when I encounter people who are heedful? “Ānanda, when you encounter people who are heedful, you should act with even greater heedfulness through body, speech, and mind. This is how you should act when you encounter people who are heedful. “But, venerable sir, how should I act when I encounter people who are both heedless and heedful? “Ānanda, when you encounter people who are both heedless and heedful, you should examine them carefully. Having examined them carefully, you should act with equanimity through body, speech, and mind. This is how you should act when you encounter people who are both heedless and heedful. “But, venerable sir, how should I act when I encounter people who are neither heedless nor heedful? “Ānanda, when you encounter people who are neither heedless nor heedful, you should act with mindfulness and clear comprehension. This is how you should act when you encounter people who are neither heedless nor heedful. “But, venerable sir, how should I act when I encounter people who are full of lust? “Ānanda, when you encounter people who are full of lust, you should act with the perception of foulness through body, speech, and mind. This is how you should act when you encounter people who are full of lust. “But, venerable sir, how should I act when I encounter people who are free from lust? “Ānanda, when you encounter people who are free from lust, you should act with the perception of peace through body, speech, and mind. This is how you should act when you encounter people who are free from lust. “But, venerable sir, how should I act when I encounter people who are both full of lust and free from lust? “Ānanda, when you encounter people who are both full of lust and free from lust, you should examine them carefully. Having examined them carefully, you should act with equanimity through body, speech, and mind. This is how you should act when you encounter people who are both full of lust and free from lust. “But, venerable sir, how should I act when I encounter people who are neither full of lust nor free from lust? “Ānanda, when you encounter people who are neither full of lust nor free from lust, you should act with mindfulness and clear comprehension. This is how you should act when you encounter people who are neither full of lust nor free from lust. “But, venerable sir, how should I act when I encounter people who are angry? “Ānanda, when you encounter people who are angry, you should act with loving-kindness through body, speech, and mind. This is how you should act when you encounter people who are angry. “But, venerable sir, how should I act when I encounter people who are not angry? “Ānanda, when you encounter people who are not angry, you should act with compassion through body, speech, and mind. This is how you should act when you encounter people who are not angry. “But, venerable sir, how should I act when I encounter people who are both angry and not angry? “Ānanda, when you encounter people who are both angry and not angry, you should examine them carefully. Having examined them
“Venerable sir, it is said: ‘Harmony in the Saṅgha, harmony in the Saṅgha.
To what extent, venerable sir, is the Saṅgha harmonious?”
“Here, Ānanda, monks point out what is not Dhamma as ‘not Dhamma,’ and they point out the Dhamma as ‘Dhamma.
They point out what is not Vinaya as ‘not Vinaya,’ and they point out the Vinaya as ‘Vinaya.

They point out what was neither spoken nor uttered by the Tathāgata as ‘neither spoken nor uttered by the Tathāgata,’ and they point out what was spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata as ‘spoken and uttered by the Tathāgata.’”

They proclaim what was not practiced by the Tathāgata as "not practiced by the Tathāgata," they proclaim what was practiced by the Tathāgata as "practiced by the Tathāgata," they proclaim what was not laid down by the Tathāgata as "not laid down by the Tathāgata," and they proclaim what was laid down by the Tathāgata as "laid down by the Tathāgata."
“By these ten bases, Ānanda, they do not draw away, they do not pull apart, they do not perform legal acts separately, and they do not recite the Pātimokkha separately.
To this extent, Ānanda, the Saṅgha is united.
“But, Bhante, having reunited a divided Saṅgha, what does one produce?”
“Ānanda, it produces Brahmā-like merit.
“But what, Bhante, is Brahmā-like merit?
“It is this, Ānanda: ‘One rejoices in heaven for an eon.’”
Happy is concord in the Saṅgha,
and the assistance of those who are in concord;
one who delights in concord and is established in the Dhamma—
He does not fall away from the security of yoga;
having made the Saṅgha harmonious,
he rejoices in heaven for an eon.
The tenth.
The fourth chapter, the Upāli-vagga.
Its summary (uddāna):
Upāli, the setting aside [of the Saṅgha],
the formal accusation, full ordination,
dependence, the novice, and the two divisions.
"Delight in others' welfare.
— Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.41, Chapter 5: On Abuse.
Vivādasutta (AN 10.41).

Then the Venerable Upāli approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Upāli said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason, why quarrels, disputes, strife, and contention arise in the Saṅgha, and why the bhikkhus do not dwell in comfort?
“Here, Upāli, bhikkhus proclaim what is non-Dhamma as Dhamma, and they proclaim what is Dhamma as non-Dhamma;

they proclaim what is non-discipline as discipline, and they proclaim what is discipline as non-discipline; they proclaim what has not been spoken or uttered by the Tathāgata as having been spoken by him...”
They proclaim what was spoken by the Tathāgata as not spoken by the Tathāgata; they proclaim what was uttered by the Tathāgata as unuttered and unsaid by the Tathāgata;
they proclaim what was not practiced by the Tathāgata as practiced by the Tathāgata;
they proclaim what was practiced by the Tathāgata as not practiced by the Tathāgata; they proclaim what was not laid down by the Tathāgata as laid down by the Tathāgata.
“They proclaim what has been laid down by the Tathāgata as not having been laid down by the Tathāgata.

This, Upāli, is the cause, this is the reason why disputes, quarrels, strife, and contention arise in the Saṅgha, and because of which the bhikkhus do not dwell in comfort. Thus ends the first [section].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.42 5. Akkosavagga Paṭhamavivādamūlasutta (The First Discourse on the Root of Dispute) “Monks, there are these ten roots of dispute. What ten? (1) Here, monks, a monk is angry and bears ill will; he disputes with his fellow monks, saying: ‘You do not understand this Dhamma and Discipline. I understand this Dhamma and Discipline. What, you understand this Dhamma and Discipline? You practice wrongly; I practice rightly. What has been said by the Blessed One out of malice, that was not said by the Blessed One;

what has not been said by the Blessed One, that was said by the Blessed One; what has been said by the Blessed One, that is not so; what has not been said by the Blessed One, that is so. This, monks, is the first root of dispute. (2) Again, monks, a monk is insolent and arrogant; he disputes with his fellow monks... [as above] ...This, monks, is the second root of dispute. (3) Again, monks, a monk is envious and stingy; he disputes with his fellow monks... [as above] ...This, monks, is the third root of dispute. (4) Again, monks, a monk is deceitful and fraudulent; he disputes with his fellow monks... [as above] ...This, monks, is the fourth root of dispute. (5) Again, monks, a monk is obstinate and stubborn; he disputes with his fellow monks... [as above] ...This, monks, is the fifth root of dispute. (6) Again, monks, a monk holds wrong view and possesses perverse perspective; he disputes with his fellow monks... [as above] ...This, monks, is the sixth root of dispute. (7) Again, monks, a monk, having fallen into a dispute, clings to it and does not let go; he disputes with his fellow monks... [as above] ...This, monks, is the seventh root of dispute. (8) Again, monks, a monk, having fallen into a dispute, speaks in praise of it and does not let go; he disputes with his fellow monks... [as above] ...This, monks, is the eighth root of dispute. (9) Again, monks, a monk, having fallen into a dispute, speaks in dispraise of those who oppose him and does not let go; he disputes with his fellow monks... [as above] ...This, monks, is the ninth root of dispute. (10) Again, monks, a monk, having fallen into a dispute, speaks in dispraise of himself and does not let go; he disputes with his fellow monks, saying: ‘You do not understand this Dhamma and Discipline. I understand this Dhamma and Discipline. What, you understand this Dhamma and Discipline? You practice wrongly; I practice rightly. What has been said by the Blessed One out of malice, that was not said by the Blessed One; what has not been said by the Blessed One, that was said by the Blessed One; what has been said by the Blessed One, that is not so; what has not been said by the Blessed One, that is so. This, monks, is the tenth root of dispute. These, monks, are the ten roots of dispute.”
“Venerable sir, how many roots of dispute are there?
“Upāli, there are ten roots of dispute.”
Which ten?
Here, Upāli, monks proclaim what is non-Dhamma as Dhamma, they proclaim what is Dhamma as non-Dhamma;

they proclaim what is non-discipline as discipline, they proclaim what is discipline as non-discipline; they proclaim what was neither spoken nor uttered by the Tathāgata as having been spoken by him...
They proclaim what was spoken by the Tathāgata as not spoken by the Tathāgata; they proclaim what was uttered by the Tathāgata as unuttered and unsaid by the Tathāgata;
they proclaim what was not practiced by the Tathāgata as practiced by the Tathāgata;
they proclaim what was practiced by the Tathāgata as not practiced by the Tathāgata; they proclaim what was not laid down by the Tathāgata as laid down by the Tathāgata.
They proclaim what has been laid down by the Tathāgata as not having been laid down by the Tathāgata, and what has not been laid down by the Tathāgata as having been laid down by the Tathāgata.
These, Upāli, are the ten roots of dispute. This is the second [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.43 5.

Akkosavagga The Second Discourse on the Root of Dispute “Bhikkhus, there are these ten roots of dispute. What ten? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is angry and bears ill will; he is divisive and seeks to cause division; he speaks harshly and is a speaker of what is untrue; he is covetous and has a mind of ill will; he holds wrong view and has a distorted perspective. These, bhikkhus, are the ten roots of dispute.”
“Venerable sir, how many roots of dispute are there?
“There are ten roots of dispute, Upāli.”
Which ten?
Here, Upāli, monks explain what is not an offense as an offense; they explain what is an offense as not an offense;
they explain a light offense as a heavy offense; they explain a heavy offense as a light offense; [they explain] a grave offense...
They represent a non-gross offense as a gross offense; they represent a gross offense as a non-gross offense;
they represent a curable offense as an incurable offense; they represent an incurable offense as a curable offense;
they represent an offense that can be remedied as an offense that cannot be remedied; and they represent an offense that cannot be remedied as an offense that can be remedied.
“Upāli, these indeed are the ten roots of dispute.
The third [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.44.

5. Akkosavagga: Kusinārasutta (AN 10.44, PTS AN v 79) At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was staying at Kusinārā in Upavattana, the sal-tree grove of the Mallas. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘the end of the world, the end of the world. In what way, venerable sir, might one describe the end of the world? “Ānanda, it is by means of the four great elements—the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element—that this body is constructed and fabricated. But when one is liberated from these four great elements, one is no longer reckoned by name or clan; one is a sage at peace, unreckonable by anything in the world. “But, venerable sir, where do these four great elements cease without remainder? “When, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is liberated through the destruction of craving, he has transcended this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans; he has reached the goal, lived the holy life, done what was to be done, and there is nothing further beyond this. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, venerable sir, it is marvelous! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘When, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is liberated through the destruction of craving, he has transcended this world... and there is nothing further beyond this. And have you heard, Ānanda, which of my disciples among the female lay followers are foremost in exhortation? “I have heard, venerable sir, that the female lay follower Khujjuttarā is foremost among the Blessed One’s disciples among the female lay followers in exhortation.

On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Kusinārā in the Baliharaṇa Grove.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who wishes to reprove another should first examine five qualities within himself and establish five qualities within himself before reproving the other.”
What five things should be examined within oneself?
Monks, a monk who wishes to reprove another should examine himself thus:
"Am I pure in my bodily conduct? Am I endowed with pure bodily conduct that is flawless and irreproachable?"
"Does this quality exist in me, or does it not?
If, monks, a monk is not pure in his bodily conduct, and is not endowed with pure bodily conduct that is flawless and untarnished, there will be those who say of him:
"Come now, let the venerable one train in bodily conduct. Such will be the reproachers of him.
Furthermore, monks, a monk who wishes to reprove another should reflect thus:
‘Am I pure in my verbal conduct? Am I endowed with verbal conduct that is pure, flawless, and irreproachable?
Is this quality found in me, or is it not?’
“Monks, if a monk is not pure in his verbal conduct, and does not possess verbal conduct that is pure, flawless, and irreproachable, there will be those who say of him:
‘Come now, let the venerable one train in speech. Such will be the reproachers of him.
Furthermore, monks, when a monk who is a reproacher desires to reproach another, he should reflect thus:”
‘Is my mind established in loving-kindness toward my fellow practitioners of the holy life, free from ill will?
Does this quality exist in me or not?
If, monks, a monk’s mind is not established in loving-kindness toward his fellow practitioners of the holy life, free from ill will, there will be those who say of him:
‘Come now, venerable sir, establish a mind of loving-kindness toward your fellow practitioners in the holy life’—thus will there be those who speak to him.
Furthermore, monks, a monk who wishes to reprove another should reflect thus:
‘Am I learned, a retainer of what has been heard, and one who has accumulated what has been heard? Are those teachings which are beautiful in the beginning, beautiful in the middle, and...’
They proclaim the holy life that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, entirely complete and pure;
such teachings have been heard much by me, retained in mind, mastered verbally,
examined by the intellect, and well-penetrated by view.
“Does this Dhamma exist within me,
or does it not? If, monks, a monk is not learned, does not retain what he has heard, and does not accumulate what he has heard— those teachings which are good in the beginning,
good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, utterly perfect and pure— then [he does not know].
They praise the holy life; such teachings as these have been heard much by him, retained, mastered verbally, examined with the mind, and well-penetrated by view. There are those who say of him:
"Come now, let the venerable one master the tradition," and there are those who speak thus to him.
Furthermore, monks, a monk who wishes to reprove another should reflect thus:
‘Are both Pātimokkhas well-learned by me in detail, well-analyzed, well-mastered, and well-determined, both as to the rules and their sub-clauses?
Does this quality exist in me or not?’”
If, monks, a bhikkhu has not properly learned both Pātimokkhas in detail, nor has he analyzed them well,
mastered them well, and investigated them well, both in terms of the rules and their detailed exposition, then when asked, "Where was this said by the Blessed One, venerable sir?
he will not be able to provide an answer.
There will be those who say to him:
"Come now, let the venerable one train in the Vinaya. Such will be those who speak to him.
These five qualities should be examined within oneself.
Which five qualities should be established within oneself?
"I shall speak at the proper time, not at an improper time;
I shall speak what is true, not what is untrue."
‘I will speak gently, not harshly;
I will speak in accordance with what is beneficial, not in accordance with what is harmful;
I will speak with a mind of loving-kindness, not with inner hatred.’”
"These five qualities should be established within oneself.
Monks, a monk who wishes to reprove another should first examine these five qualities within himself and establish these five qualities within himself before reproving the other.
This is the fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.45 5.

Akkosavagga Rājantepurappavesanasutta (The Discourse on Entering the King’s Inner Palace) “Bhikkhus, there are these ten qualities of one who enters the king’s inner palace. What ten? (1) He is well-born; (2) he is handsome; (3) he is eloquent; (4) he is a skilled speaker; (5) he speaks at the right time; (6) he speaks what is true; (7) he speaks what is beneficial; (8) he speaks with a mind of loving-kindness; (9) he does not speak in a way that leads to his own harm; (10) he does not speak in a way that leads to the harm of others. These, bhikkhus, are the ten qualities of one who enters the king’s inner palace.”
“Monks, there are these ten dangers in entering a king’s inner palace.
What are the ten?
In this case, monks, a king is sitting together with his chief queen.
A monk enters there.
Either the chief queen, upon seeing the monk, displays a smile, or the monk, upon seeing the chief queen, displays a smile.
In that regard, it occurs to the king:
‘Surely they have done something, or they will do something.
This, monks, is the first danger in entering the royal inner quarters.
Furthermore, monks, a king who has many duties and many responsibilities, having approached a certain woman, does not remember:
"She conceived a child by him.
Then it occurs to the king:
‘No one else enters here except for one who has gone forth.
Could there be some offense for one who has gone forth?
This, monks, is the second danger in entering a royal palace.
Furthermore, monks, suppose some treasure is lost in a king’s inner palace.
Then it occurs to the king:
‘No one else enters here except for a renunciant.’
"Could there not be work for one who has gone forth?
This, monks, is the third danger in entering a king’s inner palace.
Furthermore, monks, secret counsels within a king’s inner palace leak out to the outside.
Thereupon, it occurs to the king:
“No one else enters here except for one who has gone forth into homelessness.
Could this be the work of one who has gone forth?”
This, monks, is the fourth danger in entering a king’s inner palace.
Furthermore, monks, in a king’s inner palace, either the father longs for the son or the son longs for the father.
It occurs to them thus:
‘No one else enters here except for one who has gone forth into homelessness.
Could there perhaps be some offense for one who has gone forth?
This, monks, is the fifth danger in entering a royal palace.
Furthermore, monks, a king appoints one of low status to a high position.
Those who find this displeasing think:
"The king is indeed associating with a renunciant."
"Could there not be work for one who has gone forth?
This, monks, is the sixth danger in entering a king's inner palace.
Furthermore, monks, a king may appoint someone of high status to a low position.
Those for whom this was unpleasant thought:
"The king is indeed associating with one who has gone forth.
Could this be a transgression for the one who has gone forth?"
This, monks, is the seventh danger in entering a king’s inner palace.
Furthermore, monks, a king may dispatch his army at an improper time.
Those for whom this is unpleasant think thus:
“The king is indeed closely associated with one who has gone forth.
Could this not lead to trouble for the one who has gone forth?
This, monks, is the eighth danger in entering a royal palace.
Furthermore, monks, after a king has dispatched his army at the proper time, he may turn it back from midway on the road.
Those who find this disagreeable think:
“The king is indeed associating with one who has gone forth.”
"Could there not be work for one who has gone forth?
This, monks, is the ninth disadvantage in entering a king’s inner palace.

Furthermore, monks, the king’s inner palace is crowded with elephants, crowded with horses, and crowded with chariots; it contains alluring forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tactile objects, which are not suitable for one who has gone forth.
“Monks, this is the tenth danger in entering a royal palace.
These, monks, are the ten dangers in entering a royal palace.
Thus was the fifth [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.46 5. Akkosavagga Sakkasutta Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then Sakka, lord of the devas, approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him: “Sakka, when a person possesses ten qualities, he is deposited in heaven as if brought there. What ten? Here, Sakka, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One. “He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. “He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. “He is virtuous; he possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones, unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. “He is learned, possessing the Dhamma; he has retained the Dhamma he learned from the Teacher or his disciples in mind; these teachings, learned and retained in mind, are well-penetrated by view. “He is content with any kind of robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites.

“He dwells with energy aroused for abandoning unwholesome qualities and acquiring wholesome qualities; he is strong, firm in exertion, not casting off the duty of cultivating wholesome qualities. “He is a speaker on the Dhamma, one who speaks at the right time, speaks what is factual, speaks on the Dhamma, speaks on the discipline; at the right time he speaks such words as are connected with the goal, reasonable, succinct, and definitive. “He is one who gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life. “He possesses the wisdom of arising and passing away which is noble and penetrative and leads to the complete destruction of suffering. “When a person possesses these ten qualities, Sakka, he is deposited in heaven as if brought there. When this was said, Sakka, lord of the devas, said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! The Blessed One has made the Dhamma clear in many ways, as though he were turning upright what had been overturned, revealing what was hidden, showing the way to one who was lost, or holding up a lamp in the darkness so those with eyes might see forms. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life shall last. Then Sakka, lord of the devas, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, paid homage to him, circumambulated him keeping the right side toward him, and vanished right there. Not long after Sakka had gone, a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to him: “Venerable sir, who was that being who just now approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and then vanished right there? “That was Sakka, lord of the devas, bhikkhu,” the Blessed One replied. “Sakka, lord of the devas, has developed these ten qualities, and because he has done so, he dwells in the deva world enjoying sovereignty over the devas. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But, venerable sir, how has Sakka, lord of the devas, developed these ten qualities, and because he has done so, does he dwell in the deva world enjoying sovereignty over the devas? “Here, bhikkhu, Sakka possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha... [as above] ...he possesses the wisdom of arising and passing away which is noble and penetrative and leads to the complete destruction of suffering. It is in this way, bhikkhu, that Sakka, lord of the devas, has developed these ten qualities, and because he has done so, he dwells in the deva world enjoying sovereignty over the devas. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is amazing how the Blessed One has made the Dhamma clear in many ways, as though he were turning upright what had been overturned, revealing what was hidden, showing the way to one who was lost, or holding up a lamp in the darkness so those with eyes might see forms. Venerable sir, Sakka, lord of the devas, has indeed developed these ten qualities, and because he has done so, he dwells in the deva world enjoying sovereignty over the devas. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, that bhikkhu delighted in the Blessed One’s words. Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then Sakka, lord of the devas, approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to him: “Sakka, when a person possesses ten qualities, he is deposited in hell as if brought there. What ten? Here, Sakka, a noble disciple does not possess confirmed confidence in the Buddha... [as above] ...he is not a speaker on the Dhamma... he does not gain at will the four jhānas... he does not possess the wisdom of arising and passing away which is noble and penetrative and leads to the complete destruction of suffering.
