(AN 10.46, PTS AN v 83) On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Nigrodha Park.
Then, on that very Uposatha day, a number of Sakyan lay followers approached the Blessed One; having approached, they...
Having paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. As the lay followers of Sakka were sitting there, the Blessed One said this to them:
“Sakka, do you observe the Uposatha complete with the eight factors?
“Sometimes, Bhante, we observe the Uposatha complete with the eight factors; sometimes we do not.”

“It is a misfortune for you, Sakyans, it is a great loss for you, that while living in this life fraught with sorrow and living in this life fraught with death, you sometimes observe the uposatha complete in eight factors and sometimes do not observe it.
What do you think, Sakyans?
Suppose here a man, without committing any unwholesome deed by way of any occupation, were to earn half a kahāpaṇa every day.”
“Is it enough to say that a man who is skillful and endowed with diligence?”—
“Yes, venerable sir.”—
“What do you think, Sakyans?”
“Suppose, here, a man were to earn a kahāpaṇa coin every day without committing any unwholesome deed by means of some work.
Would it be appropriate to say that he is a clever man endowed with initiative?”—
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“What do you think, Sakyans?
Suppose here a man, by means of some meditation subject, were to earn two kahāpaṇas a day without doing anything unwholesome… were to earn three kahāpaṇas a day….”
He would pay out four kahāpaṇas...
he would pay out five kahāpaṇas...
he would pay out six kahāpaṇas...
He would pay out seven kahāpaṇas ...
he would pay out eight kahāpaṇas ...
he would pay out nine kahāpaṇas ...
He should pay ten kahāpaṇas as a fine;
he should pay twenty kahāpaṇas as a fine;
he should pay thirty kahāpaṇas as a fine.
He would pay out forty kahāpaṇas...
he would pay out fifty kahāpaṇas...
he would pay out a hundred kahāpaṇas.
“‘A man who is skillful and endowed with initiative’—is this sufficient as a description?
“Yes, venerable sir.
“What do you think, Sakyans?”

“Would that man, receiving a hundred or a thousand *kahāpaṇas* every day and setting aside each amount as he received it, acquire a great mass of wealth if he were to live for a hundred years and have a lifespan of a hundred years?
“Yes, venerable sir.
“What do you think, Sakkā?”

“Would that man, for the sake of wealth, on account of wealth, and with wealth as his basis, dwell experiencing absolute happiness for one night, or for one day, or for half a night, or for half a day?
“Certainly not, venerable sir. “And why is that?”
“Sensual pleasures, venerable sir, are indeed impermanent, empty, false,
and subject to deception. “But here, Sakyans, my disciple who dwells for ten years diligent,
ardent, and resolute, practicing according to my instructions, might [attain] even a hundred years, a hundred times a hundred years, or a hundred times a thousand years…”
He would dwell experiencing absolute happiness for thousands of years.
And he would be either a once-returner, a non-returner, or at least a stream-enterer with certainty.
Let alone ten years, Sakka.
In this case, my disciple [has practiced] for nine years...
eight years...
seven years...
Six years … five years … four years …
Dwelling diligent, ardent, and resolute for three years… two years… one year, practicing according to my instructions...
One might dwell experiencing exclusively happiness for a hundred years, or a hundred thousand years, or even a hundred thousand times a hundred thousand years;
yet such a person would be either a once-returner, a non-returner, or at least one who has entered the stream with certainty.
Let alone one year, Sakkā.
In this case, my disciple, dwelling for ten months diligent, ardent, and resolute, practicing according to my instructions,
might dwell experiencing exclusive happiness for a hundred years, a hundred centuries, or even a hundred thousand years;
yet he would be either a once-returner, a non-returner, or at least one who has entered the stream with certainty.
"Let alone ten months, Sakyans;
here my disciple [remains] for nine months...
eight months..."
Seven months...
six months...
five months...
four months … three months … two months …
Dwelling diligently, ardent, and resolute for one month… or half a month, practicing according to my instructions,
he will experience absolute happiness for a hundred years, a hundred times a hundred years, or even a hundred times a thousand years.
He would dwell [in this way], and he would surely be either a once-returner, a non-returner, or at least a stream-enterer with certainty.
Let alone half a month, Sakka, here my disciple,
dwelling for ten days and nights diligent, ardent, and resolute, according to my instruction—
Practicing in such a way, he might dwell for a hundred years, a hundred thousand years, or even a million years experiencing exclusively happiness;
and he would indeed be either a once-returner, a non-returner, or at least one who has entered the stream with certainty.
Let alone ten days and nights, Sakkā.
Here, my disciple, in nine days and nights...
in eight days and nights...
in seven days and nights...
Six days and nights...
five days and nights...
four days and nights...
Dwelling diligently, ardent, and resolute for three days and nights… for two days and nights… for one day and night, practicing according to my instruction, he will—
“Even if one were to dwell for a hundred years, a hundred hundred years, or a hundred thousand years experiencing nothing but absolute happiness,
yet if that person were a once-returner, a non-returner, or at least a stream-enterer with certainty—

then for you, Sakyans, it is a loss, it is a misfortune, that while living in this life fraught with sorrow and this life fraught with death, you only occasionally observe the Uposatha complete in its eight factors, and do not observe it at other times.”
“Venerable sir, from this day forward, we shall observe the Uposatha complete with these eight factors.
This is the sixth [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.47
5. Akkosavagga Mahālisutta (AN 10.47, PTS AN v 86)
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Gabled Hall.

Then Mahāli the Licchavi approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Mahāli the Licchavi said this to the Blessed One:
“What, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the reason for the performance of evil kamma, for the undertaking of evil kamma?”
“Greed, Mahāli, is the cause, greed is the condition for the performance of evil karma, for the occurrence of evil karma.
Hatred, Mahāli, is the cause, hatred is the condition for the performance of evil karma, for the occurrence of evil karma.
Delusion, Mahāli, is the cause, delusion is the condition for the performance of evil karma, for the occurrence of evil karma.”
“Improper attention, Mahāli, is the cause, improper attention is the condition for the performance of evil kamma, for the occurrence of evil kamma.
A mind directed wrongly, Mahāli, is the cause, a mind directed wrongly is the condition for the performance of evil kamma, for the occurrence of evil kamma.
This, Mahāli, is the cause, this is the condition for the performance of evil kamma, for the occurrence of evil kamma.”
“But what, Bhante, is the cause, what is the condition for the performance of wholesome kamma, for the occurrence of wholesome kamma?
“Non-greed, Mahāli, is the cause, non-greed is the condition for the performance of wholesome kamma, for the occurrence of wholesome kamma.
Non-hatred, Mahāli, is the cause, non-hatred is the condition for the performance of wholesome kamma, for the occurrence of wholesome kamma.”
Non-delusion, Mahāli, is the cause, non-delusion is the condition for the performance of wholesome kamma, for the occurrence of wholesome kamma.
Wise attention, Mahāli, is the cause, wise attention is the condition for the performance of wholesome kamma, for the occurrence of wholesome kamma.
A rightly directed mind, Mahāli, is the cause, a rightly directed mind is the condition for the performance of wholesome kamma, for the occurrence of wholesome kamma.
“This, Mahāli, is the cause, this is the condition for the performance of wholesome kamma, for the occurrence of wholesome kamma.

And, Mahāli, if these ten things did not exist in the world, neither misconduct nor right conduct would be discerned here—neither unrighteous conduct and uneven conduct, nor righteous conduct and even conduct.

But because, Mahāli, these ten things do exist in the world, therefore misconduct and right conduct are discerned—unrighteous conduct and uneven conduct, as well as righteous conduct and even conduct.”
The Seventh. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.48 5.
Akkosavagga (The Chapter on Abuse)
The Discourse on the Frequent Reflections of One Who Has Gone Forth (Pabbajitābhiṇhasutta):
“Monks, these ten things should be frequently reflected upon by one who has gone forth.”
Which ten?
“I have entered upon a state of disfigurement”—this should be frequently reflected upon by one who has gone forth.
“My livelihood is dependent on others”—this should be frequently reflected upon by one who has gone forth.
‘Another mode of conduct must be practiced by me,’ this should be frequently reflected upon by one who has gone forth.
‘Does my own self not reproach me for my virtue? this should be frequently reflected upon by one who has gone forth.
‘Do wise companions in the holy life, having investigated me, not reproach me for my virtue? this should be frequently reflected upon by one who has gone forth.
‘I shall be separated and parted from all that is dear and beloved’—this should be frequently reflected upon by one who has gone forth.
‘I am the owner of my karma, the heir of my karma, born of my karma, related to my karma, and have my karma as my refuge;
whatever karma I shall do, whether good or evil, of that I will be the heir’—this should be frequently reflected upon by one who has gone forth.
‘How are my days and nights passing?’—this is what one who has gone forth should frequently reflect upon.
‘Do I indeed take delight in empty huts?’—this is what one who has gone forth should frequently reflect upon.
‘Have I attained any superhuman state, a distinction in noble knowledge and vision, by means of which I [might...’]
‘In the final period, when questioned by my fellow celibates, I shall not be ashamed’—this is what one who has gone forth should frequently reflect upon.
“Monks, these ten things are what one who has gone forth should frequently reflect upon.
The eighth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.49 5. Akkosavagga Sarīraṭṭhadhammasutta “Monks, there are these ten qualities of one who is dear, beloved, and cherished by their fellows in the holy life. What ten? Here, monks, a monk is virtuous;

he dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest transgressions, and having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. This is the first quality of one who is dear, beloved, and cherished by their fellows in the holy life. Furthermore, monks, a monk has learned much, remembers what he has heard, and accumulates what he has learned. These teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure spiritual life—such teachings he has learned much of, retained in mind, recited verbally, mentally examined, and penetrated well by view. This is the second quality... Furthermore, monks, a monk is a speaker on the Dhamma; he speaks at the right time, speaks what is true, speaks what is beneficial, speaks on the Dhamma and the Vinaya; at the right time he utters speech that is worth treasuring. This is the third quality... Furthermore, monks, a monk is one who encourages, inspires, and emboldens his fellows in the holy life when they are despondent. This is the fourth quality... Furthermore, monks, a monk is one who does not seek out the faults of others, nor does he speak of them. This is the fifth quality... Furthermore, monks, a monk is one who does not conceal his own faults, but reveals them. This is the sixth quality... Furthermore, monks, a monk is one who is patient, enduring, and possesses a long-suffering temperament. This is the seventh quality... Furthermore, monks, a monk is one who is easy to correct and accepts instruction respectfully. This is the eighth quality... Furthermore, monks, a monk is one who has few desires. This is the ninth quality... Furthermore, monks, a monk is one who is contented. This is the tenth quality of one who is dear, beloved, and cherished by their fellows in the holy life. These, monks, are the ten qualities of one who is dear, beloved, and cherished by their fellows in the holy life.”
“Monks, there are these ten things that are beneficial to the body.
What are the ten?
Cold, heat, hunger, thirst, excrement, urine, restraint of body, restraint of speech, restraint of livelihood, and the volitional formation of existence leading to renewed becoming—
these, monks, are the ten things that belong to the physical body. Thus ends the ninth [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.50 5. Akkosavagga Bhaṇḍanasutta (The Discourse on Quarreling) “Monks, there are these ten qualities of one who quarrels. What ten? (1) He is angry and bears malice; (2) he is envious and stingy; (3) he is crafty and deceitful; (4) he has evil desires and wrong view; (5) he is miserly with regard to dwellings; (6) he is miserly with regard to families; (7) he is miserly with regard to gains; (8) he is miserly with regard to praise; (9) he is miserly with regard to the Dhamma; (10) he does not wish others to be superior, nor does he wish them to be equal, but rather he wishes them to be inferior to himself. These, monks, are the ten qualities of one who quarrels.”
(AN 10.50, PTS AN v 88) On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, after returning from their alms round following the meal, a number of bhikkhus were in the assembly hall.
Seated together and assembled, they were engaged in quarreling, brawling, and falling into disputes, dwelling while piercing one another with verbal daggers.
Then, in the evening, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion and went to the assembly hall; having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, for what discussion are you gathered and seated here now, and what was the conversation among you that remained unfinished?

“Venerable sir, having returned from the alms round after our meal, we were gathered and seated here in the assembly hall when we fell into quarreling, brawling, and disputes, dwelling while piercing one another with verbal daggers.”
“Monks, it is not fitting for you— sons of good family who have gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith—
to dwell engaged in quarrels, engaged in strife, fallen into disputes, piercing one another with the weapons of the tongue.
“Monks, there are these ten qualities that are memorable, which create endearment, create respect, lead to being gathered together, to non-dispute, to harmony, and to unity.
What are the ten?

Here, monks, a monk is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains himself in the rules of training.

Furthermore, monks, when a monk is virtuous—[as previously described]—and having undertaken them, trains in the rules of training, this too is a quality that is memorable, endearing, and respectful; it leads to inclusion, to non-dispute, to harmony, and to unity.
Furthermore, monks, a monk is learned, one who has retained what he has heard and accumulated what he has heard; those teachings which...
They proclaim the holy life that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with its meaning and its phrasing, entirely complete and pure;
such teachings as these he has heard much of, retained in mind, mastered through speech,
examined by the mind, and well penetrated by view.
Furthermore, monks, when a monk is learned … [as above] … and has well-penetrated right view, this quality is memorable, endearing, and inspiring;
it leads to inclusion, to non-dispute, to harmony, and to unity.
Furthermore, monks, a monk has good friends, good companions, and good associates.
Furthermore, monks, that a monk has good friends, good companions, and good associates—this quality is also memorable, endearing, and respectful;
it leads to inclusion, to absence of dispute, to harmony, and to unity.
Furthermore, monks, a monk is easy to speak to, endowed with qualities that make him easy to speak to, patient, receptive to instruction, and compliant with advice.
Furthermore, monks, when a monk is easy to speak to, endowed with qualities that make him easy to speak to, patient, receptive to instruction, and compliant,
this too is a principle of cordiality that creates affection, creates respect, leads to inclusion, to non-dispute, to harmony, and to unity. Furthermore, monks,

when a monk is skillful and diligent regarding those various major and minor duties for his fellow celibates— endowed with the wisdom of means therein, capable of acting and capable of organizing— he [is endowed with a principle of cordiality].

Furthermore, monks, whatever various duties there may be for his fellow celibates, a monk is skillful therein, diligent, endowed with the appropriate means of investigation, and capable of acting and capable of arranging things.
This quality, too, is memorable, endearing, and inspiring; it leads to inclusion, to lack of dispute, to harmony, and to unity.
Furthermore, monks, a monk is a lover of the Dhamma, speaks with affection, and finds great joy in the higher Dhamma and the higher Vinaya.

Furthermore, monks, when a monk is a lover of the Dhamma, one who delights in its proclamation, and finds great joy in the higher Dhamma and the higher Vinaya—this quality, too, is memorable, endearing, and respectful;
it leads to being gathered together, to lack of dispute, to harmony, and to unity.

Furthermore, monks, a monk dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in effort, and does not relinquish his burden regarding wholesome states.

Furthermore, monks, when a monk dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the attainment of wholesome states—steadfast, firm in effort, not casting off the burden regarding wholesome states—this quality, too, is memorable, endearing, and respectful;
it leads to gathering together, to absence of dispute, to harmony, and to unity.
Furthermore, monks, a monk is content with whatever robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick he may receive.
“Furthermore, monks, when a monk is content with any kind of robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick, this too is a principle that is memorable… which leads to [nibbāna].
Furthermore, monks, a monk is mindful, endowed with supreme mindfulness and circumspection; he remembers and recalls what was done long ago and what was said long ago.”

Furthermore, monks, when a monk is mindful, endowed with supreme mindfulness and circumspection, one who remembers and recollects what was done long ago and what was spoken long ago—this too is a quality that is memorable...
[as before] ...it leads to such a state.
Furthermore, monks, a monk is wise, endowed with the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away, noble, penetrative, and leading to the complete destruction of suffering.

“Furthermore, monks, when a monk is wise, endowed with the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away—noble, penetrative, and leading to the complete destruction of suffering—this too is a quality that is consoling...
[as before] ...it leads to this state.
These, monks, are the ten qualities that are consoling, which create affection, create respect, and lead to being gathered together, to lack of dispute, to harmony, and to unity.”
The tenth.
The fifth chapter, on Abuse.
Its summary verse:
The two roots of dispute,
the entry into Kusinārā,
and Sakka’s frequent visit to Mahāli.
"And quarrels regarding the body.
The first fifty [discourses] are completed.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.51

6. Sacittavagga Sacittasutta (AN 10.51, PTS AN v 92) “Bhikkhus, there are these five things that lead to the non-decline of a bhikkhu who possesses a mind. What five? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu possesses a mind that is mindful, alert, concentrated, and liberated. These are the five things that lead to the non-decline of a bhikkhu who possesses a mind. Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We shall possess a mind that is mindful, alert, concentrated, and liberated. It is in this way that you should train yourselves.”
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu is not skilled in the method of understanding the minds of others, then he should think: ‘I shall become skilled in the method of understanding my own mind.’”
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
And how, monks, is a monk skilled in the method of examining his own mind?
Suppose, monks, a woman or a man—young, youthful, fond of ornaments—were to look at their reflection in a clear mirror,"
Just as one examining the reflection of one’s own face in a clear, bright bowl of water would,
if one sees therein dust or a blemish, strive for the removal of that dust or blemish;
but if one does not see therein dust or a blemish, one is satisfied with that, one’s purpose being fulfilled:
‘It is indeed a gain for me; it is indeed a purification for me.
In the same way, monks, reflection is of great benefit to a bhikkhu regarding wholesome states:
‘Do I usually dwell with covetousness, or do I usually dwell without covetousness? Do I have a mind of ill will…’”
Do I dwell frequently with a mind free from ill will? Do I dwell frequently with a mind free from ill will?
Do I dwell frequently overwhelmed by sloth and torpor? Do I dwell frequently free from sloth and torpor?
Do I dwell frequently agitated? Do I dwell frequently unagitated? Do I dwell frequently full of doubt?
Do I usually dwell having crossed over doubt? Do I usually dwell in anger, or do I usually dwell without anger?
Do I usually dwell with a defiled mind, or do I usually dwell with an undefiled mind?
Do I usually dwell with an agitated body, or do I usually dwell with an unagitated body?
‘Do I usually dwell lazily, or do I usually dwell with energy aroused?
Do I usually dwell unconcentrated, or do I usually dwell concentrated?
Monks, if, upon reviewing, a monk knows thus:
‘I dwell frequently with covetousness; I dwell frequently with a mind of ill will; I dwell frequently overwhelmed by sloth and torpor;
I dwell frequently agitated; I dwell frequently with doubt;
I dwell frequently with anger; I dwell frequently with a defiled mind; I dwell frequently with a restless body.’
‘I dwell often in idleness; I dwell often without concentration,’ then, monks,
that bhikkhu must apply himself with superior desire, effort, exertion, ardor, indefatigability, mindfulness, and clear comprehension for the abandoning of those very same evil, unwholesome states.
Just as, monks, one whose clothes are on fire or whose head is on fire would exert an extraordinary degree of zeal,
effort, enthusiasm, ardor, indefatigability, mindfulness, and clear comprehension for the purpose of extinguishing those very clothes or that very head.

In the same way, monks, that bhikkhu must apply himself with excessive zeal, effort, exertion, ardor, indefatigability, mindfulness, and clear comprehension for the sake of abandoning those very same evil, unwholesome states.
But if, monks, while reviewing, a monk knows thus:
‘I dwell frequently without covetousness, I dwell frequently with a mind free from ill will, I dwell frequently free from sloth and torpor,
I dwell frequently undisturbed, I dwell frequently having crossed over doubt, I am without anger’—
‘I dwell frequently with a mind that is undefiled, I dwell frequently with a body that is not agitated,
I dwell frequently with energy aroused, and I dwell frequently in concentration. Then, monks,
having established himself in those very wholesome states, that bhikkhu should apply himself further to the destruction of the taints.”
First.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.52 6.
Sacittavagga (The Chapter on One’s Own Mind)
There, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus: [Sāriputtasutta (AN 10.52, PTS AN v 94)] "In this regard,
the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus:"
“Friends, monks.
“Friend,” those monks replied to the Venerable Sāriputta.
The Venerable Sāriputta said this:
“If, friends, a bhikkhu is not skilled in the method of others’ minds, then he should train himself thus: ‘I will be skilled in the method of my own mind.
And how, friends, is a bhikkhu skilled in the method of his own mind?
Just as, friends, a woman or a man— youthful, young, and fond of adornment—
examining his own reflection in a clear, bright, and polished mirror or in a bowl of pure water, if he sees therein any dust or blemish,
exerts himself for the removal of that very dust or blemish.
If he does not see therein any speck or blemish, he becomes glad at heart, his purpose fulfilled, thinking:
"It is a gain for me, it is well-purified for me.
In the same way, friends, a monk’s self-examination is very helpful regarding wholesome states.
‘Do I usually dwell with covetousness, or do I usually dwell without covetousness?
Do I usually dwell with a mind of ill will, or do I usually dwell with a mind free from ill will?
Do I usually dwell overwhelmed by sloth and torpor, or do I usually dwell free from sloth and torpor? Am I usually restless?’
Do I dwell frequently agitated? Do I dwell frequently full of doubt?
Do I dwell frequently having crossed over doubt? Do I dwell frequently angry? Do I dwell frequently without anger?
Do I dwell frequently with a defiled mind? Do I dwell frequently with an undefiled mind?
‘Do I usually dwell with a restless body, or do I usually dwell with an un-restless body?
Do I usually dwell lazy, or do I usually dwell with energy aroused?
Do I usually dwell unconcentrated, or do I usually dwell concentrated?’”
If, friends, while reflecting, a bhikkhu knows thus:

“I often dwell with covetousness... I often dwell without concentration,” then, friends, that bhikkhu should exert intense desire, effort, and perseverance for the abandoning of those very same evil unwholesome states.
And there must be ardor, perseverance, exertion, fortitude, indefatigability, mindfulness, and clear comprehension. Just as if, friends,
one’s clothes were on fire or one’s head were on fire,

one would apply an extraordinary degree of desire, effort, exertion, fortitude, indefatigability, mindfulness, and clear comprehension for the sole purpose of extinguishing those clothes or that head.

"In the same way, friends, that bhikkhu must apply superior desire, effort, enthusiasm, exertion, indefatigability, mindfulness, and clear comprehension for the sake of abandoning those very same evil, unwholesome states. However, friends,
if while reflecting a bhikkhu knows thus:"

‘I dwell frequently without covetousness... ... ‘I dwell frequently concentrated,’ friend, that bhikkhu, having established himself in those very wholesome states, should apply himself further to the destruction of the taints. Thus it was said.
Second.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.53

6. Sacittavagga Ṭhitisutta (Discourse on Stability) "Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is established in a mind that is stable, he understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering. He understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering. He understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering. He understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. When a bhikkhu is established in a mind that is stable, he understands as it really is: ‘These are the taints. He understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of the taints. He understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of the taints. He understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints. Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We will be established in a mind that is stable. It is in this way that you should train yourselves."
“Bhikkhus, I do not praise stability in regard to wholesome qualities, much less decline.
Rather, bhikkhus, I praise growth in regard to wholesome qualities, not stability and not decline.
And how, bhikkhus, is there decline in regard to wholesome qualities, rather than stability or growth?
“Here, monks, whatever extent a monk has in terms of faith, virtue, learning, generosity, wisdom, and eloquence— if those qualities neither remain nor increase in him,
I say this is a decline in wholesome qualities, monks, not their stability or growth. It is in this way, monks, that there is a decline in wholesome qualities, not their stability or growth.”
And how, monks, is there stability in wholesome states, neither decline nor growth?
Here, monks, whatever a monk possesses of faith, virtue, learning, generosity, wisdom, and eloquence—those qualities neither diminish nor increase for him.
This, monks, I call stability in wholesome states, neither decline nor growth.
In this way, monks, there is stability in wholesome states, neither growth nor decline.
And how, monks, is there growth in wholesome states, neither stability nor decline?
Here, monks, whatever measure of faith, virtue, learning, generosity, wisdom, and eloquence a monk possesses, those qualities neither remain stagnant nor decline.
“Bhikkhus, I say this is growth in wholesome qualities, not stagnation nor decline.
It is in this way, bhikkhus, that there is growth in wholesome qualities, not stagnation nor decline.
If a bhikkhu is not skilled in the ways of others’ minds, then he should think: ‘I shall become skilled in the ways of my own mind.’”
"In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
And how, monks, is a monk skilled in the method of examining his own mind?
Just as, monks, a woman or a man—youthful, young, and fond of adornment—would look at their reflection in a clear mirror,"
Just as when a man, looking at the reflection of his own face in a clear,
bright pool of water, if he sees therein some dust or blemish, strives for the removal of that dust or blemish;
but if he does not see therein any dust or blemish, he is satisfied with that, his purpose being fulfilled:
‘It is indeed a gain for me; it is indeed well-purified for me.
In the same way, monks, reflection is of great benefit to a monk regarding wholesome states:
‘Do I often dwell with covetousness, or do I often dwell without covetousness? Do I dwell with a mind of ill will...’?
Do I dwell frequently with a mind free from ill will? Do I dwell frequently with a mind free from ill will?
Do I dwell frequently overwhelmed by sloth and torpor? Do I dwell frequently free from sloth and torpor?
Do I dwell frequently agitated? Do I dwell frequently unagitated? Do I dwell frequently possessed by doubt?
Do I dwell frequently with doubt overcome? Do I dwell frequently in anger? Or do I dwell frequently without anger?
Do I dwell frequently with a defiled mind? Or do I dwell frequently with an undefiled mind?
Do I dwell frequently with an agitated body? Or do I dwell frequently without an agitated body?
‘Do I usually dwell with energy slackened, or do I usually dwell with energy aroused?
Do I usually dwell with mind unconcentrated, or do I usually dwell with mind concentrated?
Monks, if, upon reviewing, a monk knows thus:
‘I dwell frequently with covetousness; I dwell frequently with a mind of ill will; I dwell frequently overwhelmed by sloth and torpor;
I dwell frequently with restlessness; I dwell frequently with doubt; I dwell frequently with anger;
I dwell frequently with a defiled mind; I dwell frequently with a body agitated.’
‘I dwell often in idleness; I dwell often without concentration,’ then, monks,

that bhikkhu must apply himself with superior desire, effort, exertion, ardor, indefatigability, mindfulness, and clear comprehension for the sake of abandoning those very same evil, unwholesome states.
“Just as, monks, one whose clothes are on fire or whose head is on fire would exert an extraordinary degree of zeal,
effort, enthusiasm, persistence, indefatigability, mindfulness, and clear comprehension for the sake of extinguishing those very clothes or that very head— even so, monks,
should that bhikkhu [exert himself] for the sake of the total abandoning of those very same evil, unwholesome states.”
For the sake of abandoning [them], an intense desire, effort, exertion, perseverance, non-retrogression, mindfulness,
and clear comprehension must be practiced.
But if, monks, while reflecting, a monk knows thus:
‘I dwell frequently without covetousness; I dwell frequently with a mind free from ill will; I dwell frequently free from sloth and torpor;
I dwell frequently without restlessness; I dwell frequently having crossed over doubt;
I dwell frequently without anger; I dwell frequently with an undefiled mind; I dwell frequently with an unagitated body.’
‘I dwell frequently with energy aroused, and I dwell frequently with mind concentrated,’ then, monks, that bhikkhu,
having established himself in those very wholesome states, should apply himself further to the destruction of the taints.
The third.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.54 6. Sacittavagga Samathasutta “Monks, when one thing is developed and cultivated, it leads to a great sense of peace. What is that one thing? Tranquility of mind. And how, monks, is tranquility of mind developed and cultivated so that it leads to a great sense of peace? Here, monks, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... He dwells contemplating mind in the mind... He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. It is in this way, monks, that tranquility of mind is developed and cultivated so that it leads to a great sense of peace.”
“Bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu is not skilled in the method of discerning the minds of others, then he should train himself thus: ‘I will become skilled in the method of discerning my own mind.
It is in this way, bhikkhus, that you should train yourselves.”
And how, monks, is a monk skilled in the method of examining his own mind?
Just as if, monks, a woman or a man— young, youthful, fond of ornaments—
were looking at the reflection of their own face in a clear, bright, polished mirror or in a bowl of pure water, and were to see therein...
Whether it be dust or a stain, he strives for the removal of that very dust or stain.
If he does not perceive any dust or stain there, he becomes satisfied with that very fact, his purpose fulfilled:
"It is a gain for me; indeed, I am purified."
In the same way, monks, self-examination is very helpful for a monk regarding wholesome states:
‘Am I one who has attained internal tranquility of mind, or am I not?
Am I one who has attained higher wisdom and insight into phenomena, or am I not?’”
“Bhikkhus, if, upon reviewing, a bhikkhu knows thus:

‘I am a possessor of internal serenity of mind, but I am not a possessor of higher wisdom consisting in insight into phenomena,’ then, bhikkhus, that bhikkhu, having established himself in internal serenity of mind, should apply himself to the development of higher wisdom consisting in insight into phenomena.
After some time, he becomes a possessor both of internal serenity of mind and of higher wisdom consisting in insight into phenomena.”
But if, monks, while reviewing, a monk knows thus:

‘I am a possessor of insight into phenomena through higher wisdom, but I am not a possessor of internal mental serenity,’ then, monks, that monk, having established himself in insight into phenomena through higher wisdom, should apply himself to internal mental serenity.
After some time, he becomes a possessor both of insight into phenomena through higher wisdom and of internal mental serenity.
But if, monks, while reviewing, a monk knows thus:
‘I am not an attainer of internal serenity of mind, nor am I an attainer of higher wisdom through insight into phenomena,’ then,
monks, that monk should apply himself with excessive zeal for the sake of obtaining those very same wholesome states.
Exertion, effort, persistence, indefatigability, mindfulness, and clear comprehension must be practiced. Just as if, monks,
one’s clothes were on fire or one’s head were on fire,

one would apply an extraordinary degree of desire, exertion, effort, persistence, indefatigability, mindfulness, and clear comprehension for the sole purpose of extinguishing those very clothes or that very head.

In the same way, monks, for the sake of attaining those very wholesome states, that bhikkhu must exercise intense desire, effort, exertion, perseverance, undaunted mindfulness, and clear comprehension.
After some time, he becomes a possessor of internal mental serenity and a possessor of higher wisdom through insight into phenomena.
But if, monks, while reviewing himself, the bhikkhu knows thus:

‘I am one who has attained internal tranquility of mind, and I am one who has attained higher wisdom through insight into phenomena. Monks, that monk, having established himself in those very wholesome states, should apply himself further to the destruction of the taints.
Monks, I say that robes are of two kinds:
those to be used and those not to be used.
“Monks, I declare that almsfood is of two kinds:
that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated.
Monks, I declare that lodgings are of two kinds:”
There is that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated.
Monks, I declare that even villages and market towns are of two kinds:
those that should be cultivated and those that should not be cultivated.
“Monks, I declare that a region is of two kinds:
one to be frequented and one not to be frequented.
Monks, I declare that a person is also of two kinds:”
"There is that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated.
'Monks, I declare that even the robe-cloth is of two kinds:
that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated.'"
Thus it was said. With reference to what was this said?
In this regard, if one should know of a robe:
"When I use this robe, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline," such a robe should not be used.
In this regard, if one should know of a robe:
"While using this robe of mine, unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase," such a robe should be used.
"Monks, I say that a robe is of two kinds—"
‘There is that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated’—
it is with reference to this that it was said.
“Monks, I declare that even almsfood is of two kinds.”
‘There is that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated’—thus it was said. With reference to what was this said?
In this regard, one should know of almsfood: [that it is to be cultivated or not].
‘If, while consuming this almsfood of mine, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline,’ such almsfood should not be consumed.
In that regard, if one should know of an almsfood:
‘If, while consuming this almsfood of mine, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase,’ such almsfood should be consumed.
“Bhikkhus, I say that almsfood is of two kinds:
that which is to be cultivated and that which is not to be cultivated.
It was with reference to this that it was said.
‘Monks, I say that lodgings are of two kinds:
those to be cultivated and those not to be cultivated.
Thus it was said. With reference to what was this said?
In that regard, if one should know of a lodging:
"While I am using this lodging, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline," such a lodging should not be used.
In that regard, if one should know of a lodging:
‘When I frequent this lodging, unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase’—such a lodging should be frequented.
“Monks, I say that lodgings are of two kinds:
those to be frequented and those not to be frequented.”
Thus, that which was said, this was said with reference to this:
“Monks, I declare that villages and market towns are of two kinds:
those to be cultivated and those not to be cultivated.”
Thus it was said. With reference to what was this said?
In this regard, if one should know of a village or town:
"When I frequent this village or town, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline," then such a village or town should not be frequented.
In that regard, if one should know of a village or town:
"By frequenting this village or town, unwholesome states diminish in me and wholesome states increase," such a village or town should be frequented.
"Monks, I say that even a village or town is of two kinds."
‘There are things to be cultivated and things not to be cultivated’—
this is what was said, and it was said with reference to this.
“Monks, I say that even countries and regions are of two kinds:”
‘There is that which should be cultivated and that which should not be cultivated.
Thus it was said. With reference to what was this said?
In this regard, one should know of a certain region or district:
‘While I am frequenting this region, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline’—such a region should not be frequented.
But in that case where one should know of a region:
‘While I am frequenting this region, unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase’—such a region should be frequented.
“Monks, when I said that ‘countries and regions are of two kinds—
I say they are either to be cultivated or not to be cultivated’—
it was with reference to this that I said that.”
“Monks, I say that there are two kinds of persons:
those who are to be associated with and those who are not to be associated with.
Thus it was said. With reference to what was this said?
In this regard, if one should know of a person:
“When I associate with this person, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline,” such a person should not be associated with.
In this regard, if one should know of a person:
‘When I associate with this person, unwholesome qualities diminish and wholesome qualities increase’—such a person should be associated with.
“Monks, I say that there are two kinds of persons:
those who should be associated with, and those who should not be associated with.”
Thus, that which was said was said with reference to this.
The fourth [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.55

6. Sacittavagga: Parihānasutta (AN 10.55, PTS AN v 102) “Bhikkhus, there are these five causes for the decline of a bhikkhu who is a trainee. What five? Here, a bhikkhu dwells without reverence and deference toward the Teacher, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, the training, and concentration. These, bhikkhus, are the five causes for the decline of a bhikkhu who is a trainee. There are, bhikkhus, these five causes for the non-decline of a bhikkhu who is a trainee. What five? Here, a bhikkhu dwells with reverence and deference toward the Teacher, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, the training, and concentration. These, bhikkhus, are the five causes for the non-decline of a bhikkhu who is a trainee.”
There, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus:
"Friends, bhikkhus.
"Friend," those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Sāriputta.
The Venerable Sāriputta said this:
"Friend, it is said: 'a person subject to decline, a person subject to decline';
and it is said: 'a person not subject to decline, a person not subject to decline.'"
“In what way, friend, has the person subject to decline been described by the Blessed One, and in what way has the person not subject to decline been described by the Blessed One?
“Friend, we come from afar to learn the meaning of this statement from the venerable Sāriputta.
It would be well indeed if the venerable Sāriputta himself were to clarify the meaning of this statement.”
“Having heard it from the Venerable Sāriputta, the bhikkhus will retain it.
“Then, friends, listen and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Sāriputta.
The Venerable Sāriputta said this:
"To what extent, friends, has the person subject to decline been described by the Blessed One?
Here, friends, a bhikkhu does not hear the Dhamma he has not heard before, and the teachings he has already heard fall into forgetfulness."
And those states that were previously untouched by his mind do not manifest for him, and he does not cognize what has not been cognized.
To this extent, friends, a person subject to decline has been described by the Blessed One.
But to what extent, friends, has a person not subject to decline been described by the Blessed One?

"Here, friends, a bhikkhu hears a teaching he has not heard before; the teachings he has already heard do not fade from his memory; those teachings that were previously untouched by his mind now become manifest to him; and he understands what was previously unknown.
To this extent, friends, a person is said by the Blessed One to be of a nature not subject to decline.
If, friends, a bhikkhu is not skilled in the way of others' minds, then he should think: 'I shall be skilled in the way of my own mind.'"
"In this way, friends, you should train yourselves.
And how, friends, is a bhikkhu skilled in the method of examining his own mind?
Suppose, friends, a woman or a man—young, youthful, fond of ornaments—were to look at their reflection in a clear mirror,"
Just as when a man, looking at the reflection of his own face in a clear, bright pool of water, if he sees therein some dust or blemish,
exerts himself for the removal of that dust or blemish;
but if he does not see therein any dust or blemish, he is satisfied with that, his purpose being fulfilled:
‘It is a gain for me indeed! It is a great purification for me indeed!
In the same way, friends, reflection is very helpful to a bhikkhu regarding wholesome states:
‘Do I frequently dwell without covetousness? Is this quality found in me or not?’”
"Do I usually dwell with a mind free from ill will? Does this quality exist in me or not?
Do I usually dwell free from sloth and torpor? Does this quality exist in me or not?
Do I usually dwell undisturbed? Does this quality exist in me or not?"
"Do I often dwell having crossed over doubt? Does this quality exist in me or not? Do I often dwell without anger?
Does this quality exist in me or not? Do I often dwell with an undefiled mind? Does this quality exist in me or not? Am I one who attains [these states]?"
‘Does this state of joy in the Dhamma exist within me or not? Am I one who has attained internal tranquility of mind; does this state exist within me or not?
Am I one who has attained higher wisdom and insight into phenomena; does this state exist within me or not?’”
But if, friend, while reviewing, a bhikkhu does not perceive all these wholesome states within himself,
then that bhikkhu must apply intense desire, effort, exertion, ardor, indefatigability, mindfulness, and clear comprehension for the sake of acquiring all these wholesome states.
"Friend, it is just as if one’s clothes were on fire, or one’s head were on fire.
One would exert extraordinary zeal, effort, energy, persistence, indefatigability, mindfulness, and clear comprehension for the sake of extinguishing those very clothes or that very head.
In the same way, friend, that bhikkhu must exert extraordinary zeal, effort, energy, persistence, indefatigability, mindfulness, and clear comprehension for the attainment of all wholesome states."
But if, friends, while reflecting, a bhikkhu perceives some wholesome qualities within himself and does not perceive other wholesome qualities within himself, then that bhikkhu,
having established himself in those wholesome qualities which he perceives within himself, [should apply himself] to those wholesome qualities which he does not perceive within himself.
He considers that for the acquisition of those wholesome states, there must be undertaken an intense desire,
effort, exertion, perseverance, undauntedness, mindfulness, and clear comprehension—
just as one whose clothes are on fire or whose head is on fire [would act].
Just as one would exert excessive zeal, effort, energy, perseverance, indefatigability, mindfulness, and clear comprehension for the sake of extinguishing that very lamp or head,
even so, friend, that bhikkhu— having established himself in those wholesome qualities which he perceives within himself—
should [exert himself] regarding those wholesome qualities which he does not perceive within himself.
For the sake of attainment, there must be intense desire, effort, exertion, perseverance, indefatigability, mindfulness,
and clear comprehension. However, friends,
if a bhikkhu, upon reviewing, perceives all these wholesome qualities within himself, [he should remain established in them].
"Therefore, friends, a bhikkhu, having established himself in all these wholesome states, should apply himself further to the destruction of the taints.
The fifth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.56 6.

Sacittavagga Paṭhamasaññāsutta (The First Discourse on Perceptions) “Monks, there are these ten perceptions. What ten? The perception of a bloated corpse, the perception of a livid corpse, the perception of a festering corpse, the perception of a fissured corpse, the perception of a mangled corpse, the perception of a scattered corpse, the perception of a hacked-and-scattered corpse, the perception of a bleeding corpse, the perception of a worm-infested corpse, and the perception of a skeleton. These, monks, are the ten perceptions.”
“Monks, these ten perceptions, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit and great benefit; they have the Deathless as their ground and the Deathless as their consummation.
What are the ten?

“The perception of foulness, the perception of death, the perception of the repulsiveness of food, the perception of non-delight in the entire world, the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in what is impermanent, the perception of non-self in what is suffering, the perception of abandoning, the perception of dispassion, and the perception of cessation—these ten perceptions, monks, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit and great benefit; they culminate in the Deathless and have the Deathless as their final goal.
The sixth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.57 6.

Sacittavagga Second Discourse on Perceptions “Monks, there are these ten perceptions. What ten? The perception of a bloated corpse, the perception of a livid corpse, the perception of a festering corpse, the perception of a fissured corpse, the perception of a mangled corpse, the perception of a hacked-and-scattered corpse, the perception of a bleeding corpse, the perception of a worm-infested corpse, the perception of a skeleton, and the perception of a bone. These, monks, are the ten perceptions.”
“Bhikkhus, these ten perceptions, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit and great benefit; they have the Deathless as their ground and the Deathless as their consummation.
What ten?

“The perception of impermanence, the perception of non-self, the perception of death, the perception of the repulsiveness of food, the perception of non-delight in the entire world, the perception of a skeleton, the perception of a worm-infested corpse, the perception of a livid corpse, the perception of a fissured corpse, and the perception of a bloated corpse—these ten perceptions, bhikkhus, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit and great benefit; they have the Deathless as their ground and the Deathless as their consummation.
Thus it was said. The seventh.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.58 6.

Sacittavagga Mūlakasutta “Bhikkhus, there are these ten roots of disputes. What ten? Disputes rooted in greed, rooted in hatred, rooted in delusion, rooted in views, rooted in conceit, rooted in envy, rooted in stinginess, rooted in deceit, rooted in craftiness, and rooted in bad friendship. These, bhikkhus, are the ten roots of disputes.”
“Bhikkhus, if wanderers of other sects should ask you thus:
‘Friends, what is the root of all phenomena? What is their origin? What is their source? (AN 10.58, PTS AN v 106)
“Of what convergence are all phenomena? What is the foremost of all phenomena? What is the dominant factor of all phenomena?
What is the highest of all phenomena? What is the core of all phenomena? What is the refuge of all phenomena?
What is the consummation of all phenomena? Thus questioned, monks, you [should answer] those wanderers of other sects.
“How would you answer?
“Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One, guided by the Blessed One, and have the Blessed One as their refuge.
It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One himself would explain the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it.”
“Therefore, bhikkhus, listen and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, if wanderers of other sects should ask you thus:
‘Friends, what is the root of all phenomena? What is their origin? What is their source? What is their convergence? What is their foremost? What is their sovereign?’”
“What is the root of all phenomena? What is their essence? What is their foundation? What is their conclusion?
Being asked thus, monks, you should answer those wanderers of other sects as follows:
“Friends, all phenomena have desire as their root; all phenomena arise from attention; all phenomena originate from contact.”
‘All phenomena converge in feeling; all phenomena have concentration as their chief; all phenomena have mindfulness as their sovereign;
all phenomena have wisdom as their supreme; all phenomena have liberation as their essence; all phenomena are grounded in the deathless; all phenomena culminate in Nibbāna.’”
“Being asked thus, bhikkhus, you should answer those wanderers of other sects in this way.
The eighth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.59

6. Sacittavagga: Pabbajjāsutta (AN 10.59, PTS AN v 107) “Monks, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world. What three? The person who has gone forth out of faith; the person who has gone forth out of fear; and the person who has gone forth out of neither faith nor fear, but who has gone forth for the sake of the holy life itself. These, monks, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus:
‘Our minds will be familiar with our state as we went forth, and arisen evil unwholesome states will not persist by taking possession of the mind;
our minds will be familiar with the perception of impermanence, and our minds will be familiar with the perception of non-self.’”
Our mind will be cultivated in the perception of foulness; our mind will be cultivated in the perception of danger;
having known both the even and the uneven of the world, our mind will be cultivated in that perception;
having known both the arising and the passing away of the world, our mind will be cultivated in that perception; [and] the origin of the world...
‘Having known its passing away, our mind will be familiar with that perception;
our mind will be familiar with the perception of abandoning, familiar with the perception of dispassion, and familiar with the perception of cessation.’”
In this way, monks, you should train yourselves.
For when, monks, a bhikkhu’s mind is familiar with his original going-forth, and arisen evil unwholesome states do not remain obsessing the mind;
and when his mind is familiar with the perception of impermanence and familiar with the perception of non-self—
The mind becomes familiar with the perception of foulness; the mind becomes familiar with the perception of danger;
having known what is even and uneven in the world, the mind becomes familiar with that perception;
having known existence and non-existence in the world, the mind becomes familiar with that perception; [having known] the arising and the passing away of the world...

Knowing that, his mind becomes familiar with the perception of abandoning, his mind becomes familiar with the perception of dispassion, his mind becomes familiar with the perception of cessation; for him, one of two fruits is to be expected:
either final knowledge in this very life, or, if there is a residue of clinging, the state of a non-returner.
The Ninth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.60 6.
Sacittavagga (The Chapter on One’s Own Mind)
The Discourse to Girimānanda (AN 10.60).
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the Venerable Girimānanda was afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill.

Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, the Venerable Girimānanda is afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill."
“It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One would approach the Venerable Girimānanda out of compassion.
“If you, Ānanda, were to recite the ten perceptions to the bhikkhu Girimānanda,
it is possible that upon hearing those ten perceptions, his affliction might be immediately allayed.”
Which ten?

The perception of impermanence, the perception of non-self, the perception of the unattractive, the perception of danger, the perception of relinquishment, the perception of dispassion, the perception of cessation, the perception of non-delight in the entire world, the perception of non-desire for all conditioned phenomena, and mindfulness of breathing.
And what, Ānanda, is the perception of impermanence?
In this case, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects thus:
"Form is impermanent, feeling is impermanent, perception is impermanent, volitional formations are impermanent, consciousness is impermanent.
Thus he dwells contemplating impermanence in these five aggregates of clinging.
This, Ānanda, is called the perception of impermanence.
And what, Ānanda, is the perception of non-self?
Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects thus:

‘The eye is non-self, forms are non-self; the ear is non-self, sounds are non-self; the nose is non-self, odors are non-self; the tongue is non-self, tastes are non-self; the body is non-self, tangibles are non-self; the mind is non-self, mental phenomena are non-self.
Thus, Ānanda, one dwells contemplating non-self in these six internal and external sense bases.
This, Ānanda, is called the perception of non-self.
And what, Ānanda, is the perception of foulness?
Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu contemplates this very body, from the soles of the feet upwards and from the hair of the head downwards, bounded by the skin, as full of various kinds of impurity:
"In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone-marrow, kidneys, liver..."
"The heart, liver, midriff, spleen, lungs; the intestines, mesentery, stomach, and excrement;
bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat; tears, grease, spittle, snot, synovial fluid, and urine.
Thus he dwells contemplating the foulness in this body.
This, Ānanda, is called the perception of foulness.
And what, Ānanda, is the perception of danger?
Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects thus:
‘This body is indeed full of suffering and full of peril. Thus, various diseases arise in this body, such as these:

eye disease, ear disease, nose disease, tongue disease, body disease, head disease, ear-ache, mouth disease, tooth disease, lip disease, cough, asthma, catarrh, burning fever, chills, stomach ache, fainting, dysentery, colic, and cholera.’
Leprosy, boils, ringworm, consumption, apamāra, daddu, itch, scabies, nail-ailment, vitacchikā, blood-disease, bile-disease, diabetes, abscesses, carbuncles, fistulas,
ailments arising from bile, ailments arising from phlegm, ailments arising from wind, ailments arising from a combination of humors,
ailments born of changes in the seasons, ailments born of irregular conduct, and ailments resulting from external injury.
"Disease is born of the ripening of kamma; there are disease, cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and the need for excrement and urine.
Thus, Ānanda, one dwells contemplating the danger in this body.
This, Ānanda, is called the perception of danger.
And what, Ānanda, is the perception of abandoning?
Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu does not tolerate an arisen thought of sensual desire; he abandons it, dispels it, brings it to an end, and makes it non-existent.
He does not tolerate an arisen thought of ill will; he abandons it, dispels it, brings it to an end, and [makes it non-existent].
He brings it to non-existence. He does not tolerate a thought of cruelty that has arisen; he abandons it, dispels it, eliminates it, and brings it to non-existence.
Whatever evil, unwholesome states have arisen, he does not tolerate them; he abandons them, dispels them, eliminates them, and brings them to non-existence.
This, Ānanda, is called the perception of abandoning.
And what, Ānanda, is the perception of dispassion?
Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects thus:
‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, dispassion, Nibbāna.
This, Ānanda, is called the perception of dispassion.
And what, Ānanda, is the perception of cessation?
"Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects thus:
‘This is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions, the destruction of craving, cessation, Nibbāna.
This, Ānanda, is called the perception of cessation."
And what, Ānanda, is the perception of non-delight in the entire world?
Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu dwells abandoning those clingings in the world that are mental fixations, adherences, and underlying tendencies, not clinging to them.
This, Ānanda, is called the perception of non-delight in the entire world.
And what, Ānanda, is the perception of non-delight in all conditioned phenomena?
Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu is repelled by, ashamed of, and disgusted with all conditioned phenomena.
This, Ānanda, is called the perception of non-delight in all conditioned phenomena.
And what, Ānanda, is mindfulness of breathing?

Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down; folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him, he breathes in mindfully and breathes out mindfully.
Breathing in long, he knows, "I am breathing in long"; breathing out long, he knows, "I am breathing out long.
Breathing in short, he knows, "I am breathing in short"; breathing out short, he knows, "I am breathing out short.
He trains himself, "I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body"; he trains himself, "I shall breathe out experiencing the whole body."
‘Calming the bodily formation, I shall breathe in,’ he trains himself. ‘Calming the bodily formation, I shall breathe out,’ he trains himself.
‘Experiencing rapture, I shall breathe in,’ he trains himself. ‘Experiencing rapture, I shall breathe out,’ he trains himself.
‘Experiencing pleasure, I shall breathe in,’ he trains himself. ‘Experiencing pleasure, I shall breathe out,’ he trains himself.
‘Experiencing the mental formations, I shall breathe in,’ he trains himself. ‘Experiencing the mental formations, I shall breathe out,’ he trains himself.
‘Tranquillizing the mental formations, I shall breathe in,’ he trains himself. ‘Tranquillizing the mental formations, I shall breathe out,’ he trains himself.
‘Experiencing the mind, I shall breathe in,’ he trains himself. ‘Experiencing the mind, I shall breathe out,’ he trains himself.
Gladdening the mind...
concentrating the mind...
liberating the mind... [and so forth].
Contemplating impermanence …pe… contemplating fading away …pe… contemplating cessation …pe…
‘Contemplating relinquishment, I shall breathe in,’ he trains himself; ‘contemplating relinquishment, I shall breathe out,’ he trains himself.
This, Ānanda, is called mindfulness of breathing.
If you, Ānanda, were to speak these ten perceptions to the bhikkhu Girimānanda, it is possible that his fever would subside.
"However, it is possible that upon hearing these ten perceptions, the monk Girimānanda’s affliction might be immediately allayed.

Then the Venerable Ānanda, having learned these ten perceptions in the presence of the Blessed One, approached the Venerable Girimānanda; having approached, he recited these ten perceptions to the Venerable Girimānanda.
Then, upon hearing these ten perceptions from the Venerable Girimānanda, that affliction of his subsided immediately.
The Venerable Girimānanda recovered from that affliction; indeed, that affliction of the Venerable Girimānanda was thus abandoned.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.61 7. Yamakavagga Avijjāsutta (The Discourse on Ignorance)
“Bhikkhus, no prior limit of ignorance is discerned such that one could say: ‘Before this, ignorance did not exist; then afterwards it came into being.
Although this is said, bhikkhus, nevertheless it is discerned that: ‘With this as condition, there is ignorance.’”
"Bhikkhus, I say that ignorance has a nutriment; it is not without nutriment.
And what is the nutriment for ignorance?
It should be said: 'The five hindrances.'"
“Bhikkhus, I say that the five hindrances have a nutriment; they are not without nutriment.
And what is the nutriment for the five hindrances?
It should be said: ‘The three kinds of misconduct.’”
“Bhikkhus, I say that the three kinds of misconduct have a nutriment; they are not without nutriment.
And what is the nutriment for the three kinds of misconduct?
It should be said: ‘Lack of restraint over the sense faculties.’”
“Monks, I say that lack of restraint of the sense faculties has a nutriment; it is not without nutriment.
And what is the nutriment for lack of restraint of the sense faculties?
It should be said: ‘lack of clear comprehension in one who is unmindful.’”
“Monks, I say that lack of clear comprehension is also with nutriment, not without nutriment.
And what is the nutriment for lack of clear comprehension?
It should be said: ‘Inappropriate attention.’”
“Bhikkhus, I say that even unwise attention has a nutriment; it is not without nutriment.
And what is the nutriment for unwise attention?
It should be said: lack of faith.”
"Lack of faith, monks, I say has a nutriment; it is not without a nutriment.
And what is the nutriment for lack of faith?
It should be said: 'Hearing what is not the true Dhamma.'"
“Monks, I say that even listening to what is not the true Dhamma has a nutriment; it is not without a nutriment.
And what is the nutriment for listening to what is not the true Dhamma?
It should be said: ‘Association with unworthy persons.’”
Thus, monks, the fullness of associating with unworthy persons fulfills the hearing of what is not the true Dhamma;
the fullness of hearing what is not the true Dhamma fulfills lack of faith; the fullness of lack of faith fulfills improper attention;
the fullness of improper attention fulfills lack of mindfulness and lack of clear comprehension; and the fullness of lack of mindfulness and lack of clear comprehension—
One fulfills the lack of restraint of the sense faculties; the fulfilled lack of restraint of the sense faculties fulfills the three types of misconduct;
the fulfilled three types of misconduct fulfill the five hindrances; the fulfilled five hindrances fulfill ignorance.
In this way, this is the nutriment for that ignorance, and in this way it reaches fulfillment.
Just as, monks, when it is raining in thick drops on a mountain above, that water, flowing down according to the slope, fills the mountain clefts, gullies, and creeks;
the mountain clefts, gullies, and creeks being filled, fill the small pools; the small pools being filled, fill the large pools; the large pools...
The small streams, being full, fill the large streams; the large streams, being full, fill the great rivers;
the great rivers, being full, fill the great ocean, the sea.
Such is the nourishment for this great ocean, the sea, and such is its fulfillment.
In the same way, monks, association with unworthy persons, when fulfilled, fulfills hearing what is not the true Dhamma;
hearing what is not the true Dhamma, when fulfilled, fulfills lack of faith; lack of faith, when fulfilled, fulfills improper attention;
improper attention, when fulfilled, fulfills lack of mindfulness and lack of clear comprehension. Lacking mindfulness and clear comprehension—
The fulfillment of the non-restraint of the sense faculties fulfills [them]; the fulfilled non-restraint of the sense faculties fulfills the three types of misconduct;
the fulfilled three types of misconduct fulfill the five hindrances; the fulfilled five hindrances fulfill ignorance.
In this way, there is nutriment for this ignorance, and in this way it reaches fulfillment.
And, monks, I say that true knowledge and liberation also have a nutriment; they are not without nutriment.
And what is the nutriment for true knowledge and liberation?
‘The seven factors of enlightenment,’ it should be said.
For I say, monks, that the seven factors of enlightenment have a nutriment, not that they are without nutriment.
And what is the nutriment for the seven factors of enlightenment?
‘The four foundations of mindfulness,’ it should be said.
“Monks, I declare that the four foundations of mindfulness have a nutriment; they are not without nutriment.
And what is the nutriment for the four foundations of mindfulness?”
‘The three kinds of good conduct,’ it should be said.
“Monks, I say that these three kinds of good conduct have a nutriment; they are not without nutriment.
And what is the nutriment for the three kinds of good conduct?”
“It should be said: ‘Restraint of the sense faculties.
Monks, I say that restraint of the sense faculties has a nutriment; it is not without nutriment.
And what is the nutriment for restraint of the sense faculties?”
"It should be said: 'mindfulness and clear comprehension.
And I say, monks, that mindfulness and clear comprehension have a nutriment; they are not without nutriment.
And what is the nutriment for mindfulness and clear comprehension?"
‘Appropriate attention’ is the answer to be given.
Monks, I say that even appropriate attention has a nutriment; it is not without nutriment.
And what is the nutriment for appropriate attention?
‘Faith,’ it should be said.
For I say, monks, that faith has its nutriment; it is not without nutriment.
And what is the nutriment for faith?
‘Listening to the true Dhamma’ is what should be said.
Monks, I say that listening to the true Dhamma has a nutriment; it is not without nutriment.
And what is the nutriment for listening to the true Dhamma?
‘Association with superior persons’ is what should be said here.
Thus, monks, association with superior persons, when fulfilled, fulfills hearing the true Dhamma; hearing the true Dhamma, when fulfilled, fulfills faith;
faith, when fulfilled, fulfills wise attention; wise attention—
When full, mindfulness and clear comprehension fulfill themselves; when mindfulness and clear comprehension are fulfilled, they fulfill restraint of the sense faculties;
when restraint of the sense faculties is fulfilled, it fulfills the three types of good conduct; when the three types of good conduct are fulfilled, they fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness;
when the four foundations of mindfulness are fulfilled, they fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment.
The seven factors of enlightenment, when fulfilled, fulfill true knowledge and liberation.
Such is the nutriment for this true knowledge and liberation, and such is their fulfillment.
Just as, monks, when it rains in thick drops from a cloud above the high mountains, that water flows down according to the slope...
As it flows, it fills the mountain clefts, ravines, and gullies; the mountain clefts, ravines, and gullies being filled, fill the small pools;
the small pools being filled, fill the large pools; the large pools being filled, fill the small streams;
the small streams being filled, fill the great rivers; the great rivers being filled...
They fill the great ocean, the sea;
such is the nourishment for this great ocean, the sea, and such is its fulfillment.
In the same way, monks, the cultivation of the company of true persons, when fulfilled, fulfills the hearing of the true Dhamma.
The hearing of the true Dhamma, when fulfilled, fulfills faith; faith, when fulfilled, fulfills wise attention;
wise attention, when fulfilled, fulfills mindfulness and clear comprehension;
mindfulness and clear comprehension, when fulfilled, fulfill restraint of the sense faculties; and restraint of the sense faculties, when fulfilled, fulfills the three types of good conduct.
The three types of good conduct, when fulfilled, fulfill the four foundations of mindfulness;
the four foundations of mindfulness, when fulfilled, fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment; the seven factors of enlightenment, when fulfilled, fulfill true knowledge and liberation.
In this way, there is a nutriment for this true knowledge and liberation, and in this way its fulfillment comes about.”

“Bhikkhus, no prior limit of craving for existence is discerned such that one could say: ‘Before this, craving for existence did not exist; after this, it came into being.’”

Thus, monks, association with unworthy persons, when fulfilled, fulfills hearing the false Dhamma;

Improper attention, when fulfilled, fulfills lack of clear comprehension;

the three kinds of misconduct, when fulfilled, fulfill the five hindrances; and the five hindrances, when fulfilled, fulfill ignorance.
They fulfill it; ignorance fulfills the craving for existence.

Just as, monks, when rain falls in heavy drops upon a mountain peak above, that water flows down according to the slope...
As it flows, it fills the mountain clefts, ravines, and gullies; the mountain clefts, ravines, and gullies being filled, fill the small pools;

lack of mindfulness and lack of clear comprehension fulfilled fulfills lack of restraint of the sense faculties; lack of restraint of the sense faculties fulfilled fulfills the three types of misconduct.
It fulfills them: the three types of misconduct, when fulfilled, fulfill the five hindrances; the five hindrances, when fulfilled, fulfill ignorance;
ignorance, when fulfilled, fulfills craving for existence.
In this way, this is the nutriment for that craving for existence, and in this way it reaches fulfillment.

“Bhikkhus, whoever has reached finality in me,

Of which five is there finality here?

“Bhikkhus, whoever has unwavering confidence in me,

Of which five is there finality here?

(AN 10.65, PTS AN v 120) On one occasion the Venerable Sāriputta was dwelling among the Magadhans at the village of Nālakagāma.
Then the wanderer Sāmaṇḍakāni approached the Venerable Sāriputta and exchanged greetings with him.
Having exchanged greetings and pleasantries with him, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the wanderer Sāmaṇḍakāni said this to the Venerable Sāriputta:
"Friend Sāriputta, what is suffering, and what is happiness?
"Rebirth, friend, is suffering; non-rebirth is happiness."
"Friends, when there is rebirth, this suffering is to be expected:
cold, heat, hunger, thirst, the touch of excrement and urine, the touch of fire, the touch of sticks, and the touch of weapons; and kinsmen and friends, having gathered together, reproach one.
Friends, when there is rebirth, this suffering is to be expected."
"Friends, when there is no further rebirth, this happiness is to be expected:

neither cold nor heat, neither hunger nor thirst, neither excrement nor urine, no contact with fire, no contact with sticks, and no contact with weapons; even kinsmen and friends, having gathered and come together, do not cause one distress.
Friends, when there is no further rebirth, this happiness is to be expected."

On one occasion the Venerable Sāriputta was dwelling among the Magadhans at the village of Nālakagāma.
