The First Naḷakapāna Discourse (AN 10.67, PTS AN v 122)
On one occasion, while wandering on tour among the Kosalans with a large community of monks, the Blessed One arrived at a market town of the Kosalans named Naḷakapāna.
There, the Blessed One stayed in the Palāsa Grove at Naḷakapāna.
Now at that time, on the Uposatha day, the Blessed One was seated surrounded by the community of monks.
Then the Blessed One, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the bhikkhus with a discourse on the Dhamma for much of the night,
surveyed the silent community of bhikkhus and addressed the Venerable Sāriputta:
“Sāriputta, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus is free from sloth and torpor.
Let a Dhamma talk occur to you, Sāriputta, for the bhikkhus.
My back is aching.”
“I shall attend upon him.
“Very well, Bhante,” the Venerable Sāriputta replied to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, having spread out his outer robe folded fourfold, lay down on his right side in the lion’s posture, placing one foot upon the other, mindful and clearly comprehending, with his mind fixed on the thought of rising.
There, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus:
"Friends, bhikkhus.
"Friend," those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Sāriputta.
The Venerable Sāriputta said this:
“Friends, whoever lacks faith in wholesome states, lacks a sense of shame,
and lacks a sense of moral dread— ”
If one lacks energy and lacks wisdom regarding wholesome states, then whether night or day comes for such a person, only decline in wholesome states is to be expected,
not growth. Just as, friends, in the dark fortnight, as night or day comes for the moon, it wanes in beauty, wanes in its orb, wanes in radiance, and wanes in height and circumference;
In the same way, friends, for whoever lacks faith in wholesome states,
lacks moral shame, lacks moral dread,
and lacks energy...
There is no wisdom regarding wholesome states; for such a person, whether night or day comes, only decline in wholesome states is to be expected, not growth.
"A person who lacks faith," friends, is a cause for decline;
"a person who lacks a sense of shame," friends, is a cause for decline.
‘A person who lacks moral dread,’ friends, is a cause for decline;
‘a person who is lazy,’ friends, is a cause for decline;
‘a person who is lacking in wisdom,’ friends, is a cause for decline.
“‘A person who is angry,’ friends, is a cause for decline;
‘a person who is resentful,’ friends, is a cause for decline;
‘a person who has evil desires,’ friends, is a cause for decline.”
“Friends, for a person who has bad friends, this is a cause of decline;
for a person who holds wrong view, friends, this is a cause of decline.
But whoever, friends, possesses faith in wholesome states, possesses a sense of shame…”
There is moral dread...
there is wisdom regarding wholesome states. For such a person, whether night or day comes, only growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline.
Just as, friends, during the waxing fortnight of the moon, whether night or day comes, it increases in beauty, increases in its orb, increases in radiance, and increases in height and circumference;
In the same way, friends, whoever possesses faith in wholesome states, possesses moral shame,
possesses moral dread,
and possesses energy...
There is wisdom regarding wholesome states; for such a person, whether night or day comes, only growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline.
"A person who is endowed with faith," friends, this is non-decline;
"a person who possesses a sense of shame," friends, this is non-decline.
‘A person who has a sense of moral dread,’ friends, is a sign of non-decline;
‘a person who has aroused energy,’ friends, is a sign of non-decline;
‘a person who possesses wisdom,’ friends, is a sign of non-decline.
“‘A person who is free from anger,’ friends, is a case of non-decline;
‘a person who is free from malice,’ friends, is a case of non-decline;
‘a person who has few desires,’ friends, is a case of non-decline.”
“Friends, a person who has a virtuous friend: this is non-decline.
A person who holds right view: this, friends, is non-decline.
Then the Blessed One rose and addressed the Venerable Sāriputta:
“Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta!
For anyone, Sāriputta, who lacks faith in wholesome states, lacks moral shame,
and lacks moral dread— ”
If one lacks energy and lacks wisdom regarding wholesome states, then whether night or day comes for such a person, only decline in wholesome states is to be expected,
not growth. Just as, Sāriputta, during the dark fortnight of the moon, whether night or day comes, it wanes in beauty, wanes in its orb, wanes in radiance, and wanes in height and circumference;

lacks wisdom in wholesome qualities, for them, whether it be night or day ... there is no growth.
"A person who is faithless," Sāriputta, this is a cause for decline.
one who is shameless … one who lacks moral dread … one who is indolent …
one who is lacking in wisdom … one who is prone to anger … one who is resentful …
‘A person who has evil desires… evil friends… wrong view,’ Sāriputta, this is a cause for decline.
“Sāriputta, whoever has faith in wholesome states, has a sense of shame,
has moral dread,
and has energy— ”
If one possesses wisdom regarding wholesome states, then whether night or day comes upon them, only growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline.
Just as, Sāriputta, in the bright fortnight, as night or day comes upon the moon, it increases in beauty, increases in its orb, increases in radiance, and increases in height and circumference;
even so, Sāriputta, for anyone who has faith in wholesome states, who has a sense of shame…
When there is moral dread, energy,
and wisdom regarding wholesome states, then whether night or day comes, only growth in wholesome states is to be expected for him, not decline.
‘A person who is endowed with faith,’ Sāriputta, this is a state of non-decline; one who has a sense of shame … one who has a sense of moral dread … [is likewise a state of non-decline].
...one who has aroused energy ...
one who possesses wisdom ... one who is free from anger ...
one who is free from resentment … one who has few desires … one who has virtuous friends …
“‘A person of right view,’ Sāriputta, this is a state of non-decline.
The seventh. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.68
7. Yamaka Chapter:
The Second Naḷakapāna Discourse (AN 10.68, PTS AN v 125)
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Naḷakapāna in the Palāsa Grove.
Now on that occasion, on the Uposatha day, the Blessed One was seated surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
Then the Blessed One, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened the bhikkhus with a discourse on the Dhamma for much of the night, [arose from his seat].
Having inspired and gladdened them, he surveyed the silent community of monks and addressed the Venerable Sāriputta:
“Sāriputta, the community of monks is free from sloth and torpor.”
“Let a Dhamma talk occur to you, Sāriputta, for the bhikkhus.
My back is aching;
I shall stretch it.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Sāriputta replied to the Blessed One.

Then the Blessed One, having folded his outer robe into four layers, lay down on his right side in the lion’s posture, placing one foot upon the other, mindful and clearly comprehending, having fixed his mind on the thought of rising.
Thereupon, the Venerable Sāriputta addressed the bhikkhus:
“Friends, monks. The monks replied to the Venerable Sāriputta,
“Friend,” and the Venerable Sāriputta said this:
“Friends, whoever lacks faith in wholesome states, lacks a sense of shame,
lacks moral dread,
and lacks energy….”
There is no wisdom;
there is no hearkening to the Dhamma; there is no retention of the Dhamma.
There is no investigation of the meaning;
there is no practice in accordance with the Dhamma;
there is no heedfulness regarding wholesome states. For such a person, whether night or day comes, only decline and not growth in wholesome states is to be expected.
"Friend, just as during the dark fortnight, whatever night or day comes, the moon wanes in beauty, wanes in its orb, wanes in radiance,
and wanes in height and circumference; even so, friend, for anyone who lacks faith in wholesome qualities,
lacks moral shame, and lacks moral dread..."
There is no energy … there is no wisdom … there is no application of the ear …
There is no retention of the Dhamma… there is no investigation of the meaning… there is no practice in accordance with the Dhamma…
If there is no heedfulness regarding wholesome states, then whether night or day comes for him, only decline in wholesome states is to be expected, not growth.
But for anyone, friend, who has faith in wholesome states, who has a sense of shame... who has a sense of moral dread... [these qualities will lead to growth].
There is energy;
there is wisdom;
there is attentive listening.
There is the retention of the Dhamma;
there is the investigation of the meaning;
there is the practice in accordance with the Dhamma.
"There is heedfulness regarding wholesome states. For one who possesses this, whether night or day comes, only growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline.
Just as, friends, in the bright fortnight, as night or day comes, the moon increases in beauty, increases in its orb, increases in radiance, and increases in height and circumference;
even so, friends, for anyone who has faith in wholesome states... [and so on]."
“Diligence regarding wholesome states exists; for one who possesses it, whether night or day comes, only growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline.
Then the Blessed One rose and addressed the Venerable Sāriputta:
“Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta!”
Sāriputta, whoever lacks faith in wholesome states, lacks moral shame,
lacks moral dread,
and lacks wisdom—
There is no energy;
there is no lending an ear;
there is no retention of the Dhamma.
For him there is no investigation of the meaning,
no practice in accordance with the Dhamma,
and no heedfulness regarding wholesome states; whether night or day comes upon him, one can only expect decline in wholesome states, not growth.
"Just as, Sāriputta, during the dark fortnight, whether night or day comes, the moon wanes in beauty, wanes in its orb, wanes in radiance, and wanes in height and circumference;
even so, Sāriputta, for anyone who lacks faith in wholesome states...
[and so on] ...who lacks diligence in wholesome states, whether night or day comes, only decline in wholesome states is to be expected, not growth."
"Whoever, Sāriputta, has faith in wholesome states, has a sense of shame,
has moral dread,
and has energy..."
There is wisdom;
there is attentive listening;
there is the retention of the Dhamma.
There is investigation of the meaning;
there is practice in accordance with the Dhamma;
there is diligence regarding wholesome states. For one who possesses these, whether night or day comes, only growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline.

“Sāriputta, just as during the bright fortnight, whether night or day comes, the moon only increases in beauty, increases in its orb, increases in radiance, and increases in height and circumference; even so, Sāriputta,
for anyone who has faith in wholesome states … [and so on] … who has diligence in wholesome states,
whether night or day comes, only growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline.”
The Eighth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.69 7.
Yamaka Chapter (Pairs)
Paṭhamakathāvatthusutta (AN 10.69).
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, after returning from their alms round following the meal, a number of bhikkhus were seated together and gathered in the assembly hall,
dwelling engaged in various kinds of worldly talk, such as: talk of kings, talk of thieves, talk of ministers, talk of armies, talk of dangers, talk of wars, talk of food,
talk of drinks, talk of clothing, talk of bedding, talk of garlands, talk of perfumes, talk of relatives, and talk of vehicles.

"Talk about villages, talk about market towns, talk about cities, talk about the countryside, talk about women, talk about heroes, talk about streets, talk about wells, talk about the departed, talk about various matters, talk about speculations concerning the world, talk about speculations concerning the ocean, talk about 'thus it was' and 'thus it will be.
Then, in the evening, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion and went to the assembly hall; having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, for what discussion are you gathered and seated here now? And what was the conversation of yours that remained unfinished?

“Venerable sir, having returned from our almsround after the meal, we were gathered and seated here in the assembly hall when we remained engaged in various kinds of worldly talk, such as this: [and so forth].
“Talk about kings, talk about thieves… [and so on] … or talk about ‘thus it was’ and ‘thus it will be.

“But this, monks, is not fitting for you, sons of good family who have gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith, that you should dwell devoted to various kinds of worldly chatter, such as:

talk about kings, talk about thieves, talk about ministers, talk about armies, talk about dangers, talk about battles, talk about food, [talk about drink, talk about clothes, talk about beds, talk about garlands, talk about perfumes, talk about relatives, talk about vehicles, talk about villages, talk about towns, talk about cities, talk about countries, talk about women, talk about men, talk about heroes, talk about streets, talk about wells, talk about those who have departed, talk about various trifles, talk about the origin of the world, talk about the origin of the ocean, talk about whether things exist or do not exist].”
Talk about drinks, talk about clothes, talk about beds, talk about garlands, talk about scents, talk about relatives,
talk about vehicles, talk about villages, talk about towns, talk about cities, talk about countries, talk about women, talk about heroes, talk about streets, talk about wells,

talk about departed ancestors, talk about various matters, talk about speculations concerning the world, talk about speculations concerning the ocean, and talk about "thus it was" and "thus it will be."
“Monks, there are these ten bases for discourse.
What are the ten?

Discourse on fewness of desires, discourse on contentment, discourse on seclusion, discourse on non-association, discourse on the arousal of energy, discourse on virtue, discourse on concentration, discourse on wisdom, discourse on liberation, and discourse on the knowledge and vision of liberation.”
“Monks, these are the ten bases of discourse. Monks,
if you were to engage in discussion by taking each of these ten bases of discourse as a starting point,
you could outshine with your own brilliance even the brilliance of the sun and moon, so powerful and so majestic.”
“What need is there to mention other wanderers of different sects?
Thus ends the ninth [discourse]. *Aṅguttara Nikāya* 10.70.
7. Yamaka Chapter:
The Second Discourse on the Basis of Talk (AN 10.70, PTS AN v 129)
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

Now on that occasion, after the meal, on returning from their alms round, a number of bhikkhus were sitting gathered together in the assembly hall, engaged in various kinds of worldly talk, such as talk about kings, thieves, and ministers of state...
[and so forth] ...talk about whether things are so or are not so.
“Monks, there are these ten grounds for praise.
What are the ten?
Here, monks, a monk himself is of few desires, and he is one who speaks to the monks on the topic of fewness of desires.”
‘A bhikkhu who is of few desires and who speaks to the bhikkhus about having few desires’—this is a ground for praise.
He himself is contented and he speaks to the bhikkhus about contentment.
‘A bhikkhu who is contented and who speaks to the bhikkhus about contentment’—this is a ground for praise.
One is secluded oneself and is a speaker of talk on seclusion for the bhikkhus.
This is a ground for praise: ‘The bhikkhu is secluded and is a speaker of talk on seclusion for the bhikkhus.
One is unassociated oneself and is a speaker of talk on non-association for the bhikkhus.
‘A bhikkhu who is unattached and who speaks to the bhikkhus about non-attachment’—this is a ground for praise.
He himself is one who has aroused energy and he speaks to the bhikkhus about the arousal of energy.
‘A bhikkhu who has aroused energy and who speaks to the bhikkhus about the arousal of energy’—this is a ground for praise.
He himself is endowed with virtue and is one who speaks to the bhikkhus on the perfection of virtue.
That this bhikkhu is endowed with virtue and speaks to the bhikkhus on the perfection of virtue is a ground for praise.
He himself is endowed with concentration and is one who speaks to the bhikkhus on the perfection of concentration.
‘A bhikkhu accomplished in concentration, who speaks to the bhikkhus on the accomplishment of concentration’—this is a ground for praise.
He himself is accomplished in wisdom and speaks to the bhikkhus on the accomplishment of wisdom.
‘A bhikkhu accomplished in wisdom, who speaks to the bhikkhus on the accomplishment of wisdom’—this is a ground for praise.
One is oneself accomplished in liberation and is a speaker to the bhikkhus on the accomplishment of liberation.
This is a ground for praise: ‘A bhikkhu is accomplished in liberation and is a speaker to the bhikkhus on the accomplishment of liberation.
One is oneself accomplished in the knowledge and vision of liberation and is a speaker to the bhikkhus on the accomplishment of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
‘A bhikkhu endowed with the knowledge and vision of liberation is one who speaks to the bhikkhus on the perfection of the knowledge and vision of liberation’—this is a ground for praise.
These, monks, are the ten grounds for praise.
The tenth [sutta].
The Second Chapter on Pairs.
Its summary verse:
Ignorance, craving, and the goal.
"Having understood, and two on happiness;
two were spoken at Naḷakapāna,
and two more on the bases of discourse."

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.71 8. Ākaṅkhavagga Ākaṅkhasutta (The Discourse on Wishing) “Monks, there are these ten things that one who wishes for what is wholesome, who wishes for what is beneficial, who wishes for what is pleasant, who wishes for what is agreeable, who wishes for happiness, who wishes for security from bondage, who wishes for the unsurpassed security from bondage, who wishes for the unsurpassed bliss, who wishes for the unsurpassed awakening, should develop. What ten? (1) One who wishes for what is wholesome, who wishes for what is beneficial, who wishes for what is pleasant, who wishes for what is agreeable, who wishes for happiness, who wishes for security from bondage, who wishes for the unsurpassed security from bondage, who wishes for the unsurpassed bliss, who wishes for the unsurpassed awakening, should develop unwavering confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. (2) One who wishes for what is wholesome… should develop unwavering confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. (3) One who wishes for what is wholesome… should develop unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. (4) One who wishes for what is wholesome… should develop the virtue that is untorn, unbroken, unspotted, unsplattered, liberating, praised by the wise, untarnished, leading to concentration. (5) One who wishes for what is wholesome… should develop the perception of impermanence regarding the body, the perception of non-self regarding all phenomena, the perception of death, the perception of the repulsiveness of food, the perception of non-delight in the entire world, the perception of the suffering in what is subject to arising, the perception of the non-self in what is subject to cessation, the perception of abandoning, the perception of dispassion, and the perception of cessation. (6) One who wishes for what is wholesome… should develop loving-kindness as a basis for meditation, extensive, exalted, measureless, without enmity, without ill will. (7) One who wishes for what is wholesome… should develop compassion as a basis for meditation, extensive, exalted, measureless, without enmity, without ill will. (8) One who wishes for what is wholesome… should develop altruistic joy as a basis for meditation, extensive, exalted, measureless, without enmity, without ill will. (9) One who wishes for what is wholesome… should develop equanimity as a basis for meditation, extensive, exalted, measureless, without enmity, without ill will. (10) One who wishes for what is wholesome, who wishes for what is beneficial, who wishes for what is pleasant, who wishes for what is agreeable, who wishes for happiness, who wishes for security from bondage, who wishes for the unsurpassed security from bondage, who wishes for the unsurpassed bliss, who wishes for the unsurpassed awakening, should develop insight into the nature of phenomena as they really are, which leads to the complete destruction of suffering. These, monks, are the ten things that one who wishes for what is wholesome, who wishes for what is beneficial, who wishes for what is pleasant, who wishes for what is agreeable, who wishes for happiness, who wishes for security from bondage, who wishes for the unsurpassed security from bondage, who wishes for the unsurpassed bliss, who wishes for the unsurpassed awakening, should develop.”
(AN 10.71, PTS AN v 131) On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Monks,” [the Blessed One said]. “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One spoke as follows:

“Monks, dwell with virtue perfected, with the Pātimokkha perfected; dwell restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, endowed with proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and train yourselves by undertaking the rules of training.

Monks, if a monk should desire: ‘May I be dear to my fellow celibates, pleasing to them, respected, and esteemed,’ he should fulfill the precepts of virtue, be devoted to internal tranquility of mind, and not neglect meditative absorption.”
One endowed with insight is a cultivator of empty huts.
Monks, if a monk should wish, "May I be a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick," he should be one who fulfills his moral discipline,
is devoted to internal mental tranquility, does not neglect meditative absorption, and is intent on insight.
One who possesses these qualities is a cultivator of empty huts.

Monks, if a monk should desire: "May the services of those for whom I enjoy robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick be of great fruit and great benefit to them," he should, in that very regard, [be established] in the virtues... [as before] ...be a cultivator of empty huts.

“Monks, if a monk should wish: ‘May that which my deceased relatives and kinsmen, who have passed away, remember with a confident heart, be of great fruit and great benefit for them,’ then he should, in this very life, be perfect in virtue...

[as before] ...and be one who frequents empty dwellings. “Monks, if a monk should wish: ‘May I be content with whatever robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick may be available,’ then he should, in this very life, be perfect in virtue... [as before] ...and be one who frequents empty dwellings.”
“Monks, if a monk should wish: ‘May I be patient with cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things;
may I be patient with offensive and unwelcome modes of speech, and with arisen bodily feelings that are painful, racking, sharp, piercing, bitter, disagreeable, unpleasant, and life-threatening,”
“May I be one who is patient,” [thinking thus,] he should fulfill the training rules...
[and so on] ...be one who frequents empty huts. Monks, if a monk should wish: “May I be one who endures both the unpleasant and the pleasant; may neither the unpleasant nor the pleasant overcome me;
may I dwell having repeatedly overcome whatever unpleasantness or pleasure has arisen,” he should fulfill the training rules... [and so on] ...be one who frequents empty huts.
“Monks, if a monk should wish: ‘May I be a conqueror of fear and dread, and may fear and dread not conquer me;

may I dwell having repeatedly overcome whatever fear and dread has arisen,’ then he should, for that purpose, be devoted to the higher training in virtue, be devoted to the higher training in concentration, be devoted to the higher training in wisdom, be devoted to solitude, be devoted to non-affliction, be devoted to non-contention, and be one who frequents empty huts.”

“Monks, if a monk should wish: ‘May I be one who gains at will, without difficulty, and without hardship, the four jhānas that are higher mental states and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life,’ he should, in that case, [fulfill] the precepts... [and so on]... be a cultivator of empty huts.
If a monk should wish: ‘Through the destruction of the taints, may I realize for myself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom...’”
‘May I dwell having realized for myself with direct knowledge in this very life, having attained it. To this end,
he should be one who fulfills virtuous conduct, is devoted to internal mental serenity, does not neglect meditative absorption,
is endowed with insight, and frequents empty dwellings.
“‘Monks, dwell possessed of virtue, possessed of the Pātimokkha; dwell restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha,
possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and train yourselves by undertaking the rules of training’—
it was with reference to this that it was said.”
First.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.72 8.
Ākaṅkhavagga (The Chapter on Wishes)
The Kaṇṭaka Sutta (AN 10.72).
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Hall with the Peaked Roof, together with many well-known and renowned elder disciples.
Together with the Venerable Cāla, the Venerable Upacāla, the Venerable Kukkuṭa, the Venerable Kaḷimba, the Venerable Nikaṭa, the Venerable Kaṭissaha,
and many other well-known and renowned elder disciples.
Now at that time, a great many well-known Licchavis, in magnificent and splendid carriages, entered deep into the Great Forest with loud noises and great clamor, in order to see the Blessed One.
Then it occurred to those venerable ones:
"These many well-known Licchavis, filling their fine carriages, are plunging deep into the Great Forest with loud noises and great clamor to see the Blessed One.
But the Blessed One has said that sounds are a thorn to meditative absorption."
"Perhaps we should go to the Gosiṅga Sāla-tree grove.
There we may dwell in comfort, free from noise and free from crowds.
Then those venerable ones went to the Gosiṅga Sāla-tree grove.
There those venerable ones dwelt at ease, free from noise and free from crowds.
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Where, bhikkhus, are Cāla, Upacāla, Kukkuṭa, Kaḷimbha, Nikaṭa, and Kaṭissaha?”
“Where, monks, have those elder disciples gone?
“Here, venerable sir, it occurred to those venerable ones:
‘These many well-known Licchavis, with their various magnificent carriages, are filling the city.’”
"Making loud noises and great clamor, they plunge deep into the great forest to see the Blessed One;
yet the Blessed One has said that meditative absorptions have sound as their thorn.
Suppose we were to go to the Gosiṅga Sāl Forest grove, where we might dwell in comfort, free from noise and free from crowds."
“Then, Bhante, those venerable ones approached the Gosiṅga Sāl-tree grove.
There, those venerable ones dwelt in comfort, free from noise and free from crowds.
“Excellent, excellent, bhikkhus! It is just as those great disciples would speak when speaking correctly: for I have said, bhikkhus, that noise is a thorn to jhāna.”
"Monks, there are these ten thorns.
What are the ten?
For one who delights in solitude, delighting in company is a thorn; for one devoted to the practice of the sign of the unattractive, devotion to the sign of the attractive is a thorn."
Thorns: for one who guards the doors of the sense faculties, looking at shows is a thorn; for the holy life, the presence of women is a thorn; for the first *jhāna*, sound is a thorn;
for the second *jhāna*, applied and sustained thought (*vitakka-vicāra*) are thorns;
for the third *jhāna*, rapture (*pīti*) is a thorn; for the fourth *jhāna*, inhalation and exhalation are thorns; and for the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling...
Perception and feeling are thorns; lust is a thorn, hatred is a thorn, and delusion is a thorn.
Monks, dwell free from thorns; monks, dwell with thorns removed.
“Monks, dwell free from thorns and free from brambles.
Monks, the arahants are free from thorns; the arahants are free from brambles.”
“Bhikkhus, the arahants are free from thorns and without thorns.
The second [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.73

8. Ākaṅkhavagga Iṭṭhadhammasutta (AN 10.73, PTS AN v 135) “Bhikkhus, there are these four things that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, and dear, which are not easy to obtain in the world. What four? Long life, bhikkhus, is a thing that is desirable, lovely, agreeable, and dear, which is not easy to obtain in the world. Beauty, bhikkhus, is a thing that is desirable, lovely, agreeable, and dear, which is not easy to obtain in the world. Happiness, bhikkhus, is a thing that is desirable, lovely, agreeable, and dear, which is not easy to obtain in the world. A good reputation, bhikkhus, is a thing that is desirable, lovely, agreeable, and dear, which is not easy to obtain in the world. These, bhikkhus, are the four things that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, and dear, which are not easy to obtain in the world.”
“Monks, there are these ten things that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, and rare in the world.
What are the ten?
Wealth that is desirable, lovely, agreeable, and rare in the world;”
Beauty is desirable, lovely, pleasing, and rare in the world;
health is desirable, lovely, pleasing, and rare in the world;
virtue is desirable, lovely, pleasing, and rare in the world.
The holy life is desirable, lovely, pleasing, and rare in the world;
friends who are desirable, lovely, and pleasing are rare in the world;
great learning is desirable, lovely, pleasing, and rare in the world.
Wisdom is desirable, lovely, and pleasing, yet it is rare in the world;
the teachings are desirable, lovely, and pleasing, yet they are rare in the world;
the heavenly realms are desirable, lovely, and pleasing, yet they are rare in the world.
“Monks, for these ten things that are desirable, lovely, pleasing, and rare in the world, there are ten things that act as obstacles:
laziness and lack of exertion are obstacles to wealth; lack of grooming and lack of adornment are obstacles to beauty;
unwholesome conduct is an obstacle to health; association with evil friends is an obstacle to virtuous conduct; lack of restraint over the sense faculties...”
Deceit is an obstacle to the holy life; deceiving friends is an obstacle to friendship; lack of recitation is an obstacle to great learning;
lack of desire to hear and lack of inquiry are obstacles to wisdom; lack of application and lack of reflection are obstacles to the teachings;
and wrong practice is an obstacle to the heavens.
“Monks, for these ten things that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, and rare in the world, there are these ten states that act as obstacles.
Monks, for these ten states that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, and rare in the world, there are ten things that serve as their nourishment:
exertion and lack of laziness are the nourishment for wealth; grooming and adornment are the nourishment for beauty; and appropriate conduct is the nourishment for health.”
Health is the nourishment for freedom from disease; association with good friends is the nourishment for virtuous conduct; restraint of the sense faculties is the nourishment for the holy life;
non-deceitfulness is the nourishment for friends; recitation and practice are the nourishment for great learning;
listening and inquiry are the nourishment for wisdom; application and reflection are the nourishment for the teachings; and right practice is the nourishment for the heavenly realms.
“Monks, these ten things are the nourishment for these ten things that are desirable, lovely, pleasing, and rare in the world.
The third.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.74

8. Ākaṅkhavagga Vaḍḍhisutta (AN 10.74) “Monks, when a noble disciple possesses four qualities, he is one who increases in wealth, grain, silver, and gold; he is one who increases in servants, workers, and laborers; he is one who increases in wives, sons, and daughters; he is one who increases in elephants, cattle, horses, and mules; he is one who increases in fields and lands; he is one who increases in reputation; he is one who increases in longevity; and he is one who increases in wisdom. What four? Here, monks, a noble disciple possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. He possesses unwavering confidence in the Dhamma: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. He possesses unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals. This Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. And he possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—virtues that are untorn, unrent, unblotched, unmottled, liberating, praised by the wise, unadhered-to, and leading to concentration. When a noble disciple possesses these four qualities, monks, he is one who increases in wealth, grain, silver, and gold... he is one who increases in wisdom.”
“Bhikkhus, growing by ten kinds of growth, a noble disciple grows by noble growth; he becomes one who takes hold of the essence and takes hold of the excellence of the body.
What are the ten? He grows in fields and lands; he grows in wealth and grain; he grows in children and wives; he grows in slaves, laborers, and servants...”
It increases: it increases in four-footed creatures, it increases in faith, it increases in virtue, it increases in learning, it increases in generosity, and it increases in wisdom.

Monks, when an noble disciple increases by these ten kinds of increase, he increases by the noble increase; he becomes one who takes hold of the essence and takes hold of what is excellent for his body.
The person who prospers through wealth,
grain, children, wife, and four-footed livestock,
becomes wealthy, renowned, and honored.
Whether by kinsmen, friends, or even kings,
he who increases in faith, virtue, wisdom, generosity, and learning— both of these [groups]— will prosper.
Thus such a true person, discerning,
prospers in both ways even in this very life. Thus ends the fourth [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.75 8. Ākaṅkhavagga Migasālāsutta At Sāvatthī. Then the female lay follower Migasālā approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to him: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I may dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute.

“It is not easy, Migasālā, for one who has not seen form as it really is, who has not seen feeling as it really is, who has not seen perception as it really is, who has not seen volitional formations as they really are, and who has not seen consciousness as it really is, to abandon desire for them. “But when one has seen form as it really is, feeling as it really is, perception as it really is, volitional formations as they really are, and consciousness as it really is, one abandons desire for them. “When, Migasālā, a noble disciple has abandoned desire for form, abandoned desire for feeling, abandoned desire for perception, abandoned desire for volitional formations, and abandoned desire for consciousness, he is called a noble disciple who has cut off craving, stripped off the fetter, and by completely breaking through conceit, has made an end of suffering. “Suppose, Migasālā, there was a householder or a householder’s son, rich, with great wealth and property, with abundant gold, silver, bullion, and treasure, abundant fields, lands, and estates, abundant vehicles, both yoked and unyoked, abundant wives, male and female slaves, and workers and servants, abundant grain, fodder, and fuel. Then his house would be set on fire. When the house was burning, he would first try to pull out from the burning house his sons, his daughters, and his daughters-in-law. Having pulled out his sons, his daughters, and his daughters-in-law from the burning house, he would afterwards himself come out. “In the same way, Migasālā, when a noble disciple has abandoned desire for form, abandoned desire for feeling, abandoned desire for perception, abandoned desire for volitional formations, and abandoned desire for consciousness, he is called a noble disciple who has cut off craving, stripped off the fetter, and by completely breaking through conceit, has made an end of suffering. When this was said, the female lay follower Migasālā said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir!... From today let the Blessed One remember me as a female lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”
(AN 10.75, PTS AN v 137) On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then, in the morning, the Venerable Ānanda dressed, took his bowl and robe, and went to the residence of the female lay follower Migasālā. Having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Then the female lay follower Migasālā approached the Venerable Ānanda;
having approached, she paid homage to the Venerable Ānanda and sat down to one side. As she was sitting there, the female lay follower Migasālā said this to the Venerable Ānanda:

"In what way, Bhante Ānanda, is the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One so difficult to understand, that both the celibate practitioner and the non-celibate practitioner will have exactly the same destination in the life hereafter?"
“Venerable sir, my father Purāṇa was a celibate, one who lived apart and abstained from sexual intercourse, the village practice.
When he passed away, the Blessed One declared: ‘The being Purāṇa is a once-returner; he has been reborn in the Tusita body.
Venerable sir, my grandfather Isidatta was not a celibate; he was content with his own wife.”
“He too has passed away, and the Blessed One has declared: ‘The being who was a once-returner has been reborn in the Tusita host.

How, venerable Ānanda, is the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One so difficult to understand, that both one who leads a holy life and one who does not lead a holy life will have exactly the same destination in the life hereafter?
“It is indeed thus, sister, that this has been declared by the Blessed One.”
Then the Venerable Ānanda, having received almsfood at the residence of the female lay follower Migasālā, rose from his seat and departed.
Then, after his meal, having returned from his almsround, the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable...
Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“Here, Bhante, having dressed in the morning and taking my bowl and robe, I approached the residence of the female lay follower Migasālā; having approached, I sat down on the prepared seat.

Then, Bhante, the female lay follower Migasālā approached me; having approached and paid homage to me, she sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Bhante, the female lay follower Migasālā said this to me:”

“How, venerable Ānanda, is the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One so that it can be understood? For here, indeed, both one who leads the holy life and one who does not lead the holy life will have the same destination in the life to come.
My father, venerable sir, Purāṇa, was one who led the holy life; he lived far from sensual pleasures and abstained from the village practice of sexual intercourse.
When he passed away, the Blessed One declared: ‘This being is a once-returner; having returned once more to this world, he will make an end of suffering.’”
“Venerable sir, my grandfather Isidatta was not a practitioner of the holy life; he was content with his own wife.
Yet when he passed away, the Blessed One declared: ‘This being is a once-returner who has been reborn in the Tusita body.

Venerable Ānanda, how is it that the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One can be understood in such a way, where both one who practices the holy life and one who does not practice the holy life will have exactly the same destination in the life hereafter?”
When this was said, Bhante, I said to the female lay follower Migasālā:
“Sister, it has indeed been declared thus by the Blessed One.

“But Ānanda, who is this female lay follower Migasālā—foolish, incompetent, a mere woman with a woman’s wit—and who are those [who are experts] in the knowledge of the higher and lower qualities of persons?”
"Ānanda, these ten types of persons are found existing in the world.
Which ten?
Here, Ānanda, a certain person is immoral."
And he does not understand, as it really is, that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein his immorality ceases without remainder.
He has neither heard [the teaching], nor mastered it through great learning, nor penetrated it with right view; he does not even attain temporary liberation.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he goes to deterioration, not to distinction.
He goes only toward decline, not toward distinction.
But here, Ānanda, a certain person is immoral,
yet he understands, as it really is, that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein his immorality ceases without remainder.
For him, it is accomplished through hearing, accomplished through learning, and his view has been penetrated; he also attains temporary liberation.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he proceeds to distinction, not to decline;
he is one who goes toward distinction, not one who goes toward decline.
In this regard, Ānanda, those who measure by means of a measuring-stick judge thus:
‘These qualities belong to this one, and those same qualities belong to the other. Why then is one inferior and the other superior?
For that, Ānanda, leads to their harm and suffering for a long time.
In this regard, Ānanda, as for that person who is immoral:
he understands, as it really is, that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein his immorality ceases without remainder.
He has done so through hearing, he has done so through great learning, he has penetrated it through right view, and he even attains temporary liberation.
This person, Ānanda, is more excellent and more sublime than that former person.
Why is that? Because, Ānanda, the stream of Dhamma carries this person across.
Who else but a Tathāgata could know that?
Therefore, Ānanda, do not be one who measures persons;
do not take the measure of persons.
One incurs harm, Ānanda, by taking a measure of persons.
Either I, Ānanda, might take a measure of persons, or one who is like me.
But here, Ānanda, a certain person is virtuous.
And he does not understand, as it really is, that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein his virtue ceases without remainder.
He has neither heard [the Dhamma], nor mastered it through learning, nor penetrated it with vision; he does not even attain temporary liberation.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he goes to deterioration, not to distinction.
He is one who goes only toward decline, not toward distinction.
But here, Ānanda, a certain person is virtuous;
he understands, as it really is, that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein his virtue ceases without remainder.
For him, it has been accomplished through hearing, it has been accomplished through great learning, and it has been penetrated by view; he also attains temporary liberation.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he proceeds to distinction, not to decline;
he is one who goes toward distinction, not one who goes toward decline.
In this regard, Ānanda, those who measure by means of a measure...
[as before] ...either I, Ānanda, might take a measure of persons, or someone like me.
But here, Ānanda, a certain person is one of intense passion.
And he does not understand, as it really is, that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein his lust ceases without remainder.
He has neither heard [the teaching], nor mastered it through learning, nor penetrated it with vision; he does not even attain temporary liberation.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he goes to deterioration, not to distinction.
He goes only toward decline, not toward distinction.
But here, Ānanda, a certain person is one of intense passion;
yet he understands, as it really is, that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein his passion ceases without remainder.
For him, it has been accomplished through hearing, it has been accomplished through great learning, and it has been penetrated through right view; he also attains temporary liberation.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he proceeds to distinction, not to decline;
he is one who goes toward distinction, not one who goes toward decline.
In this regard, Ānanda, those who measure measure...
[as before] ...Either I, Ānanda, or someone like me, would take the measure of persons.
Now, Ānanda, here a certain person is prone to anger.
And he does not understand, as it really is, that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein his anger ceases without remainder.
He has neither heard about it, nor mastered it through learning, nor penetrated it with vision; he does not even attain temporary liberation.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he goes to deterioration, not to distinction.
He goes only toward decline, not toward distinction.
But here, Ānanda, a certain person is prone to anger;
yet he understands, as it truly is, that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein his anger ceases without remainder.
For him, it has been accomplished through hearing, it has been accomplished through great learning, and it has been penetrated through right view; he also attains temporary liberation.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he proceeds to distinction, not to decline;
he is one who goes to distinction, not one who goes to decline.
In this regard, Ānanda, those who measure measure...
[as before] ...Either I, Ānanda, might take the measure of persons, or one who is like me.
But here, Ānanda, a certain person is restless.
And he does not understand, as it really is, that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein his restlessness ceases without remainder.
For him, there has been no hearing, no mastery of the scriptures, and no penetration of the view; he does not even attain temporary liberation.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he goes to deterioration, not to distinction.
He goes only toward decline, not toward distinction.
But here, Ānanda, a certain person is restless;
yet he understands, as it really is, that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein his restlessness ceases without remainder.
For him, it has been accomplished through hearing, it has been accomplished through great learning, and it has been penetrated through right view; he also attains temporary liberation.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he proceeds to distinction, not to decline;
he is one who goes toward distinction, not one who goes toward decline.
In this regard, Ānanda, those who judge by measure say:
"These same qualities belong to this one; these same qualities belong to that other. Why is one inferior and the other superior?
For that, Ānanda, leads to their harm and suffering for a long time.
In this regard, Ānanda, as for that person who is restless, yet understands as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein his restlessness ceases without remainder:
he has accomplished it through hearing, he has accomplished it through great learning, he has penetrated it through right view, and he attains temporary liberation.
This person, Ānanda, is more excellent and more sublime than the former person.
For what reason?
Because, Ānanda, the stream of Dhamma carries this person across.
Who else but the Tathāgata could know that interval?
Therefore, Ānanda, do not be one who measures persons;
do not take the measure of persons.
For one who takes the measure of persons, Ānanda, is harmed.
"Or, Ānanda, I myself might measure persons, or someone like me might do so.

But what is Migasālā the female lay follower, who is foolish, incompetent, a mere woman with a woman's wit, compared to those who possess the knowledge of discerning the higher and lower qualities of persons?
These, Ānanda, are the ten persons found existing in the world."
“Ānanda, if Isidatta had been endowed with the same kind of virtue as Purāṇa was, then Purāṇa would not have known even the destination of Isidatta after death.
And, Ānanda, if Purāṇa had been endowed with the same kind of wisdom as Isidatta was, then Isidatta would not have known even the destination of Purāṇa after death.
Thus, Ānanda, both these individuals were deficient in one respect.”
Fifth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.76. Chapter 8:
On Wishes (Ākaṅkhavagga).

“Bhikkhus, if these three things did not exist in the world, a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One would not arise in the world, nor would the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata shine forth in the world. What are the three? They are: birth, aging, and death.”
Which three?
Birth, aging, and death—these three things, monks, would not be found in the world;
the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, would not arise in the world; and the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata would not shine forth in the world.

But because, monks, these three things are found in the world, therefore a Tathāgata arises in the world—an Arhat, a perfectly enlightened Buddha—and therefore the Dhamma-Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata shines forth in the world.
Monks, without abandoning these three things, one is incapable of abandoning birth, abandoning aging, and abandoning death.
What are the three?
“Without abandoning lust, without abandoning hatred, and without abandoning delusion— monks,
it is impossible for one who has not abandoned these three things to abandon birth, to abandon aging, and to abandon death. And, monks,
it is impossible for one who has not abandoned these three things to abandon lust, to abandon hatred, and to abandon delusion.”
Which three? Without having abandoned personality-belief, without having abandoned doubt, and without having abandoned adherence to rules and observances—
these, monks, are the three things that, if not abandoned, one is incapable of abandoning lust, abandoning hatred, and abandoning delusion.
“Bhikkhus, without abandoning three things, one is incapable of abandoning the view of a personal identity, abandoning doubt, and abandoning adherence to rules and observances.
What are the three?
Without abandoning improper attention, without abandoning following a wrong path, and without abandoning mental sluggishness.”

“Monks, without abandoning these three things, one is incapable of abandoning the view of a self-existent body (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), abandoning doubt (*vicikicchā*), and abandoning adherence to rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*).

Monks, without abandoning these three things, one is incapable of abandoning improper attention (*ayoniso manasikāra*), abandoning the pursuit of wrong paths (*kummaggasevana*), and abandoning mental sluggishness (*cetaso līnatta*).
What are the three?”

“Without abandoning these three things, monks, one is incapable of abandoning careless attention, following a wrong path, and mental sluggishness: namely, without abandoning forgetfulness, without abandoning lack of clear comprehension, and without abandoning mental distraction.
Furthermore, monks, without abandoning these three things, one is incapable of abandoning forgetfulness, lack of clear comprehension, and mental distraction.”

Which three? Without having abandoned the desire not to see the noble ones, without having abandoned the desire not to hear the noble Dhamma, and without having abandoned a mind intent on fault-finding—
it is impossible, monks, for one who has not abandoned these three things to abandon forgetfulness, to abandon lack of clear comprehension, and to abandon mental distraction.
“Bhikkhus, without having abandoned three things, one is incapable of abandoning the desire not to see the noble ones, the desire not to hear the noble Dhamma, and a mind intent on fault-finding.
What are the three?
Without having abandoned restlessness, without having abandoned lack of restraint, and without having abandoned immorality.”
“Monks, without abandoning these three things, one is incapable of abandoning the desire not to see the noble ones, the desire not to hear the noble Dhamma, and a mind intent on finding fault.
Monks, without abandoning these three things, one is incapable of abandoning restlessness, lack of restraint, and immorality.
Which three?”
Without abandoning lack of faith, without abandoning stinginess, and without abandoning laziness— monks,
it is impossible for one who has not abandoned these three things to abandon restlessness, to abandon lack of restraint, and to abandon immorality. Furthermore, monks,
without abandoning these three things, it is impossible to abandon lack of faith, to abandon stinginess, and to abandon laziness.
Which three? Without having abandoned disrespect, without having abandoned difficult-to-correctness, and without having abandoned evil friendship—
these, monks, are the three things that, if not abandoned, one is incapable of abandoning lack of faith, stinginess, and laziness.
"Bhikkhus, without having abandoned three things, one is incapable of abandoning disrespect, abandoning difficult-to-correctness, and abandoning evil friendship.
Which three?
Without having abandoned moral shamelessness, without having abandoned moral fearlessness, and without having abandoned negligence."
“Monks, without having abandoned these three things, one is incapable of abandoning disrespect, abandoning difficult speech, and abandoning evil friendship.
One who is shameless and lacking in moral dread is heedless.
Being heedless, he is incapable of abandoning disrespect, abandoning difficult speech, and abandoning evil friendship.”
Thus, being a bad friend, he is incapable of abandoning lack of faith, stinginess, and laziness.
Being lazy, he is incapable of abandoning restlessness, lack of restraint, and immorality.
Being immoral, he is incapable of abandoning the desire not to see the noble ones, the desire not to hear the Dharma of the noble ones, and a mind intent on finding fault.
Thus, being possessed of a mind prone to reproach, he is incapable of abandoning forgetfulness, abandoning lack of clear comprehension, and abandoning mental distraction.
Being possessed of a distracted mind, he is incapable of abandoning improper attention, abandoning the pursuit of wrong paths, and abandoning mental sluggishness.
Being possessed of a sluggish mind, he is incapable of abandoning identity view, abandoning doubt, and abandoning adherence to rules and observances.
Being full of doubt, one is incapable of abandoning lust, abandoning hatred, and abandoning delusion.
Without having abandoned lust, hatred, and delusion, one is incapable of abandoning birth, abandoning aging, and abandoning death.
By abandoning these three things, monks, one is capable of abandoning birth, abandoning aging, and abandoning death.
Which three? Having abandoned lust, having abandoned hatred, and having abandoned delusion—
these, monks, are the three things that, when abandoned, one is capable of abandoning birth, abandoning aging, and abandoning death.
“Bhikkhus, having abandoned three things, one is capable of abandoning lust, abandoning hatred, and abandoning delusion.
What are the three?
Having abandoned identity view, having abandoned doubt, and having abandoned adherence to rules and observances.”
“Monks, having abandoned these three things, one is capable of abandoning lust, abandoning hatred, and abandoning delusion.
Monks, having abandoned these three things, one is capable of abandoning identity view, abandoning doubt, and abandoning adherence to rules and observances.
Which three?”

“By abandoning these three things, monks, one is capable of abandoning personality-belief, abandoning doubt, and abandoning adherence to rules and observances. By abandoning these three things, monks,
one is capable of abandoning improper attention, abandoning the pursuit of wrong paths, and abandoning mental sluggishness.”
Which three? Having abandoned forgetfulness, having abandoned lack of clear comprehension, and having abandoned mental distraction—
these, monks, are the three things that, when abandoned, one is able to abandon improper attention, abandoning the following of a wrong path, and abandoning mental sluggishness.
“Bhikkhus, having abandoned three things, one is capable of abandoning forgetfulness, abandoning lack of clear comprehension, and abandoning mental distraction.
Which three?
Having abandoned the desire not to see the noble ones; having abandoned the desire not to hear the noble Dhamma; and having abandoned a mind intent on fault-finding.”
“Monks, by abandoning these three things, one is capable of abandoning forgetfulness, abandoning lack of clear comprehension, and abandoning mental distraction.

Monks, by abandoning these three things, one is capable of abandoning the desire not to see the noble ones, abandoning the desire not to hear the noble Dhamma, and abandoning a mind intent on fault-finding.
What are the three?”
"Having abandoned restlessness, having abandoned lack of restraint,

and having abandoned immorality— having abandoned these three things, monks, one is capable of abandoning the desire not to see the noble ones, the desire not to hear the noble Dhamma, and a mind intent on finding fault.
Having abandoned these three things, monks, one is capable of abandoning restlessness, lack of restraint, and immorality."
Which three? Having abandoned lack of faith, having abandoned stinginess, and having abandoned laziness—
these, monks, are the three things that, when abandoned, one is capable of abandoning restlessness, abandoning lack of restraint, and abandoning immorality.
“Bhikkhus, having abandoned three things, one is capable of abandoning lack of faith, lack of generosity, and laziness.
Which three?
Having abandoned disrespect, having abandoned difficult-to-correctness, and having abandoned bad friendship.”
“Monks, having abandoned these three things, one is capable of abandoning lack of faith, abandoning stinginess, and abandoning laziness.
Monks, having abandoned these three things, one is capable of abandoning disrespect, abandoning difficult-to-correctness, and abandoning evil friendship.
Which three?”
“Having abandoned shamelessness, having abandoned lack of moral dread, and having abandoned negligence—
having abandoned these three qualities, monks, one is capable of abandoning disrespect, abandoning difficult speech, and abandoning bad friendship.
One who possesses a sense of shame, monks, is conscientious and diligent.”
Being diligent, he is capable of abandoning disrespect, abandoning difficult speech, and abandoning evil friendship.
Being a friend of the virtuous, he is capable of abandoning lack of faith, abandoning stinginess, and abandoning laziness.
Being one who has aroused energy, he is capable of abandoning restlessness, abandoning lack of restraint, and abandoning immorality.
Being thus possessed of virtue, he is capable of abandoning the desire not to see the noble ones, the desire not to hear the noble Dhamma, and the intentness on finding fault.
Being free from the intentness to find fault, he is capable of abandoning muddled mindfulness, lack of clear comprehension, and mental distraction.
Being undistracted in mind, he is capable of abandoning improper attention, following the wrong path, and mental sluggishness.
Being thus undaunted in mind, one is capable of abandoning personality-belief, abandoning doubt, and abandoning adherence to rules and observances.
Being free from doubt, one is capable of abandoning lust, abandoning hatred, and abandoning delusion.
Having abandoned lust, having abandoned hatred, and having abandoned delusion, one is capable of abandoning birth, abandoning aging, and abandoning death.”
The Sixth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.77.

The Discourse on the Crow (Kākasutta): “Monks,
the crow is possessed of ten things that are not true Dhamma.”
Which ten? He is corrupt, impudent, greedy, gluttonous, cruel, merciless, weak, shrieking, forgetful, and deceitful—
it is by possessing these ten unrighteous qualities, monks, that a crow is so called.
In the same way, monks, a wicked monk is possessed of ten things that are not true Dhamma.
What are the ten?
He is shameless, impudent, greedy, gluttonous, cruel, merciless, weak, a boaster, forgetful, and a schemer.
“Monks, it is by possessing these ten things that a wicked monk is so called.
The seventh. *Aṅguttara Nikāya* 10.78.

8. Ākaṅkhavagga Nigaṇṭhasutta (AN 10.78, PTS AN v 150) “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of Nigaṇṭhas. What four? The one who is bound by all bonds; the one who is bound by some bonds and not by others; the one who is freed from some bonds but not from others; and the one who is freed from all bonds. And how, bhikkhus, is one a Nigaṇṭha bound by all bonds? Here, someone has not abandoned lust for sensual pleasures, ill will, and cruelty; he has not abandoned the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to views; he has not abandoned conceit, agitation, and ignorance, nor the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to agitation, and the underlying tendency to ignorance. This is called a Nigaṇṭha bound by all bonds. And how, bhikkhus, is one a Nigaṇṭha bound by some bonds and not by others? Here, someone has abandoned lust for sensual pleasures, ill will, and cruelty; he has abandoned the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to views; he has abandoned conceit, agitation, and ignorance, as well as the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to agitation, and the underlying tendency to ignorance. Yet he still possesses the five lower fetters. This is called a Nigaṇṭha bound by some bonds and not by others. And how, bhikkhus, is one a Nigaṇṭha freed from some bonds but not from others? Here, someone has abandoned lust for sensual pleasures, ill will, and cruelty; he has abandoned the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to views; he has abandoned conceit, agitation, and ignorance, as well as the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to agitation, and the underlying tendency to ignorance. He has also abandoned the five lower fetters, yet he still possesses the five higher fetters. This is called a Nigaṇṭha freed from some bonds but not from others. And how, bhikkhus, is one a Nigaṇṭha freed from all bonds? Here, someone has abandoned lust for sensual pleasures, ill will, and cruelty; he has abandoned the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to views; he has abandoned conceit, agitation, and ignorance, as well as the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to agitation, and the underlying tendency to ignorance. He has abandoned the five lower fetters and the five higher fetters. This is called a Nigaṇṭha freed from all bonds.”
“Monks, the Nigaṇṭhas are possessed of ten things that are contrary to the true Dhamma. Which ten?
Monks, the Nigaṇṭhas lack faith;”
"Bhikkhus, the Nigaṇṭhas are immoral;
bhikkhus, the Nigaṇṭhas are shameless;
bhikkhus, the Nigaṇṭhas are fearless of wrongdoing."
Monks, the Nigaṇṭhas associate with those who are not true men;
monks, the Nigaṇṭhas praise themselves and disparage others;
monks, the Nigaṇṭhas cling to their own views, obstinately grasp them, and are difficult to disabuse of them.
“Bhikkhus, the Nigaṇṭhas are deceivers;
the Nigaṇṭhas have evil desires;
the Nigaṇṭhas have evil friends.”
“Monks, it is because they possess these ten things contrary to the true Dhamma that the Nigaṇṭhas are so called.
The eighth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.79

8. Ākaṅkhavagga Āghātavatthusutta (AN 10.79, PTS AN v 150) "Bhikkhus, there are these six bases for resentment. What six? (1) ‘He has done me harm,’ this is the first base for resentment. (2) ‘He is doing me harm,’ this is the second base for resentment. (3) ‘He will do me harm,’ this is the third base for resentment. (4) ‘He has done harm to those who are dear and pleasing to me,’ this is the fourth base for resentment. (5) ‘He is doing harm to those who are dear and pleasing to me,’ this is the fifth base for resentment. (6) ‘He will do harm to those who are dear and pleasing to me,’ this is the sixth base for resentment. These, bhikkhus, are the six bases for resentment."
“Bhikkhus, there are these ten grounds for resentment.
What are the ten?
‘He has done me harm,’ one harbors resentment;”
“He harbors resentment, thinking: ‘He has acted for my harm’;
he harbors resentment, thinking: ‘He will act for my harm’; [he harbors resentment, thinking:
‘He has acted for the harm of one who is dear and pleasing to me’... (and so forth).
‘He has acted for my harm’ … ‘He will act for my harm,’ one harbors resentment;
‘He has acted for the benefit of one who is unpleasant and disagreeable to me’ … [and so on].
One harbors resentment thinking, “He is acting for my benefit,” or “He will act for my benefit”;
and one becomes angry where there is no cause for anger.
“Monks, these are the ten grounds for resentment.
The ninth [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.80

8. Ākaṅkhavagga Āghātapaṭivinayasutta (AN 10.80, PTS AN v 150) “Monks, there are these five ways of removing resentment. What five? Here, monks, when anger arises in a monk toward someone, he reflects thus: ‘This person has done me harm; it is possible that this person will do me harm. Having reflected thus, he gives rise to resentment. Or else, when anger arises in him, he reflects: ‘This person has done me harm; it is possible that this person is doing me harm. Having reflected thus, he gives rise to resentment. Or else, when anger arises in him, he reflects: ‘This person has done me harm; it is possible that this person will do me harm in the future. Having reflected thus, he gives rise to resentment. Or else, when anger arises in him, he reflects: ‘This person has done harm to those dear and pleasing to me; it is possible that this person will do harm to those dear and pleasing to me. Having reflected thus, he gives rise to resentment. Or else, when anger arises in him, he reflects: ‘This person has done harm to those who are not dear or pleasing to me; it is possible that this person will do harm to those who are not dear or pleasing to me. Having reflected thus, he gives rise to resentment. These, monks, are the five ways of giving rise to resentment. But there are, monks, these five ways of removing resentment. What five? Here, monks, when anger arises in a monk toward someone, he reflects thus: ‘This person has done me harm; it is impossible that this person will do me harm. Having reflected thus, he removes his resentment. Or else, when anger arises in him, he reflects: ‘This person has done me harm; it is impossible that this person is doing me harm. Having reflected thus, he removes his resentment. Or else, when anger arises in him, he reflects: ‘This person has done me harm; it is impossible that this person will do me harm in the future. Having reflected thus, he removes his resentment. Or else, when anger arises in him, he reflects: ‘This person has done harm to those dear and pleasing to me; it is impossible that this person will do harm to those dear and pleasing to me. Having reflected thus, he removes his resentment. Or else, when anger arises in him, he reflects: ‘This person has done harm to those who are not dear or pleasing to me; it is impossible that this person will do harm to those who are not dear or pleasing to me. Having reflected thus, he removes his resentment. These, monks, are the five ways of removing resentment.”
“Monks, there are these ten ways of removing resentment.
What are the ten?
One removes resentment by thinking: ‘He has done me harm; what can be done about it?’”
One dispels resentment by thinking, “He has acted for my harm; how could that be? One dispels resentment by thinking, “He will act for my harm;
how could that be? [And one dispels resentment by thinking,] “He has acted for the harm of one who is dear and pleasing to me... and so forth.

"He acted... he will act... for the welfare of one who is dear and pleasing to me"—how could such a thing happen? Thus he dispels resentment. "He acted... he acts... for the welfare of one who is neither dear nor pleasing to me"—how could such a thing happen? Thus he dispels resentment.
“He will act for my welfare; how could such a thing happen?”—thus one dispels resentment;
and one does not become angry when it is unwarranted.
These, monks, are the ten ways of dispelling resentment.”
The tenth.
The third chapter, the Ākaṅkha-vagga.

Longing, the thorn, and the desired;
growth, and Migasālā;
three qualities, and the crow.
The Nigaṇṭhas and the two types of animosity.

On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Campā on the bank of the Gaggarā lotus pond.

Then the Venerable Vāhana approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Vāhana said this to the Blessed One:
“By means of how many qualities, Bhante, does a Tathāgata dwell detached, disjoined, and liberated, with a mind that has transcended all boundaries?
“Vāhana, by means of ten qualities, a Tathāgata dwells detached, disjoined, and liberated, with a mind that has transcended all boundaries.”
"By which ten?
Vāhana, the Tathāgata dwells with a mind that has escaped from form, is detached from it, and is liberated from it, having made it free from boundaries;
he dwells with a mind that has escaped from feeling... [and so on]..."
"By perception, Vāhana...
by volitional formations, Vāhana...
by consciousness, Vāhana..."
Indeed, Vāhana, by birth...
indeed, Vāhana, by aging...
indeed, Vāhana, by death...
"Vāhana, the Tathāgata has indeed emerged from suffering, Vāhana, he has emerged from the defilements; he dwells detached, liberated, and with a mind free from boundaries.
Just as, Vāhana, a blue lotus, a red lotus, or a white lotus, born in water and grown in water, stands having risen up above the water, unsullied by the water."
“In this very way, Vāhana, by means of these ten qualities, the Tathāgata dwells having escaped, detached, and liberated, with a mind that has transcended all boundaries.

9. Theravagga Ānandasutta (AN 10.82, PTS AN v 152) Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Therefore, bhikkhus, if anyone should speak in praise of me, or of the Dhamma, or of the Saṅgha, you should not, on that account, feel elated or uplifted or joyful. “Bhikkhus, if anyone should speak in dispraise of me, or of the Dhamma, or of the Saṅgha, you should not, on that account, feel dejected or downcast or sorrowful. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata has fully understood what is to be fully understood; the Tathāgata has abandoned what is to be abandoned; the Tathāgata has realized what is to be realized; the Tathāgata has developed what is to be developed. Therefore, bhikkhus, if anyone should speak in dispraise of me, or of the Dhamma, or of the Saṅgha, you should not, on that account, feel dejected or downcast or sorrowful. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is marvelous, venerable sir! Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As the Venerable Ānanda was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Indeed, Ānanda, it is impossible that a bhikkhu who lacks faith should attain growth, increase, and maturity in this Dhamma and Discipline.”
"Indeed, Ānanda, it is impossible that a monk who is immoral should attain growth, increase, and maturity in this Dhamma and Vinaya.
Indeed, Ānanda, it is impossible that a monk who has heard little should attain growth, increase, and maturity in this Dhamma and Vinaya.
Indeed, Ānanda, it is impossible that a monk who is difficult to correct should attain growth, increase, and maturity in this Dhamma and Vinaya."
"Indeed, Ānanda, it is impossible that a bhikkhu who is a bad friend should attain growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma and Discipline.
Indeed, Ānanda, it is impossible that a bhikkhu who is lazy should attain growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma and Discipline.
Indeed, Ānanda, it is impossible that a bhikkhu who is muddle-minded should attain growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma and Discipline."
