9. Theravagga (The Chapter on Elders).
Puṇṇiya Sutta (AN 10.83).

Then the Venerable Puṇṇiya approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Puṇṇiya said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason why at times the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma occurs to him, while at other times it does not?
“Puṇṇiya, when a bhikkhu has faith but does not approach [the Teacher], then the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma does not occur to him.
But when, Puṇṇiya, a bhikkhu has both faith and approaches [the Teacher], then the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma occurs to him.”
"Puṇṇiya, a bhikkhu may be endowed with faith and approach [a teacher], yet he does not attend upon him...
he may attend upon him, yet he does not inquire...
he may inquire, yet he does not listen to the Dhamma with attentive ear."
One listens to the Dhamma with attentive ear, yet having heard it, one does not retain the Dhamma;
or, having heard the Dhamma, one retains it, yet one does not examine the meaning of the teachings retained;
or, one examines the meaning of the teachings retained, yet having understood the meaning and understood the Dhamma, one does not practice in accordance with the Dhamma.

Having understood the goal and understood the Dhamma, one practices in accordance with the Dhamma; yet one is not a speaker of what is good, nor is one possessed of a good delivery, endowed with speech that is polished, distinct, flawless, and capable of making the meaning known...
[but] one is a speaker of what is good, possessed of a good delivery, endowed with speech that is polished, distinct, flawless, and capable of making the meaning known;
yet one does not instruct, encourage, inspire, or gladden one’s fellow practitioners of the holy life.
The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma does not yet manifest itself.
But when, Puṇṇiya, a bhikkhu is endowed with faith, approaches [the teacher], pays respect, inquires,

listens to the Dhamma with attentive ears, and having heard it, retains the Dhamma in mind, and understands the meaning of the teachings he has retained— then [the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dhamma manifests].
He investigates thoroughly; having understood the meaning and understood the Dhamma, he practices in accordance with the Dhamma.
He is a good speaker, possessing a beautiful voice, endowed with speech that is polished, clear, flawless, and expressive of the meaning;
and he is one who instructs, encourages, inspires, and gladdens his fellow celibates.
"In this way, Puṇṇiya, does the Dhamma teaching occur to the Tathāgata.
Possessing these ten qualities, Puṇṇiya, the Dhamma teaching of the Tathāgata is invariably inspired.
The third [discourse].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.84 9. Theravagga Byākaraṇasutta (The Discourse on the Declaration) “Bhikkhus, there are these ten qualities of one who has declared final knowledge.

What ten? (1) Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults; having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. (2) He has learned much, remembers what he has learned, and accumulates what he has learned. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure holy life—such teachings as these he has learned much of, retained in mind, recited verbally, mentally investigated, and penetrated well by view. (3) He gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life. (4) With the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma. (5) With the destruction of the taints, he has realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having attained it, he dwells therein. These, bhikkhus, are the ten qualities of one who has declared final knowledge.”
There, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna addressed the bhikkhus:
"Friends, bhikkhus!"
“Friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna.
The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this:
“In this case, friends, a bhikkhu declares final knowledge:”
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being’—this is how he understands.

Then a Tathāgata, or a disciple of the Tathāgata, who is a meditator skilled in attainments, skilled in others' minds, and skilled in the ways of others' minds, examines, interrogates, and cross-examines him.
By that Tathāgata or disciple of the Tathāgata—who is a meditator skilled in attainments, skilled in others' minds...
When being questioned, cross-examined, and interrogated by one skilled in the methods of discerning the minds of others,
he falls into distress, falls into confusion, falls into misfortune, falls into calamity, and falls into both misfortune and calamity.

Then the Tathāgata, or a disciple of the Tathāgata, who is a meditator, skilled in attainments, skilled in the minds of others, and skilled in the methods of discerning the minds of others, attends to him with his own mind, encompassing that person's mind, as follows:
‘Why does this venerable one declare final knowledge, saying:
“I understand: birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being”?

Then the Tathāgata, or a disciple of the Tathāgata, who is a meditator skilled in attainments, skilled in others’ minds, and skilled in the ways of others’ minds, understands his mind with his own mind thus:
‘This venerable one is indeed prone to anger;
he frequently dwells with a mind obsessed by anger.
Now, obsession by anger is a cause of decline in the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by the Tathāgata.’
Furthermore, this venerable one is prone to resentment;
he often dwells with a mind obsessed by resentment.
Now, obsession by resentment is a cause of decline in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
Moreover, this venerable one is deceitful;
he dwells frequently with a mind obsessed by deceit.
Now, obsession by deceit is a cause of decline in the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
Moreover, this venerable one is contentious;
he frequently dwells with a mind obsessed by contentiousness.
Now, obsession by contentiousness in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata is a cause of decline.
Moreover, this venerable one is envious;
he frequently dwells with a mind obsessed by envy.
Now, obsession by envy is a cause of decline in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
Moreover, this venerable one is stingy;
he often dwells with a mind obsessed by stinginess.
Now, obsession by stinginess is a cause of decline in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, this venerable one is deceitful;
he frequently dwells with a mind obsessed by deceit.
Now, obsession by deceit in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata is a cause of decline.
Moreover, this venerable one is deceitful;
he frequently dwells with a mind obsessed by deceit.
Now, obsession by deceit is a cause of decline in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
Moreover, this venerable one has evil desires;
he frequently dwells with a mind obsessed by desire.
Now, obsession by desire in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata is a cause of decline.
Yet this venerable one has reached a state of complacency midway, having attained only a minor distinction when there was more yet to be done.
Indeed, reaching a state of complacency midway in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata is a form of decline.
Truly, friends, it is impossible for a monk to attain growth, increase, and maturity in this Dhamma and Vinaya without abandoning these ten things.
"Truly, friends, it is possible that a bhikkhu, having abandoned these ten things, will attain growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma and Discipline.
The fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.85

9. Theravagga Katthīsutta (AN 10.85, PTS AN v 157) “Bhikkhus, suppose there were a great bonfire burning for a hundred years, and a man would come along bringing wood for the fire. What do you think, bhikkhus, would that great bonfire burn even longer because of that man’s bringing of wood? “Venerable sir, it would burn even longer. “So too, bhikkhus, for a noble disciple, when four things are present, the Tathāgata is declared to be fully enlightened, his teaching to be well-expounded, and the Saṅgha of disciples to be practicing the good way. What four? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One. “He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. “He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. “He possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. “When these four things are present for a noble disciple, the Tathāgata is declared to be fully enlightened, his teaching to be well-expounded, and the Saṅgha of disciples to be practicing the good way. “Suppose, bhikkhus, there were a great tree standing possessed of heartwood, and a man would come along bringing an axe. He would cut through its root-suckers, its roots, its trunk, its branches, and its foliage, and he would fell it, cut it into logs, split the logs, and reduce them to splinters. Then, having soaked them in water and worked them with his feet, he would burn them in a fire until they became ashes. Having collected the ashes, he would winnow them in a high wind or let them be carried away by the swift current of a river. Thus, bhikkhus, that great tree would be described as destroyed at the root, severed from the top, made non-existent, not subject to future arising. “So too, bhikkhus, for a noble disciple, when these four things are present, the Tathāgata is declared to be fully enlightened, his teaching to be well-expounded, and the Saṅgha of disciples to be practicing the good way. And that noble disciple is described as having destroyed the I-making, mine-making, and the underlying tendency to conceit regarding this conscious body; and regarding all external objects, he is described as having destroyed the I-making, mine-making, and the underlying tendency to conceit, severed them at the root, made them like a palm stump, done away with them so that they are no longer subject to future arising.”
On one occasion the Venerable Mahācunda was dwelling among the Cetis at Sahajāti.
There the Venerable Mahācunda addressed the bhikkhus:
“Friends, bhikkhus!”
“Friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Mahācunda.
The Venerable Mahācunda said this:
“In this case, friends, a bhikkhu is one who boasts and vaunts himself regarding his attainments:”
‘I enter into and emerge from the first jhāna; I enter into and emerge from the second jhāna;
I enter into and emerge from the third jhāna; I enter into and emerge from the fourth jhāna;
I enter into and emerge from the base of infinite space. I—
‘I enter and emerge from the base of infinite consciousness; I enter and emerge from the base of nothingness;
I enter and emerge from the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; I enter and emerge from the cessation of perception and feeling.’”

Then the Tathāgata, or a disciple of the Tathāgata— being one who meditates, skilled in attainments, skilled in others' minds, and skilled in the ways of others' minds— questions him, presses him, and cross-examines him. While being questioned, pressed,

and cross-examined by the Tathāgata or the disciple of the Tathāgata— who is a meditator, skilled in attainments, skilled in others' minds, and skilled in the ways of others' minds— he [discloses] his conduct...
He falls into misfortune; he falls into ruin; he falls into calamity; he falls into both ruin and calamity.

Then a Tathāgata, or a disciple of the Tathāgata—one who is a meditator, skilled in attainments, skilled in others' minds, and skilled in the ways of others' minds—directs his mind to that person's mind and reflects thus:
"Why is this venerable one boastful and self-aggrandizing regarding his attainments?"
‘I enter the first jhāna and emerge from it...
[and so on] ...I enter the cessation of perception and feeling and emerge from it.

Then a Tathāgata, or a disciple of the Tathāgata, who is a meditator skilled in attainments, skilled in others’ minds, and skilled in the ways of others’ minds, having encompassed his mind with his own mind, understands thus:

“For a long time, indeed, this venerable one has been a doer of brokenness, a doer of flaws, a doer of strength-wounds, and a doer of impurities; he is not a doer of continuity, nor is his conduct continuous regarding the precepts.
This venerable one is immoral.
Now, immorality is a cause for decline in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.”
Moreover, this venerable one lacks faith;
indeed, lack of faith in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata is a cause of decline.
Moreover, this venerable one has heard little and is of improper conduct.
Moreover, lack of learning is a cause of decline in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, this venerable one is difficult to speak with;
indeed, being difficult to speak with is a cause of decline in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
Moreover, this venerable one has evil friends;
now, having evil friends in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata is a cause of decline.
Furthermore, this venerable one is indolent.
Moreover, laziness is a cause of decline in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, this venerable one is muddle-minded;
indeed, muddle-mindedness is a cause of decline in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
Moreover, this venerable one is a deceiver;
indeed, deceitfulness within the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata is a cause of decline.
Moreover, this venerable one is difficult to support.
Moreover, being difficult to support is a decline in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, this venerable one is lacking in wisdom;
indeed, lack of wisdom is a decline in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.”
"Suppose, friends, a companion were to say to another companion:
'When you have need of wealth, my friend, ask me for it; I will give you wealth.
Then, when some business requiring wealth has arisen, that companion might say to his companion: 'I have need of wealth, my friend; give me wealth.'"
Then one might say to him:
"Well then, friend, dig here. While digging there, he would not find anything.
Then one might say:
‘My friend, you have spoken falsely to me; my friend, you have spoken vainly to me—dig here!
He would say:
‘I did not speak falsely to you, my friend, nor did I speak vainly. Nevertheless, my friend, dig here.’”
Thus, even while digging there, he would not find it.
He would say:
"My friend, you spoke falsely to me; my friend, you spoke emptily to me when you said, 'Dig here.'"
He might say this:
“I did not speak falsely to you, friend; I did not speak an empty thing. Come then, friend, dig here.
Even while digging there, he would not find anything.
He might say this:
“My friend, you have spoken falsely to me; my friend, you have spoken in vain to me—‘Dig here!
He might say this:
“‘Friend, I did not speak falsely; I did not speak vainly. Rather, it was I myself who fell into madness and a derangement of mind.
In the same way, friends, a bhikkhu is a boaster and a braggart regarding his attainments:
‘I enter and emerge from the first jhāna; I enter and emerge from the second jhāna…’”
I emerge from it; I attain the third jhāna and emerge from it; I attain the fourth jhāna and emerge from it;
I attain the base of infinite space and emerge from it;
I attain the base of infinite consciousness and emerge from it; I attain the base of nothingness...
‘I emerge from it; I enter the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and emerge from it; I enter the cessation of perception and feeling and emerge from it.

Then a Tathāgata, or a disciple of the Tathāgata, who is a meditator skilled in attainments, skilled in others’ minds, and skilled in the ways of others’ minds, questions him, presses him, and cross-examines him.

Thus, when being questioned, examined, and exhorted by a Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata— one who is meditative, skilled in attainments, skilled in others' minds, and skilled in the methods for discerning others' minds—
he falls into error, he falls into confusion, he falls into misfortune, he falls into calamity, and he falls into both misfortune and calamity.

Then a Tathāgata or a disciple of the Tathāgata—being one who meditates, skilled in attainments, skilled in others' minds, and skilled in the ways of others' minds—directs his mind to that person's mind and considers thus:
"Why is this venerable one boastful and vainglorious regarding his attainments, saying:
'I enter the first jhāna... [and so on].
‘I enter and emerge from the cessation of perception and feeling.
A Tathāgata, or a disciple of the Tathāgata, who is a meditator skilled in attainments and skilled in the methods for discerning the minds of others, understands his mind with his own mind:

‘For a long time this venerable one has been a doer of brokenness, a doer of gaps, a doer of flaws, and a doer of stains; he has not been a doer of continuity, nor has he been consistent in his conduct regarding the precepts.’
This venerable one is indeed immoral;
and in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, immorality is a cause of decline.
Furthermore, this venerable one is indeed lacking in faith.
Lack of faith in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata is indeed a cause of decline.
Furthermore, this venerable one is of little learning and lacks proper conduct;
lack of true knowledge in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata is indeed a cause of decline.
Moreover, this venerable one is difficult to speak to;
indeed, being difficult to speak to in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata is a cause of decline.
Moreover, this venerable one has evil friends.
Moreover, having evil friends in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata is a cause of decline.
Furthermore, this venerable one is indolent;
indeed, indolence in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata is a cause of decline.
Moreover, this venerable one is muddle-minded;
for in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, muddle-mindedness is a cause of decline.
Moreover, this venerable one is a hypocrite.
Indeed, hypocrisy is a decline in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, this venerable one is difficult to support;
indeed, being difficult to support is a decline in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
"But this venerable one is of poor wisdom;
and in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, poor wisdom is a cause of decline.
Indeed, friends, it is impossible that a bhikkhu, without abandoning these ten things, will attain growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma and Vinaya.
"Therefore, friends, it is possible that a bhikkhu who has abandoned these ten things will attain growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma and Discipline.
Thus was the fifth [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.86.

9. The Chapter on Elders: The Discourse on Overweening Pride (Adhimānasutta) “Bhikkhus, there are these five kinds of overweening pride. What five? (1) One who is inferior considers himself equal; this is the first kind of overweening pride. (2) One who is equal considers himself superior; this is the second kind of overweening pride. (3) One who is superior considers himself equal; this is the third kind of overweening pride. (4) One who has not attained what is superior considers himself to have attained it; this is the fourth kind of overweening pride. (5) One who is possessed of evil qualities considers himself to be possessed of good qualities; this is the fifth kind of overweening pride. These, bhikkhus, are the five kinds of overweening pride.”
On one occasion the Venerable Mahākassapa was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
There the Venerable Mahākassapa addressed the bhikkhus:
“Friends, bhikkhus!”
“Friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Mahākassapa.
The Venerable Mahākassapa said this:
“In this case, friends, a bhikkhu declares final knowledge:”
‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being,’ he understands.

Then the Tathāgata, or a disciple of the Tathāgata—one who is a meditator, skilled in attainments, skilled in others’ minds, and skilled in the ways of others’ minds—questions him, presses him, and cross-examines him.
He [is questioned] by that Tathāgata or disciple of the Tathāgata, who is a meditator, skilled in attainments, and skilled in others’ minds.
When being questioned, cross-examined, and interrogated by one skilled in the methods of discerning the minds of others,
he falls into distress, falls into confusion, falls into misfortune, falls into ruin, and falls into both misfortune and ruin.

Then the Tathāgata, or a disciple of the Tathāgata, who is a meditator, skilled in attainments, skilled in the minds of others, and skilled in the methods of discerning the minds of others, attends to him with his own mind, encompassing that mind, thus:
‘Why does this venerable one declare final knowledge, saying:
“Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being”?

Then the Tathāgata, or a disciple of the Tathāgata, who is a meditator, skilled in attainments, skilled in the minds of others, and skilled in the ways of the minds of others, understands his mind with his own mind thus:

‘This venerable one is indeed conceited and committed to conceit; he perceives that he has attained what he has not attained, that he has accomplished what he has not accomplished, and that he has achieved what he has not achieved.
Out of conceit, he declares final knowledge:
“I understand: birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.”’

Then a Tathāgata, or a disciple of the Tathāgata, who is a meditator skilled in attainments, skilled in others' minds, and skilled in the methods of discerning others' minds, directs his mind toward that person's mind and considers:

"What indeed is this venerable one relying upon that he is so conceited, so truly possessed of conceit; one who perceives himself as having attained what he has not attained, as having accomplished what he has not accomplished, and as having realized what he has not realized?
Out of conceit, he declares final knowledge."

‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being’—this the Tathāgata, or a disciple of the Tathāgata, who is a meditator skilled in attainments, skilled in the minds of others, and skilled in the ways of the minds of others, understands by encompassing his mind with his own mind thus:
‘This venerable one is indeed learned, a bearer of the teachings, one who has accumulated what he has heard; those teachings which are beautiful in the beginning, beautiful in the middle, and...’
They proclaim the holy life, which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, entirely complete and pure;
such teachings as these he has heard much of, retained, mastered verbally, examined with the mind,
and well penetrated through view.

Therefore, this venerable one is conceited and possesses the truth of conceit; he perceives that he has attained what he has not attained, that he has accomplished what he has not accomplished, and that he has realized what he has not realized.
Out of conceit, he declares final knowledge:
‘I understand: “Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.”’”

Then a Tathāgata, or a disciple of the Tathāgata, who is a meditator skilled in attainments, skilled in others' minds, and skilled in the ways of others' minds, comprehends his mind with his own mind and understands:
"This venerable one is indeed covetous;
he frequently dwells with a mind obsessed by covetousness."
Furthermore, obsession with covetousness is a cause of decline in the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
Moreover, this venerable one is malevolent;
he frequently dwells with a mind obsessed by ill will.
Furthermore, obsession by ill will is a cause of decline in the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
Moreover, this venerable one is slothful and torpid;
he frequently dwells with a mind obsessed by sloth and torpor.
Moreover, being obsessed by sloth and torpor is a cause of decline in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, this venerable one is restless;
he often dwells with a mind obsessed by restlessness.
Furthermore, restlessness-obsession is a cause of decline in the Dhamma and Discipline proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
Moreover, this venerable one is full of doubt;
he frequently dwells with a mind obsessed by doubt.
Furthermore, obsession by doubt is a cause of decline in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
Moreover, this venerable one delights in action, takes pleasure in action, and is devoted to delighting in action.
Now, delighting in action is a cause of decline in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
Moreover, this venerable one delights in talk, takes pleasure in talk, and is devoted to delighting in talk.
Now, delighting in talk in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata is a cause of decline.
Furthermore, this venerable one delights in sleep, takes pleasure in sleep, and is devoted to delighting in sleep.
Now, delighting in sleep is a cause of decline in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
This venerable one delights in company, takes pleasure in company, and is devoted to delighting in company.
Indeed, delighting in company is a cause of decline in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
Yet this venerable one has reached a state of complacency midway, having achieved only a minor distinction when there was more to be done.
Now, reaching a state of complacency midway in the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata is a cause of decline.
Indeed, friends, it is impossible for a bhikkhu to attain growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma and Vinaya without abandoning these ten things.
"It is indeed possible, friends, that a bhikkhu who has abandoned these ten things will attain growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma and Discipline.
The sixth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.87

9. Theravagga Nappiyasutta (AN 10.87, PTS AN v 164) “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is unpleasant to see and unpleasant to associate with; the person who is unpleasant to see but pleasant to associate with; the person who is pleasant to see but unpleasant to associate with; and the person who is pleasant to see and pleasant to associate with. And how, monks, is one a person unpleasant to see and unpleasant to associate with? Here, monks, someone is of evil conduct in body, speech, and mind. He dwells without having abandoned the defilements that lead to rebirth in a state of misery, a bad destination, the lower world, or hell. This, monks, is called a person unpleasant to see and unpleasant to associate with. And how, monks, is one a person unpleasant to see but pleasant to associate with? Here, monks, someone is of evil conduct in body, speech, and mind. Yet he dwells having abandoned the defilements that lead to rebirth in a state of misery, a bad destination, the lower world, or hell. This, monks, is called a person unpleasant to see but pleasant to associate with. And how, monks, is one a person pleasant to see but unpleasant to associate with? Here, monks, someone is of good conduct in body, speech, and mind. Yet he dwells without having abandoned the defilements that lead to rebirth in a state of misery, a bad destination, the lower world, or hell. This, monks, is called a person pleasant to see but unpleasant to associate with. And how, monks, is one a person pleasant to see and pleasant to associate with? Here, monks, someone is of good conduct in body, speech, and mind. And he dwells having abandoned the defilements that lead to rebirth in a state of misery, a bad destination, the lower world, or hell. This, monks, is called a person pleasant to see and pleasant to associate with. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
There, the Blessed One addressed the monks concerning the monk who had passed away: "Monks!
"Venerable Sir," those monks replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“In this case, monks, a monk is a litigant and does not speak in praise of the settling of legal issues.

Monks, that a monk is a litigant and does not speak in praise of the settling of legal issues—this quality does not lead to endearment, nor to respect, nor to esteem, nor to the state of a recluse, nor to unity.”
Furthermore, monks, a monk does not desire training and does not speak in praise of undertaking the training.

Monks, that a monk does not desire training and does not speak in praise of undertaking the training—this quality does not lead to endearment, nor to respect, nor to esteem, nor to the state of a recluse, nor to unity.
Furthermore, monks, a monk has evil desires and does not speak in praise of the removal of desire.

Furthermore, monks, when a monk has evil desires and does not speak in praise of the removal of desire, this quality does not lead to endearment, to respect, to development, to the state of a recluse, or to unity.
Moreover, monks, a monk is prone to anger and does not speak in praise of the removal of anger.

In that a monk is prone to anger and does not speak in praise of the removal of anger, this quality also does not lead to endearment, to respect, to development, to the state of a recluse, or to unity.
Furthermore, monks, a monk is one who is contemptuous and does not speak in praise of the removal of contempt.

That a monk is contemptuous and does not speak in praise of the removal of contempt—this quality does not lead to endearment, nor to respect, nor to esteem, nor to the state of a recluse, nor to unity.
Furthermore, monks, a monk is one who is deceitful and does not speak in praise of the removal of deceit.

Furthermore, monks, when a monk is deceitful and does not speak in praise of the removal of deceit, this quality does not lead to endearment, to respect, to development, to the state of a recluse, or to unity.
Moreover, monks, a monk is deceptive and does not speak in praise of the removal of deception.

Furthermore, monks, when a monk is deceptive and does not speak in praise of the removal of deception, this quality also does not lead to endearment, to respect, to development, to the state of a recluse, or to unity.
Furthermore, monks, a monk is not inclined to attend to the teachings and does not speak in praise of attending to the teachings.

Monks, because a monk is not inclined to attend to the teachings and does not speak in praise of attending to the teachings, this quality does not lead to endearment, nor to respect, nor to development, nor to the state of a recluse, nor to unity.
Furthermore, monks, a monk does not dwell in seclusion and does not speak in praise of seclusion.

Furthermore, monks, when a monk does not dwell in seclusion and does not speak in praise of seclusion, this quality does not lead to endearment, respect, development, the state of a recluse, or to unity.

Again, monks, when a monk does not extend hospitality to his fellow celibate practitioners and does not speak in praise of those who do so extend hospitality—when, monks, a monk does not extend hospitality to his fellow celibate practitioners... [and does not speak in praise of those who do]... [this quality does not lead to endearment, respect, development, the state of a recluse, or to unity].
One who speaks in praise [of such things]— this quality also does not lead to endearment, nor to respect, nor to esteem, nor to the state of a recluse,
nor to unity. Monks, even if such a monk should have this wish arise:
‘Oh, that my fellow-celibates would honor me, respect me, esteem me, and worship me!’—yet his fellow-celibates do not honor him, respect him, esteem him, or worship him.
Why is that? Because, monks, his wise fellow-celibates perceive that those evil, unwholesome states have not been abandoned by him.
“Just as, monks, even though a wild colt might have the wish: ‘Oh,
that people would place me in the position of a thoroughbred, feed me the food of a thoroughbred,
and groom me with the grooming of a thoroughbred,’ yet people do not place him in the position of a thoroughbred nor feed him the food of a thoroughbred.”
They feed them, yet they do not groom them with the grooming of a thoroughbred. Why is that?
Because, monks, wise people perceive that those deceptions, frauds, crookednesses, and perversions have not been abandoned by him.
"In the same way, monks, even if such a monk should have this wish arise:

'Oh, that my fellow practitioners of the holy life would honor me, respect me, esteem me, and revere me,' yet his fellow practitioners do not honor him, respect him, esteem him, or revere him. Why is that?"
For in this way, monks, wise fellow-celibates perceive that those evil, unwholesome states have not been abandoned by him.
Furthermore, monks, a monk is not one who initiates legal disputes, but is a speaker in praise of the settling of legal disputes.

That a monk is not one who initiates legal disputes, but is a speaker in praise of the settling of legal disputes—this too is a quality that leads to endearment, to respect, to development, to the state of a recluse, and to unity.
Furthermore, monks, a monk is desirous of training and speaks in praise of undertaking the training.
That, monks, a monk is desirous of training and speaks in praise of undertaking the training—this quality leads to endearment, to respect, to development, to the state of a recluse, and to unity.
Furthermore, monks, a monk has few desires and speaks in praise of the removal of desire.
Furthermore, monks, when a monk has few desires and speaks in praise of the removal of desire, this too is a quality... that leads to unity.
Furthermore, monks, a monk is free from anger and speaks in praise of the removal of anger.
That a monk is free from anger and speaks in praise of the removal of anger—this too is a quality... that leads to unity.
Furthermore, monks, a monk is not one who slanders; he speaks in praise of the removal of slander.
In that a monk is not one who slanders and speaks in praise of the removal of slander, this too is a quality... [as before] ...which leads to unity.
Furthermore, monks, a monk is not one who is deceitful; he speaks in praise of the removal of deceit.
Furthermore, monks, when a monk is not deceitful and speaks in praise of the removal of deceit, this too is a quality... that leads to unity.
Furthermore, monks, a monk is not guileful and speaks in praise of the removal of guile.
That a monk is not guileful and speaks in praise of the removal of guile—this too is a quality... that leads to unity.
Furthermore, monks, a monk is intent on attending to the teachings and speaks in praise of attending to the teachings.

Monks, that a monk is intent on attending to the teachings and speaks in praise of attending to the teachings—this too is a quality that leads to unity... [and so forth] ...it conduces to being of one mind.
Furthermore, monks, a monk is withdrawn in seclusion and speaks in praise of seclusion.
Furthermore, monks, when a monk is secluded and speaks in praise of seclusion, this too is a quality that leads to being dear, respected, esteemed, to the state of a recluse, and to unity.
Furthermore, monks, a monk is hospitable toward his fellow celibates and speaks in praise of hospitality.
That a monk is hospitable toward his fellow celibates and speaks in praise of hospitality—this too is a quality that leads to being dear, respected, esteemed, to the state of a recluse, and to unity.
“Bhikkhus, even though such a bhikkhu might not have the wish arise in him thus:
‘Oh, that my fellow celibates would honor me, respect me, esteem me, and worship me,’ yet his fellow celibates do indeed honor him, respect him, esteem him, and worship him. Why is that?
[Because of his qualities.]”
For in this way, monks, his wise fellow-celibates perceive that those evil, unwholesome states have been abandoned by him.
Just as, monks, even though no such wish might arise in a noble thoroughbred horse:
‘Oh, that people would place me in the position of a thoroughbred, feed me the food of a thoroughbred, and groom me with the grooming of a thoroughbred!’...
‘...and they would groom it. Then, indeed, people place it in the position of a thoroughbred, feed it the food of a thoroughbred, and groom it with the grooming of a thoroughbred.
For what reason?
For in such a case, monks, wise people perceive that those instances of deceit, fraud, crookedness, and insincerity have been abandoned.
Even so, monks, although such a bhikkhu might not even form the wish:
"Oh, may my fellow practitioners honor me, revere me, esteem me, and worship me," nevertheless his fellow practitioners do honor him, revere him, esteem him, and worship him.
And why is that? Because, monks, his wise fellow-celibates perceive those evil, unwholesome states as abandoned by him.
Thus ends the seventh [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.88 9. Theravagga Akossakasutta (The Discourse on Abusers) “Monks, there are these ten kinds of persons found existing in the world. What ten? The one who abuses; the one who returns abuse; the one who strikes back; the one who returns blows; the one who speaks ill of those who speak ill; the one who speaks well of those who speak well; the one who does not retaliate against those who strike back; the one who does not return blows to those who strike; the one who does not speak ill of those who speak ill; and the one who speaks well of those who speak well. These, monks, are the ten kinds of persons found existing in the world.”

“Bhikkhus, it is possible that a bhikkhu who is abusive and insulting, who reviles his fellow celibates and the noble ones, will meet with one of ten calamities. What ten? [The text continues as follows:]”
He does not attain what has not yet been attained; he falls away from what has already been attained; he does not purify himself in the true Dhamma;
or he becomes conceited regarding the true Dhamma and leads the holy life without joy;
or he commits some defiled offense; or he is afflicted by a severe illness; or he falls into madness and mental derangement.
He dies confused; with the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.

Monks, for that monk who is abusive, reviling, and a slanderer of his fellow practitioners of the holy life, it is possible and within the range of experience that he will incur one or another of these ten calamities.
Thus it was for the eighth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.89 9. Theravagga Kokālikasutta At Sāvatthī. Then the Venerable Kokālika approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, I do not see even one other bhikkhu who possesses such great supernormal power and might as the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. “It is wonderful, Kokālika! It is marvelous, Kokālika! How can you, having seen them with your own eyes, say: ‘I do not see even one other bhikkhu who possesses such great supernormal power and might as the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna’? “Venerable sir, it is because I have heard from the lips of the Blessed One himself that the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna are possessed of great supernormal power and might. But I do not see even one other bhikkhu who possesses such great supernormal power and might as they.

“Kokālika, do not speak thus; do not speak thus! Do not disparage those venerable ones, for those venerable ones would not disparage you. Kokālika, those venerable ones are wise, and they would not disparage you. Kokālika, do not disparage the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. Those venerable ones are wise; they would not disparage you. For if you disparage them, you will go to hell for an eon, and there you will suffer torment. Suppose, Kokālika, a man were to take a firebrand of wood or bamboo and run with it against a great pile of dry grass or hay. What do you think, Kokālika? Would that firebrand burn that great pile of dry grass or hay? “Yes, venerable sir. “So too, Kokālika, if you disparage the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna—those venerable ones being wise and not disparaging you—you will go to hell for an eon, and there you will suffer torment. But suppose, Kokālika, a man were to take a firebrand of wood or bamboo and run with it against a great pile of wet, sappy grass or hay. What do you think, Kokālika? Would that firebrand burn that great pile of wet, sappy grass or hay? “No, venerable sir. “So too, Kokālika, if you were to take a firebrand of wood or bamboo and run with it against the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, those venerable ones, being wise, would extinguish that firebrand before it could reach them. And you, Kokālika, would go to hell for an eon, and there you would suffer torment. Therefore, Kokālika, do not disparage the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. Those venerable ones are wise; they would not disparage you. For if you disparage them, you will go to hell for an eon, and there you will suffer torment. Then the Venerable Kokālika, having been rebuked by the Blessed One, rose from his seat and departed. Not long after he had left, the Venerable Sāriputta approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, the Venerable Kokālika has just been rebuked by the Blessed One and has risen from his seat and departed. What will become of the Venerable Kokālika? “Sāriputta, Kokālika will go to hell for an eon, and there he will suffer torment. “But, venerable sir, how far away is the Venerable Kokālika now? “Sāriputta, Kokālika is standing at the gateway to the Jeta Grove. Then the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna went to the gateway to the Jeta Grove. (AN 10.89, PTS AN v 170) Then the bhikkhu Kokālika approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the bhikkhu Kokālika said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, Sāriputta and Moggallāna have evil desires; they have fallen under the sway of evil desires."
“Do not say so, Kokālika; do not say so, Kokālika.
Set your mind at rest regarding Sāriputta and Moggallāna, Kokālika.
Sāriputta and Moggallāna are virtuous.”
A second time, the bhikkhu Kokālika said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, although the Blessed One is trustworthy and reliable to me, nevertheless Sāriputta and Moggallāna have evil desires; they have fallen under the sway of evil desires.
"Do not say so, Kokālika! Do not say so, Kokālika!"
“Kokālika, direct your mind toward Sāriputta and Moggallāna with confidence;
Sāriputta and Moggallāna are virtuous.
For a third time, the bhikkhu Kokālika said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, although the Blessed One is trustworthy and reliable to me, nevertheless Sāriputta and Moggallāna have evil desires; they have fallen under the sway of evil desires.
“Do not say so, Kokālika! Do not say so, Kokālika!
Set your mind at rest regarding Sāriputta and Moggallāna, Kokālika.”
“Pesalā are Sāriputta and Moggallāna!
Then the bhikkhu Kokālika rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed.
Not long after the bhikkhu Kokālika had left, his entire body became covered with boils the size of mustard seeds.
Having been the size of mustard seeds, they became the size of mung beans; having been the size of mung beans, they became the size of chickpeas;
having been the size of chickpeas, they became the size of jujube stones; having been the size of jujube stones, they became the size of jujubes;
having been the size of jujubes, they became the size of myrobalans; having been the size of myrobalans, they became the size of *tiṇḍuka* fruits.
Having become the size of *tiṇḍuka* fruits, they became the size of bamboo shoots; having become the size of bamboo shoots, they became the size of *billa* fruits;
having become the size of *billa* fruits, they burst open and pus and blood flowed out.
He indeed lay upon plantain leaves like a fish that has swallowed poison.
Then the paccekabrahmā Turū approached the bhikkhu Kokālika; having approached, he stood in the air and said this to the bhikkhu Kokālika:
“Set your mind at rest regarding Sāriputta and Moggallāna, Kokālika.
Sāriputta and Moggallāna are virtuous.”
“Who are you, friend?
“I am the independent Brahmā Turu.
“But, friend, were you not declared by the Blessed One to be a non-returner? Then for what reason have you come here?”
“Behold how far you have gone astray!
Then the Paccekabrahmā Turu addressed the bhikkhu Kokālika in verses:
“For a person who has been born...”
An axe is born in the mouth by which the fool cuts himself when uttering ill-spoken words.
He who praises one who deserves blame,
or blames one who deserves praise,
gathers misfortune with his own mouth.
Through that [ordinary] loss, one finds no true misfortune.

This defeat of wealth at dice is but a minor misfortune; it is a far worse misfortune than this, when one loses oneself through gambling. Through that [great] misfortune, one finds no happiness. This defeat of wealth at dice is but a minor misfortune.
Even if one loses everything, including one's very self,
this alone is the greater misfortune:
that one should corrupt the mind toward the Sugatas.
For one hundred thousand nirabbudas,
and thirty-six plus five abbudas,
does he who reviles the noble ones go to hell.
“Having directed speech and mind toward evil.
Then the bhikkhu Kokālika died from that very affliction.
Having died, because he harbored a mind of resentment toward Sāriputta and Moggallāna, the bhikkhu Kokālika was reborn in the Paduma Hell.
Then, when the night had advanced, Brahmā Sahampati—of surpassing beauty, illuminating the entire Jeta Grove—approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he stood to one side.
Standing to one side, Brahmā Sahampati addressed the Blessed One in this way:
“Venerable sir, the bhikkhu Kokālika has died.
Having died, venerable sir, the bhikkhu Kokālika has been reborn in the Paduma hell because he harbored a mind of malice toward Sāriputta and Moggallāna.
This is what Brahmā Sahampati said.
Having said this, he paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping him to his right, and vanished right there.
Then, with the passing of that night, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
"Bhikkhus, last night, when the night was far spent, Brahmā Sahampati—of surpassing beauty—approached me and illuminated the entire extent of the world."
Having illuminated the Jeta Grove, he approached me; having approached, he paid homage to me and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, monks, Brahmā Sahampati said this to me:
“Venerable sir, the bhikkhu Kokālika has passed away.”
“Venerable sir, the bhikkhu Kokālika has passed away and has been reborn in the Paduma hell because he harbored a mind of malice toward Sāriputta and Moggallāna.
This is what Brahmā Sahampati said, monks.
Having spoken this, he paid homage to me, circumambulated me keeping me to his right, and vanished right there.
When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, how long is the lifespan in the Paduma hell?
“Bhikkhu, the lifespan in the Paduma hell is indeed long.”
“It is not easy to calculate it as ‘this many years,’ or ‘this many hundreds of years,’ or ‘this many thousands of years,’ or ‘this many hundreds of thousands of years. “But,
Bhante, is it possible to give a simile?”
“It is possible, bhikkhus,” the Blessed One said.
“Suppose, bhikkhu, there were a Kosalan cartload of twenty measures of sesame seeds, and a man were to remove a single seed from it at the end of every hundred years.
That Kosalan cartload of twenty measures of sesame seeds, bhikkhu, would more quickly be exhausted and come to an end by this method than one *abbuda* hell would [be exhausted].”
“Just as, bhikkhu, there are twenty Abbuda hells, so is one Nirabbuda hell.
Just as, bhikkhu, there are twenty Nirabbuda hells, so is one Ababa hell.
Just as, bhikkhu, there are twenty Ababa hells, so is one Aṭaṭa hell.”
Just as, monk, twenty Aṭaṭā hells are equal to one Ahaha hell;
just as, monk, twenty Ahaha hells are equal to one Kumuda hell;
just as, monk, twenty Kumuda hells are equal to one Sogandhika hell.
“Just as, bhikkhu, there are twenty Sogandhika hells, so is one Uppalaka hell.
Just as, bhikkhu, there are twenty Uppalaka hells, so is one Puṇḍarīka hell.
Just as, bhikkhu, there are twenty Puṇḍarīka hells, so is one Paduma hell.”
“Furthermore, bhikkhu, the bhikkhu Kokālika has been reborn in the Paduma hell because he harbored a mind of malice toward Sāriputta and Moggallāna.
This is what the Blessed One said.
Having said this, the Sublime One, the Teacher, further spoke these words:
For when a person is born,
an axe is born in his mouth,
with which he cuts himself.
The fool speaks ill words when he praises one who deserves blame,
or blames one who is worthy of praise.
He gathers misfortune with his mouth;
through that misfortune, he finds no happiness.
This misfortune is but a trifle.
That loss of wealth at dice— even compared to the loss of all one's possessions together with one's very self—
this alone is the greater evil.
Whoever corrupts his mind toward the Sugatas shall dwell for thirty-six and five hundred thousand *nirabbuda* aeons, and fifty-six *abbuda* aeons.
One who reviles noble ones goes to hell,
having directed speech and mind toward evil.
Thus ends the ninth [verse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.90 9. Theravagga Khīṇāsavabalasutta (The Discourse on the Powers of One Whose Taints Are Destroyed) “Monks, there are these ten powers of one whose taints are destroyed. What ten? (1) Here, monks, the Tathāgata understands as it really is the possible as possible and the impossible as impossible. This is the first power of one whose taints are destroyed. (2) Again, the Tathāgata understands as it really is the result of the undertaking of karmic actions past, future, and present, with their causes and conditions, in their ways and manifestations. This is the second power of one whose taints are destroyed. (3) Again, the Tathāgata understands as it really is the meditative absorption, its emergence, and its abiding, with their causes and conditions, in their ways and manifestations. This is the third power of one whose taints are destroyed. (4) Again, the Tathāgata understands as it really is the faculties of other beings, other persons, their keenness or dullness, their excellence or mediocrity, and how they are practiced. This is the fourth power of one whose taints are destroyed. (5) Again, the Tathāgata understands as it really is the defilement, the cleansing, and the emergence from the jhānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments. This is the fifth power of one whose taints are destroyed. (6) Again, the Tathāgata recollects his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, many eons of world-dissolution, many eons of world-evolution, and many eons of both dissolution and evolution, [recollecting]: ‘There I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a lifespan; passing away from there, I was reborn elsewhere, and there too I had such a name... Thus he recollects his manifold past lives in their modes and details. This is the sixth power of one whose taints are destroyed. (7) Again, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, the Tathāgata sees beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma: ‘These beings who engaged in misconduct by body, speech, and mind, who reviled the noble ones, held wrong views, and undertook actions based on wrong views, at the breaking up of the body, after death, have been reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a lower realm, or in hell; but these beings who engaged in good conduct by body, speech, and mind, who did not revile the noble ones, held right views, and undertook actions based on right views, at the breaking up of the body, after death, have been reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. Thus, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, he sees beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma. This is the seventh power of one whose taints are destroyed. (8) Again, by the destruction of the taints, the Tathāgata has realized for himself in this very life, through direct knowledge, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, he dwells therein. This is the eighth power of one whose taints are destroyed. (9) Again, the Tathāgata understands as it really is the range of the powers of other ascetics and brahmins, whether they precede him or follow him. This is the ninth power of one whose taints are destroyed. (10) Again, when the Tathāgata claims the place of the Bull of Men, roars his lion’s roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Wheel of Brahmā, no ascetic or brahmin, no deva, Māra, or Brahmā, nor anyone in the world, can turn back that wheel. This is the tenth power of one whose taints are destroyed. These, monks, are the ten powers of one whose taints are destroyed.”
(AN 10.90, PTS AN v 174) Then the Venerable Sāriputta approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As the Venerable Sāriputta was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
“Sāriputta, how many powers does a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed possess, by virtue of which powers a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed claims the destruction of the taints:”
“‘My taints are exhausted,’ [he says].
“Venerable sir, there are ten powers of a bhikkhu whose taints are exhausted, possessed of which a bhikkhu whose taints are exhausted claims the exhaustion of his taints:
‘My taints are exhausted.’”
Which ten?
Here, venerable sir, for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, all conditioned phenomena have been well seen as they really are with correct wisdom as impermanent.
Furthermore, venerable sir, for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, all conditioned phenomena [have been well seen] as they really are with correct wisdom as impermanent...
They are well seen. This too, venerable sir, is a power of a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, by virtue of which power a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed claims the destruction of the taints:
"The taints are destroyed in me."
Furthermore, venerable sir, for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, sensual pleasures have been well seen as they really are with correct wisdom,
like a pit of glowing embers. That, venerable sir, for which a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed has well seen sensual pleasures as they really are with correct wisdom,
like a pit of glowing embers— this too is a power of a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, by relying upon which power...
A bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed declares the destruction of the taints:
"My taints are destroyed.

Furthermore, venerable sir, the mind of a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed inclines toward seclusion, leans toward seclusion, tends toward seclusion, is established in seclusion, delights in renunciation, and has completely transcended all states that are the basis for the taints.

Furthermore, venerable sir, when a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed has a mind that slants, slopes, and inclines toward seclusion, that is established in seclusion, delights in renunciation, and is entirely freed from states that are the basis for the taints—this too, venerable sir, is a power of a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, by virtue of which power a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed claims the destruction of the taints: [“I understand: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’”]
‘My taints are destroyed.
Furthermore, Bhante, for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, the four foundations of mindfulness have been developed and well-developed.
And, Bhante, that the four foundations of mindfulness have been developed and well-developed by a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed—
This too, Bhante, is a power of a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, by virtue of which power a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed claims the destruction of the taints, saying:
"The taints are destroyed in me."

Furthermore, Bhante, for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, the four right endeavors have been developed and well-developed … the four bases of psychic power have been developed and well-developed … the five faculties … [have been developed and well-developed].”
The five powers have been developed, well-developed;
the seven factors of enlightenment have been developed, well-developed;
the noble eightfold path has been developed, well-developed.
Furthermore, venerable sir, when the noble eightfold path has been developed and well-developed by a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed,
this too is a power of that bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, by virtue of which power a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed claims the destruction of the taints: [as follows].
‘My taints are destroyed.
These, venerable sir, are the ten powers of a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed, endowed with which a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed claims the destruction of the taints, saying:
‘My taints are destroyed.’”
The tenth.
