The Discourse on Enjoyers of Sensual Pleasures (Kāmabhogīsutta).
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As the householder Anāthapiṇḍika was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
"Householder, these ten enjoyers of sensual pleasures are found existing in the world."
Which ten?
Here, householder, a certain enjoyer of sensual pleasures seeks wealth unrighteously and by violence;
having sought wealth unrighteously and by violence, he does not make himself happy, nor does he gladden himself, nor does he share it, nor does he perform meritorious deeds.
"But here, householder, a certain enjoyer of sensual pleasures seeks wealth unrighteously and by violence;
having sought wealth unrighteously and by violence, he makes himself happy and pleased, yet he does not share it nor perform meritorious deeds.
And here, householder, another certain enjoyer of sensual pleasures seeks wealth unrighteously and by violence..."
Having sought wealth unrighteously and by force, one makes oneself happy and joyful, shares it, and performs meritorious deeds.
But here, householder, a certain enjoyer of sensual pleasures seeks wealth both righteously and unrighteously, both by force and without force;
having sought wealth both righteously and unrighteously, both by force and without force, he does not make himself happy or joyful, nor does he share it or perform meritorious deeds.
Furthermore, householder, here a certain enjoyer of sensual pleasures seeks wealth both by lawful and unlawful means, both by violence and without violence;
having sought wealth both by lawful and unlawful means, both by violence and without violence, he makes himself happy and pleased, yet he does not share it nor perform meritorious deeds.
Furthermore, householder, here a certain enjoyer of sensual pleasures seeks wealth both by lawful and unlawful means, both by violence and without violence... [and so on].
Having sought wealth both by right means and by wrong means, both through violence and without violence, one makes oneself happy and glad, shares it, and performs meritorious deeds.
But here, householder, some enjoyer of sensual pleasures seeks wealth by right means and without violence;
yet having sought wealth by right means and without violence, he does not make himself happy or glad, nor does he share it, nor does he perform meritorious deeds.
Furthermore, householder, here a certain enjoyer of sensual pleasures seeks wealth righteously and without violence;
having sought wealth righteously and without violence, he makes himself happy and pleased, yet he does not share it nor perform meritorious deeds.
Furthermore, householder, here a certain enjoyer of sensual pleasures seeks wealth righteously and without violence...
Having sought wealth righteously and without violence, one makes oneself happy and pleased, shares it, and performs meritorious deeds.
Yet, one enjoys that wealth while being gripped by it, infatuated with it, and clinging to it—failing to see its danger and lacking wisdom regarding escape from it.
But here, householder, some enjoyer of sensual pleasures seeks wealth righteously and without violence;
Having sought wealth righteously and without violence, he makes himself happy and joyful, shares it, and performs meritorious deeds.
And he enjoys that wealth without being attached to it, infatuated with it, or obsessed by it; seeing its danger and possessing wisdom regarding escape, he uses it.
In this regard, householder, as for that enjoyer of sensual pleasures who seeks wealth unrighteously and through violence—unrighteously...
Having sought wealth through violence, he does not make himself happy, nor does he gladden himself, nor does he share it, nor does he perform meritorious deeds.
Householder, this enjoyer of sensual pleasures is to be censured for three reasons.
First, he is to be censured for this first reason: "He seeks wealth unrighteously and through violence."
‘He does not make himself happy nor does he gladden himself’—on account of this second ground he is to be criticized.
‘He does not share [his wealth] nor does he perform meritorious deeds’—on account of this third ground he is to be criticized.
Householder, this enjoyer of sensual pleasures is to be criticized on these three grounds.
In this regard, householder, that enjoyer of sensual pleasures who seeks wealth unrighteously and by violence,
and having sought wealth unrighteously and by violence, makes himself happy and pleased but neither shares it nor performs meritorious deeds—
this enjoyer of sensual pleasures, householder, is to be blamed for two reasons and praised for one reason.
‘He seeks wealth unrighteously and by violence’—on account of this first ground he is to be censured.
‘He makes himself happy and glad’—on account of this one ground he is to be praised.
‘He does not share [the wealth] nor perform meritorious deeds’—on account of this second ground he is to be censured.
“Householder, this enjoyer of sensual pleasures is to be censured for these two reasons and praised for this one reason.
In this regard, householder, as for that enjoyer of sensual pleasures who seeks wealth unrighteously and by violence,
and having sought wealth unrighteously and by violence, makes himself happy and pleased, shares it, and performs meritorious deeds— this [is the case].”
Householder, one who enjoys sensual pleasures is to be blamed for one reason and praised for two reasons.
"He seeks wealth by unrighteous means, through violence"—for this one reason he is to be blamed.
"He makes himself happy and pleased"—for this first reason he is to be praised.
‘He shares [his wealth] and performs meritorious deeds’—by this second ground he is to be praised.
Householder, this enjoyer of sensual pleasures is to be censured for this one ground, but praised for these two grounds.
In this regard, householder, as for that enjoyer of sensual pleasures who seeks wealth both by lawful and unlawful means, whether by violence or without violence...
Having sought wealth both by righteous and unrighteous means, and both by violent and non-violent means, one does not make oneself happy,
nor does one gladden oneself, nor does one share it, nor does one perform meritorious deeds— this person who enjoys sensual pleasures, householder,
is praiseworthy for one reason and censurable for three reasons.
‘He seeks wealth righteously and without violence’—on this one ground he is to be praised.
‘He seeks wealth unrighteously and by violence’—on this first ground he is to be censured.
‘He does not make himself happy or joyful’—on this second ground he is to be censured.
‘He does not share [his wealth] and does not perform meritorious deeds’—on account of this third ground, he is to be censured.
Householder, this enjoyer of sensual pleasures is to be praised on this one ground and censured on these three grounds.
In that regard, householder, as for this enjoyer of sensual pleasures who seeks wealth both by lawful and unlawful means, whether by violence or without violence...
Having sought wealth both by righteous means and unrighteous means, and both by violent means and non-violent means, one makes oneself happy and pleased,
yet does not share it nor perform meritorious deeds— this person, householder, who enjoys sensual pleasures is praiseworthy in two respects and blameworthy in two respects.
“He seeks wealth by righteous means and by non-violent means”— in this first respect he is praiseworthy.
‘He seeks wealth unrighteously and by violence’—on account of this first ground, he is to be censured.
‘He makes himself happy and pleased’—on account of this second ground, he is to be praised.
‘He does not share [the wealth] nor perform meritorious deeds’—on account of this third ground, he is to be censured.
“Householder, this enjoyer of sensual pleasures is to be praised for these two reasons and censured for these two reasons.
In this regard, householder, that enjoyer of sensual pleasures who seeks wealth both by lawful and unlawful means,

and both by violent and non-violent means, and having sought wealth both by lawful and unlawful means, and both by violent and non-violent means, makes himself happy and pleased and shares it [with others]— ”
"He performs meritorious deeds. Householder, this enjoyer of sensual pleasures is praiseworthy for three reasons and censurable for one reason.
"He seeks wealth righteously and without violence"—for this first reason he is praiseworthy.
"He seeks wealth unrighteously and by violence"—for this one reason he is censurable.
“He makes himself happy and pleased”—this is the second ground for praise.
“He shares [his wealth] and performs meritorious deeds”—this is the third ground for praise.
Householder, this enjoyer of sensual pleasures is praiseworthy on account of these three grounds, but censurable on account of this one ground.
In this regard, householder, that enjoyer of sensual pleasures who seeks wealth righteously and without violence,
yet having sought wealth righteously and without violence, does not make himself happy or joyful, nor shares it, nor performs meritorious deeds—
this enjoyer of sensual pleasures, householder, is praiseworthy in one respect and censurable in two respects.
"He seeks wealth righteously and without violence"—on this one ground he is to be praised.
"He does not make himself happy or joyful"—on this first ground he is to be censured.
"He does not share it nor perform meritorious deeds"—on this second ground he is to be censured.
“Householder, this enjoyer of sensual pleasures is to be praised for this one ground, but he is to be criticized for these two grounds. In this regard, householder,
that enjoyer of sensual pleasures who seeks wealth righteously and without violence, yet having sought wealth righteously and without violence,
makes himself happy and pleased but does not share it nor perform meritorious deeds— this one, householder, [is to be criticized for those two grounds].”
“Householder, one who enjoys sensual pleasures is to be praised for two reasons and criticized for one.
‘He seeks wealth righteously and without violence’—for this first reason he is to be praised.
‘He makes himself happy and pleased’—for this second reason he is to be praised.”
“He does not share [his wealth] and does not perform meritorious deeds”—on account of this one ground, he is to be censured.
Householder, this enjoyer of sensual pleasures is to be praised on these two grounds and censured on this one ground.
In this regard, householder, as for that enjoyer of sensual pleasures who seeks wealth righteously and without violence... [he seeks wealth] righteously.
Having sought wealth, he enjoys it without violence, gladdens himself, shares it, and performs meritorious deeds;
yet he consumes those riches while being bound by them, infatuated with them, and clinging to them, seeing neither their danger nor the way of escape from them.
This person who enjoys sensual pleasures, householder, is praiseworthy in three respects and censurable in one respect.
“He seeks wealth righteously and without violence”—this is the first ground for praise.
“He makes himself happy and joyful”—this is the second ground for praise.
“He shares [his wealth] and performs meritorious deeds”—this is the third ground for praise.

‘He enjoys those possessions while being obsessed with them, infatuated with them, and clinging to them, seeing neither the danger in them nor possessing the wisdom for their escape’—on account of this one ground he is to be censured.
Householder, this enjoyer of sensual pleasures is to be praised on these three grounds and censured on this one ground.
In that regard, householder, as for the enjoyer of sensual pleasures who seeks wealth righteously and without violence... [he seeks] wealth righteously.
Having sought them out, he makes himself happy and joyful without violence, shares them, and performs meritorious deeds;
and he enjoys those possessions without being bound by them, without being infatuated with them, and without being addicted to them, seeing their danger and possessing wisdom regarding escape.
In these four respects, householder, such an enjoyer of sensual pleasures is praiseworthy.
“He seeks wealth righteously and without violence”—this is the first ground for praise.
“He makes himself happy and joyful”—this is the second ground for praise.
“He shares it and performs meritorious deeds”—this is the third ground for praise.

‘And he enjoys those riches without being tied to them, without being infatuated with them, without being obsessed by them; seeing the danger in them and discerning the escape from them’—on account of this fourth ground, he is praiseworthy.
This, householder, is the enjoyer of sensual pleasures who is praiseworthy on these four grounds.
These, householder, are the ten kinds of enjoyers of sensual pleasures found existing in the world.
Of these ten types of enjoyers of sensual pleasures, householder, the one who seeks wealth righteously and without violence,
and having sought wealth righteously and without violence, makes himself happy and pleased, shares it, and performs meritorious deeds—
and who is unattached, uninfatuated, and unclinging to that wealth, seeing its danger and possessing wisdom regarding escape— [is the foremost].
...enjoys them; this one is the foremost, the best, the chief, the highest, and the most excellent among these ten types of enjoyers of sensual pleasures.

Just as, householder, from a cow comes milk, from milk curd, from curd butter, from butter ghee, and from ghee the cream of ghee—and the cream of ghee is declared to be the best therein—so too, householder, among these ten types of enjoyers of sensual pleasures, that enjoyer of sensual pleasures who [obtains wealth] through the Dhamma...
He seeks wealth without violence; having sought wealth righteously and without violence, he makes himself happy and glad, shares it, and performs meritorious deeds.
Furthermore, he enjoys that wealth without being tied to it, infatuated with it, or obsessed by it, seeing its danger and possessing the wisdom of escape.
This one is the foremost and the best among these ten types of enjoyers of sensual pleasures.
“Foremost, supreme, and excellent.
First.
*Aṅguttara Nikāya* 10.92.

10. Upāli Chapter: The Discourse on Fear (Upālivagga Bhayasutta) “Monks, there are these five fears that have not yet arisen which will arise in the future, and which, when they have arisen, will lead to the harm and suffering of many people, to the detriment, harm, and suffering of devas and humans. What five? The fear of famine has not yet arisen, but it will arise in the future; when it has arisen, it will lead to the harm and suffering of many people, to the detriment, harm, and suffering of devas and humans. The fear of weapons has not yet arisen, but it will arise in the future; when it has arisen, it will lead to the harm and suffering of many people, to the detriment, harm, and suffering of devas and humans. The fear of disease has not yet arisen, but it will arise in the future; when it has arisen, it will lead to the harm and suffering of many people, to the detriment, harm, and suffering of devas and humans. The fear of non-Buddhist teachers has not yet arisen, but it will arise in the future; when it has arisen, it will lead to the harm and suffering of many people, to the detriment, harm, and suffering of devas and humans. The fear of the appearance of a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Perfectly Enlightened One, who is more excellent and more sublime than me, has not yet arisen, but it will arise in the future; when it has arisen, it will lead to the harm and suffering of many people, to the detriment, harm, and suffering of devas and humans. These are the five fears that have not yet arisen which will arise in the future, and which, when they have arisen, will lead to the harm and suffering of many people, to the detriment, harm, and suffering of devas and humans.”
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As the householder Anāthapiṇḍika was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said this to him:
"Householder, when five fears and enmities have been stilled for a noble disciple, by four..."
And he possesses the factors of stream-entry; the noble method has been well seen and well penetrated by his wisdom.
Desiring it, he could declare of himself: "I have exhausted hell; I have exhausted the animal realm;

I have exhausted the sphere of hungry ghosts; I have exhausted the states of deprivation, the evil destinations, and the lower worlds. I am a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as my destination."
What are the five fears and enmities that have been stilled?
Householder, when one who destroys life, on account of the destruction of life, engenders fear and enmity both in this present life and in future lives,
and experiences mental pain and grief— [these are the first].
One who abstains from taking life engenders neither fear nor enmity pertaining to the present life,
nor does he engender fear or enmity pertaining to future lives, nor does he experience mental pain or dejection.
For one who abstains from taking life, that fear and enmity are thus stilled.
Householder, one who takes what is not given...
one who engages in sexual misconduct... one who speaks falsehood... [is reborn in hell].
One who indulges in fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants that cause negligence produces fear and enmity both in this present life and in future lives, and experiences mental pain and grief;
whereas one who abstains from fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants that cause negligence produces neither fear nor enmity in this present life... [and so forth].
One generates enmity that brings fear even in the future life, and one experiences mental pain and dejection.
For one who abstains from fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence, that fear and enmity are thus stilled.
These five fears and enmities are stilled.
With which four factors of stream-entry is he endowed?
Here, householder, the noble disciple is endowed with verified confidence in the Buddha:
"Thus indeed is the Blessed One … [as above] … the Buddha, the Blessed One."
He is endowed with verified confidence in the Dhamma:
"The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be personally realized by the wise.
He is endowed with verified confidence in the Saṅgha:

‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing well; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing straightly; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing methodically;

the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing appropriately—namely, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals. This Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality, worthy of gifts.’
‘He is worthy of salutation with joined palms, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
He is endowed with the virtues dear to the noble ones—virtues that are unbroken, untorn, unspotted, unmottled, liberating, praised by the wise, unadhered-to, and conducive to concentration.
Thus, he is endowed with these four factors of stream-entry.
And what is that noble method well seen and thoroughly penetrated by wisdom?
Here, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus:
"When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises."
When this is not, that is not; with the cessation of this, that ceases. That is to say:
with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise;
with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises.
With consciousness as condition, name-and-form;
with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases;
with the six sense bases as condition, contact.
With contact as condition, feeling arises;
with feeling as condition, craving arises;
with craving as condition, clinging arises.
With clinging as condition, existence comes to be;
with existence as condition, birth;
and with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise.
‘In this way there is the arising of this entire mass of suffering;
but from the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations...
[and so on] ...in this way there is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering.’”
And this noble method has been well seen and well penetrated by his wisdom.
Householder, when these five fears and enmities have subsided for a noble disciple,
and he is endowed with these four factors of stream-entry, and this noble method has been well seen by his wisdom—
It has been well-penetrated; desiring it, one could declare of oneself:

“I have exhausted hell, exhausted the animal realm, exhausted the sphere of hungry ghosts; I have exhausted the states of deprivation, the evil destinations, and the lower worlds. I am a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as my destination.
This is the second [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.93 10. Upālivagga Kiṃdiṭṭhikasutta (The Discourse on What Kinds of Views) “Venerable sir, what kind of view does one hold who holds such a view as this: ‘There is nothing given, nothing offered, nothing sacrificed; there is no fruit or result of good and bad actions’? “Bhikkhus, one who holds such a view holds the view of a nihilist. “But, venerable sir, what kind of view does one hold who holds such a view as this: ‘There is a self that is permanent, stable, eternal, and not subject to change’? “Bhikkhus, one who holds such a view holds the view of an eternalist. “Venerable sir, what kind of view does one hold who holds such a view as this: ‘The Tathāgata exists after death’? “Bhikkhus, one who holds such a view holds the view of an eternalist. “But, venerable sir, what kind of view does one hold who holds such a view as this: ‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death’? “Bhikkhus, one who holds such a view holds the view of an annihilationist.

“Venerable sir, what kind of view does one hold who holds such a view as this: ‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death’? “Bhikkhus, one who holds such a view holds the view of an eternalist and an annihilationist. “But, venerable sir, what kind of view does one hold who holds such a view as this: ‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death’? “Bhikkhus, one who holds such a view holds the view of an eternalist and an annihilationist. “Venerable sir, what kind of view does one hold who holds such a view as this: ‘There is this world, there is the next world’? “Bhikkhus, one who holds such a view holds the view of an eternalist. “But, venerable sir, what kind of view does one hold who holds such a view as this: ‘There is no this world, there is no next world’? “Bhikkhus, one who holds such a view holds the view of an annihilationist. “Venerable sir, what kind of view does one hold who holds such a view as this: ‘There is both this world and the next world’? “Bhikkhus, one who holds such a view holds the view of an eternalist and an annihilationist. “But, venerable sir, what kind of view does one hold who holds such a view as this: ‘There is neither this world nor the next world’? “Bhikkhus, one who holds such a view holds the view of an eternalist and an annihilationist. “Venerable sir, what kind of view does one hold who holds such a view as this: ‘There is liberation through the exertion of will’? “Bhikkhus, one who holds such a view holds the view of an eternalist. “But, venerable sir, what kind of view does one hold who holds such a view as this: ‘There is no liberation through the exertion of will’? “Bhikkhus, one who holds such a view holds the view of an annihilationist. “Venerable sir, what kind of view does one hold who holds such a view as this: ‘There is both liberation through the exertion of will and no liberation through the exertion of will’? “Bhikkhus, one who holds such a view holds the view of an eternalist and an annihilationist. “But, venerable sir, what kind of view does one hold who holds such a view as this: ‘There is neither liberation through the exertion of will nor no liberation through the exertion of will’? “Bhikkhus, one who holds such a view holds the view of an eternalist and an annihilationist. “Venerable sir, what kind of view does one hold who holds such a view as this: ‘There is this world and the next world, and there is liberation through the exertion of will’? “Bhikkhus, one who holds such a view holds the view of an eternalist. “But, venerable sir, what kind of view does one hold who holds such a view as this: ‘There is no this world, no next world, and no liberation through the exertion of will’? “Bhikkhus, one who holds such a view holds the view of an annihilationist. “Venerable sir, what kind of view does one hold who holds such a view as this: ‘There is this world and the next world, and there is no liberation through the exertion of will’? “Bhikkhus, one who holds such a view holds the view of an eternalist. “But, venerable sir, what kind of view does one hold who holds such a view as this: ‘There is no this world, no next world, and there is liberation through the exertion of will’? “Bhikkhus, one who holds such a view holds the view of an annihilationist. “Venerable sir, what kind of view does one hold who holds such a view as this: ‘There is this world and the next world, and there is both liberation through the exertion of will and no liberation through the exertion of will’? “Bhikkhus, one who holds such a view holds the view of an eternalist and an annihilationist. “But, venerable sir, what kind of view does one hold who holds such a view as this: ‘There is no this world, no next world, and there is neither liberation through the exertion of will nor no liberation through the exertion of will’? “Bhikkhus, one who holds such a view holds the view of an eternalist and an annihilationist. “Venerable sir, what kind of view does one hold who holds such a view as this: ‘There is this world and the next world, and there is neither liberation through the exertion of will nor no liberation through the exertion of will’? “Bhikkhus, one who holds such a view holds the view of an eternalist. “But, venerable sir, what kind of view does one hold who holds such a view as this: ‘There is no this world, no next world, and there is neither liberation through the exertion of will nor no liberation through the exertion of will’? “Bhikkhus, one who holds such a view holds the view of an annihilationist. “Venerable sir, what kind of view does one hold who holds such a view as this: ‘There is this world and the next world, and there is liberation through the exertion of will, and there is neither liberation through the exertion of will nor no liberation through the exertion of will’? “Bhikkhus, one who holds such a view holds the view of an eternalist. “But, venerable sir, what kind of view does one hold who holds such a view as this: ‘There is no this world, no next world, and there is liberation through the exertion of will, and there is neither liberation through the exertion of will nor no liberation through the exertion of will’? “Bhikkhus, one who holds such a view holds the view of an annihilationist. “Venerable sir, what kind of view does one hold who holds such a view as this: ‘There is this world and the next world, and there is neither liberation through the exertion of will nor no liberation through the exertion of will’? “Bhikkhus, one who holds such a view holds the view of an eternalist. “But, venerable sir, what kind of view does one hold who holds such a view as this: ‘There is no this world, no next world, and there is neither liberation through the exertion of will nor no liberation through the exertion of will’? “Bhikkhus, one who holds such a view holds the view of an annihilationist. “Venerable sir, what kind of view does one hold who holds such a view as this: ‘There is this world and the next world, and there is liberation through the exertion of will, and there is neither liberation through the exertion of will nor no liberation through the exertion of will’? “Bhikkhus, one who holds such a view holds the view of an eternalist. “But, venerable sir, what kind of view does one hold who holds such a view as this: ‘There is no this world, no next world, and there is liberation through the exertion of will, and there is neither liberation through the exertion of will nor no liberation through the exertion of will’? “Bhikkhus, one who holds such a view holds the view of an annihilationist. “Venerable sir, what kind of view does one hold who holds such a view as this: ‘There is this world and the next world, and there is liberation through the exertion of will, and there is neither liberation through the exertion of will nor no liberation through the exert
(AN 10.93, PTS AN v 185) On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. Then,
in the middle of the day, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika departed from Sāvatthī to see the Blessed One.
Then it occurred to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika:
"It is not yet the right time to see the Blessed One;
the Blessed One is in seclusion."
"It is not the time for visiting the monks who are worthy of esteem;
those monks who are worthy of esteem are in seclusion.
Suppose I were to go to the park of the wanderers of other sects?"
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika approached the park of the wanderers of other sects.
Now at that time, those wanderers of other sects were sitting together in a crowd, making a great clamor and a loud noise, engaged in various kinds of frivolous talk.
Those wanderers of other sects saw the householder Anāthapiṇḍika coming from afar.
Having seen him, they settled one another, saying:
"Be quiet, sirs; do not make a noise.
This householder Anāthapiṇḍika, a disciple of the ascetic Gotama, is coming to the monastery."
"Furthermore, among the white-robed lay disciples of the ascetic Gotama who reside in Sāvatthī, this householder Anāthapiṇḍika is one of them.
Those venerable ones desire little noise, are trained in little noise, and speak in praise of little noise.
It might be that, perceiving a gathering with little noise, he would think it appropriate to approach."
Then those wanderers of other sects became silent.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika approached those wanderers of other sects; having approached, he exchanged greetings with them.

When they had finished exchanging polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. As the householder Anāthapiṇḍika was sitting there to one side, those wanderers of other sects said this to him:
“Tell me, householder, what is the ascetic Gotama’s view?
“I do not know, venerable sir, all of the Blessed One’s views.
“So it seems, householder, that you do not know all of the ascetic Gotama’s views.”
“Tell me, householder, what is the view of the bhikkhus?
“Venerable sir, I do not even know the entire view of the bhikkhus.
“So it seems, householder, that you do not know the entire view of the ascetic Gotama, nor do you know the entire view of the bhikkhus.”
“Tell us, householder, what is your view?
“Venerable sir, it is not difficult for us to declare what our views are.
Come now, let the venerable ones first declare their own respective views; afterwards, it will not be difficult for us to declare what our views are.”
When this was said, a certain wanderer said to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika:
“The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false—such, householder, is my view.”
Then another wanderer said this to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika:
“The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false—such is my view, householder.”
Then another wanderer said this to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika:
“The world is finite … [or] the world is infinite …”
"The soul and the body are the same" … "the soul is one thing and the body another" … "a Tathāgata exists after death" …
“The Tathāgata does not exist after death… both exists and does not exist after death… neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is the truth, all else is vain”— thus they hold.
“I hold such a view, householder.
When this was said, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika said to those wanderers:
“Venerable sirs, as for that venerable one who spoke thus:”
‘The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false’—such was my view, householder.
This view of this venerable one has arisen either due to his own improper attention or conditioned by the voice of another.
Moreover, this view is a thing that has come to be, conditioned, volitionally produced, and dependently arisen.
Whatever is a thing that has come to be, conditioned, volitionally produced, and dependently arisen, that is impermanent.
What is impermanent is suffering.
Whatever is suffering, that very thing this venerable one has clung to; that very thing this venerable one has accepted.
As for what this venerable one says, Bhante:
"The world is eternal; this alone is the truth, all else is false"—it is precisely suffering that he has clung to and accepted.
‘Householder, such is my view.
This view of this venerable one has arisen either due to his own improper attention or conditioned by the voice of another.
Furthermore, that view is real, conditioned, volitionally produced, and dependently originated.
Whatever is conditioned, constructed, volitionally produced, and dependently arisen is impermanent.
What is impermanent is suffering.
This venerable one has clung to that very thing; this venerable one has adhered to that very thing.
"Venerable sir, as for this venerable one who speaks thus:
‘The world is finite...
[or] the world is infinite...’"
"The soul and the body are the same" … "the soul is one thing and the body another" … "a Tathāgata exists after death" …
"The Tathāgata does not exist after death...
the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death...
the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is the truth, all else is vain"—this is a speculative view.
‘Householder, such is my view.
This view of this venerable one has arisen either through his own unwise attention or with the voice of another as its condition.
Furthermore, that view is real, conditioned, volitionally produced, and dependently originated.
"Whatever is born, conditioned, volitionally produced, and dependently arisen is impermanent.
What is impermanent is suffering.
This venerable one has clung to that very thing; this venerable one has taken up that very thing."
When this was said, those wanderers said this to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika:
“Householder, we have all indeed declared our respective views.
Tell us, householder, what is your own view?”
“Venerable sir, whatever is conditioned, fabricated, volitionally produced, and dependently arisen is impermanent.
What is impermanent is suffering.
Regarding what is suffering: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’”
“I hold such a view, Bhante.
“Householder, whatever is conditioned, formed, volitionally produced, and dependently arisen is impermanent.
What is impermanent is suffering.”
“Householder, you have clung to that which is suffering; householder, you have accepted that which is suffering.
“Venerable sir, whatever is become, conditioned, volitionally produced, and dependently arisen is impermanent.
What is impermanent is suffering.”
‘Whatever is suffering, that is not mine; I am not this; this is not my self’—thus has this been well seen as it really is with correct wisdom.
And I understand its further escape as it really is.
When this was said, those wanderers sat silent, ashamed, with shoulders slumped and heads downcast, brooding and unable to respond.

Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, perceiving that those wanderers were silent, crestfallen, with shoulders drooping and faces downcast, brooding and speechless, rose from his seat and approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika...
The householder reported to the Blessed One everything that had been the conversation and discussion with those wanderers of other sects.
"Excellent, excellent, householder! [the Blessed One said].
“In this way, householder, those foolish men should from time to time be properly rebuked with a reasoned argument.
Then the Blessed One instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened the householder Anāthapiṇḍika with a discourse on the Dhamma.

Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, having been instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened by the Blessed One with a discourse on the Dhamma, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed.
Then, not long after the householder Anāthapiṇḍika had departed, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus,

even a bhikkhu who has been ordained for a hundred years in this Dhamma and Vinaya would be able to refute those wanderers of other sects with such thoroughness according to the Dhamma, just as Anāthapiṇḍika has done.”
“[He] was rebuked by the householder.
The third [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.94

10. Upāli Chapter: The Discourse to Vajjiyamāhita (AN 10.94, PTS AN v 189) At Sāvatthī. Then the householder Vajjiyamāhita approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how many things does a noble disciple possess to be declared ‘one who has arrived at the fruit,’ ‘one who stands upon the fruit,’ and ‘one who is no longer subject to falling back’? “There are five things, householder, that a noble disciple possesses to be declared ‘one who has arrived at the fruit,’ ‘one who stands upon the fruit,’ and ‘one who is no longer subject to falling back. What five? Here, householder, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. He possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—untorn, unbroken, unspotted, unsplattered, liberating, praised by the wise, untarnished, leading to concentration. He possesses the aggregate of wisdom that is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. Possessing these five things, householder, a noble disciple is declared ‘one who has arrived at the fruit,’ ‘one who stands upon the fruit,’ and ‘one who is no longer subject to falling back. When this was said, the householder Vajjiyamāhita said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir!... From today let the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life. Then the householder Vajjiyamāhita, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Not long after he had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, there are these five things that lead to the decline of a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life. What five? Here, bhikkhus, a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life frequents those who are not virtuous, not those who are virtuous; he honors those who are not virtuous, not those who are virtuous; he listens to the Dhamma from those who are not virtuous, not from those who are virtuous; he learns the Dhamma from those who are not virtuous, not from those who are virtuous; and he examines the meaning of the Dhamma with those who are not virtuous, not with those who are virtuous. These, bhikkhus, are the five things that lead to the decline of a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life. There are, bhikkhus, these other five things that lead to the non-decline of a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life. What five? Here, bhikkhus, a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life does not frequent those who are not virtuous, but frequents those who are virtuous; he honors those who are virtuous, not those who are not virtuous; he listens to the Dhamma from those who are virtuous, not from those who are not virtuous;

he learns the Dhamma from those who are virtuous, not from those who are not virtuous; and he examines the meaning of the Dhamma with those who are virtuous, not with those who are not virtuous. These, bhikkhus, are the five things that lead to the non-decline of a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s words. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these five kinds of persons found existing in the world. What five? The person who is like a stone pillar, the person who is like a wooden post, the person who is like a balance scale, the person who is like a pool of water, and the person who is like a lotus. And how, bhikkhus, is a person like a stone pillar? Here, bhikkhus, some person is firm in his views, holding them tightly, stubbornly clinging to them, and refusing to release them even when being pressed and questioned by others. This is called a person like a stone pillar. And how, bhikkhus, is a person like a wooden post? Here, bhikkhus, some person is dull-witted and slow to understand the Dhamma and discipline taught by the Tathāgata. This is called a person like a wooden post. And how, bhikkhus, is a person like a balance scale? Here, bhikkhus, some person goes up and down, rising and falling, like a balance scale. This is called a person like a balance scale. And how, bhikkhus, is a person like a pool of water? Here, bhikkhus, some person is one who gains his livelihood by means of the Dhamma, not by means of what is not the Dhamma. This is called a person like a pool of water. And how, bhikkhus, is a person like a lotus? Here, bhikkhus, some person is an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, reached the true goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through final knowledge. This is called a person like a lotus. These, bhikkhus, are the five kinds of persons found existing in the world. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Sublime One rose from his seat and went to his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had gone, a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it was said: ‘A person like a stone pillar... a person like a lotus. In what way, venerable sir, is a person like a stone pillar? In what way is a person like a wooden post? In what way is a person like a balance scale? In what way is a person like a pool of water? In what way is a person like a lotus? “Here, bhikkhu, some person is firm in his views, holding them tightly, stubbornly clinging to them, and refusing to release them even when being pressed and questioned by others. In this way, bhikkhu, a person is like a stone pillar. Here, bhikkhu, some person is dull-witted and slow to understand the Dhamma and discipline taught by the Tathāgata. In this way, bhikkhu, a person is like a wooden post. Here, bhikkhu, some person goes up and down, rising and falling, like a balance scale. In this way, bhikkhu, a person is like a balance scale. Here, bhikkhu, some person is one who gains his livelihood by means of the Dhamma, not by means of what is not the Dhamma. In this way, bhikkhu, a person is like a pool of water. Here, bhikkhu, some person is an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed... and is liberated through final knowledge. In this way, bhikkhu, a person is like a lotus. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, that bhikkhu delighted in the Blessed One’s words. Thus have I heard. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these five kinds of persons found existing in the world. What five? On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Campā on the bank of the Gaggarā Lotus Pond.
Then the householder Vajjiyamāhita departed from Campā during the middle of the day to see the Blessed One.
Then it occurred to the householder Vajjiyamāhita:
“It is not yet the right time to see the Blessed One;
the Blessed One is in seclusion.
It is also not the right time to see the venerable monks.”
“Even the monks who are worthy of esteem are in seclusion.
What if I were to go to the park of the wanderers of other sects?
Then the householder Vajjiyamāhita went to the park of the wanderers of other sects.
Now at that time, those wanderers of other sects were sitting together in a crowd, making a great clamor and loud noise, engaged in various kinds of frivolous talk.
Those wanderers of other sects saw the householder Vajjiyamāhita coming from afar; seeing him, they quieted one another, saying:
"Be quiet, sirs! Do not make a noise, sirs!"
"Here comes the householder Vajjiyamāhita, a disciple of the ascetic Gotama.
Of all the white-robed lay disciples of the ascetic Gotama residing in Campā, this householder Vajjiyamāhita is one of them.
Now, those venerable ones desire little noise; they are disciplined in the avoidance of noise and are speakers in praise of little noise."
“Perhaps, having perceived that the assembly is quiet, he might think it fit to approach.
Then those wanderers of other sects became silent.
Then the householder Vajjiyamāhita approached those wanderers of other sects; having approached, he exchanged greetings with them.
Having exchanged polite and courteous greetings, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, those wanderers of other sects said this to the householder Vajjiyamāhita:
“Is it true, householder, that the ascetic Gotama disparages all austerity, and that he single-mindedly censures and reviles every ascetic who lives a harsh life?
“Venerable sirs, the Blessed One does not disparage all austerity, nor does he single-mindedly censure and revile every ascetic who lives a harsh life.”
“Venerable sir, the Blessed One censures what is censurable and praises what is praiseworthy.
Since the Blessed One censures what is censurable and praises what is praiseworthy, venerable sir, the Blessed One is one who speaks analytically;
he is not one who speaks categorically in this matter.”
When this was said, a certain wanderer said to the householder Vajjiyamāhita:
“Wait a moment, householder! Regarding that ascetic Gotama whose praise you speak, is it not the case that the ascetic Gotama is an annihilationist and one who does not prescribe rules?
“On this point, venerable sir, I shall speak to you in accordance with the Dhamma:”
“‘This is wholesome,’ venerable sir, has been declared by the Blessed One;
‘this is unwholesome,’ venerable sir, has been declared by the Blessed One.
Thus, while the Blessed One declares what is wholesome and unwholesome, the Blessed One is one who possesses such declarations.”
“The Blessed One is not a mere disciplinarian who issues no instructions.
When this was said, those wanderers sat silent, ashamed, with shoulders slumped and heads downcast, brooding and unable to respond.
Then the householder Vajjiyamāhita [addressed] those wanderers who were silent, ashamed, with shoulders slumped...
Seeing them sitting with their heads bowed, brooding and speechless, Vajjiyamāhita rose from his seat,
approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side.
As he was seated there, he reported to the Blessed One everything that had been said in his conversation with those wanderers of other sects.
“Excellent, excellent, householder!
It is indeed in this way, householder, that those foolish men should from time to time be properly restrained by you with the Dhamma.
Householder, I do not say that every kind of austerity should be practiced.”
Furthermore, householder, I do not say that every kind of austerity should not be practiced;
nor, householder, do I say that every kind of undertaking should be undertaken;
nor, householder, do I say that every kind of undertaking should not be undertaken.
“Householder, I do not say that every kind of striving should be undertaken;
nor, householder, do I say that no kind of striving should be undertaken.
Householder, I do not say that every kind of relinquishment should be relinquished.”
"But, householder, I do not say that every relinquishment is not to be relinquished;
nor, householder, do I say that every liberation is not to be liberated;
nor, householder, do I say that every liberation must not be liberated."
"For whatever austerity, householder, that one practicing leads to the increase of unwholesome states and the decline of wholesome states, such an austerity, I say, should not be practiced.
But whatever austerity, householder, that one practicing leads to the decline of unwholesome states and the increase of wholesome states, such an austerity, I say, should be practiced.
For whatever undertaking, householder, that one undertaking leads to the increase of unwholesome states and the decline of wholesome states, such an undertaking, I say, should not be undertaken."
"Householder, I say that one should undertake such an undertaking as, by undertaking it, unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase.
For I say that one should not exert such an effort as, by exerting it, unwholesome states increase and wholesome states diminish."
"Householder, when for one who exerts effort unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase, I say that such effort should be exerted.
But, householder, when for one who relinquishes [attachment] unwholesome states increase and wholesome states diminish, I say that such relinquishment should not be practiced."
"Householder, when by relinquishing a certain relinquishment unwholesome states decline and wholesome states increase, I say that such a relinquishment should be relinquished.
For if, householder, by being liberated through a certain liberation unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline, I say that such a liberation should not be liberated."
“Householder, when unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase as one is liberated by this liberation, I say that such a liberation is to be liberated.

Then the householder Vajjiyamāhita, having been instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened by the Blessed One with a discourse on the Dhamma, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed.
Not long after the householder Vajjiyamāhita had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, even that bhikkhu who has long had little dust in his eyes regarding this Dhamma and Discipline would likewise refute those wanderers of other sects with reasoned argument,
just as they were refuted by the householder Vajjiyamāhita.”
The Fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.95 10. Upālivagga
Uttiya Sutta.
Then the wanderer Uttiya approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.
Having exchanged greetings and pleasantries, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the wanderer Uttiya said this to the Blessed One:
"Master Gotama, is it the case that the world is eternal; that this alone is true and anything else is false?
"Uttiya, this has not been declared by me."
‘The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false.
‘But, Master Gotama, is it the case that the world is not eternal; this alone is true, all else is false?
‘This too, Uttiya, has been left undeclared by me.’
“The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false.
“But, Master Gotama, is the world finite … or is the world infinite …?”
"The soul and the body are the same" … "the soul is one thing and the body another" … "a Tathāgata exists after death" …

‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death… the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death… the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is the truth, all else is foolish’?”
“Uttiya, this too has been left undeclared by me:
‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is the truth, all else is vain.

“When asked, ‘Venerable Gotama, is it the case that “the world is eternal; this alone is the truth, all else is vain,” and have you declared this? you replied, ‘Uttiya, this too has been left undeclared by me.’”
‘The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false,’ you say.

But when asked, ‘Venerable Gotama, is it the case that “the world is not eternal; this alone is true, all else is false”?’—being thus questioned, you say, ‘Uttiya, this too has been left undeclared by me: “the world is not eternal; this alone is true, all else is false.”’”
‘But, Master Gotama, is the world finite?
… Is the world infinite?
… Are the soul and the body the same? … [and so on] …”
The soul is one thing and the body another...
the Tathāgata exists after death...
the Tathāgata does not exist after death...
‘The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death… the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is true, all else is false’— when asked thus,
O Uttiya, I have left this also undeclared.”
“‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is the truth, all else is vain’—this is what you say.
So then, for what purpose has Master Gotama made a declaration?
“Having directly known it myself, Uttiya, I teach the Dhamma to my disciples for the purification of beings, for the removal of sorrow and lamentation...”
“...for the surmounting of suffering and dejection, for the disappearance of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true way, and for the realization of Nibbāna.
“But as for this Dhamma that Master Gotama teaches to his disciples through direct knowledge—
for the purification of beings, for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true way...”
“...for the realization of Nibbāna, is the whole world led by him, or half, or a third?
When this was said, the Blessed One remained silent.
Then it occurred to the Venerable Ānanda:
“Let it not be that the wanderer Uttiya adopts such an evil view as this:
‘The ascetic Gotama, when asked a question about the most excellent of all things, evades it and does not answer; surely he is unable.
For that would lead to the long-term harm and suffering of the wanderer Uttiya.”
Then the Venerable Ānanda said this to the wanderer Uttiya:
"In that case, friend Uttiya, I shall give you a simile.
For by means of a simile, some wise people here understand the meaning of what has been said."
"Friend Uttiya, it is just as if there were a king’s frontier city with strong foundations, strong walls and gates, and a single gate.
Therein would be a gatekeeper who is wise, competent, and intelligent—a keeper-out of strangers and an usher-in of acquaintances.

He would patrol the circumvallation path all around that city. While patrolling the circumvallation path, he would not see a breach in the wall or an opening in the wall, even one large enough for a cat to slip through."
But it does not occur to him to know: "So many living beings enter or exit this city.
Rather, it occurs to him in this way: "Whatever gross living beings enter or exit this city, they all enter or exit through this gate.
In the same way, friend Uttiya, it does not occur to the Tathāgata to concern himself with whether the whole world is led away by that [Dhamma], or half of it, or a third part.
Then, indeed, it occurs to the Tathāgata in this regard: "Whatever beings have been led away from the world, are being led away, or will be led away,
all of them do so by abandoning the five hindrances— which are defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom—
by having their minds well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness, and by developing the seven factors of enlightenment as they really are."
"Thus these have been led away from the world, are being led away, or will be led away.
"Friend Uttiya, the very question you asked the Blessed One, you have asked the Blessed One again in another way.
Therefore, the Blessed One did not answer it to you."
The Fifth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.96.
Chapter Ten: The Section on Upāli.
The Kokanuda Sutta (AN 10.96).
On one occasion the Venerable Ānanda was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Tapoda Monastery.
Then, as the night was fading, the Venerable Ānanda rose and went to the Tapodā hot springs to bathe his limbs.
Having bathed his limbs in the Tapodā and come out, he stood there wearing a single robe, drying his limbs.
At that same time, the wanderer Kokanuda also rose as the night was fading and went to the Tapodā hot springs to bathe his limbs.
The wanderer Kokanuda saw the Venerable Ānanda coming from afar.
Having seen him, he said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
“Where are you going there, friend?”
“I am one of the bhikkhus, friend. “Of which bhikkhus, friend?
“Of the ascetics who are sons of the Sakyan, friend.”
“Venerable sir, we would ask the venerable one about a certain point, if the venerable one would grant us the opportunity for an answer to the question.
“Ask, friend; having heard it, I shall know.
“But, sir, do you hold the view: ‘The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false’?”
“Friend, I do not hold the view:
‘The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false.
“But, sir, do you hold the view: ‘The world is non-eternal; this alone is true, all else is false’?”
“I do not hold such a view, friend, as:
‘The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false.
“Then what, sir, is the case: Is the world finite...? [and so forth].
The world is infinite;
that soul is the same as the body;
the soul is one thing and the body another.
Does the Tathāgata exist after death? ...
Does the Tathāgata not exist after death? ...
Does the Tathāgata both exist and not exist after death? ...
“Do you hold the view: ‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is the truth, all else is foolish’?
“I do not hold such a view, friend:
‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is the truth, all else is foolish.’”
“Then, sir, you neither know nor see?
“I do not, friend, neither know nor see.
I do know, friend, I do see.”
“When asked, ‘Sir, do you hold the view: “The world is eternal; this alone is the truth, all else is foolishness”?’—being thus questioned, he replied:
‘I do not hold such a view, friend.’”
‘The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false,’ you say.
When asked, ‘But sir, do you hold the view that “the world is not eternal; this alone is true, all else is false”?’—being thus questioned:
“Friend, I do not hold the view that ‘the world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false.
Why then, sir, [do you ask] whether the world is finite...?”
The world is infinite … that the soul is identical with the body … that the soul is distinct from the body …
Does the Tathāgata exist after death?
Does the Tathāgata not exist after death?
Does the Tathāgata both exist and not exist after death?
‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death;
this alone is true, all else is false’—those who hold such a view, when asked thus, say:
‘Friends, I do not hold such a view.’”
‘The Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is true, all else is false.
When you were asked, ‘In that case, sir, you neither know nor see,’ you replied:
‘It is not that I do not know, friend, nor that I do not see.’”
“I know, friend, I see,” you say.
But how, friend, is the meaning of this statement to be understood?
“The view, friend, that ‘the world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false’—this is a mere speculative position.”
‘The world is eternal; this alone is true, all else is false’—this, friend, is a speculative view.
‘The world is finite’ … ‘the world is infinite’ … [and so on].
"The soul and the body are the same...
the soul is one thing and the body another...
a Tathāgata exists after death..."

‘The Tathāgata does not exist after death… the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death… the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death; this alone is the truth, all else is foolishness’— this, friend, is a speculative view.
To whatever extent there is view, to whatever extent there is the basis for views, the foundation of views, the obsession of views, the origination of views, and the eradication of views—I know that;
I see that. Knowing that and seeing that, how could I say:
"I do not know, I do not see"?
“I know it, friend; I see it.
“What is the Venerable One’s name, and how do his fellow celibates know him?
“My name, friend, is ‘Ānanda.’”
"And yet my fellow-celibates know me as 'Ānanda'.
"Indeed, sir, we did not realize that we were consulting with the Great Teacher himself when we thought it was the Venerable Ānanda!"
"For if we had known,
'This is the Venerable Ānanda,' we would not have spoken even this much.
May the Venerable Ānanda forgive me."
The Sixth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.97.
Chapter Ten: With Upāli.
“Bhikkhus, possessing ten qualities, a bhikkhu is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.”
By which ten?

Here, monks, a monk is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains himself in the rules of training.
He is learned, a bearer of what he has heard, and a storehouse of what he has heard. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end...
They proclaim the holy life in its entirety, perfect and pure, with its meaning and its phrasing;
such teachings as these he has heard much of, retained, mastered verbally, examined with the mind, and well penetrated by view.
He is one who has good friends, good companions, and good associates.
He possesses right view and is endowed with right vision.
He wields the various kinds of psychic power: having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one;
he appears and disappears; he passes through walls, through enclosures, and through mountains without being obstructed.
Just as in the air, he dives in and out of the earth as if it were water; he walks on water without breaking the surface as if on earth;
he travels cross-legged through the air like a winged bird;
and with his hand he touches and strokes the moon and sun, so mighty and powerful.
He wields mastery with his body even as far as the Brahma-world.
With the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing that of humans, he hears both kinds of sounds—the divine and the human, whether far or near.
He understands the minds of other beings and other persons by encompassing their minds with his own.
He understands a mind with lust as "a mind with lust";
he understands a mind without lust as "a mind without lust";
he understands a mind with hatred...
A mind free from hatred...
a mind with delusion...
or a mind free from delusion...
Whether the mind is contracted … or whether the mind is distracted … or whether the mind is exalted …
Or a mind that is not sublime … or a surpassable mind … or an unsurpassable mind …
Whether the mind is concentrated or unconcentrated,
whether the mind is liberated or unliberated...
Or, he understands an unliberated mind as ‘an unliberated mind.
He recollects his manifold past abodes, that is to say:
one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births...
For forty births, for fifty births, for a hundred births, for a thousand births, for a hundred thousand births, for many aeons of world-contraction,
for many aeons of world-expansion, and for many aeons of both world-contraction and expansion, [he recollects]: "In that place I was,
with such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan."
"Having passed away from there, I arose there; there I was with such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan;
having passed away from there, I have reappeared here"—thus he recollects his manifold past lives in their modes and details.
With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—
low and high, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate— and he understands how beings fare according to their karma:
"Alas, these worthy beings were possessed of misconduct in body, misconduct in speech, and misconduct in mind..."
These beings were endowed with [evil conduct], revilers of the noble ones, holding wrong views, and undertaking actions based on wrong views;
at the breaking up of the body, after death, they have reappeared in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
But these worthy beings were endowed with good conduct of body, endowed with good conduct of speech, and endowed with good conduct of mind.
‘They do not revile the noble ones; they hold right view and undertake actions based on right view.

With the breakup of the body, after death, they have reappeared in a happy destination, a heavenly world. Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—low and high, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate.
He understands beings according to their kamma.

Through the destruction of the taints, he realizes for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, he dwells therein.
Monks, a monk endowed with these ten qualities is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, and is an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.”
Seventh. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.98.
Chapter 10: The Section on Upāli.
The Discourse on the Elder (Therasutta):
"Bhikkhus, endowed with ten qualities, an elder bhikkhu dwells in comfort in whatever direction he may reside."
By which ten?
He is an elder, of long-standing seniority, long-ordained;
he is virtuous... [and so on].
He trains by undertaking the rules of training; he is learned …pe… well-penetrated in view;
moreover, both Pātimokkhas have been properly handed down to him in detail, well-analyzed, well-mastered, and well-determined, both in terms of the rules and their specific phrasing;
and he is skilled in the arising and the settling of legal issues.
He is one who loves the Dhamma, whose speech is pleasing, and who finds sublime joy in the higher Dhamma and the higher Discipline;
he is content with any kind of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick;
and he is inspiring, being well-restrained in his going forth and returning, and in his sitting within inhabited areas.
“He is one who gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and provide a pleasant dwelling in this very life;
and with the destruction of the taints, he enters and dwells in the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, having realized them for himself through direct knowledge in this very life.
It is when a senior bhikkhu is endowed with these ten qualities, monks, that in whatever direction he dwells, he dwells in comfort.”
The Eighth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.99.
Chapter Ten: The Section on Upāli.
The Upāli Sutta (AN 10.99).

Then the Venerable Upāli approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Upāli said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I wish to resort to remote lodgings in forest thickets and jungle retreats.
“Indeed, Upāli, remote lodgings in forest thickets and jungle retreats are difficult to master.
Solitude is hard to practice and hard to enjoy.”
“Alone, I think, the thoughts carry away the mind of a bhikkhu who does not attain concentration.
Upāli, if anyone were to say:
‘Not attaining concentration, I will resort to remote lodgings in forest thickets and jungle retreats,’ it is to be expected of him that he will [be carried away].”
‘He will sink or he will float. It is just as if,
Upāli, there were a great lake of water,
and then an elephant king seven or eight cubits high were to come along.
It might occur to him:
“Suppose I were to plunge into this lake and play at splashing water up to my ears, and play at splashing water up to my back;
and having played at splashing water up to my ears and having played at splashing water up to my back, and having bathed and drunk and emerged, I would depart wherever I wish.”
Having plunged into that lake, he might play at the game of washing his ears and play at the game of washing his back;
and having played at the game of washing his ears and played at the game of washing his back, and having bathed, drunk, and emerged, he would depart wherever he wished. Why is that?
"Mahā, Upāli, this physical form finds a footing in what is deep.
Suppose a hare or a cat were to come there;
it would think thus:"
‘Who am I, and who is this elephant?
Suppose I were to plunge into this pool and play at splashing water against its ears, and play at splashing water against its back;
and having played at splashing water against its ears and having played at splashing water against its back, and having bathed and drunk and emerged, I might depart wherever I wish.’
If he were to suddenly plunge into that lake of water without reflection,
it is to be expected of him:
"He will either sink or float."
And why is that? Upāli, this personal existence is limited; it does not find a firm footing in what is deep.
In the same way, Upāli, whoever should say:
‘If, not attaining concentration, I resort to remote lodgings in forests and jungle-thickets,’ it is to be expected of him that he will either sink or float away.
Just as, Upāli, a young, weak infant lying on its back plays with its own urine and excrement.
“What do you think, Upāli?
Is this not purely and entirely childish play?
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“After some time, Upāli, as that boy grew up and his faculties matured, he played with whatever toys are common for boys, such as:
the crooked stick, the spindle, the top, the ball, the leaf-cup, the little chariot, and the bow.
What do you think, Upāli?”
“Is this play not more excellent and more sublime than the former play?
“Yes, venerable sir.
“Then, Upāli, after some time, as that boy grew up and his faculties matured...”
Endowed with and possessed of the five strands of sensual pleasure, he enjoys them:
forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust;
sounds cognizable by the ear...
By means of odors cognizable by the nose...
by means of tastes cognizable by the tongue...
by means of tangibles cognizable by the body—those that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, endearing, connected with sensual pleasure, and provocative of lust.
“What do you think, Upāli?
Is this play not more excellent and more sublime than the former play?
“Yes, Bhante.”

“Furthermore, Upāli, here the Tathāgata arises in the world, an arahant, a perfectly awakened Buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, well-gone, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
Having realized this world—with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans—by his own direct knowledge, he makes it known.”

He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he reveals the holy life (brahmacariya) in its entirety, complete and pure.
A householder, or a householder’s son, or one born into some other family, hears that Dhamma.
Having heard that Dhamma, he gains faith in the Tathāgata.
Endowed with that acquisition of faith, he reflects thus:
“The household life is crowded, a path of dust; going forth is the open air.
It is not easy for one dwelling at home to practice the holy life in its absolute fullness, absolute purity, and in its polished perfection.”
‘What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, don saffron robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness?
Then, at a later time, having abandoned a small or a large mass of wealth,
and having abandoned a small or a large circle of relatives, he shaves off his hair and beard.
Having clothed himself in saffron robes, he goes forth from the household life into homelessness.

Having thus gone forth, having undertaken the training and the way of life of the bhikkhus, he abandons the taking of life and abstains from taking life. With rod laid aside and weapon laid aside, conscientious and compassionate, he dwells sympathetic toward the welfare of all living beings.
Abandoning the taking of what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given; he takes only what is given, expects only what is given, and dwells with a heart free from theft.
Abandoning unchastity, he lives a life of celibacy; he dwells apart and abstains from the vulgar practice of sexual intercourse.
Abandoning false speech, he abstains from false speech; he speaks the truth, is devoted to truth, is trustworthy, reliable, and not a deceiver of the world.
Abandoning malicious speech, he abstains from malicious speech; having heard something here, he does not repeat it elsewhere.

He does not repeat elsewhere what he has heard here for the purpose of dividing these people from those, nor does he repeat here what he has heard elsewhere for the purpose of dividing those people from these.

Thus, he is a reconciler of those who are divided and a promoter of harmony among those who are united; he delights in concord, rejoices in concord, and finds joy in concord; he speaks words that create concord.
Having abandoned harsh speech, he abstains from harsh speech. He speaks such words as are gentle, pleasing to the ear, endearing, heart-reaching, urbane, agreeable to many, and dear to many.
Having abandoned idle chatter, he abstains from idle chatter; he speaks at the proper time, speaks what is true, speaks what is meaningful, speaks on the Dhamma, and speaks on the Vinaya.
He is one who utters speech that is worth treasuring—timely, reasoned, measured, and connected with the goal.
He abstains from injuring seeds and plants.
He eats but one meal a day, refraining from eating at night, abstaining from food outside the proper time.
He abstains from attending dances, songs, music, and performances;
he abstains from wearing garlands, using perfumes and unguents, and from the use of ornaments and finery.
He abstains from high and luxurious beds;
he abstains from accepting gold and silver;
he abstains from accepting raw grain.
He abstains from accepting raw meat;
he abstains from accepting women and girls;
he abstains from accepting male and female slaves.
He abstains from accepting goats and sheep;
he abstains from accepting chickens and pigs;
he abstains from accepting elephants, cattle, horses, and mares.
He abstains from accepting fields and land;
he abstains from the practice of running errands and acting as a messenger;
he abstains from buying and selling.
He abstains from cheating with scales, cheating with measures, and cheating with weights;
he abstains from bribery, deception, and fraud;
he abstains from mutilation, murder, abduction, robbery, and violence.
Thus he is content with robes that merely protect the body and almsfood that merely sustains the belly.
Wherever he goes, he sets out taking only these;
just as a winged bird, wherever it flies, flies with only its own wings as its burden.
In the same way, a bhikkhu is content with robes to protect the body and almsfood to sustain the belly. Wherever he goes, he sets out taking only these with him.
Endowed with this noble aggregate of virtuous behavior, he experiences within himself the happiness that is blameless.
Having seen a form with the eye, he does not grasp at its signs or its secondary characteristics.
Since, if one were to dwell with this faculty of the eye unguarded, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might flow in upon him, he practices for its restraint;
he guards the faculty of the eye, he achieves restraint over the faculty of the eye.
Having heard a sound with the ear...
Having smelled an odor with the nose...
having tasted a flavor with the tongue...
having touched a tangible object with the body...
Having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he does not grasp at its signs or its secondary characteristics.
Since, if he were to dwell with this faculty of mind unguarded, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might flow in upon him, he practices for its restraint;
he guards the faculty of mind and achieves restraint over the faculty of mind.
Thus, endowed with this noble restraint of the faculties, he experiences within himself the unadulterated happiness.
He acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning; he acts with clear comprehension when looking ahead and looking aside;
he acts with clear comprehension when bending and stretching his limbs; he acts with clear comprehension when wearing his outer robe, bowl, and inner robe.
He acts with clear comprehension when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; he acts with clear comprehension in attending to the calls of nature;
he acts with clear comprehension when going, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and remaining silent.
Thus, endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue, endowed with this noble restraint of the sense faculties, and endowed with this noble mindfulness and clear comprehension...
He resorts to a secluded lodging: a forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, an open space, or a heap of straw.
Having gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, he sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him.
Abandoning covetousness for the world, he dwells with a mind free from covetousness; he purifies his mind of covetousness.
Having abandoned ill will and hatred, he dwells with a mind free from ill will, compassionate for the welfare of all living beings; he purifies his mind of ill will and hatred.
