Having abandoned sloth and torpor, he dwells free from sloth and torpor, percipient of light, mindful and clearly comprehending; he purifies his mind of sloth and torpor.
Having abandoned restlessness and remorse, he dwells unagitated, with a mind inwardly tranquil; he purifies his mind of restlessness and remorse.
Having abandoned doubt, he dwells having crossed over doubt, free from indecision regarding wholesome states; he purifies his mind of doubt.

Having abandoned these five hindrances—defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom—and being secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and possesses the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.
“What do you think, Upāli,
is this dwelling not indeed more excellent and more sublime than the previous dwellings?
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“Furthermore, Upāli, my disciples, perceiving this quality within themselves, resort to remote lodgings in forests and jungle-thickets; yet they do not yet dwell having attained their own goal.
Again, Upāli, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna….
What do you think, Upāli?”
“Is this dwelling not indeed more excellent and more sublime than the previous dwellings?
“Yes, venerable sir.

“In this way too, Upāli, my disciples, seeing a particular quality within themselves, resort to remote lodgings in forest thickets and jungle retreats; yet they do not yet dwell having attained their own goal.”
"Furthermore, Upāli, with the fading away of rapture, a bhikkhu dwells having attained the third jhāna...
What do you think, Upāli:
is this dwelling not more excellent and more sublime than the previous dwellings?"
“Yes, venerable sir.

“Upāli, it is because they perceive this quality within themselves that my disciples resort to remote lodgings in forest thickets and wilderness areas; yet they do not yet dwell having attained their own goal.
Furthermore, Upāli, with the abandoning of pleasure... [as before] ...a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna...”

"Furthermore, Upāli, with the complete transcendence of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impingement, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the base of infinite space,
[perceiving] 'space is infinite. What do you think, Upāli,
is this dwelling not more excellent and more sublime than the previous dwellings?"
“Yes, venerable sir.

“Upāli, it is because they perceive this quality within themselves that my disciples resort to remote lodgings in forest thickets and wilderness areas; yet, they do not yet dwell having attained their own goal.
Furthermore, Upāli, by completely transcending the base of infinite space, thinking ‘consciousness is infinite,’ a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness… [and so on].”
"Having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness, thinking 'there is nothing,' one enters and dwells in the base of nothingness...
Having completely transcended the base of nothingness, thinking 'this is peaceful, this is sublime,' one enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
What do you think, Upāli?"
“Is this dwelling not indeed more excellent and more sublime than the previous dwellings?
“Yes, venerable sir.

“In this way too, Upāli, my disciples, seeing a particular quality within themselves, resort to remote lodgings in forest thickets and jungle retreats; yet they do not yet dwell having attained their own goal.”

“Furthermore, Upāli, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling; and having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed.
What do you think, Upāli:
is this dwelling not more excellent and more sublime than the previous dwellings?”
“Yes, venerable sir.
“Upāli, it is because they perceive this quality within themselves that my disciples resort to remote lodgings in forest thickets and wilderness areas, and they dwell having attained their own goal.
Come now, Upāli, dwell in the Saṅgha.”
"While you dwell in the Saṅgha, there will be comfort for you.
The ninth [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.100.

10. Upāli Chapter: Discourse on the Impossibility (Abhabbasutta) (AN 10.100, PTS AN v 209) “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “Upāli, there are these five qualities that make one incapable and unfit for the destruction of the taints in this very life. What five? Here, Upāli, a bhikkhu is devoid of faith, devoid of shame, devoid of fear of wrongdoing, devoid of learning, and devoid of wisdom. These, Upāli, are the five qualities that make one incapable and unfit for the destruction of the taints in this very life. “There are, Upāli, these other five qualities that make one capable and fit for the destruction of the taints in this very life. What five? Here, Upāli, a bhikkhu possesses faith, possesses shame, possesses fear of wrongdoing, possesses learning, and possesses wisdom. These, Upāli, are the five qualities that make one capable and fit for the destruction of the taints in this very life.”
“Monks, without abandoning these ten things, one is incapable of realizing arahantship.
What are the ten?
Lust, hatred, delusion, anger, resentment, contempt, spite, envy, avarice, and conceit.”
“Monks, without abandoning these ten things, one is incapable of realizing arhatship.
Monks, by abandoning these ten things, one is capable of realizing arhatship.
What are the ten?”
“Bhikkhus, having abandoned these ten things— lust, hatred, delusion, anger, enmity, hypocrisy, spite, envy, avarice, and conceit— one is capable of realizing arahantship.
The tenth.
The fifth chapter, the Upāli-vagga.
Its summary verse:
The enjoyer of sensual pleasures, fear, and views.
Vajjiyamāhita, Uttiya,
Kokanuda, Āhuneyya, Thera, and Upāli— these are incapable.
The Second Fifty is completed. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.101, Chapter 11:
On the Perception of a Recluse.
“Bhikkhus, these three perceptions of a recluse,
when developed and cultivated, fulfill seven qualities.”
Which three?
"I have entered upon a change of appearance," "My livelihood is dependent on others," and "My deportment must be maintained"— these, monks,
are the three perceptions of a recluse which, when developed and cultivated, fulfill seven qualities.

“What seven? One acts continuously and conducts oneself continuously in the precepts; one is free from covetousness; one is free from ill will; one is not conceited; one desires training; one regards the requisites for life as being ‘for this purpose’; and one dwells with energy aroused.
These, monks, are the three perceptions of a recluse which, when developed and cultivated, fulfill these seven qualities.”
First.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.102.
Chapter 11: Perceptions of a Recluse (Samaṇasaññāvagga).
The Discourse on the Factors of Enlightenment (Bojjhaṅgasutta): “Bhikkhus,
these seven factors of enlightenment, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the three types of true knowledge.”
Which seven?

The enlightenment factor of mindfulness, the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena, the enlightenment factor of energy, the enlightenment factor of rapture, the enlightenment factor of tranquility, the enlightenment factor of concentration, and the enlightenment factor of equanimity.
These, monks, are the seven factors of enlightenment; when developed and cultivated, they fulfill the three true knowledges.
What are the three?
Here, monks, a monk recollects his manifold past abodes, that is to say:
one birth, two births, three births... [as far as] thus with their aspects and particulars he recollects his manifold past abodes.
"With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans... [he] understands beings as faring according to their kamma.
Through the destruction of the taints... [he] dwells having realized and attained [liberation].
These, monks, are the seven factors of enlightenment; when developed and cultivated, they fulfill these three kinds of true knowledge."
The Second.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.103.
Chapter 11: Perceptions of Ascetics.
The Discourse on Wrongness (Micchattasutta): “Bhikkhus,
by resorting to wrongness, there is failure, not success.”
And how, monks, does failure come about by resorting to wrongness, rather than success?
For one of wrong view, monks, wrong intention arises; for one of wrong intention, wrong speech arises;
for one of wrong speech, wrong action arises; for one of wrong action, wrong livelihood arises.
From wrong livelihood, wrong effort arises; from wrong effort, wrong mindfulness arises; from wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration arises;
from wrong concentration, wrong knowledge arises; and from one with wrong knowledge, wrong liberation arises.
It is in this way, monks, that by resorting to the wrong path there is failure, not success.
"Monks, by resorting to rightness, there is success, not failure.
And how, monks, by resorting to rightness, is there success, not failure?
For one who possesses right view, monks, right intention arises; for one with right intention, right speech arises."
For one of right speech, right action arises; for one of right action, right livelihood arises; for one of right livelihood, right effort arises;
for one of right effort, right mindfulness arises; for one of right mindfulness, right concentration arises;
for one of right concentration, right knowledge arises; and for one of right knowledge, right liberation arises.
“It is in this way, monks, that by resorting to rightness there is success, not failure.
The third [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.104

11. The Chapter on Perceptions of Ascetics Seed Sutta (AN 10.104) "Bhikkhus, there are these five seeds. What five? The seed that is whole, the seed that is broken, the seed that is rotten, the seed that is damaged by wind and heat, and the seed that lacks soil. These, bhikkhus, are the five seeds. Just so, bhikkhus, there are these five kinds of persons found existing in the world. What five? The person who is whole like a seed, the person who is broken like a seed, the person who is rotten like a seed, the person who is damaged by wind and heat like a seed, and the person who lacks soil like a seed. And how, bhikkhus, is a person whole like a seed? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person possesses faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom. This, bhikkhus, is called a person who is whole like a seed. And how, bhikkhus, is a person broken like a seed? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person possesses faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom; yet his faith wanes, his virtue wanes, his learning wanes, his generosity wanes, and his wisdom wanes. This, bhikkhus, is called a person who is broken like a seed. And how, bhikkhus, is a person rotten like a seed? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person possesses faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom; yet his faith decays, his virtue decays, his learning decays, his generosity decays, and his wisdom decays. This, bhikkhus, is called a person who is rotten like a seed. And how, bhikkhus, is a person damaged by wind and heat like a seed? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person possesses faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom; yet he is subject to the winds and heat of gain, loss, fame, disrepute, praise, and blame. This, bhikkhus, is called a person who is damaged by wind and heat like a seed. And how, bhikkhus, is a person lacking soil like a seed? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person possesses faith, virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom; yet he does not associate with those who are virtuous, nor does he honor them, nor does he listen to the Dhamma from them, nor does he practice the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma. This, bhikkhus, is called a person who lacks soil like a seed. These, bhikkhus, are the five kinds of persons found existing in the world."
“Bhikkhus, for a person who holds wrong view, who has wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action,
wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration, wrong knowledge, and wrong liberation—
whatever bodily action he undertakes and performs in accordance with that view, whatever verbal action, and whatever mental action [he undertakes and performs]...”
Whatever view one has fully accepted and undertaken, whatever intention, whatever aspiration, whatever resolve, and whatever volitional formations there may be—
all those phenomena lead to what is undesirable, unlovely, disagreeable, harmful,
and suffering. For what reason?
For his view, monks, is evil.
Just as if, monks, a seed of neem, or a seed of bitter gourd, or a seed of bitter cucumber were placed in moist soil;
whatever essence of earth it takes up, and whatever essence of water it takes up, all [that becomes bitter].
That leads to bitterness, pungency, and unsatisfactoriness.
Why is that? Because, monks, the seed itself is bad.

In the same way, monks, for a person of wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration, wrong knowledge, and wrong liberation, whatever bodily action is undertaken and performed in accordance with that view, and whatever verbal action...

[is undertaken and performed in accordance with that view]... [and whatever mental action is undertaken and performed in accordance with that view]... [all lead to what is unwholesome, not to what is wholesome].
Whatever mental action is undertaken and performed in accordance with one's view— whatever volition, whatever aspiration, whatever resolve,
and whatever formations— all those phenomena lead to what is unwished for, undesired, unpleasant, harmful,
and suffering. For what reason?
For his view, monks, is evil.
But for a person of right view, monks— one who possesses right intention, right speech, right action,
right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration, right knowledge, and right liberation—
Whatever bodily action one has undertaken and performed in accordance with one's view, whatever verbal action one has undertaken and performed in accordance with one's view,
whatever mental action one has undertaken and performed in accordance with one's view, as well as whatever volition, whatever aspiration, whatever resolve,
and whatever formations there may be— all those phenomena lead to what is desirable, lovely, pleasing, beneficial, and happy.
For what reason?
Because, monks, his view is auspicious.
Just as, monks, a seed of sugarcane, or a seed of rice, or a seed of grape, [would grow] in moist soil...
Whatever essence of earth it takes up and whatever essence of water it takes up,
all that leads to being savory, sweet,
and delightful. For what reason?
For the seed, monks, is auspicious.
In the same way, monks, for one of right view—pe—for one of right liberation, whatever bodily action is undertaken and performed in accordance with that view, whatever verbal action...

whatever mental action is undertaken and performed in accordance with that view, whatever intention, whatever aspiration, whatever resolve, and whatever volitional formations there may be—all those phenomena lead to what is wished for, desired, agreeable, beneficial, and pleasant.
And why is that? Because, monks, his view is auspicious. Thus ends the fourth [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.105 11. Samaṇasaññāvagga Vijjāsutta (The Discourse on Clear Knowledge) "Bhikkhus, there are these ten qualities of a true ascetic. What ten? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu possesses clear knowledge; he possesses the higher virtue; he possesses the higher mind; he possesses the higher wisdom; he is one who has abandoned craving for existence; he is one who has cut off the stream of existence; he is one who has destroyed the bridge [to rebirth]; he is one who has no more desire for future life; he is one who has reached the end of the journey; he is one who has done what was to be done. These, bhikkhus, are the ten qualities of a true ascetic."
“Bhikkhus, ignorance is the forerunner in the attainment of unwholesome states, followed by shamelessness and lack of moral dread.
For one who is immersed in ignorance and lacking true knowledge, wrong view arises; for one with wrong view, wrong intention arises.”
From wrong intention, wrong speech arises; from one of wrong speech, wrong action arises;
from one of wrong action, wrong livelihood arises; from one of wrong livelihood, wrong effort arises; from one of wrong effort, wrong mindfulness arises;
from one of wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration arises; and from one of wrong concentration, wrong knowledge arises.
For one with wrong knowledge, wrong liberation arises.
Knowledge, monks, is the precursor for the attainment of wholesome states, while moral shame and moral dread follow after it.
For the wise person who has reached knowledge, right view arises; for one with right view, right intention arises.
Right intention arises for one who possesses right view; right speech arises for one who possesses right intention; right action arises for one who possesses right speech;
right livelihood arises for one who possesses right action; right effort arises for one who possesses right livelihood; right mindfulness arises for one who possesses right effort;
right concentration arises for one who possesses right mindfulness; and right knowledge arises for one who possesses right concentration.
“Right liberation comes to be.
The fifth. *Aṅguttara Nikāya* 10.106.

11. Samaṇasaññāvagga Nijjarasutta (Discourse on Wearing Away) “Monks, there are these five kinds of weariness that lead to the wearing away [of the defilements]. What five? Weariness with regard to gain, weariness with regard to honor, weariness with regard to fame, weariness with regard to pleasure, and weariness with regard to praise. These, monks, are the five kinds of weariness that lead to the wearing away [of the defilements].”
“Monks, there are these ten bases for the wearing away [of kamma]. What ten?
For one with right view, monks, wrong view is worn away;”
And those numerous evil, unwholesome states that arise with wrong view as condition have been worn away by him;
and numerous wholesome states, conditioned by right view, reach fulfillment through development.
For one of right intention, monks, wrong intention is worn away;
And those many evil, unwholesome states that arise with wrong intention as their condition have been worn away by him;
and many wholesome states, conditioned by right intention, reach fulfillment through development.
For one of right speech, monks, wrong speech has been worn away.
And whatever numerous evil, unwholesome states arise conditioned by wrong speech are worn away by him;
and numerous wholesome states reach fulfillment through development conditioned by right speech.
For one of right action, monks, wrong action is worn away;
And those numerous evil, unwholesome states that arise conditioned by wrong action are worn away by him;
and numerous wholesome states reach fulfillment through development conditioned by right action.
For one of right livelihood, monks, wrong livelihood is worn away.
And those numerous evil, unwholesome states that arise conditioned by wrong livelihood have been worn away by him;
and numerous wholesome states reach full development conditioned by right livelihood.
Monks, for one of right effort, wrong effort has been worn away;
And those many evil, unwholesome states that arise with wrong effort as their condition are worn away by him;
and with right effort as their condition, many wholesome states reach fulfillment by development.
For one of right mindfulness, monks, wrong mindfulness is worn away.
And those numerous evil, unwholesome states that arise with wrong mindfulness as their condition have been worn away by him;
and numerous wholesome states reach fulfillment through development with right mindfulness as their condition.
For one of right concentration, monks, wrong concentration has been worn away;
And those numerous evil, unwholesome states that arise with wrong concentration as their condition have been worn away by him;
and numerous wholesome states, conditioned by right concentration, reach fulfillment through development.
Monks, for one of right knowledge, wrong knowledge has been worn away.
And those numerous evil, unwholesome states that arise with wrong knowledge as their condition have been worn away by him;
and numerous wholesome states, conditioned by right knowledge, reach fulfillment through development.
For one who is rightly liberated, monks, wrong liberation has been worn away.
And those numerous evil, unwholesome states that arise conditioned by wrong liberation are worn away for him;
and numerous wholesome states, conditioned by right liberation, reach fulfillment through development.
These, monks, are the ten bases for wearing away.”
The Sixth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.107. Chapter 11:
The Section on the Perceptions of a Recluse (Samaṇasaññāvagga).
Dhovanasutta:
“Monks, in the southern provinces there is a place called Dhovana.”
In that regard, there is food, drink, edible food, soft food, food to be relished, food to be swallowed, dancing, singing, and instrumental music.
This cleansing exists, monks; I do not say that it does not exist.
Yet, monks, this cleansing is inferior, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial.
It does not lead to disenchantment, nor to dispassion, nor to cessation, nor to peace, nor to direct knowledge, nor to enlightenment,

nor to Nibbāna. But I, monks, shall teach you the noble washing, that washing which leads exclusively to disenchantment, to dispassion, [to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna].
It leads to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna; by resorting to this washing,
beings subject to birth are liberated from birth, beings subject to aging are liberated from aging,
beings subject to death are liberated from death, and beings subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are liberated from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
“Listen to that and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“And what, bhikkhus, is that noble washing which leads to utter disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace,
to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, to Nibbāna; by resorting to which washing beings subject to birth are freed from birth,
beings subject to aging are freed from aging, and beings subject to death are freed from death?”
Are beings liberated from death? Are beings who are subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair liberated from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair?
Monks, for one of right view, wrong view is washed away;
and those numerous evil, unwholesome states that arise conditioned by wrong view are also washed away for them.
And with right view as condition, numerous wholesome states reach fulfillment by development.
For one of right intention, monks, wrong intention is washed away...
For one of right speech, monks, wrong speech is washed away...
“Monks, for one of right action, wrong action is washed away… for one of right livelihood,
wrong livelihood is washed away… for one of right effort, wrong effort is washed away.”
“Monks, for one who possesses right mindfulness, wrong mindfulness is washed away… for one who possesses right concentration,
monks, wrong concentration is washed away… for one who possesses right knowledge, monks, wrong knowledge is washed away… [and so on].”
“Monks, for one who is rightly liberated, wrong liberation has been washed away;
and those numerous evil, unwholesome states that arise conditioned by wrong liberation have also been washed away from him.
Furthermore, numerous wholesome states, conditioned by right liberation, reach the fulfillment of their development.”
This, monks, is that noble cleansing which leads to utter disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace,
to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna; by resorting to this cleansing, beings subject to birth are liberated from birth,
beings subject to aging are liberated from aging, and beings subject to death are liberated from death.
“Beings subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are liberated from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
Thus was the seventh [sutta]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.108.

11. Samaṇasaññāvagga Tikicchakasutta (AN 10.108) “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of physicians. What four? Here, bhikkhus, a certain physician is unskilled in diagnosis; he prescribes the wrong treatment for a disease; his medicine is not effective; and he is not skilled in curing a disease that has arisen. This, bhikkhus, is the first kind of physician. Again, bhikkhus, a certain physician is skilled in diagnosis; he prescribes the right treatment for a disease; his medicine is effective; yet he is not skilled in curing a disease that has arisen. This, bhikkhus, is the second kind of physician. Again, bhikkhus, a certain physician is skilled in diagnosis; he prescribes the right treatment for a disease; his medicine is effective; and he is skilled in curing a disease that has arisen; yet he is not skilled in preventing a disease from arising. This, bhikkhus, is the third kind of physician. Again, bhikkhus, a certain physician is skilled in diagnosis; he prescribes the right treatment for a disease; his medicine is effective; he is skilled in curing a disease that has arisen; and he is skilled in preventing a disease from arising. This, bhikkhus, is the fourth kind of physician. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of physicians. Just so, bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons similar to physicians found existing in the world. What four? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person is unskilled in diagnosis; he prescribes the wrong treatment for a defilement; his teaching is not effective; and he is not skilled in curing a defilement that has arisen. This, bhikkhus, is the first kind of person similar to a physician. Again, bhikkhus, a certain person is skilled in diagnosis; he prescribes the right treatment for a defilement; his teaching is effective; yet he is not skilled in curing a defilement that has arisen. This, bhikkhus, is the second kind of person similar to a physician. Again, bhikkhus, a certain person is skilled in diagnosis; he prescribes the right treatment for a defilement; his teaching is effective; and he is skilled in curing a defilement that has arisen; yet he is not skilled in preventing a defilement from arising. This, bhikkhus, is the third kind of person similar to a physician. Again, bhikkhus, a certain person is skilled in diagnosis; he prescribes the right treatment for a defilement; his teaching is effective; he is skilled in curing a defilement that has arisen; and he is skilled in preventing a defilement from arising. This, bhikkhus, is the fourth kind of person similar to a physician. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons similar to physicians found existing in the world.”

“Physicians, bhikkhus, administer purgatives for the purpose of counteracting diseases arising from bile, for the purpose of counteracting diseases arising from phlegm, and for the purpose of counteracting diseases arising from wind.
Such a purgative exists, bhikkhus; I do not say that it does not exist.
Yet, bhikkhus, that purgative sometimes succeeds and sometimes fails.”
"And I, monks, will teach you the noble purgative, that purgative which succeeds and never fails;
by means of which purgative beings subject to birth are liberated from birth; beings subject to aging are liberated from aging;
beings subject to death are liberated from death; and beings subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair [are liberated from them]."
“Beings are liberated from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
Listen to that; attend closely, and I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
"And what, bhikkhus, is that noble purgative which succeeds and never fails,
by resorting to which beings subject to birth are liberated from birth, and beings subject to aging are liberated from aging?"
Are beings subject to death liberated from death? Are beings subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair liberated from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair?
Monks, for one with right view, wrong view has been discarded.
And those numerous evil, unwholesome states that arise with wrong view as their condition are expelled from him;
and numerous wholesome states reach fulfillment by development with right view as their condition.
For one of right intention, monks, wrong intention is expelled... [and so on]...
“Monks, for one of right speech, wrong speech has been vomited out… for one of right action,
wrong action has been vomited out… for one of right livelihood, wrong livelihood has been vomited out.”
“Monks, for one of right effort, wrong effort is expelled… Monks,
for one of right mindfulness, wrong mindfulness is expelled… Monks,
for one of right concentration, wrong concentration is expelled.”
“Monks, for one of right knowledge, wrong knowledge is discarded … [and so on] … Monks,
for one of right liberation, wrong liberation is discarded;
and those numerous evil, unwholesome states that arise with wrong liberation as their condition are also discarded by him.”
"And with right liberation as condition, numerous wholesome states reach fulfillment by development.
This, monks, is that noble purgative which succeeds and does not fail;
by resorting to this purgative, beings subject to birth are liberated from birth … [and so on] … they are liberated from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair."
The Eighth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.109.
Chapter 11: Perceptions of Ascetics (Samaṇasaññāvagga).
The Vamana Sutta (AN 10.109): “Monks,

physicians administer emetics for the sake of warding off diseases arising from bile, for the sake of warding off diseases arising from phlegm, and for the sake of warding off diseases arising from wind.”
“There is this emetic, monks; I do not say that it does not exist.
Yet, monks, this emetic sometimes succeeds and sometimes fails.
And I, monks, will teach the noble emetic, which always succeeds and never fails.”
By means of this vomiting, beings subject to birth are liberated from birth; beings subject to aging are liberated from aging;
beings subject to death are liberated from death; and beings subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are liberated from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
Listen to that...
What, monks, is that noble emetic which succeeds and does not fail, by resorting to which beings subject to birth are liberated from birth... [and] from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair?
How are beings liberated from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair?
For one with right view, monks, wrong view has been vomited out;
and those numerous evil, unwholesome states that arise conditioned by wrong view have also been vomited out by him.
And with right view as condition, numerous wholesome states reach fulfillment by development.
For one of right intention, monks, wrong intention has been vomited out...
For one of right speech, monks, wrong speech has been vomited out...
“Monks, for one of right action, wrong action has been vomited out… for one of right livelihood,
wrong livelihood has been vomited out… for one of right effort, wrong effort has been vomited out.”
“Bhikkhus, for one who possesses right mindfulness, wrong mindfulness has been vomited up… for one who possesses right concentration,
bhikkhus, wrong concentration has been vomited up… for one who possesses right knowledge,
bhikkhus, wrong knowledge has been vomited up…” [and so forth].
“Monks, for one who is rightly liberated, wrong liberation has been vomited up;
and those numerous evil, unwholesome states that arise conditioned by wrong liberation have also been vomited up by him.
Furthermore, numerous wholesome states, conditioned by right liberation, reach fulfillment through development.”
“This, monks, is that noble emetic which succeeds and does not fail;
by resorting to which emetic, beings subject to birth are liberated from birth … [and so on] … they are liberated from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair.
Thus ends the ninth [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.110 11. Samaṇasaññāvagga Niddhamanīyasutta (The Discourse on What Should Be Expelled) “Monks, there are these ten things that should be expelled from a monastery. What ten? One who destroys life should be expelled from the monastery; one who takes what is not given should be expelled from the monastery; one who engages in sexual misconduct should be expelled from the monastery; one who speaks falsely should be expelled from the monastery; one who drinks fermented or distilled liquor should be expelled from the monastery; one who is a maker of strife should be expelled from the monastery; one who is a maker of quarrels should be expelled from the monastery; one who is a maker of disputes should be expelled from the monastery; one who is a maker of contention should be expelled from the monastery; and one who dwells as a follower of another sect should be expelled from the monastery. These, monks, are the ten things that should be expelled from a monastery.”
“Bhikkhus, there are these ten things that should be expelled. What are the ten? [The Buddha continued: (AN 10.110, PTS AN v 220)
“Bhikkhus, for one of right view, wrong view is blown away;
those numerous evil unwholesome states that arise with wrong view as condition are also blown away;
and numerous wholesome states reach fulfillment by development through right view as their condition.”
“Monks, for one of right intention, wrong intention is blown away … for one of right speech,
monks, wrong speech is blown away … for one of right action, monks, wrong action is blown away.”
“Monks, for one of right livelihood, wrong livelihood is expelled;
monks, for one of right effort, wrong effort is expelled;
monks, for one of right mindfulness, wrong mindfulness is expelled.”
“Monks, for one with right concentration, wrong concentration is blazed out… Monks,
for one with right knowledge, wrong knowledge is blazed out… Monks,
for one with right liberation, wrong liberation is blazed out.”
“And those numerous evil, unwholesome states that arise with wrong liberation as their condition are blown away by him,
and numerous wholesome states reach fulfillment through development with right liberation as their condition.
These, monks, are the ten things that must be blown away.”
The Tenth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.111.
Chapter Eleven: Perceptions of Ascetics.
The First Discourse on the Trainee (Paṭhama-asekha-sutta).
Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, that bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, it is said, ‘one beyond training, one beyond training.
In what way, venerable sir, is a bhikkhu one beyond training?
“In this case, bhikkhu, a bhikkhu is endowed with the right view of one beyond training, with the right intention of one beyond training...”
He is endowed with right speech of one beyond training, he is endowed with right action of one beyond training,
he is endowed with right livelihood of one beyond training, he is endowed with right effort of one beyond training,
he is endowed with right mindfulness of one beyond training, and he is endowed with right concentration of one beyond training.
He is endowed with right knowledge of one beyond training; he is endowed with right liberation of one beyond training.
It is in this way, bhikkhu, that a bhikkhu is one beyond training.
Thus ends the eleventh [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.112 11. Samaṇasaññāvagga Dutiyaasekhasutta (The Second Discourse on the Non-Trainee) "Bhikkhus, there are these ten qualities of a non-trainee. What ten? Here, bhikkhus, a non-trainee dwells with a mind obsessed by sensual lust, without having abandoned the underlying tendency to sensual lust;

he dwells with a mind obsessed by ill will, without having abandoned the underlying tendency to ill will; he dwells with a mind obsessed by sloth and torpor, without having abandoned the underlying tendency to sloth and torpor; he dwells with a mind obsessed by restlessness and remorse, without having abandoned the underlying tendency to restlessness and remorse; he dwells with a mind obsessed by doubt, without having abandoned the underlying tendency to doubt. "He does not possess unwavering confidence in the Buddha: 'Thus indeed is the Blessed One: worthy, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One. "He does not possess unwavering confidence in the Dhamma: 'The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. "He does not possess unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha: 'The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. "He does not possess the virtues dear to the noble ones—virtues that are untorn, unrent, unblotched, unmottled, liberating, praised by the wise, not adhered to, leading to concentration. "These, bhikkhus, are the ten qualities of a non-trainee."
“Monks, there are these ten qualities of one beyond training (*asekhā dhammā*). What are the ten? [The text continues with the list of the ten qualities.]”
The right view of one beyond training, the right intention of one beyond training, the right speech of one beyond training, the right action of one beyond training,

the right livelihood of one beyond training, the right effort of one beyond training, the right mindfulness of one beyond training, the right concentration of one beyond training, the right knowledge of one beyond training,
and the right liberation of one beyond training.
“Monks, these indeed are the ten qualities of one beyond training.
The twelfth [sutta].
The first chapter, the Chapter on the Perception of a Recluse, is finished.
Its summary verse:
Perception, the factors of enlightenment,
wrongness, the seed, clear knowledge, and the wearing away.
Washing is medicine; vomiting is purging;
the two types of adepts are ejection.
(Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.113)

12. Paccorohaṇivagga First Discourse on What is Not Dhamma (Paṭhama-adhamma-sutta) At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The one who is devoted to what is not Dhamma and does not practice according to Dhamma; the one who is devoted to what is not Dhamma but practices according to Dhamma; the one who is devoted to what is Dhamma but does not practice according to Dhamma; and the one who is devoted to what is Dhamma and practices according to Dhamma. These are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “But how, Bhante, is one a person devoted to what is not Dhamma and not practicing according to Dhamma? “Here, bhikkhu, someone holds such a view as this: ‘There is nothing given, nothing offered, nothing sacrificed; there is no fruit or result of good and bad actions; there is no this world, no other world; there is no mother, no father; there are no beings spontaneously reborn; there are in the world no ascetics and brahmins of right conduct and right practice who have realized for themselves by direct knowledge and declare this world and the other world. Thus he is one who holds a wrong view. Since his view is thus, he intends for his own affliction, for the affliction of others, and for the affliction of both, and he experiences mental suffering and dejection. This is called a person devoted to what is not Dhamma and not practicing according to Dhamma. And how, bhikkhu, is one a person devoted to what is not Dhamma but practicing according to Dhamma? Here, someone holds such a view as this: ‘There is what is given… there are in the world ascetics and brahmins of right conduct and right practice who have realized for themselves by direct knowledge and declare this world and the other world. Thus he is one who holds a right view. Since his view is thus, he does not intend for his own affliction, nor for the affliction of others, nor for the affliction of both, and he does not experience mental suffering and dejection. This is called a person devoted to what is not Dhamma but practicing according to Dhamma. And how, bhikkhu, is one a person devoted to what is Dhamma but not practicing according to Dhamma? Here, someone holds such a view as this: ‘There is what is given… there are in the world ascetics and brahmins of right conduct and right practice who have realized for themselves by direct knowledge and declare this world and the other world. Thus he is one who holds a right view. Since his view is thus, he does not intend for his own affliction, nor for the affliction of others, nor for the affliction of both, and he does not experience mental suffering and dejection. However, he does not live the holy life under the Teacher or under fellow disciples of the Teacher, out of faith, for the full realization of the goal of the holy life, that is, for the utter destruction of suffering. This is called a person devoted to what is Dhamma but not practicing according to Dhamma. And how, bhikkhu, is one a person devoted to what is Dhamma and practicing according to Dhamma? Here, someone holds such a view as this: ‘There is what is given… there are in the world ascetics and brahmins of right conduct and right practice who have realized for themselves by direct knowledge and declare this world and the other world. Thus he is one who holds a right view. Since his view is thus, he does not intend for his own affliction, nor for the affliction of others, nor for the affliction of both, and he does not experience mental suffering and dejection. Furthermore, he lives the holy life under the Teacher or under fellow disciples of the Teacher, out of faith, for the full realization of the goal of the holy life, that is, for the utter destruction of suffering. This is called a person devoted to what is Dhamma and practicing according to Dhamma. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, Bhante! It is marvelous, Bhante! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘There are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. “Indeed, bhikkhu, it is so. It is so, bhikkhu. There are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Elated, that bhikkhu delighted in the Blessed One’s words. *The Book of the Tens, Chapter XII: The Descent from the Throne (Paccorohaṇivagga), First Discourse on What is Not Dhamma.*
“Monks, what is unrighteousness should be understood as disadvantageous,
and what is righteous should be understood as advantageous.

Having understood what is unrighteous and disadvantageous, and having understood what is righteous and advantageous, one should practice in accordance with what is righteous and what is advantageous.”
"And what, monks, is unrighteousness and what is harmful?
Wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration, wrong knowledge,
and wrong liberation— this, monks, is called unrighteousness and what is harmful."
"And what, monks, is the Dhamma and the goal?
Right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration, right knowledge,
and right liberation— this, monks, is called the Dhamma and the goal."
“Monks, what is non-Dhamma and what is harmful should be understood;
what is Dhamma and what is beneficial should also be understood.

Having understood what is non-Dhamma and what is harmful, and having understood what is Dhamma and what is beneficial, one should practice in accordance with the Dhamma and in accordance with what is beneficial.”
Thus, that which was said was said with reference to this.
The first.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.114

12. Paccorohaṇivagga The Second Discourse on What is Unrighteous (Dutiya-adhamma-sutta) “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Which four? The person who is unrighteous and of unrighteous nature; the person who is unrighteous but of righteous nature; the person who is righteous but of unrighteous nature; and the person who is righteous and of righteous nature. And how, monks, is one a person who is unrighteous and of unrighteous nature? Here, monks, a certain person is unrighteous in his bodily action, unrighteous in his verbal action, and unrighteous in his mental action. This, monks, is called a person who is unrighteous and of unrighteous nature. And how, monks, is one a person who is unrighteous but of righteous nature? Here, monks, a certain person is unrighteous in his bodily action, unrighteous in his verbal action, and unrighteous in his mental action, yet he possesses faith, possesses virtue, possesses learning, possesses generosity, and possesses wisdom. This, monks, is called a person who is unrighteous but of righteous nature. And how, monks, is one a person who is righteous but of unrighteous nature? Here, monks, a certain person is righteous in his bodily action, righteous in his verbal action, and righteous in his mental action, yet he lacks faith, lacks virtue, lacks learning, lacks generosity, and lacks wisdom. This, monks, is called a person who is righteous but of unrighteous nature. And how, monks, is one a person who is righteous and of righteous nature? Here, monks, a certain person is righteous in his bodily action, righteous in his verbal action, and righteous in his mental action, and he possesses faith, possesses virtue, possesses learning, possesses generosity, and possesses wisdom. This, monks, is called a person who is righteous and of righteous nature. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Farer, the Teacher, further said this: “The unrighteous person of unrighteous nature, And the unrighteous person of righteous nature, The righteous person of unrighteous nature, And the righteous person of righteous nature— These, monks, are the four kinds of persons Found existing in the world. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those monks rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One. *The Book of the Tens, Chapter XII: The Descent from the Ladder* (Paccorohaṇivagga), Discourse 114.*
“Monks, what is non-Dhamma should be understood, and what is Dhamma should be understood;
what is harmful should be understood, and what is beneficial should be understood.

Having understood what is non-Dhamma and what is Dhamma, and having understood what is harmful and what is beneficial, one should practice in accordance with the Dhamma and in accordance with what is beneficial.”
And what, bhikkhus, is non-Dhamma, and what is Dhamma? What is harmful, and what is beneficial?
Wrong view, bhikkhus, is non-Dhamma;
right view is Dhamma.
And whatever numerous evil, unwholesome states arise with wrong view as their condition—this is harm;
and whatever numerous wholesome states reach fulfillment through development with right view as their condition—this is benefit.
Wrong intention, monks, is non-Dhamma;
Right intention is a wholesome state;
the many evil, unwholesome states that arise conditioned by wrong intention are an affliction;
and the many wholesome states that reach fulfillment through development conditioned by right intention are a benefit.
“Monks, wrong speech is non-Dhamma;
right speech is Dhamma.
And those numerous evil, unwholesome states that arise conditioned by wrong speech—this is harm.”
And with right speech as condition, numerous wholesome states reach fulfillment through development: this is the meaning.
Monks, wrong action is non-Dhamma;
right action is Dhamma.
And whatever numerous evil, unwholesome states arise with wrong action as their condition—this is disadvantage.
And whatever numerous wholesome states reach fulfillment by development with right action as their condition—this is advantage.
Wrong livelihood, monks, is unrighteousness;
Right livelihood is the Dhamma;
those numerous evil, unwholesome states that arise conditioned by wrong livelihood are disadvantageous;
and those numerous wholesome states that reach fulfillment through development conditioned by right livelihood are beneficial.
“Bhikkhus, wrong effort is non-Dhamma;
right effort is Dhamma.
And those numerous evil, unwholesome states that arise with wrong effort as condition—this is harm.”
And with right effort as condition, numerous wholesome states reach fulfillment by development; this is the meaning.
Wrong mindfulness, monks, is non-Dhamma;
right mindfulness is Dhamma.
And whatever numerous evil, unwholesome states arise with wrong mindfulness as their condition—this is a disadvantage.
But with right mindfulness as their condition, numerous wholesome states reach fulfillment by development—this is an advantage.
Wrong concentration, monks, is non-Dhamma;
Right concentration is a wholesome state (*dhamma*);
the many evil, unwholesome states that arise conditioned by wrong concentration are disadvantageous;
and the many wholesome states that reach fulfillment through development conditioned by right concentration are beneficial.
“Bhikkhus, wrong knowledge is non-Dhamma;
right knowledge is the Dhamma.
And the many evil, unwholesome states that arise with wrong knowledge as condition—this is harm.”
And with right knowledge as condition, numerous wholesome states reach fulfillment through development; this is the meaning.
Wrong liberation, monks, is non-Dhamma;
right liberation is Dhamma.
And whatever numerous evil, unwholesome states arise with wrong liberation as their condition—this is disadvantage.
And whatever numerous wholesome states reach fulfillment through development with right liberation as their condition—this is advantage.
“Monks, what is non-Dhamma and what is Dhamma should be understood;”
“Both the harmful and the beneficial should be understood;
having understood both the unrighteous and the righteous, and having understood both the harmful and the beneficial, one should practice in accordance with what is righteous and what is beneficial.
It was with reference to this that it was said.
The Second.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.115 12.
The Chapter on the Descent (Paccorohaṇi)
Tatiyaadhammasutta: “Monks,
what is non-Dhamma and what is Dhamma must be understood.”
“Both what is harmful and what is beneficial must be understood.

Having understood both what is contrary to the Dhamma and what is the Dhamma, and having understood both what is harmful and what is beneficial, one should practice in accordance with the Dhamma and in accordance with what is beneficial.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Having said this, the Sugata rose from his seat and entered his dwelling.
Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, it occurred to those bhikkhus:
"Friends, the Blessed One, having given us this brief summary and without explaining the meaning in detail, rose from his seat and entered his dwelling:..."
“Monks, what is non-Dhamma must be understood, and what is Dhamma must be understood;
what is harmful must be understood, and what is beneficial must be understood.

Having understood what is non-Dhamma and what is Dhamma, and having understood what is harmful and what is beneficial, one should practice in accordance with the Dhamma and in accordance with the beneficial.”
“Who could analyze in detail the meaning of this brief summary taught by the Blessed One, the meaning of which has not yet been analyzed?
Then it occurred to those bhikkhus:
“This venerable Ānanda is praised and esteemed by the Teacher and by his wise fellow-celibates.”
“Venerable Ānanda is capable of analyzing in detail the meaning of this brief summary taught by the Blessed One, the meaning of which has not yet been analyzed in detail.
What if we were to approach the venerable Ānanda and inquire about this matter?
We shall bear it in mind according as the venerable Ānanda explains it to us.”
Then those bhikkhus approached the Venerable Ānanda; having approached, they exchanged greetings with the Venerable Ānanda.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, they sat down to one side. Sitting there, those bhikkhus said this to the Venerable Ānanda:

"Friend Ānanda, the Blessed One, having given us this brief summary and without explaining the meaning in detail, rose from his seat and entered his dwelling: [the discourse on the four foundations of mindfulness]."
‘What is unrighteousness... [as before] ...and so should one practice.
Then, friends, not long after the Blessed One had departed, this thought occurred to us:
"Friends, this is what the Blessed One taught to us in brief by way of a summary, without analyzing the meaning in detail, before rising from his seat and entering his dwelling:
'Non-Dhamma... [and so on] ...
one should practice accordingly.'"
"Who might be able to analyze in detail the meaning of this brief summary taught by the Blessed One, the meaning of which has not yet been analyzed in detail?
Then, friends, it occurred to us:
"This venerable Ānanda is praised and esteemed by the Teacher himself and by his wise fellow-celibates."
“The Venerable Ānanda is capable of analyzing in detail the meaning of this brief summary taught by the Blessed One, the meaning of which has not yet been analyzed.
Suppose we were to approach the Venerable Ānanda and inquire about this matter?
We shall bear it in mind exactly as the Venerable Ānanda explains it.”
“Let the Venerable Ānanda analyze this.
“Suppose, friend, a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood,
were to pass right by the root and the trunk of a great standing tree possessed of heartwood, looking instead for heartwood in the branches and foliage.”
you would think it should be sought after.
In the same way, friends, while the Teacher is present before you, you pass over that Blessed One and think that this matter should be asked of us.

For that Blessed One, friends, knows what should be known and sees what should be seen; he is become vision, become knowledge, become the Dhamma, become the Brahma; he is the speaker, the proclaimer, the guide to the goal, the giver of the Deathless, the Lord of the Dhamma, the Tathāgata.
"It was indeed the right time for you to have approached the Blessed One and asked about this matter yourselves;
you should have retained it exactly as the Blessed One would have explained it to you.

"Surely, friend Ānanda, the Blessed One knows what should be known and sees what should be seen. He is the eye, he is knowledge, he is the Dhamma, he is the Brahma. He is the speaker, the proclaimer, the guide to the goal, the giver of the Deathless, the Lord of the Dhamma, the Tathāgata."
It was indeed the right time for us to have approached the Blessed One himself and asked about this matter,
so that we might have remembered it exactly as the Blessed One would have explained it.
Moreover, the Venerable Ānanda is praised and esteemed by the Teacher and by his wise fellow-celibates.
“Venerable Ānanda is capable of analyzing in detail the meaning of this brief summary taught by the Blessed One, the meaning of which has not yet been analyzed in detail.
May the venerable Ānanda analyze it in detail without finding it troublesome.
“In that case, friends, listen and pay close attention; I shall speak.”
“Yes, friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Ānanda.
Then the Venerable Ānanda said this:
“Friends, regarding that brief summary which the Blessed One recited and then, without explaining the meaning in detail, rose from his seat and entered his dwelling:”
“Monks, what is non-Dhamma must be understood, and what is Dhamma must be understood;
what is harmful must be understood, and what is beneficial must be understood.

Having understood what is non-Dhamma and what is Dhamma, and having understood what is harmful and what is beneficial, one should practice in accordance with the Dhamma and in accordance with what is beneficial.”
And what, friends, is non-Dhamma, and what is Dhamma? What is harmful, and what is beneficial?
Wrong view, friends, is non-Dhamma;
right view is Dhamma.
And whatever numerous evil, unwholesome states arise with wrong view as their condition—this is harm;
and whatever numerous wholesome states reach fulfillment through development with right view as their condition—this is benefit.
Wrong intention, friends, is non-Dhamma;
Right intention is Dhamma...
Wrong speech, friends, is non-Dhamma;
right speech is Dhamma...
"Friends, wrong action is non-Dhamma;
right action is Dhamma...
Wrong livelihood, friends, is non-Dhamma."
Right livelihood is Dhamma...
Wrong effort, friends, is non-Dhamma;
right effort is Dhamma...
"Friends, wrong mindfulness is non-Dhamma;
right mindfulness is Dhamma...
Friends, wrong concentration is non-Dhamma."
Right concentration is the Dhamma… Wrong knowledge, friend, is non-Dhamma;
right knowledge is the Dhamma….
"Friends, wrong liberation is non-Dhamma;
right liberation is the Dhamma.
And those numerous evil, unwholesome states that arise with wrong liberation as their condition—this is harm."
And with right liberation as condition, numerous wholesome states reach fulfillment through development; this is the meaning.
Now, friends, the Blessed One, having given us this brief summary and without explaining the meaning in detail, rose from his seat and entered his dwelling, saying:
"Bhikkhus, what is non-Dhamma and what is Dhamma should be understood... [as before] ...".
"Thus should one practice. This, friends, is how I understand in detail the meaning of this brief summary taught by the Blessed One, the detailed meaning of which was not yet analyzed.
However, friends, if you wish, you should approach the Blessed One himself and ask him about this matter.
As the Blessed One explains it to you, so should you remember it.
“Very well, friend,” those bhikkhus replied, rejoicing and expressing their appreciation for the Venerable Ānanda’s words.
They rose from their seats and approached the Blessed One. Having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Sitting there, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:
“Bhante, the Blessed One has risen from his seat and entered his dwelling after giving us a brief summary without explaining the meaning in detail, saying:
‘Monks, what is non-Dhamma should be understood...
[and so on] ...one should practice accordingly.’”
"Venerable sir, not long after the Blessed One had departed, this occurred to us:
'Friends, the Blessed One has risen from his seat and entered his dwelling after giving us a brief summary of the teaching without explaining its meaning in detail:
"Bhikkhus, non-Dhamma should be understood... [and so on]."
‘Thus should one practice.
‘Who indeed might analyze in detail the meaning of this brief summary taught by the Blessed One, the meaning which has not yet been analyzed?
Then, Bhante, it occurred to us:
“This Venerable Ānanda is indeed praised by the Teacher and esteemed by his wise fellow-celibates.
The Venerable Ānanda is capable of analyzing in detail the meaning of this brief summary taught by the Blessed One, the meaning of which has not yet been analyzed in detail.
What if we were to approach the Venerable Ānanda and, having approached him, question him regarding this matter?”
‘We shall remember it exactly as the venerable Ānanda explains it.
Then, Bhante, we approached the venerable Ānanda; having approached, we asked the venerable Ānanda about this matter.
It has been well-expounded for us, Bhante, by the venerable Ānanda in these ways, with these words, and with these phrases.”
“Excellent, excellent, monks!
Ānanda is wise, monks;
Ānanda possesses great wisdom.”
“Bhikkhus, even if you were to approach me and ask about this matter, I would answer it in exactly the same way that Ānanda has answered it.
This is its meaning, and thus you should remember it. The third [sutta].

He has contemplated five hundred points of thought by which those belonging to other sects know that they have been overcome.
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, do you remember the bases of wisdom?
“It is the time for this, Blessed One; it is the time for this, Sugata, that the Blessed One should speak.

“Therefore, monks, listen and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.

Consequently, that unrighteous assembly makes a great clamor and noise, saying:

"Furthermore, monks, here someone suppresses and oppresses a legitimate discussion with an illegitimate discussion, and thereby pleases an illegitimate assembly.
Because of that, the illegitimate assembly becomes loud and noisy, crying out:
'Oh, what a wise man! Oh, what a wise man!'"
But here, monks, a certain person uses an unrighteous argument to suppress and crush both a righteous argument and an unrighteous argument, and thereby he pleases an unrighteous assembly.
Consequently, that unrighteous assembly makes a great noise and a loud clamor, saying:
"Oh, what a wise man! Oh, what a wise man!"

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.117 12. Paccorohaṇivagga Saṅgāravasutta Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then the brahmin Saṅgārava approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their polite conversation, he sat down to one side and said to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama, I am a brahmin who maintains the sacred fires, one who has kept the five fires kindled for eighty years. Yet, Master Gotama, I do not see any ascetic or brahmin who possesses such great psychic power and might as Master Gotama. “Brahmin, it is because you have not seen me when I possess great psychic power and might that you speak thus. But, brahmin, when I possess great psychic power and might, you will see me. Then the brahmin Saṅgārava rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, knelt down with his right knee on the ground, raised his joined palms in reverential salutation toward the Blessed One, and said: “May Master Gotama accept my invitation for tomorrow’s meal, together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. The Blessed One consented by remaining silent. Then the brahmin Saṅgārava, having understood the Blessed One’s consent, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Now on that occasion, the brahmin householders of Sāvatthī had made an appointment, saying: “The meal for tomorrow will be prepared for the ascetic Gotama and his retinue.

Then the brahmin Saṅgārava went to his own residence and gave instructions to his slaves and laborers: “Prepare a large amount of hard food and soft food for the ascetic Gotama and his retinue. “Yes, sir,” those slaves and laborers replied to the brahmin Saṅgārava. Then the brahmin Saṅgārava went to the Blessed One and, having arrived, said to him: “It is time, Master Gotama; the meal is ready. May Master Gotama come at his own convenience. Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and outer robe, and entered Sāvatthī for alms. Now on that occasion, the brahmin householders of Sāvatthī, having prepared a large amount of hard food and soft food for the ascetic Gotama and his retinue, stood along the road watching for the Blessed One, thinking: “This way the Blessed One comes; this way the Blessed One approaches. When they saw the Blessed One coming in the distance, they went forth to meet him and paid homage to him. Then they said to the Blessed One: “Let the Blessed One enter Sāvatthī by this road. This road has been prepared by us for the Blessed One and his retinue. Then the Blessed One entered Sāvatthī by that road. The brahmin Saṅgārava then went to his own residence and set out a large amount of hard food and soft food. When the Blessed One had washed his hands and feet and taken his seat, the brahmin Saṅgārava personally served the Blessed One and his retinue with the large amount of hard food and soft food. When the Blessed One had eaten and had withdrawn his hand from the bowl, the brahmin Saṅgārava took a low seat, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama, I am a brahmin who maintains the sacred fires, one who has kept the five fires kindled for eighty years. Yet, Master Gotama, I do not see any ascetic or brahmin who possesses such great psychic power and might as Master Gotama. “Brahmin, it is because you have not seen me when I possess great psychic power and might that you speak thus. But, brahmin, when I possess great psychic power and might, you will see me. “Master Gotama, let the Blessed One demonstrate great psychic power and might right here in Sāvatthī. “Brahmin, if you were to say, ‘Let the fire be produced from this wet, sappy log,’ would it be possible to produce fire from that wet, sappy log? “It would not be possible, Master Gotama. “Brahmin, if you were to say, ‘Let fire be produced from this wet, sappy log by means of a drill,’ would it be possible to produce fire from that wet, sappy log by means of a drill? “It would not be possible, Master Gotama. “Brahmin, if you were to say, ‘Let fire be produced from this wet, sappy log by means of a drill and a stick,’ would it be possible to produce fire from that wet, sappy log by means of a drill and a stick? “It would not be possible, Master Gotama. “Brahmin, if you were to say, ‘Let fire be produced from this wet, sappy log by means of a drill, a stick, and effort,’ would it be possible to produce fire from that wet, sappy log by means of a drill, a stick, and effort? “It would not be possible, Master Gotama. “Just so, brahmin, if you were to say, ‘Let the ascetic Gotama demonstrate great psychic power and might right here in Sāvatthī,’ it is impossible for me to demonstrate great psychic power and might right here in Sāvatthī. “Master Gotama, let the Blessed One demonstrate great psychic power and might elsewhere than right here in Sāvatthī. “Brahmin, if you were to say, ‘Let fire be produced from this dry, sapless log,’ would it be possible to produce fire from that dry, sapless log? “It would be possible, Master Gotama. “Brahmin, if you were to say, ‘Let fire be produced from this dry, sapless log by means of a drill,’ would it be possible to produce fire from that dry, sapless log by means of a drill? “It would be possible, Master Gotama. “Brahmin, if you were to say, ‘Let fire be produced from this dry, sapless log by means of a drill and a stick,’ would it be possible to produce fire from that dry, sapless log by means of a drill and a stick? “It would be possible, Master Gotama. “Brahmin, if you were to say, ‘Let fire be produced from this dry, sapless log by means of a drill, a stick, and effort,’ would it be possible to produce fire from that dry, sapless log by means of a drill, a stick, and effort? “It would be possible, Master Gotama. “Just so, brahmin, if you were to say, ‘Let the ascetic Gotama demonstrate great psychic power and might elsewhere than right here in Sāvatthī,’ it is possible for me to demonstrate great psychic power and might elsewhere than right here in Sāvatthī. “Master Gotama, where could the Blessed One demonstrate great psychic power and might? “Brahmin, there is the Himalayas, the king of mountains, where various medicinal herbs grow: the herb called *tāsa*, the herb called *rohiṇī*, the herb called *pukkharasāti*, the herb called *sujātā*, the herb called *nāgasāhvayā*, the herb called *elā*, the herb called *uppalā*, the herb called *padumā*, the herb called *pāṭalā*, the herb called *mahāpāṭalā*, the herb called *sinduvāra*, and the herb called *campaka*. There is also the *kuṭaja* tree, the *kaṇṇikāra* tree, the *nāgapāda* tree, and the *yugandhara* tree. There is the river Ganges, flowing full of water, pleasant, delightful, and cool. Brahmin, suppose a man were to go to the Himalayas, the king of mountains, and there he would dig up the medicinal herb called *tāsa*, take it with him, and depart. Having traveled a long distance, he would think: ‘I shall now prepare a fire-producing apparatus. He would then split the medicinal herb called *tāsa* in half lengthwise, split it in half crosswise, and split each of those halves in half again lengthwise and crosswise. He would then take a chip of the medicinal herb called *tāsa* and, having moistened it with saliva, place it in a fire-producing apparatus. He would then think: ‘I shall now produce fire by friction. But, brahmin, would it be possible for him to produce fire by friction? “No, Master Gotama. Why is that? Because that medicinal herb called *tāsa* is too moist, Master Gotama. “Suppose, brahmin, a man were to go to
