Wrong speech is this shore, right speech is the further shore;
wrong action is this shore, right action is the further shore;
wrong livelihood is this shore, right livelihood is the further shore.
Wrong effort is this shore, right effort is the further shore;
wrong mindfulness is this shore, right mindfulness is the further shore;
wrong concentration is this shore, right concentration is the further shore.
Wrong knowledge is this shore, right knowledge is the further shore;
wrong liberation is this shore, right liberation is the further shore.
This, brahmin, is "this shore," and this is "the further shore."
Few among humans are those people who go to the further shore;
but this other generation—
They merely run along the shore.
But those who follow the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma in the well-expounded teaching—
Those people will cross over to the far shore,
the realm of Death so difficult to transcend,
having utterly abandoned dark qualities.
Let the wise person cultivate purity,
having gone from home to homelessness,
to a secluded place that is difficult to reach.
One who has abandoned sensual pleasures and possesses nothing should desire delight therein;
one should purify oneself.
The wise one is freed from the defilements of the mind—
those whose minds have been rightly and thoroughly cultivated in the factors of enlightenment.
Those who delight in the relinquishing of grasping, being without clinging,
have destroyed the taints and possess radiance.
“They have attained final nibbāna in the world.
The fifth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.118

12. Paccorohaṇivagga Orimatīrasutta (The Discourse on This Shore) “Bhikkhus, this Dhamma is for one who stands on this shore, not for one who stands on the further shore. And how, bhikkhus, is the Dhamma for one who stands on this shore, not for one who stands on the further shore? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells with his mind obsessed by sensual lust, burning with sensual lust; he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen sensual lust. He dwells with his mind obsessed by ill will, burning with ill will; he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen ill will. He dwells with his mind obsessed by sloth and torpor, burning with sloth and torpor; he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen sloth and torpor. He dwells with his mind obsessed by restlessness and remorse, burning with restlessness and remorse; he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen restlessness and remorse. He dwells with his mind obsessed by doubt, burning with doubt; he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen doubt. This, bhikkhus, is how the Dhamma is for one who stands on this shore, not for one who stands on the further shore. But, bhikkhus, this Dhamma is for one who stands on the further shore, not for one who stands on this shore. And how, bhikkhus, is the Dhamma for one who stands on the further shore, not for one who stands on this shore? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells with a mind that is not obsessed by sensual lust, free from burning passion for sensual lust; he understands as it really is the escape from the arisen sensual lust. He dwells with a mind that is not obsessed by ill will, free from burning passion for ill will; he understands as it really is the escape from the arisen ill will. He dwells with a mind that is not obsessed by sloth and torpor, free from burning passion for sloth and torpor; he understands as it really is the escape from the arisen sloth and torpor. He dwells with a mind that is not obsessed by restlessness and remorse, free from burning passion for restlessness and remorse; he understands as it really is the escape from the arisen restlessness and remorse. He dwells with a mind that is not obsessed by doubt, free from burning passion for doubt; he understands as it really is the escape from the arisen doubt. This, bhikkhus, is how the Dhamma is for one who stands on the further shore, not for one who stands on this shore.”
“Monks, I will teach you the near shore and the far shore.
Listen to it and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“And what, bhikkhus, is the near shore? And what is the far shore?
Wrong view is the near shore; right view is the far shore... [and so on] ...”
Wrong liberation is this shore; right liberation is the further shore.
This, monks, is the near shore; this is the far shore.
Few indeed are those among human beings...
Those people who go to the further shore,
while this other generation merely runs along the near shore.
But those people who follow the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma as it has been rightly proclaimed,
they shall go beyond.
The realm of death is very difficult to cross.
Having utterly abandoned dark qualities,
the wise person should cultivate bright ones.
Having come from home to the homeless state,
where seclusion is far removed,
one should seek delight therein.
Having abandoned sensual pleasures, possessing nothing,
the wise person should purify themselves from the defilements of the mind.
Those whose minds are well-developed in the factors of enlightenment,
regarding the relinquishing of grasping—
Those who delight in non-clinging,
whose taints are exhausted and who possess radiance—
they are fully extinguished in this world.
The Sixth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.119.
Chapter 12: On the Descent (Paccorohaṇivagga).

At that time, on the Uposatha day, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi— having washed his head and put on a pair of new linen garments— stood to one side not far from the Blessed One, carrying a handful of fresh kusa grass.
On that very Uposatha day, the Blessed One saw the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi standing to one side, having washed his head, wearing a new pair of linen garments, and carrying a handful of fresh kusa grass.
Having seen him, he said this to the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi:
"Why is it, brahmin, that on this Uposatha day you have washed your head, are wearing a new pair of linen garments, and are standing to one side carrying a handful of fresh kusa grass?"
“What is it for the brahmin clan today?
“Today, Master Gotama, there is the *paccorohaṇī* ceremony for the brahmin clan.
“But how, brahmin, is the *paccorohaṇī* performed by the brahmins?”
“Here, Master Gotama, on the Uposatha day, the brahmins wash their heads, put on a pair of new linen garments,
smear the ground with fresh cow dung, spread it over with green kuśa grass,
and prepare a bed between the boundary and the fire-hall.
Three times during that night they would rise and, with palms joined, pay homage to the fire, saying:
"We descend from you, O Lord; we descend from you, O Lord.
And they gratified the fire with abundant ghee, oil, and butter.
"And at the end of that night, they satisfy the brahmins with choice foods, both hard and soft.
In this way, Master Gotama, the *paccorohaṇī* festival of the brahmins takes place.
"But, brahmin, the *paccorohaṇī* of the brahmins is one thing, whereas the *paccorohaṇī* in the discipline of the Noble One is quite another."
“But how, Master Gotama, is there a ‘descent’ in the Noble One’s discipline?
It would be well if Master Gotama would teach me the Dhamma as to how there is a descent in the Noble One’s discipline.
“In that case, brahmin, listen and attend closely; I shall speak.”
“Yes, sir,” the brahmin Jāṇussoṇī replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“In this case, brahmin, a noble disciple reflects thus:”
‘The result of wrong view is indeed evil,
both in this very life and in the future.
Having reflected thus, he abandons wrong view.
One descends from wrong view.
… “The result of wrong intention is indeed evil,
both in this very life and in the future.”
Having reflected thus, he abandons wrong intention;
he descends from wrong intention.
… “Now, wrong speech has an evil result—”
"both in this very life and in future lives.
Having reflected thus, he abandons wrong speech and descends from wrong speech.
‘... There is indeed an evil result for wrong action, both in this very life and in future lives.
Having reflected thus, he abandons wrong action.
He descends from wrong action.
… “The result of wrong livelihood is evil,
both in this very life and in future lives.”
Having reflected thus, one abandons wrong livelihood and descends from wrong livelihood.
… “The result of wrong effort is indeed evil— ”
“both in this very life and in future lives.
Having reflected thus, he abandons wrong effort and descends from wrong effort.
‘The result of wrong mindfulness is indeed evil,
both in this very life and in future lives.
Having reflected thus, he abandons wrong mindfulness.
One descends from wrong mindfulness.
… “The result of wrong concentration is indeed evil,
both in this very life and in the future.”
Having reflected thus, he abandons wrong concentration and descends from wrong concentration.
… “The result of wrong knowledge is indeed evil— ”
‘both in this very life and in future lives.
Having reflected thus, he abandons wrong knowledge and descends from wrong knowledge.
‘... Wrong liberation indeed has an evil result, both in this very life and in the future.
Having reflected thus, he abandons wrong liberation.
“He descends from wrong liberation.
It is in this way, brahmin, that there is a ‘descent’ in the discipline of the Noble One.
“Master Gotama, the descent of the brahmins is one thing, but the descent in the discipline of the Noble One is another.”
“Master Gotama, compared to this Descent of the Noble Ones in the Ariyan discipline, the Brāhmaṇas’ Descent does not count for even a sixteenth part.
Excellent, Master Gotama!
… May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last.”
Seventh. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.120.
Chapter 12: On the Descent (Paccorohaṇivagga).
The Second Discourse on the Descent (Dutiyapaccorohaṇīsutta):
“Monks, I will teach you the noble descent.”
Listen to that… And what,
bhikkhus, is the noble Paccorohaṇī festival?
Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple reflects thus:
‘The result of wrong view is indeed evil,
both in this very life and in the future.
Having reflected thus, he abandons wrong view.
One descends from wrong view.
There is an evil result for wrong intention… for wrong speech… [and so forth].
For one of wrong action...
for one of wrong livelihood...
for one of wrong effort...
Of wrong mindfulness...
of wrong concentration...
of wrong knowledge...
The result of wrong liberation is indeed evil,
both in this very life and in the future.
Having reflected thus, he abandons wrong liberation.
He descends from wrong liberation.
This, monks, is called the noble Paccorohaṇī festival.
The eighth.

“Bhikkhus, this is the forerunner and precursor of the rising of the sun, namely, the dawn.

12. Paccorohaṇivagga Āsavakkhayasutta (AN 10.122, PTS AN v 237) “Monks, there are these four taints. What four? The taint of sensuality, the taint of existence, the taint of views, and the taint of ignorance. These, monks, are the four taints. When this was said, a certain monk addressed the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the condition, for the arising of these four taints? “Contact, monk, is the cause, contact is the condition, for the arising of these four taints. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the condition, for the arising of that contact? “The sixfold sense base, monk, is the cause, the sixfold sense base is the condition, for the arising of that contact. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the condition, for the arising of that sixfold sense base? “Name-and-form, monk, is the cause, name-and-form is the condition, for the arising of that sixfold sense base. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the condition, for the arising of that name-and-form? “Consciousness, monk, is the cause, consciousness is the condition, for the arising of that name-and-form. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the condition, for the arising of that consciousness? “Volitional formations, monk, are the cause, volitional formations are the condition, for the arising of that consciousness. “But, venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the condition, for the arising of those volitional formations? “Ignorance, monk, is the cause, ignorance is the condition, for the arising of those volitional formations. “Monk, when ignorance is abandoned and true knowledge has arisen, contact ceases due to the cessation of ignorance; with the cessation of contact, the taints cease. When this was said, that monk addressed the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘When ignorance is abandoned and true knowledge has arisen, contact ceases due to the cessation of ignorance; with the cessation of contact, the taints cease. “Indeed, monk, it is so. When ignorance is abandoned and true knowledge has arisen, contact ceases due to the cessation of ignorance; with the cessation of contact, the taints cease. “Venerable sir, how should one know, how should one see, for the destruction of the taints to occur? “Monk, one should know all, one should see all. For one who knows all and sees all, the mind becomes dispassionate toward all; through dispassion, it is liberated; through liberation, the knowledge arises: ‘It is liberated. One understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being. “It is wonderful, venerable sir, it is marvelous! A man would come along needing heartwood. He would cut down that great tree at its foot and, having cut it down, he would peel away the outer bark, the inner bark, and the softwood, and then take the heartwood. Then a second man would come along needing heartwood. He would cut down that great tree at its foot and, having cut it down, he would peel away the outer bark, the inner bark, and the softwood, and then take the heartwood. But, venerable sir, that great tree standing possessed of heartwood—when its outer bark, inner bark, and softwood have been peeled away, it is called ‘heartwood-less.

13. Parisuddhavagga First Discourse (AN 10.123, PTS AN v 237) "Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is completely pure; the person who is not completely pure; the person who is both completely pure and not completely pure; and the person who is neither completely pure nor not completely pure. And how, monks, is one a person who is completely pure? Here, monks, a bhikkhu is virtuous, restrained with the restraint of the Pātimokkha, perfect in conduct and resort, and seeing fear in the slightest fault, he trains by undertaking the training rules. He dwells with a mind well-restrained by mindfulness, his senses guarded, possessing the wealth of wisdom, and he is one who has attained the destruction of the taints. This, monks, is called a person who is completely pure. And how, monks, is one a person who is not completely pure? Here, monks, a bhikkhu is immoral, unrestrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, deficient in conduct and resort, and not seeing fear in transgression, he does not train by undertaking the training rules. He dwells with a mind not restrained by mindfulness, his senses unguarded, lacking the wealth of wisdom, and he is one who has not attained the destruction of the taints. This, monks, is called a person who is not completely pure. And how, monks, is one a person who is both completely pure and not completely pure? Here, monks, a bhikkhu is virtuous, restrained with the restraint of the Pātimokkha, perfect in conduct and resort, and seeing fear in the slightest fault, he trains by undertaking the training rules. Yet he dwells with a mind not restrained by mindfulness, his senses unguarded, lacking the wealth of wisdom, and he is one who has not attained the destruction of the taints. This, monks, is called a person who is both completely pure and not completely pure. And how, monks, is one a person who is neither completely pure nor not completely pure? Here, monks, a bhikkhu is virtuous, restrained with the restraint of the Pātimokkha, perfect in conduct and resort, and seeing fear in the slightest fault, he trains by undertaking the training rules. And he dwells with a mind well-restrained by mindfulness, his senses guarded, possessing the wealth of wisdom, and he is one who has attained the destruction of the taints. This, monks, is called a person who is neither completely pure nor not completely pure. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world."
“Bhikkhus, these ten things are pure and bright, and they exist nowhere else than in the discipline of the Sugata.
What are the ten?
Right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration, right knowledge, and right liberation.”
“Monks, these ten things are pure and bright, and they exist nowhere else but in the discipline of the Sugata.
Thus was the first [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.124
13. Parisuddhavagga Second Discourse (AN 10.124, PTS AN v 237)
“Monks, these ten things arise that have not arisen before, and they do so nowhere else than in the discipline of the Well-Gone One.
What ten?
Right view … [and so on] … right liberation.”
“Monks, these ten things arise when they have not yet arisen, and not apart from the discipline of the Well-Gone One.
The second [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.125

13. Parisuddhavagga The Third Discourse (AN 10.125) “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is pure in conduct but impure in view; the person who is impure in conduct but pure in view; the person who is impure both in conduct and in view; and the person who is pure both in conduct and in view. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Monks, these ten things are of great fruit and great benefit, and they are found nowhere else than in the discipline of the Well-Gone One.
What are the ten?
Right view … [and so on] … right liberation.”
“Monks, these ten things are of great fruit and great benefit, and they do not exist apart from the discipline of the Well-Gone One.
The third [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.126

13. Parisuddhavagga The Fourth Discourse (AN 10.126) "Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? "The person who is pure; the person who is impure; the person who is both pure and impure; and the person who is neither pure nor impure. "And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who is pure? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is virtuous, restrained with the restraint of the Pātimokkha, perfect in conduct and resort, and seeing fear in the slightest fault, he trains by undertaking the training rules. He dwells with a mind that is purified from lust, hate, and delusion. This, bhikkhus, is called a person who is pure. "And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who is impure? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is not virtuous, not restrained with the restraint of the Pātimokkha, deficient in conduct and resort, and not seeing fear in transgression, he does not train by undertaking the training rules. His mind is not purified from lust, hate, and delusion. This, bhikkhus, is called a person who is impure. "And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who is both pure and impure? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is sometimes virtuous and sometimes not virtuous, sometimes restrained with the restraint of the Pātimokkha and sometimes not, sometimes perfect in conduct and resort and sometimes not, sometimes seeing fear in the slightest fault and sometimes not, and sometimes training by undertaking the training rules and sometimes not. At times his mind is purified from lust, hate, and delusion, and at times it is not. This, bhikkhus, is called a person who is both pure and impure. "And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who is neither pure nor impure? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has abandoned the fetters of lust, hate, and delusion; he has cut them off at the root, made them like a palm stump, done away with them so that they are no longer subject to future arising. This, bhikkhus, is called a person who is neither pure nor impure. "These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world."* *This discourse is followed by verses on the same theme.*
“Bhikkhus, these ten things culminate in the removal of lust, the removal of hatred, and the removal of delusion, and nowhere else than in the discipline of the Sugata.
What are the ten?
Right view … [and so on] … right liberation.”
“Monks, these ten things culminate in the removal of lust, culminate in the removal of hatred, and culminate in the removal of delusion; nowhere else than in the discipline of the Well-Gone One.
Thus was the fourth [discourse]. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.127

13. Parisuddhavagga Pañcamasutta (AN 10.127, PTS AN v 238) “Bhikkhus, there are these five kinds of purity. What five? Purity of bodily conduct, purity of verbal conduct, purity of mind, purity of livelihood, and purity of view. These, bhikkhus, are the five kinds of purity.”

“Monks, these ten qualities lead exclusively to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna, and not otherwise than through the discipline of the Well-Gone One.
What are the ten?
Right view … [and so on] … right liberation.”

“Monks, these ten qualities lead exclusively to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to Nibbāna, and not otherwise than through the discipline of the Sugata.
The fifth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.128

13. Parisuddhavagga The Sixth Discourse (AN 10.128) [The Blessed One said: “Monks, there are these six factors for the purification of a bhikkhu who is a trainee. What six? “Here, monks, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest transgressions; having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. This is the first factor for the purification of a bhikkhu who is a trainee. “Again, monks, a bhikkhu has learned much, remembers what he has heard, and accumulates what he has heard. Those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure spiritual life—such teachings as these he has learned much of, retained in mind, recited verbally, investigated mentally, and penetrated well through view. This is the second factor for the purification of a bhikkhu who is a trainee. “Again, monks, a bhikkhu gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life. This is the third factor for the purification of a bhikkhu who is a trainee. “Again, monks, a bhikkhu, with the destruction of the taints, realizes for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having attained it, dwells therein. This is the fourth factor for the purification of a bhikkhu who is a trainee. “Again, monks, a bhikkhu possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha: ‘Thus indeed is the Blessed One: worthy, perfectly awakened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. This is the fifth factor for the purification of a bhikkhu who is a trainee. “Again, monks, a bhikkhu possesses unwavering confidence in the Dhamma: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. This is the sixth factor for the purification of a bhikkhu who is a trainee. “These, monks, are the six factors for the purification of a bhikkhu who is a trainee.”
“Bhikkhus, these ten things, when developed and cultivated, arise only when they have not yet arisen, and nowhere else than in the discipline of the Well-Gone One.
What ten?
Right view … [and so on] … right liberation.”
“Monks, these ten qualities, when developed and cultivated, arise even though they have not yet arisen; this is nowhere else except in the discipline of the Well-Gone One.
The sixth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.129

13. Parisuddhavagga Sattamasutta (AN 10.129, PTS AN v 239) “Bhikkhus, there are these seven kinds of persons found existing in the world. What seven? The person who is completely pure; the person who is purified by faith; the person who is purified by love; the person who is purified by the Dhamma; the person who is purified by both; the person who is purified by both and by the Dhamma; and the person who is purified by both, by the Dhamma, and by the Saṅgha. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who is completely pure? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is devoid of lust for the form element; he is devoid of lust for the feeling element; he is devoid of lust for the perception element; he is devoid of lust for the volitional formations element; he is devoid of lust for the consciousness element. He is devoid of lust for the eye; he is devoid of lust for forms; he is devoid of lust for eye-consciousness; he is devoid of lust for eye-contact; he is devoid of lust for whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant. He is devoid of lust for the ear; he is devoid of lust for sounds... [and so on for the nose, tongue, body, and mind] ...he is devoid of lust for whatever feeling arises with mind-contact as condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that one is a person who is completely pure. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who is purified by faith? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has faith in the Tathāgata’s enlightenment thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that one is a person who is purified by faith. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who is purified by love? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; so above, below, across, and everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—vast, exalted, measureless, without enmity, without ill will. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that one is a person who is purified by love. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who is purified by the Dhamma? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu possesses the right view of one beyond training, which is noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that one is a person who is purified by the Dhamma. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who is purified by both? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu possesses both the right view of one beyond training and the right intention of one beyond training, which are noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that one is a person who is purified by both. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who is purified by both and by the Dhamma? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu possesses both the right view and the right intention of one beyond training, and he also possesses the right speech, right action, and right livelihood of one beyond training, which are noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that one is a person who is purified by both and by the Dhamma. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person who is purified by both, by the Dhamma, and by the Saṅgha? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu possesses both the right view and the right intention of one beyond training, and he also possesses the right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration of one beyond training, which are noble and penetrative, leading to the complete destruction of suffering. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that one is a person who is purified by both, by the Dhamma, and by the Saṅgha. These, bhikkhus, are the seven kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, these ten things, when developed and cultivated, yield great fruit and bring great benefit, nowhere else but in the discipline of the Well-Gone One.
What are the ten?
Right view … [and so on] … right liberation.”
“Monks, these ten qualities, when developed and cultivated, yield great fruit and bring great benefit, nowhere else but within the discipline of the Sugata.
The seventh. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.130

13. Parisuddhavagga The Eighth Discourse (AN 10.130, PTS AN v 239) “Monks, there are these eight bases for the purification of a bhikkhu. What eight? (1) Here, monks, a bhikkhu is possessed of faith; he places faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. This is the first basis for the purification of a bhikkhu. (2) Again, monks, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in even minor transgressions. Having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. This is the second basis for the purification of a bhikkhu. (3) Again, monks, a bhikkhu has heard much, has retained what he has heard, accumulated what he has heard. Those teachings that are lovely at the beginning, lovely in the middle, and lovely at the end, in their meaning and expression, which proclaim the holy life that is utterly perfect and pure—such teachings as these he has heard much of, retained, and mastered through reflection. This is the third basis for the purification of a bhikkhu. (4) Again, monks, a bhikkhu is one who gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life. This is the fourth basis for the purification of a bhikkhu. (5) Again, monks, with the destruction of the taints, a bhikkhu has realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having attained it, dwells therein. This is the fifth basis for the purification of a bhikkhu. (6) Again, monks, a bhikkhu possesses the analytical knowledges; he is skilled in the analysis of meaning, of phenomena, of language, and of eloquence. This is the sixth basis for the purification of a bhikkhu. (7) Again, monks, a bhikkhu is one who recollects his manifold past abodes, that is, one birth, two births, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand, many eons of cosmic expansion, many eons of cosmic contraction, many eons of cosmic expansion and contraction: ‘There I had such a name, belonged to such a clan, had such an appearance; such was my food, such my experience of pleasure and pain, such my lifespan. Passing away from there, I reappeared elsewhere; and there too I had such a name... such was my lifespan. Passing away from there, I reappeared here. Thus he recollects his manifold past abodes with their aspects and details. This is the seventh basis for the purification of a bhikkhu. (8) Again, monks, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, a bhikkhu sees beings passing away and reappearing—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in fortunate states and in unfortunate states, faring according to their kamma: ‘These beings, on account of misconduct in body, speech, and mind, or of reviling the noble ones, or of holding wrong views, or of undertaking kamma based on wrong views, at the breaking up of the body after death, have reappeared in a state of deprivation, in a bad destination, in perdition, even in hell. These beings, on account of good conduct in body, speech, and mind, or of not reviling the noble ones, or of holding right views, or of undertaking kamma based on right views, at the breaking up of the body after death, have reappeared in a happy destination, even in the heavenly world. Thus, with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, he sees beings passing away and reappearing—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, in fortunate states and in unfortunate states, faring according to their kamma. This is the eighth basis for the purification of a bhikkhu. These, monks, are the eight bases for the purification of a bhikkhu.”

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.134 14. Sādhuvagga Sādhusutta: On the Good Person “Monks, there are these ten qualities of a good person. What ten? (1) Here, monks, a good person is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest transgressions, and having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. (2) He has learned much, remembers what he has heard, and accumulates what he has learned. Those teachings that are lovely in the beginning, lovely in the middle, and lovely in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure spiritual life—such teachings he has learned much of, retained in mind, recited verbally, mentally investigated, and penetrated well through view. (3) He is a speaker of what is beneficial, a speaker of what is true, a speaker at the proper time, a speaker of facts, a speaker of the Dhamma, a speaker of the Vinaya, one who utters speech that is timely, factual, meaningful, connected with the Dhamma, and connected with the Vinaya. (4) He is easy to correct, possesses qualities that make him easy to correct, and is patient with correction. (5) He does not have a hidden nature; he is open and not secretive about his faults. (6) He is gentle and mild in character. (7) He is free from envy and does not covet the gains, honor, and praise belonging to others. (8) He is without ill will and has a mind free from enmity toward all beings. (9) He holds right view and possesses a perspective that is upright. (10) He has faith in the Tathāgata’s enlightenment thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. These, monks, are the ten qualities of a good person.”
“Monks, I will teach you what is wholesome and what is unwholesome.

and wrong liberation— this, monks, is called what is unwholesome.
And what, monks, is wholesome?
"Right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration, right knowledge,
and right liberation— this, monks, is called 'the good. Thus was the first [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.135 14. Sādhuvagga Ariyadhammasutta (The Noble Dhamma) "Bhikkhus, there are these ten qualities of the noble ones that lead to non-decline. What ten? (1) Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One.

(2) He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. (3) He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. (4) He is possessed of the virtues dear to the noble ones—unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. (5) He has heard much, has retained what he has heard, has stored what he has heard. All those teachings that are lovely in the beginning, lovely in the middle, and lovely in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the spiritually fulfilled life that is utterly perfect and pure—all such teachings as these he has heard much of, retained, recited verbally, investigated with the mind, and penetrated well through view. (6) He gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life. (7) With the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, he sees beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and he understands how beings fare in accordance with their kamma. (8) By realizing it for himself with direct knowledge, he here and now enters upon and abides in the deliverance of mind and deliverance by wisdom that are taintless with the destruction of the taints. (9) He is one who gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the various kinds of supernormal power: having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one; he appears and vanishes; he goes unhindered through a wall, through a rampart, through a mountain as though through space; he dives in and out of the earth as though it were water; he walks on water without sinking as though it were earth; seated cross-legged, he travels in space like a bird; with his hand he touches and strokes the moon and sun so powerful and mighty; he exercises mastery with the body as far as the brahma world. (10) By realizing it for himself with direct knowledge, he here and now enters upon and abides in the deliverance of mind and deliverance by wisdom that are taintless with the destruction of the taints. These, bhikkhus, are the ten qualities of the noble ones that lead to non-decline."

14. Sādhuvagga: The Discourse on Purpose (Atthasutta) “Monks, there are these four purposes for which a noble disciple cultivates the cultivation of mindfulness. What four? ‘May my mind be concentrated, may my mind not be scattered!’—this is the first purpose for which a noble disciple cultivates the cultivation of mindfulness. ‘May I understand as it really is: “This is suffering”’—this is the second purpose for which a noble disciple cultivates the cultivation of mindfulness. ‘May I understand as it really is: “This is the origin of suffering”’—this is the third purpose for which a noble disciple cultivates the cultivation of mindfulness. ‘May I understand as it really is: “This is the cessation of suffering”’—this is the fourth purpose for which a noble disciple cultivates the cultivation of mindfulness. These, monks, are the four purposes for which a noble disciple cultivates the cultivation of mindfulness.”

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.138 14. Sādhuvagga Dhammasutta “Monks, there are these ten qualities of a true person (*sappurisa*). What ten? Here, monks, a true person is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults; having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. He has learned much, remembers what he has learned, and consolidates what he has learned; such teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure spiritual life—such teachings he has learned much of, retained in mind, recited verbally, mentally investigated, and penetrated well through view. He is a speaker on the Dhamma at the right time, one who speaks what is factual, what is beneficial, and what leads to the goal; he speaks on the Dhamma in season, on the Dhamma that is lovely in its beginning, lovely in its middle, and lovely in its conclusion, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaims the perfectly complete and pure spiritual life. He teaches the Dhamma out of compassion for beings. He is one who has entered the stream of the Dhamma, one who has attained vision, one who has reached certainty, one who has transcended doubt, one who has crossed over uncertainty, one who has gained intrepidity, and one who has become independent of others in the Teacher’s Dispensation. He gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life. With the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses the human, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate—and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma. With the destruction of the taints, he realizes for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having attained it, he dwells therein. These, monks, are the ten qualities of a true person.”

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.141 14. Sādhuvagga Tapanīyasutta (The Discourse on What is to Be Heated) “Monks, there are these ten things that are to be heated. What ten? One who destroys life is to be heated; one who takes what is not given is to be heated; one who engages in sexual misconduct is to be heated; one who speaks falsely is to be heated; one who is full of longing is to be heated; one who has ill will in his heart is to be heated; one who holds wrong view is to be heated; one who is miserly with regard to dwellings is to be heated; one who is miserly with regard to families is to be heated; and one who is miserly with regard to Dhamma is to be heated. These, monks, are the ten things that are to be heated.”

14. Sādhuvagga Dukkhudrayasutta (AN 10.143, PTS AN v 243) “Monks, there are these two kinds of persons found existing in the world. What two? The one who brings forth suffering and the one who brings forth happiness. And how, monks, is a person one who brings forth suffering? Here, monks, someone has gone forth from the home life into homelessness with a mind full of longing, not having overcome longing; with a mind full of ill will, not having overcome ill will; with a mind full of dullness and drowsiness, not having overcome dullness and drowsiness; with a mind full of restlessness and remorse, not having overcome restlessness and remorse; with a mind full of doubt, not having overcome doubt. He dwells pursuing unwholesome states, abandoning wholesome states. He is one who does not guard the doors of his sense faculties, who is immoderate in eating, and who is not devoted to wakefulness. He possesses no noble wisdom that leads to the complete destruction of suffering. This, monks, is called a person who brings forth suffering. And how, monks, is a person one who brings forth happiness? Here, monks, someone has gone forth from the home life into homelessness with a mind free from longing, having overcome longing; with a mind free from ill will, having overcome ill will; with a mind free from dullness and drowsiness, having overcome dullness and drowsiness; with a mind free from restlessness and remorse, having overcome restlessness and remorse; with a mind free from doubt, having overcome doubt. He dwells pursuing wholesome states, abandoning unwholesome states. He guards the doors of his sense faculties, is moderate in eating, and is devoted to wakefulness. He possesses noble wisdom that leads to the complete destruction of suffering. This, monks, is called a person who brings forth happiness.”
“Monks, I will teach you the Dhamma that has suffering as its outcome and the Dhamma that has happiness as its outcome.

Wrong view …pe… wrong liberation—

These, monks, are the ten courses of unwholesome action with a result of suffering.”

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.146 15. Ariyavagga Kaṇhamaggasutta (The Black Path) “Monks, there is a black path and a white path; a dark path and a bright path. And what, monks, is the black path? It is this: killing living beings, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view. This, monks, is called the black path. And what, monks, is the white path? It is this: abstaining from killing living beings, abstaining from taking what is not given, abstaining from sexual misconduct, abstaining from false speech, abstaining from divisive speech, abstaining from harsh speech, abstaining from idle chatter, non-covetousness, good will, and right view. This, monks, is called the white path. Monks, I do not see even one other path that leads to such great harm as this black path. Monks, I do not see even one other path that leads to such great benefit as this white path.”
“Monks, I will teach you the dark path and the bright path.
Listen to that... [as above] ...”

Wrong view … [and so on] … wrong liberation—
this, monks, is called the dark path.
“And what, bhikkhus, is the bright path?
Right view … right liberation—
this, bhikkhus, is called the bright path.”

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.152 15. Ariyavagga Bahulīkātabbasutta (The Discourse on What Should Be Cultivated) "Bhikkhus, there are these ten things that should be cultivated. What ten? (1) Loving-kindness should be cultivated; by cultivating it, one comes to possess much merit. (2) Compassion should be cultivated; by cultivating it, one comes to possess much merit. (3) Sympathetic joy should be cultivated; by cultivating it, one comes to possess much merit. (4) Equanimity should be cultivated; by cultivating it, one comes to possess much merit. (5) The perception of impermanence should be cultivated; by cultivating it, one comes to possess much merit. (6) The perception of non-self in what is impermanent should be cultivated; by cultivating it, one comes to possess much merit. (7) The perception of the repulsiveness of food should be cultivated; by cultivating it, one comes to possess much merit. (8) The perception of non-delight in the entire world should be cultivated; by cultivating it, one comes to possess much merit. (9) The perception of the danger in all conditioned phenomena should be cultivated; by cultivating it, one comes to possess much merit. (10) The perception of the liberation of the mind through the cessation of craving should be cultivated; by cultivating it, one comes to possess much merit. These, bhikkhus, are the ten things that should be cultivated."

16. Puggalavagga Sevitabbasutta (AN 10.155, PTS AN v 247) “Monks, there are these two kinds of persons to be cultivated. What two? The person who is to be cultivated and the person who is not to be cultivated. And what kind of person, monks, is not to be cultivated? Here, monks, someone is one who destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, and indulges in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence. This kind of person, monks, is not to be cultivated. And what kind of person, monks, is to be cultivated? Here, monks, someone does not destroy life, does not take what is not given, does not engage in sexual misconduct, does not speak falsely, and does not indulge in liquor, wine, and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence. This kind of person, monks, is to be cultivated. These, monks, are the two kinds of persons to be cultivated.”
“Bhikkhus, a person endowed with ten qualities should not be associated with. Which ten?

Monks, a person endowed with ten qualities should be associated with.
“By which ten?
He possesses right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration, right knowledge, and right liberation.
It is by possessing these ten qualities, monks, that a person should be associated with.”

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.156–166 16. Puggalavagga Bhajitabbādisutta (Discourse on Those to be Frequented, etc. “Monks, there are these ten kinds of persons to be frequented. What ten? The person who is like a lotus flower; the person who is like a blue lotus flower; the person who is like a jasmine flower; the person who is like a red lotus flower; the person who is like a white lotus flower; the person who is like a sandalwood tree; the person who is like a fig tree; the person who is like a banyan tree; the person who is like a *nigrodha* tree; and the person who is like a *pāricchattaka* tree. And how, monks, is one a person like a lotus flower?

Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of loving-kindness toward all beings, free from enmity and ill will, vast, exalted, measureless, and well-cultivated. Yet he does not possess the noble wisdom that leads to the complete destruction of suffering. This, monks, is called a person like a lotus flower. And how, monks, is one a person like a blue lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of compassion toward all beings... [as above] ...yet he does not possess the noble wisdom that leads to the complete destruction of suffering. This, monks, is called a person like a blue lotus flower. And how, monks, is one a person like a jasmine flower? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of sympathetic joy toward all beings... [as above] ...yet he does not possess the noble wisdom that leads to the complete destruction of suffering. This, monks, is called a person like a jasmine flower. And how, monks, is one a person like a red lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of equanimity toward all beings... [as above] ...yet he does not possess the noble wisdom that leads to the complete destruction of suffering. This, monks, is called a person like a red lotus flower. And how, monks, is one a person like a white lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of loving-kindness toward all beings... [as above] ...and he possesses the noble wisdom that leads to the complete destruction of suffering. This, monks, is called a person like a white lotus flower. And how, monks, is one a person like a sandalwood tree? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of loving-kindness toward all beings... [as above] ...and he possesses the noble wisdom that leads to the complete destruction of suffering. Furthermore, he teaches the Dhamma to others as he has seen it, as he has realized it, for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans. Just as the sandalwood tree of the Himalayas is cool, fragrant, and delightful, so too, monks, this person is cool, fragrant, and delightful. This, monks, is called a person like a sandalwood tree. And how, monks, is one a person like a fig tree? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of loving-kindness toward all beings... [as above] ...and he possesses the noble wisdom that leads to the complete destruction of suffering. Furthermore, he teaches the Dhamma to others as he has seen it, as he has realized it, for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans. Just as the fig tree is cool, fragrant, and delightful, so too, monks, this person is cool, fragrant, and delightful. This, monks, is called a person like a fig tree. Furthermore, he teaches the Dhamma to others as he has seen it, as he has realized it, for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans. Just as the banyan tree is cool, fragrant, and delightful, so too, monks, this person is cool, fragrant, and delightful. This, monks, is called a person like a banyan tree. And how, monks, is one a person like a *nigrodha* tree? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of loving-kindness toward all beings... [as above] ...and he possesses the noble wisdom that leads to the complete destruction of suffering. Furthermore, he teaches the Dhamma to others as he has seen it, as he has realized it, for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans. Just as the *nigrodha* tree is cool, fragrant, and delightful, so too, monks, this person is cool, fragrant, and delightful. This, monks, is called a person like a *nigrodha* tree. [as above] ...and he possesses the noble wisdom that leads to the complete destruction of suffering. Furthermore, he teaches the Dhamma to others as he has seen it, as he has realized it, for the welfare of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans. Just as the *pāricchattaka* tree in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven is cool, fragrant, and delightful, so too, monks, this person is cool, fragrant, and delightful. This, monks, is called a person like a *pāricchattaka* tree. These, monks, are the ten kinds of persons to be frequented.”

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.167 17. The Chapter on Jāṇussoṇi The Discourse on the Brahmin’s Descent “Brahmins, there are these ten grounds for a brahmin’s descent. What ten? (1) Here, brahmins, a brahmin is one who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness, yet he still maintains a fire-sacrifice, offers oblations, and performs the rites of the sacrificial post. This is the first ground for a brahmin’s descent. (2) Again, brahmins, a brahmin has gone forth from the household life into homelessness, but he still teaches the Vedas, recites the Vedas, and explains the Vedas. This is the second ground for a brahmin’s descent. (3) Again, brahmins, a brahmin has gone forth from the household life into homelessness, but he still accepts gifts from others, receives offerings, and enjoys alms. This is the third ground for a brahmin’s descent. (4) Again, brahmins, a brahmin has gone forth from the household life into homelessness, but he still lives in dependence upon a teacher, remains under the tutelage of a teacher, and serves his teacher. This is the fourth ground for a brahmin’s descent. (5) Again, brahmins, a brahmin has gone forth from the household life into homelessness, but he still lives in dependence upon a preceptor, remains under the tutelage of a preceptor, and serves his preceptor. This is the fifth ground for a brahmin’s descent. (6) Again, brahmins, a brahmin has gone forth from the household life into homelessness, but he still lives in dependence upon a fellow student, remains under the tutelage of a fellow student, and serves his fellow student. This is the sixth ground for a brahmin’s descent. (7) Again, brahmins, a brahmin has gone forth from the household life into homelessness, but he still lives in dependence upon a pupil, remains under the tutelage of a pupil, and serves his pupil. This is the seventh ground for a brahmin’s descent. (8) Again, brahmins, a brahmin has gone forth from the household life into homelessness, but he still lives in dependence upon a disciple, remains under the tutelage of a disciple, and serves his disciple. This is the eighth ground for a brahmin’s descent. (9) Again, brahmins, a brahmin has gone forth from the household life into homelessness, but he still lives in dependence upon a patron, remains under the tutelage of a patron, and serves his patron. This is the ninth ground for a brahmin’s descent. (10) Again, brahmins, a brahmin has gone forth from the household life into homelessness, but he still lives in dependence upon a benefactor, remains under the tutelage of a benefactor, and serves his benefactor. This is the tenth ground for a brahmin’s descent. These, brahmins, are the ten grounds for a brahmin’s descent.”

Now at that time, on the Uposatha day, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi had washed his head, put on a pair of new linen garments, and stood to one side not far from the Blessed One, holding a handful of wet kusa grass.
The Blessed One saw the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi standing to one side on the Uposatha day, having washed his head, wearing a pair of new linen garments, and holding a handful of wet kusa grass.
Having seen him, he said this to the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi:
“Why is it, brahmin, that on this Uposatha day you have washed your head, put on a new pair of linen garments, and stand to one side carrying a handful of fresh kusa grass?
What has happened today at the brahmin household?”
“Master Gotama, today is the Paccorohaṇī festival for the brahmin clan.
“But how, brahmin, is the Paccorohaṇī festival observed by the brahmins?
“In this case, Master Gotama, on that very Uposatha day, the brahmins wash their heads, put on a pair of new linen garments, and with wet hair—”
Having smeared the ground with cow dung and spread it over with green *kuśa* grass,
they prepare their beds between the sea-shore and the fire-hall.
Rising three times during that night, they pay homage to the fire with palms joined:
“Let us descend, sir! Let us descend, sir! they said.
And with much ghee, oil, and butter, they gratified the fire.
And when that night had passed, they gratified the brahmins with choice hard food and soft food.
“In this way, Master Gotama, the brahmins perform the Paccorohaṇī festival.
“Brahmin, the Paccorohaṇī of the brahmins is one thing, but the Paccorohaṇī in the Noble One’s discipline is quite another.
“But how, Master Gotama, is the Paccorohaṇī performed in the Noble One’s discipline?”
“It would be well, venerable Gotama, if you would teach me the Dhamma in such a way that there is a ‘descent’ (paccorohaṇī) within the discipline of the Noble One.
“In that case, brahmin, listen and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, sir,” the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“In this case, brahmin, a noble disciple reflects thus:
‘The result of taking life is evil, both in the present life and in future lives.’”
Having reflected thus, he abandons the taking of life;
he descends from the taking of life.
… “The result of taking what is not given is indeed evil—”
“both in this very life and in future lives.
Having reflected thus, he abandons taking what is not given;
he descends from taking what is not given.
‘... The result of sexual misconduct is indeed evil, both in this very life and in future lives.
Having reflected thus, he abandons sexual misconduct.
He descends from sexual misconduct.
… “False speech has a bad result,
both in this very life and in future lives.”
Having reflected thus, he abandons false speech;
he descends from false speech.
… “Indeed, malicious speech has a wicked result—”
“both in this very life and in future states.
Having reflected thus, he abandons malicious speech and descends from the practice of malicious speech.
‘Harsh speech indeed has an evil result,
both in this very life and in future lives.
Having reflected thus, he abandons harsh speech.
One descends from harsh speech...
[thinking]: "The result of frivolous chatter is evil, both in this very life and in the future."
Having reflected thus, he abandons idle chatter;
he descends from idle chatter.
… “Indeed, covetousness has an evil result—”
"both in this very life and in future lives.
Having reflected thus, he abandons covetousness and descends from covetousness.
‘The result of ill will is indeed evil,
both in this very life and in the future.
Having reflected thus, he abandons ill will.
One descends from ill will... [thinking]:
"The result of wrong view is indeed evil, both in this very life and in the future."
Having reflected thus, one abandons wrong view and descends from wrong view.
In this way, brahmin, there is the descent in the discipline of the Noble One.”
“Master Gotama, the descent ceremony (*paccorohaṇī*) of the brahmins is one thing, whereas the descent ceremony in the Noble One’s discipline is quite another.
Compared to this descent ceremony in the Noble One’s discipline, Master Gotama, the brahmins’ descent ceremony does not equal even a sixteenth part.
Excellent, Master Gotama! … [as before] …”
“May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
First.

17. Jāṇussoṇivagga Ariyapaccorohaṇīsutta (AN 10.168, PTS AN v 251) “Brahmin, there is this noble descent. Listen to it and attend closely; I shall speak. “Yes, sir,” the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Brahmin, when a noble disciple possesses four qualities, he is one who has descended from the noble lineage. What four? Here, brahmin, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. He possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—untorn, unbroken, unspotted, unsplattered, liberating, praised by the wise, untarnished, leading to concentration. When a noble disciple possesses these four qualities, brahmin, he is one who has descended from the noble lineage. Just as, brahmin, when a king’s frontier fortress is well-provisioned with four things, it is able to withstand for a long time any enemy host; that is, it is well-provisioned with abundant grain, with abundant fodder for draft animals, with abundant wealth and grain, and with many skilled and competent artisans; so too, brahmin, when a noble disciple possesses these four qualities, he is one who has descended from the noble lineage. When a noble disciple has descended from the noble lineage, he is capable of breaking through the five lower fetters on his own, without assistance, and realizing the state of non-returning. Or he is capable of breaking through the five lower fetters with assistance, and realizing the state of non-returning. Or he is capable of breaking through the five lower fetters with the assistance of others, and realizing the state of non-returning. Or he is capable of breaking through the five lower fetters with the assistance of others, and realizing the state of once-returning. Or he is capable of breaking through the five lower fetters with the assistance of others, and realizing the state of stream-entry. Therefore, brahmin, you should train yourself thus: ‘We will possess confirmed confidence in the Buddha… confirmed confidence in the Dhamma… confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha… we will possess the virtues dear to the noble ones. It is in such a way, brahmin, that you should train yourself. When this was said, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama!... “Indeed, malicious speech has an evil result... [as before] ...
one descends from malicious speech. ...

He descends from harsh speech.
… “The result of frivolous chatter is evil … [he] descends from frivolous chatter.”
‘Covetousness indeed has an evil result... [as before] ... one descends from covetousness. ...

He descends from ill will... [thinking:
"The result of wrong view is indeed evil, both in this very life and in the future.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.169 17. The Chapter on Jāṇussoṇi The Discourse to Saṅgārava At Sāvatthī. Then the brahmin Saṅgārava approached the Blessed One and, having approached, exchanged greetings with him.

When they had concluded their courteous greetings and amiable conversation, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, he said to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama, I have heard this: ‘The ascetic Gotama does not acknowledge any recluse or brahmin as his equal or his superior. Do those who say this speak truthfully, or do they speak falsely? “Brahmin, those who say this do not speak truthfully; they speak falsely. For I acknowledge a recluse or a brahmin who is my equal or my superior. “But, Master Gotama, who is that recluse or brahmin whom you acknowledge as your equal or your superior? “There is, brahmin, the Tathāgata, an arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha. He is one who has fully awakened to things unheard before. That is the recluse or brahmin whom I acknowledge as my equal or my superior. “But, Master Gotama, what is the reason for your saying this? What is the basis for your claim? “Brahmin, the Tathāgata is one who has abandoned the underlying tendency to lust, the underlying tendency to aversion, and the underlying tendency to delusion, both in this very life and in regard to future states of existence. That is the reason, brahmin, why I say this; that is the basis for my claim. When this was said, the brahmin Saṅgārava said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, Master Gotama! Magnificent, Master Gotama! Just as one might set upright what was overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has Master Gotama explained the Dhamma in various ways. I go to Master Gotama for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life shall last.”
(AN 10.169, PTS AN v 252) Then the brahmin Saṅgārava approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the brahmin Saṅgārava said this to the Blessed One:
“Master Gotama, what is the near shore? What is the far shore?
“Brahmin, the destruction of life is the near shore; abstention from the destruction of life is the far shore.
Taking what is not given is the near shore; abstention from taking what is not given is the far shore.”
Sexual misconduct is this shore; abstention from sexual misconduct is the further shore.
False speech is this shore; abstention from false speech is the further shore.
Divisive speech is this shore; abstention from divisive speech is the further shore.
Harsh speech is this shore; abstention from harsh speech is the further shore.
Frivolous chatter is this shore; abstention from frivolous chatter is the further shore.
Covetousness is this shore; non-covetousness is the further shore.
Ill will is this shore; non-ill will is the further shore.
Wrong view is this shore; right view is the further shore.
This, brahmin, is "this shore," and this is "the further shore."
Few among humans are those people who go to the further shore;
but this other generation—
They merely run along the bank.
But those who follow the Dhamma in accordance with the Dhamma in the well-expounded teaching—
Those people will cross over the realm of Death, so difficult to transcend,
having utterly abandoned the dark Dhamma.
The wise person should cultivate purity,
having gone from home to homelessness,
to a secluded place that is difficult to reach.
Therein one should seek delight,
having abandoned sensual pleasures and possessing nothing;
one should purify oneself.
The wise one, from the defilements of the mind—
those whose minds are rightly well-developed in the factors of enlightenment.
Those who delight in the relinquishing of grasping, being without clinging—
having exhausted the taints, they are radiant.
“They have attained final nibbāna in the world.

Jāṇussoṇivagga (The Chapter on Jāṇussoṇi)
Paṭhamadhammasutta:
“Bhikkhus, unrighteousness should be understood as harmful, and the beneficial should be understood.”
The Dhamma must be understood, as must the goal.

Having understood what is non-Dhamma and what is disadvantageous, and having understood what is Dhamma and what is beneficial, one should practice in accordance with the Dhamma and in accordance with the goal.
And what, monks, is non-Dhamma and disadvantageous?
“Bhikkhus, killing living beings, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, malicious speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, covetousness, ill will,
and wrong view— this, bhikkhus, is called both unrighteousness and harmful.
And what, bhikkhus, is righteousness and beneficial?”
Abstaining from taking life, abstaining from taking what is not given, abstaining from sexual misconduct,
abstaining from false speech, abstaining from malicious speech, abstaining from harsh speech, abstaining from idle chatter, non-covetousness,
non-ill will, and right view.
This, monks, is called both the Dhamma and the benefit.
“Monks, what is non-Dhamma and what is disadvantageous should be understood;
and what is Dhamma and what is beneficial should be understood.”

“Monks, what is non-Dhamma must be understood … [and so on] … and one should practice accordingly.
And what, friends, is non-Dhamma? And what is Dhamma?”
And what is the harmful, and what is the beneficial?
Friend, the taking of life is unrighteous;
abstaining from the taking of life is righteous.
And whatever numerous evil, unwholesome states arise conditioned by the destruction of life—this is harm;
and whatever numerous wholesome states reach fulfillment through development conditioned by abstaining from the destruction of life—this is benefit.
Taking what is not given, friends, is contrary to the Dhamma.
Abstaining from taking what is not given is a wholesome quality (*dhamma*);
the many evil, unwholesome qualities that arise conditioned by taking what is not given are the disadvantage;
and the many wholesome qualities that reach fulfillment through development conditioned by abstaining from taking what is not given are the benefit.
"Friends, sexual misconduct is unrighteousness;
abstaining from sexual misconduct is righteousness.
And those numerous evil, unwholesome states that arise conditioned by sexual misconduct—this is harm."
And because of the condition of abstaining from sexual misconduct, numerous wholesome states reach fulfillment through development; this is the benefit.
False speech, friends, is unrighteousness;
abstaining from false speech is righteousness.
And whatever numerous evil, unwholesome states arise conditioned by false speech—this is harm.
And whatever numerous wholesome states reach fulfillment through development conditioned by abstaining from false speech—this is benefit.
Malicious speech, friends, is unrighteousness.
Abstaining from malicious speech is the Dhamma.
Those numerous evil, unwholesome states that arise conditioned by malicious speech are the disadvantage.
And those numerous wholesome states that reach fulfillment through development, conditioned by abstaining from malicious speech, are the benefit.
Harsh speech, friends, is unrighteousness;
abstaining from harsh speech is righteousness;
and the many evil, unwholesome states that arise conditioned by harsh speech—this is harm.
And by reason of abstaining from harsh speech, numerous wholesome states reach fulfillment through development; this is the benefit.
Idle chatter, friends, is unrighteousness (adhamma);
abstaining from idle chatter is righteousness (dhamma).
And those numerous evil, unwholesome states that arise conditioned by idle chatter—this is disadvantage.
But conditioned by abstaining from idle chatter, numerous wholesome states reach fulfillment through development—this is advantage.
Covetousness, friends, is unrighteousness;
Non-covetousness is a wholesome state (*dhamma*);
the many evil, unwholesome states that arise conditioned by covetousness are harmful;
and the many wholesome states that reach fulfillment through development conditioned by non-covetousness are beneficial.
Ill will, friends, is unrighteousness;
non-ill will is righteousness.
And those numerous evil, unwholesome states that arise conditioned by ill will—this is harm.
And because of non-ill will, numerous wholesome states reach fulfillment through development: this is the benefit.
Wrong view, friends, is unrighteousness;
right view is righteousness.
And whatever numerous evil, unwholesome states arise with wrong view as their condition—this is harm.
And whatever numerous wholesome states reach fulfillment through development with right view as their condition—this is benefit.
“Friends, that the Blessed One, having given a brief summary and without explaining the meaning in detail, rose from his seat and entered his dwelling—”
“Bhikkhus, unrighteousness is to be understood … [as before] … and one should practice accordingly. This,
friends, is how I understand in detail the meaning of this brief summary taught by the Blessed One, which had not been explained in detail.
"But if you wish, friends, you should approach the Blessed One himself and ask him about this matter.
You should remember it exactly as the Blessed One explains it to you.
"Very well, friend," those bhikkhus, having rejoiced and approved of the Venerable Mahākaccāna’s words, [departed].
Rising from their seats, they approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.

"Venerable sir, when the Blessed One had given us a brief summary and, without analyzing the meaning in detail, rose from his seat and entered his dwelling:..."
“Bhikkhus, what is non-Dhamma should be understood … [as before] … and one should practice accordingly.

“Friends, having given us this brief summary without explaining the meaning in detail, the Blessed One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling, saying:
‘Monks, what is non-Dhamma should be understood...
[and so on] ...and one should practice accordingly.’”
"Who might be able to analyze in detail the meaning of this brief summary taught by the Blessed One, the meaning which has not yet been analyzed?
Then, venerable sir, it occurred to us:
"This venerable Mahākaccāna is indeed praised by the Teacher and esteemed by his wise fellow-celibates."
“The Venerable Mahākaccāna is capable of analyzing in detail the meaning of this brief summary taught by the Blessed One, the meaning of which has not yet been analyzed in detail.

We shall bear it in mind according as the Venerable Mahākaccāna explains it to us.”
“Then, venerable sir, we approached the Venerable Mahākaccāna and, having approached him, asked the Venerable Mahākaccāna about this matter.

“Excellent, excellent, monks!”

Tatiyaadhammasutta: “Bhikkhus,
what is non-Dhamma and what is Dhamma should be understood.
Both the harmful and the beneficial should be understood.

Having understood what is non-Dhamma and what is Dhamma, and having understood what is harmful and what is beneficial, one should practice in accordance with the Dhamma and in accordance with the beneficial.
And what, monks, is non-Dhamma? And what is Dhamma?
And what is the harmful, and what is the beneficial?
Monks, the taking of life is unrighteous;
abstaining from the taking of life is righteous.
And whatever numerous evil, unwholesome states arise conditioned by the destruction of life—this is harm.
But conditioned by abstaining from the destruction of life, numerous wholesome states reach fulfillment through development—this is benefit.
Taking what is not given, monks, is contrary to the Dhamma.
Abstaining from taking what is not given is Dhamma...
Sexual misconduct, bhikkhus, is non-Dhamma;
abstaining from sexual misconduct is Dhamma...
“Bhikkhus, false speech is non-Dhamma;
abstention from false speech is Dhamma… Malicious speech, bhikkhus, is non-Dhamma;”
Abstaining from malicious speech is Dhamma...
Harsh speech, monks, is non-Dhamma;
abstaining from harsh speech is Dhamma...
Idle chatter, monks, is non-Dhamma;
abstention from idle chatter is Dhamma… Covetousness, monks, is non-Dhamma;
Non-covetousness is Dhamma...
Ill will, monks, is non-Dhamma;
non-ill will is Dhamma...
"Monks, wrong view is non-Dhamma;
right view is Dhamma.
And those numerous evil, unwholesome states that arise conditioned by wrong view—this is disadvantage."
And with right view as condition, numerous wholesome states reach fulfillment by development: this is the meaning.
“Monks, what is non-Dhamma and what is Dhamma should be understood;
what is harmful and what is beneficial should be understood.”

“Having understood what is non-Dhamma and what is Dhamma, having understood what is harmful and what is beneficial, one should practice in accordance with the Dhamma and in accordance with what is beneficial.
This is why it was said. The seventh [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.174 17. Jāṇussoṇivagga Kammanidānasutta (The Discourse on the Source of Kamma) “Bhikkhus, there are these three sources of kamma. What three? Kamma born of greed, kamma born of hatred, and kamma born of delusion. These, bhikkhus, are the three sources of kamma. [The Blessed One said: “Bhikkhus, there are these three roots of the unwholesome. What three? Greed is a root of the unwholesome, hatred is a root of the unwholesome, and delusion is a root of the unwholesome. And what, bhikkhus, is the result of kamma born of greed? There is the case where a certain person, overcome with greed, devoid of shame and compunction, takes the life of a living being; he steals; he engages in sexual misconduct; he tells a deliberate lie; he encourages others to take the life of a living being; he encourages others to steal; he encourages others to engage in sexual misconduct; he encourages others to tell a deliberate lie.

This person, having performed and accumulated such kamma—whether as a wheel-turning monarch, a great king, a deva of the heaven of the Thirty-three, a Yāma deva, a Tusita deva, a Nimmanarati deva, a Paranimmitavasavatti deva, a Brahmā, or a human being—will experience the result of that kamma.
