“Bhikkhus, I say that the destruction of life is threefold:
it has greed as its cause, it has hatred as its cause, and it has delusion as its cause.”
“Monks, I say that taking what is not given is threefold:
having greed as its cause, having hatred as its cause, and having delusion as its cause.
Monks, I say that sexual misconduct is threefold:”
It is caused by greed, caused by hatred, and caused by delusion.
Monks, I say that false speech is also threefold:
caused by greed, caused by hatred, and caused by delusion.
“Monks, I declare that divisive speech is threefold:
it has greed as its cause, it has hatred as its cause, and it has delusion as its cause.
Monks, I declare that harsh speech is threefold.”
It is caused by greed, caused by hatred, and caused by delusion.
Monks, I say that idle chatter is also threefold:
it is caused by greed, caused by hatred, and caused by delusion.
“Monks, I say that covetousness is threefold:
it has greed as its cause, it has hatred as its cause, and it has delusion as its cause.
Monks, I say that ill will is also threefold.”
It is caused by greed, caused by hatred, and caused by delusion.
Monks, I say that wrong view is also threefold:
it is caused by greed, caused by hatred, and caused by delusion.
“Thus, monks, greed is the source and origin of kamma; hatred is the source and origin of kamma; delusion is the source and origin of kamma.

With the destruction of greed, there is the destruction of the source of kamma; with the destruction of hatred, there is the destruction of the source of kamma; with the destruction of delusion, there is the destruction of the source of kamma. This was the eighth [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.175 17. Jāṇussoṇivagga Parikkamana Sutta: The Way Around “Bhikkhus, there are these five ways around that are conducive to the non-arising of unarisen taints, and to the subsiding of arisen taints. What five?

Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. This is the first way around that is conducive to the non-arising of unarisen taints, and to the subsiding of arisen taints. Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... the mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. This is the fourth way around that is conducive to the non-arising of unarisen taints, and to the subsiding of arisen taints. Furthermore, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells as one who has fully understood the Dhamma, who has penetrated the Dhamma with wisdom, who has crossed over doubt, who has gone beyond perplexity, who has attained confidence, and who has become independent of others in the Teacher’s Dispensation. This is the fifth way around that is conducive to the non-arising of unarisen taints, and to the subsiding of arisen taints. These, bhikkhus, are the five ways around that are conducive to the non-arising of unarisen taints, and to the subsiding of arisen taints.”
“Monks, this Dhamma is for one who practices with circumspection; this Dhamma is not for one who does not practice with circumspection.
And how, monks, is this Dhamma for one who practices with circumspection, and not for one who does not practice with circumspection?”
“Monks, for one who takes life, abstaining from taking life is the means of purification.
Monks, for one who takes what is not given, abstaining from taking what is not given is the means of purification.
Monks, for one who engages in sexual misconduct, abstaining from sexual misconduct is the means of purification.”
“Monks, for one who speaks falsehood, abstaining from false speech is the means of purification.
Monks, for one who speaks maliciously, abstaining from malicious speech is the means of purification.
Monks, for one who speaks harshly, abstaining from harsh speech is the means of purification.”
“Monks, for one who engages in idle chatter, abstaining from idle chatter is the means of purification.
For one who is covetous, non-covetousness is the means of purification.
For one with a mind of ill will, non-ill will is the means of purification.”
“Bhikkhus, for one of wrong view, right view is the means of escape.
It is in this way, bhikkhus, that this Dhamma has a means of escape; this Dhamma is not without a means of escape. Thus was the ninth [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.176 17. Jāṇussoṇivagga Cundasutta Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these ten qualities of a true man. What ten? (1) Here, a true man does not deceive the Tathāgata; he does not deceive the Dhamma; he does not deceive the Saṅgha; he does not deceive a person who is an arahant; he does not deceive a person who is a non-returner; he does not deceive a person who is a once-returner; he does not deceive a person who is a stream-enterer; he does not deceive a person who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry; he does not deceive a person who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of once-returning; and he does not deceive a person who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning. These, bhikkhus, are the ten qualities of a true man. If, bhikkhus, a true man possesses even one of these ten qualities of a true man, he is still called a ‘true man’ by the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. [The Buddha then spoke further: “Bhikkhus, there are these ten qualities of a true man. What ten? (1) Here, a true man does not deceive the Tathāgata; he does not deceive the Dhamma; he does not deceive the Saṅgha; he does not deceive a person who is an arahant; he does not deceive a person who is a non-returner; he does not deceive a person who is a once-returner; he does not deceive a person who is a stream-enterer; he does not deceive a person who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry; he does not deceive a person who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of once-returning; and he does not deceive a person who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of non-returning. These, bhikkhus, are the ten qualities of a true man. If, bhikkhus, a true man possesses even one of these ten qualities of a true man, he is still called a ‘true man’ by the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. (AN 10.176, PTS AN v 263) Thus have I heard—
on one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Pāvā in Cunda the smith’s mango grove.
Then Cunda the smith approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As Cunda the smith was sitting there, the Blessed One said this to him:
"Cunda, whose purifications do you approve of?

"Bhante, the brahmins of the western lands—those who carry water-pots, wear garlands of water-moss, tend the sacrificial fire, and descend into the water—proclaim their purifications; it is these purifications that I approve of."
“But how, Cunda, do the brahmins of the western lands—carrying water-pots, wearing garlands of water-moss, tending the sacred fire, and bathing in water—proclaim their purifications?
“In this case, venerable sir, the brahmins of the western lands carry water-pots, wear garlands of water-moss, tend the sacred fire, and bathe in water. They exhort a disciple thus:
‘Come, good man! Rising from your bed at the very break of dawn, you should touch the earth;’”
If you do not touch the earth, you should touch moist cow dung;
if you do not touch moist cow dung, you should touch green grass;
if you do not touch green grass, you should tend the sacrificial fire.
‘If you do not tend the fire, you should pay homage to the sun with palms joined;
if you do not pay homage to the sun with palms joined, you should descend into the water three times a day.

Thus, Bhante, the brahmins of the western lands—carrying water-pots, wearing garlands of water-moss, tending the fire, and descending into the water—proclaim their purifications. I approve of their purifications.”

“Cunda, the brahmins of the western lands who carry water-pots, wear garlands of water-moss, tend the sacred fire, and descend into the water prescribe purifications in one way; however, in the discipline of the Noble One, purification is quite different.
“But in what way, Bhante, is there purification in the discipline of the Noble One?
It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma as to how purification comes about in the discipline of the Noble One.”
“In that case, Cunda, listen and pay close attention; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” Cunda the smith replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Cunda, there are three kinds of impurity by way of body;
four kinds of impurity by way of speech;
and three kinds of impurity by way of mind.”
And how, Cunda, is there threefold impurity of body?
Here, Cunda, someone is a destroyer of life: cruel, bloody-handed, intent on killing and striking, lacking compassion for all living beings.
He is a taker of what is not given; he takes by way of theft what belongs to another, the property and belongings of others, whether in a village or in the wilderness.

He engages in sexual misconduct. He has intercourse with women who are protected by their mother, protected by their father, protected by both parents, protected by their brother, protected by their sister, protected by their relatives, protected by their clan, protected by Dhamma, those who have a husband, those who are under threat of punishment, and even those who are merely surrounded by a garland of flowers.
He commits misconduct with such women as these.
In this way, Cunda, there is threefold impurity of body.
And how, Cunda, is there fourfold impurity of speech?
Here, Cunda, someone is a speaker of falsehood. Whether in an assembly, in a gathering, or in the midst of kinsmen...
Whether having entered the midst of a public assembly or the royal court, being summoned and questioned as a witness:
"Come, good man, speak what you know," he says, "I know" when he does not know, or he says, "I do not know" when he knows;
he says, "I see" when he has not seen, or he says, "I do not see" when he has seen. Thus, for his own sake or for the sake of another...
Or for the sake of some small material gain, he speaks a deliberate lie.
He is a speaker of divisive speech: having heard something here, he reports it there for the purpose of dividing these people;

or having heard something there, he reports it here for the purpose of dividing those people. Thus, he is one who divides those who are united, or who incites those who are divided; he delights in discord.
He delights in factions, rejoices in factions, and speaks words that create factions.
He is harsh in speech. He utters such speech as is cutting, rough, bitter, insulting to others, provocative of anger, and conducive to lack of concentration. He is a frivolous talker;

he speaks at the wrong time, speaks what is untrue, speaks what is useless, speaks according to what is not Dhamma, and speaks according to what is not Vinaya. He utters speech that is worthless, spoken at the wrong time, without foundation, indefinite, unbeneficial, and not connected with the goal.
In this way, Cunda, there is fourfold impurity of speech.
And how, Cunda, is there threefold impurity of mind?
Here, Cunda, a certain person is covetous; he covets the wealth and possessions of others, thinking: "O, that what belongs to another were mine!"
He has a mind of ill will and a corrupt intention, thinking: “May these beings be slain, or bound, or cut off, or destroyed, or may they not exist at all.
He holds wrong view and possesses a perverted perspective, thinking:
“There is no giving, there is no sacrifice, there is no offering; there is no fruit or result of deeds well done or ill done.”
‘There is no result of kamma; there is no this world, no other world; there is no mother, no father;

there are no beings who are spontaneously born; there are in the world no ascetics or brahmins who have attained the right path and practiced rightly, who having realized this world and the other world for themselves by direct knowledge, make them known to others.’”
In this way, Cunda, there is threefold impurity by means of the mind.
These, Cunda, are the ten courses of unwholesome action.
One who is possessed of these ten courses of unwholesome action is impure even if he rises early from his bed and touches the earth; and even if he does not touch the earth, he is still impure.
Even if one touches fresh cow dung, one is indeed impure; even if one does not touch fresh cow dung, one is indeed impure.
Even if one touches green grass, one is indeed impure; even if one does not touch green grass, one is indeed impure.
Even if one tends the fire, one is indeed impure; even if one does not tend the fire, one is indeed impure.
Even if one pays homage to the sun with palms joined, one remains impure; even if one does not pay homage to the sun with palms joined, one remains impure.
Even if one enters the water three times each day and night, one remains impure; even if one does not enter the water three times each day and night, one remains impure. Why is that?
"Cunda, these ten unwholesome courses of action are indeed impure and causes of impurity.

Furthermore, Cunda, it is because of being possessed of these ten unwholesome courses of action that hell is made known, the animal realm is made known, the sphere of hungry ghosts is made known, or whatever other miserable destinations there may be.
Cunda, there is, however, threefold purity by way of the body."
There is fourfold purity of speech and threefold purity of mind. And how,
Cunda, is there threefold purity of body?

In this case, Cunda, a certain person, having abandoned the taking of life, abstains from taking life; he lays aside the rod and the weapon, and dwells conscientious, compassionate, sympathetic toward the welfare of all living beings.
Having abandoned taking what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given. Whatever belongs to another, whether in a village or in the wilderness, he does not take it by way of theft.
Having abandoned sexual misconduct, he abstains from sexual misconduct; that is, those women who are protected by their mother, protected by their father, [and so forth].

One does not engage in sexual intercourse with women protected by their mother, protected by their father, protected by their brother, protected by their sister, protected by their relatives, protected by their clan, protected by the Dhamma,
those who have a husband, those who are under threat of punishment, or even those who are merely encircled by a flower garland.
In this way, Cunda, there is purity of conduct in three ways through the body.
And how, Cunda, is there fourfold purity of speech?
Here, Cunda, someone, having abandoned false speech, abstains from false speech.
Whether in an assembly, in a group, in the midst of kinsmen, in the midst of a guild, or in the midst of a royal court, when summoned as a witness and questioned:
‘Come now, good man, say what you know. If he does not know, he says, ‘I do not know’; if he knows, he says, ‘I know.
If he has not seen, he says, ‘I have not seen’; if he has seen, he says, ‘I have seen.
Thus, whether for his own sake, for the sake of another, or for the sake of some small material gain, he does not speak a conscious lie.
Having abandoned malicious speech, he abstains from malicious speech.
He does not repeat elsewhere what he has heard here for the purpose of dividing those people, nor does he repeat here what he has heard elsewhere for the purpose of dividing these people.

Thus, he is a reconciler of those who are divided and a promoter of harmony among those who are united. Delighting in concord, rejoicing in concord, finding joy in concord, he speaks words that create concord.

Having abandoned harsh speech, he abstains from harsh speech. He speaks such words as are gentle, pleasing to the ear, endearing, heart-reaching, urbane, agreeable to many people, and dear to many people.
Having abandoned idle chatter, he abstains from idle chatter; he speaks at the proper time, speaks what is true, speaks what is beneficial, speaks on the Dhamma, and speaks on the Vinaya.
He is one who speaks with a foundation, at the right time, with reason, in a measured way, and connected to the goal.
In this way, Cunda, there is fourfold purity of speech.
And how, Cunda, is there threefold purity of mind?
Here, Cunda, someone is not covetous. He does not covet the wealth and possessions of others, thinking: "Oh, may what belongs to another be mine!"

He is one whose mind is uncorrupted and whose intentions are not malicious, thinking: "May these beings be free from enmity, free from affliction, free from distress, and may they maintain themselves in happiness.
He possesses right view and has an undistorted perspective, [thinking]:
"There is what is given, there is what is sacrificed, there is what is offered; there is the fruit and result of wholesome and unwholesome deeds."
‘There is kamma and its result; there is this world and the other world; there is mother and father; there are beings who are spontaneously reborn;

there are in the world ascetics and brahmins of right conduct and right practice who, having realized this world and the other world for themselves through direct knowledge, make them known to others.’”
In this way, Cunda, there is threefold purity of mind.
These, Cunda, are the ten courses of wholesome action.
One who is endowed with these ten courses of wholesome action, Cunda, is pure even if he rises early from his bed and touches the earth; he is pure even if he does not touch the earth.
If he touches fresh cow dung, he remains pure; if he does not touch fresh cow dung, he remains pure.
If he touches green grass, he remains pure; if he does not touch green grass, he remains pure.
If he tends the fire, he remains pure; if he does not tend the fire, he remains pure.
Even if one pays homage to the sun with palms joined, one remains pure; even if one does not pay homage to the sun with palms joined, one remains pure.
Even if one enters the water three times during the evening, one remains pure; even if one does not enter the water three times during the evening, one remains pure.
For what reason?
“Cunda, these ten courses of wholesome action are themselves pure and they bring about purity.
Moreover, Cunda, it is because of possessing these ten courses of wholesome action that gods are known, humans are known, and whatever other happy destinations there may be.
When this was said, Cunda the smith’s son said this to the Blessed One:
“Excellent, Bhante!
… [as before] … May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.
The tenth.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.177 17. Jāṇussoṇivagga Jāṇussoṇisutta (The Discourse to Jāṇussoṇi) At Sāvatthī. Then the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi approached the Blessed One and, having approached, exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their polite and amiable conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi said to the Blessed One: "Master Gotama, what is the cause and condition for the appearance of a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One? And how does the Dhamma become well-expounded by that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, so that it is visible here and now, timeless, inviting inspection, leading onward, to be realized by the wise, each for themselves? "Brahmin, when a Tathāgata appears in the world, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, he teaches the Dhamma for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true way, and for the realization of Nibbāna. That is the cause and condition for the appearance of a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One. It is in this way that the Dhamma becomes well-expounded by that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, so that it is visible here and now, timeless, inviting inspection, leading onward, to be realized by the wise, each for themselves. "But, Master Gotama, what is the cause and condition for the arising of a wheel-turning monarch? And how does a wheel-turning monarch appear in the world? "Brahmin, when a wheel-turning monarch arises in the world, he is a righteous king, a conqueror of the four quarters, who has established stability in his realm and possesses the seven treasures.

What seven? He possesses the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the steward-treasure, and the counselor-treasure as the seventh. He has more than a thousand sons who are brave, heroic, and victorious over enemy armies. He dwells conquering this earth, bounded by the ocean, not by the scourge of weapons, but by righteousness, bringing peace and security. That is the cause and condition for the arising of a wheel-turning monarch. It is in this way that a wheel-turning monarch appears in the world. "But, Master Gotama, what is the cause and condition for the arising of a universal monarch? And how does a universal monarch appear in the world? "Brahmin, when a universal monarch arises in the world, he is a righteous king, a conqueror of the four quarters, who has established stability in his realm and possesses the seven treasures. What seven? He possesses the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the steward-treasure, and the counselor-treasure as the seventh. He has more than a thousand sons who are brave, heroic, and victorious over enemy armies. He dwells conquering this earth, bounded by the ocean, not by the scourge of weapons, but by righteousness, bringing peace and security. That is the cause and condition for the arising of a universal monarch. It is in this way that a universal monarch appears in the world. "But, Master Gotama, what is the cause and condition for the arising of a great Brahmā? And how does a great Brahmā appear in the world? "Brahmin, when a great Brahmā arises in the world, he is a righteous being, a conqueror of the four quarters, who has established stability in his realm and possesses the seven treasures. What seven? He possesses the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the steward-treasure, and the counselor-treasure as the seventh. He has more than a thousand sons who are brave, heroic, and victorious over enemy armies. He dwells conquering this earth, bounded by the ocean, not by the scourge of weapons, but by righteousness, bringing peace and security. That is the cause and condition for the arising of a great Brahmā. It is in this way that a great Brahmā appears in the world. "But, Master Gotama, what is the cause and condition for the arising of a Great Man? And how does a Great Man appear in the world? "Brahmin, when a Great Man arises in the world, he is a righteous being, a conqueror of the four quarters, who has established stability in his realm and possesses the seven treasures. What seven? He possesses the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the steward-treasure, and the counselor-treasure as the seventh. He has more than a thousand sons who are brave, heroic, and victorious over enemy armies. He dwells conquering this earth, bounded by the ocean, not by the scourge of weapons, but by righteousness, bringing peace and security. That is the cause and condition for the arising of a Great Man. It is in this way that a Great Man appears in the world. "But, Master Gotama, what is the cause and condition for the arising of a Buddha? And how does a Buddha appear in the world? "Brahmin, when a Buddha arises in the world, he is a righteous being, a conqueror of the four quarters, who has established stability in his realm and possesses the seven treasures. What seven? He possesses the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the steward-treasure, and the counselor-treasure as the seventh. He has more than a thousand sons who are brave, heroic, and victorious over enemy armies. He dwells conquering this earth, bounded by the ocean, not by the scourge of weapons, but by righteousness, bringing peace and security. That is the cause and condition for the arising of a Buddha. It is in this way that a Buddha appears in the world. "But, Master Gotama, what is the cause and condition for the arising of a Wheel-Turning Monarch? And how does a Wheel-Turning Monarch appear in the world? "Brahmin, when a Wheel-Turning Monarch arises in the world, he is a righteous king, a conqueror of the four quarters, who has established stability in his realm and possesses the seven treasures. What seven? He possesses the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the steward-treasure, and the counselor-treasure as the seventh. He has more than a thousand sons who are brave, heroic, and victorious over enemy armies. He dwells conquering this earth, bounded by the ocean, not by the scourge of weapons, but by righteousness, bringing peace and security. That is the cause and condition for the arising of a Wheel-Turning Monarch. It is in this way that a Wheel-Turning Monarch appears in the world. "But, Master Gotama, what is the cause and condition for the arising of a Universal Monarch? And how does a Universal Monarch appear in the world? "Brahmin, when a Universal Monarch arises in the world, he is a righteous king, a conqueror of the four quarters, who has established stability in his realm and possesses the seven treasures. What seven? He possesses the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the steward-treasure, and the counselor-treasure as the seventh. He has more than a thousand sons who are brave, heroic, and victorious over enemy armies. He dwells conquering this earth, bounded by the ocean, not by the scourge of weapons, but by righteousness, bringing peace and security. That is the cause and condition for the arising of a Universal Monarch. It is in this way that a Universal Monarch appears in the world. "But, Master Gotama, what is the cause and condition for the arising of a Great Brahmā? And how does a Great Brahmā appear in the world? "Brahmin, when a Great Brahmā arises in the world, he is a righteous being, a conqueror of the four quarters, who has established stability in his realm and possesses the seven treasures. What seven? He possesses the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the steward-treasure, and the counselor-treasure as the seventh. He has more than a thousand sons who are brave, heroic, and victorious over enemy armies. He dwells conquering this earth, bounded by the ocean, not by the scourge of weapons, but by righteousness, bringing peace and security. That is the cause and condition for the arising of a Great Brahmā. It is in this way that a Great Brahmā appears in the world."
(AN 10.177, PTS AN v 269) Then the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi said this to the Blessed One:
“Master Gotama, we are indeed called brahmins.
We give gifts and perform acts of faith, thinking:
‘May this gift benefit our deceased relatives and kinsmen; may our deceased relatives and kinsmen partake of this gift.’”
“Master Gotama, does that gift benefit the deceased relatives and kin?
Do those deceased relatives and kin enjoy that gift?
“It benefits them, brahmin, when it is given in the right place, not when it is given in the wrong place.”
“But what, Master Gotama, is the possible, and what is the impossible? “Here, brahmin,
a certain person destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsehood,
speaks maliciously, speaks harshly, indulges in idle chatter, and is covetous.”
He is full of ill will and holds wrong view.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he reappears in hell.
He subsists there and remains there on whatever food the beings in hell consume.
This too, brahmin, is an impossible situation where that gift does not benefit one who stands there.
But here, brahmin, someone is a taker of life... [and so on] ...one who holds wrong view.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the animal realm.
Whatever food belongs to beings born in the animal realm, by that he sustains himself there, and by that he remains there.
This, too, O brahmin, is an occasion where, for one who stands [in such a state], that gift does not benefit them.
But here, brahmin, a certain person abstains from taking life and abstains from taking what is not given.
He abstains from sexual misconduct, he abstains from false speech, he abstains from malicious speech,
he abstains from harsh speech, he abstains from idle chatter; he is free from covetousness,
he is of a mind without ill will, and he holds right view.
Thus, with the breakup of the body after death, he is reborn in the company of human beings.

There, he subsists on whatever food humans eat; there, he persists by means of that same food. But even this, brahmin, is an impossible case where, for one remaining there, that gift does not provide benefit.
But here, brahmin, a certain person abstains from taking life... [and so on] ...he holds right view.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the company of the devas.
Whatever is the food of the devas, by that he subsists there; by that he remains there.
This too, brahmin, is a situation where that gift is beneficial to one who stands therein.
But here, brahmin, a certain person is a destroyer of life … [and so on] … he holds wrong view.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts.
Whatever food there is for beings in that realm of ghosts, by that he sustains himself there, by that he remains there;
or whatever they send up to him from here— whether friends or companions, or kinsmen and blood relations—
by that he sustains himself there, by that he remains there.
“This, brahmin, is the state where that gift is beneficial for one who stands therein.
“But if, Master Gotama, that deceased kinsman has not been reborn in that state, who then partakes of that gift?
“Brahmin, other deceased kinsmen have been reborn in that state; they are the ones who partake of that gift.”
“But if, Master Gotama, that deceased kinsman has not been reborn in that place, and his other deceased kinsmen have also not been reborn there, who then partakes of that gift?
“It is impossible, brahmin, it cannot happen that such a place would be devoid of deceased kinsmen throughout this long stretch of time.
Moreover, brahmin, the donor is never without fruit.”
“Does Master Gotama make a qualification even in an improper case?
“I do indeed make a qualification even in an improper case, brahmin.
Here, brahmin, someone is a destroyer of life, a taker of what is not given, one who engages in sexual misconduct, and a speaker of falsehood.”
He is one who speaks maliciously, speaks harshly, indulges in idle chatter, is covetous, has a mind of ill will,
and holds wrong view; yet he is a giver of food,
drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, bedding, dwellings, and lamps to ascetics or brahmins.
Thus, with the breakup of the body after death, he is reborn into the company of elephants.
There he obtains food and drink, garlands, and various ornaments.
For, brahmin, one who here takes life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsehood, and speaks maliciously...
Harsh in speech, a speaker of idle chatter, covetous, malevolent in heart, and held by wrong view— because of that,

with the breakup of the body after death, he is reborn in the company of elephants. Yet, because he was a giver of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, perfumes, and ointments to ascetics or brahmins...
He is one who provides beds, dwellings, and lighting; thus, he gains there food, drink, garlands, and various ornaments.
But here, brahmin, another person is a destroyer of life... [as before] ...and holds wrong view.
Yet he is a giver to ascetics or brahmins of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, perfumes, ointments, beds, dwellings, and lighting.
Thus, with the breakup of the body after death, he is reborn into the company of horses...
into the company of cattle...
into the company of dogs.
Thus, in that place, he becomes a recipient of food, drink, garlands, and various ornaments.
However, Brahmin, because he was here a taker of life... [pe] ...one of wrong view, on the dissolution of the body, after death, he is reborn in the company of dogs.
But as for the fact that he was a giver of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, perfumes, and ointments to a recluse or a brahmin—
He obtains there beds, dwellings, and lighting, as well as food, drink, garlands, and various ornaments.
But here, brahmin, a certain person abstains from taking life... [as before] ...and possesses right view.
He is a giver of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, unguents, beds, dwellings, and lighting to ascetics or brahmins.
Thus, with the breakup of the body after death, he is reborn into the company of human beings.
There, he becomes a partaker of the five strands of human sensual pleasure.
Because, Brahmin, he here abstained from taking life... [and so on] ...and held right view, by that reason, with the breakup of the body after death, he is reborn into the company of human beings.

Furthermore, whatever he gives to a recluse or a brahmin—food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, perfumes, ointments, bedding, dwellings, and lamps—he thereby becomes a recipient there of the five strands of human sensual pleasure.
But here, brahmin, a certain person abstains from taking life... [and so on] ...he holds right view.
Thus, he becomes a giver of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, perfumes, ointments, bedding, dwellings, and lamps to ascetics or brahmins.
With the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn into the company of the devas.
There, he becomes a recipient of the fivefold divine sense-pleasures.
“Brahmin, because one here refrains from taking life... [and so on] ...and possesses right view, with the breakup of the body, after death, one is reborn in the company of the devas.

Furthermore, because one is a giver of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, ointments, beds, dwellings, and lamps to ascetics or brahmins, one becomes a recipient there of the fivefold divine sense-pleasures.
Moreover, Brahmin, even the donor is not without fruit.”
“It is wonderful, Master Gotama! It is marvelous, Master Gotama!
To such an extent, Master Gotama, it is indeed fitting to give gifts and fitting to perform acts of faith, since even the giver is not without fruit.
“So it is, brahmin; for even the giver, brahmin, is not without fruit.”
“Excellent, Master Gotama! Excellent, Master Gotama!
… [as before] … May Master Gotama accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last.
This is the eleventh.
The Second Chapter on Jāṇussoṇi.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.178.
Chapter 18: On the Good.
The Discourse on the Wholesome (Sādhusutta):
“Monks, I will teach you what is wholesome and what is unwholesome.”
“Listen to that and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“And what, bhikkhus, is unwholesome?
Killing living beings, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, malicious speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, covetousness, ill will,
and wrong view— this, bhikkhus, is called unwholesome.”
And what, monks, is good? Abstinence from taking life,
abstinence from taking what is not given, abstinence from sexual misconduct,
abstinence from false speech, abstinence from malicious speech, abstinence from harsh speech, abstinence from idle chatter, and non-covetousness.
“Non-ill will and right view—
this, monks, is called ‘good. Thus was the first [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.179 18. Sādhuvagga Ariyadhammasutta (The Noble Dhamma) “Monks, there are these ten noble qualities. What ten? (1) Here, monks, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. (2) He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. (3) He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. (4) He possesses the virtue that is cherished by the noble ones; it is untorn, unrent, unblotched, unmottled, liberating, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. (5) He has heard much, retained what he has heard, stored what he has heard. Whatever teachings are admirable in the beginning, admirable in the middle, and admirable in the end, which proclaim the holy life both in its particulars and in its essence, entirely complete, surpassingly pure: such teachings he has heard much of, retained, and stored. (6) He is content with any kind of robe, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick. (7) He is one who gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life. (8) With the destruction of the taints, he has realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind, liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, he dwells therein. These, monks, are the ten noble qualities.”
“Monks, I will teach you the noble Dhamma and the ignoble Dhamma.
Listen to that… [as above]….”
And what, bhikkhus, is the ignoble teaching?
Killing living beings … [and so on] … wrong view.
This, monks, is called the ignoble teaching.
And what, monks, is the noble teaching?
Abstinence from taking life... [and so forth]...
“Right view— this,
monks, is called the noble Dhamma. The second [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.180 18.

Sādhuvagga Kusalasutta “Monks, there are these ten wholesome qualities. What ten? (1) Right view, (2) right intention, (3) right speech, (4) right action, (5) right livelihood, (6) right effort, (7) right mindfulness, (8) right concentration, (9) right knowledge, (10) right liberation. These, monks, are the ten wholesome qualities.”
“Bhikkhus, I will teach you the wholesome and the unwholesome.
Listen to that… [as above]….”
And what, monks, is unwholesome?
Killing living beings …pe… wrong view.
This, monks, is called unwholesome.
And what, monks, is wholesome?
Abstinence from taking life … [and so on] …
“Right view— this,
monks, is called wholesome. The third [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.181 18. Sādhuvagga Atthasutta (The Discourse on Benefit) "Bhikkhus, there are these ten benefits in developing and cultivating the noble eightfold path. What ten? One gains wealth; one gains a good reputation; one is respected by one’s fellow monks; one is not subject to remorse at the time of death; after the breakup of the body, after death, one is reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world; even if one does not attain final knowledge here and now, one becomes one of those who will attain final knowledge upon landing; even if one does not become one of those who will attain final knowledge upon landing, one becomes one of those who will attain final knowledge in the interval; even if one does not become one of those who will attain final knowledge in the interval, one becomes one of those who will attain final knowledge upon being reborn; even if one does not become one of those who will attain final knowledge upon being reborn, one becomes one of those who will attain final knowledge without further prompting; even if one does not become one of those who will attain final knowledge without further prompting, one becomes one of those who will attain final knowledge with further prompting. These, bhikkhus, are the ten benefits in developing and cultivating the noble eightfold path."

“Bhikkhus, I will teach you the beneficial and the unbeneficial. Listen to that... [as above]... “And what, bhikkhus, is the unbeneficial? It is the destruction of life, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view. This is called the unbeneficial. “And what, bhikkhus, is the beneficial? It is abstention from the destruction of life, abstention from taking what is not given, abstention from sexual misconduct, abstention from false speech, abstention from divisive speech, abstention from harsh speech, abstention from idle chatter, non-covetousness, non-ill will, and right view. This is called the beneficial.”
And what, bhikkhus, is harmful?
Killing living beings ...
[and so on] ... wrong view.
This, monks, is called what is harmful.
And what, monks, is what is beneficial?
Abstinence from taking life... [and so forth].
“Right view—
this, monks, is called the goal.
The fourth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.182 18.

Sādhuvagga Dhammasutta “Monks, there are these ten things that are wholesome. What ten? Right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration, right knowledge, and right liberation. These, monks, are the ten wholesome things.”
“Monks, I will teach you the Dhamma and the non-Dhamma. Listen to that... [as before] ...”
And what, bhikkhus, is non-Dhamma?
Killing living beings …pe… wrong view.
This, monks, is called non-Dhamma.
And what, monks, is the Dhamma?
Abstinence from taking life … [and so on] … [as in the standard formula].
“Right view— this,
monks, is called the Dhamma.
The fifth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.183 18.

Sādhuvagga Āsavasutta (The Taints) “Monks, there are these four taints. What four? The taint of sensuality, the taint of existence, the taint of views, and the taint of ignorance. These, monks, are the four taints.”
“Monks, I will teach you the Dhamma with taints and the Dhamma without taints.
Listen to that… [as above]….”
And what, bhikkhus, is the state associated with the taints?
Killing living beings …pe… wrong view.
This, monks, is called a phenomenon associated with the taints (*sāsava*).
And what, monks, is a phenomenon free from the taints (*anāsava*)?
Abstinence from taking life... [and so forth].
“Right view— this,
monks, is called the state free from taints.
The sixth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.184 18. Sādhuvagga Vajjasutta (The Discourse on Faults) “Monks, there are these ten faults.

What ten? (1) One commits a fault oneself; (2) one causes another to commit a fault; (3) one approves of another’s committing a fault; (4) one conceals one’s own fault; (5) one conceals another’s fault; (6) one praises oneself; (7) one disparages others; (8) one holds wrong view; (9) one has a mind of ill will toward those who speak the Dhamma; (10) one does not apply oneself to the higher Dhamma and the higher Discipline. These, monks, are the ten faults.”
“Monks, I will teach you the blameworthy Dhamma and the blameless Dhamma.
Listen to that …” [as above] …
And what, monks, is the blameworthy state?
The destruction of life …pe… wrong view.
This, monks, is called a blameworthy state.
And what, monks, is a blameless state?
Abstinence from the destruction of life... [and so on]...
“Right view— this,
monks, is called the blameless state.
The seventh.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.185 18. Sādhuvagga Tapanīyasutta (The Discourse on What is to Be Regretted) “Monks, there are these ten things that are to be regretted. What ten? (1) ‘I have not practiced the higher virtuous conduct,’ this is a thing to be regretted. (2) ‘I have not developed concentration,’ this is a thing to be regretted. (3) ‘I have not developed wisdom,’ this is a thing to be regretted. (4) ‘I have not developed liberation,’ this is a thing to be regretted. (5) ‘I have not developed the knowledge and vision of liberation,’ this is a thing to be regretted. (6) ‘I did not honor those who should be honored,’ this is a thing to be regretted. (7) ‘I did not respect those who should be respected,’ this is a thing to be regretted. (8) ‘I did not venerate those who should be venerated,’ this is a thing to be regretted. (9) ‘I did not revere those who should be revered,’ this is a thing to be regretted. (10) ‘I did not pay homage to those who should be paid homage to,’ this is a thing to be regretted. These, monks, are the ten things that are to be regretted.”
“Monks, I will teach you the doctrine that leads to remorse and the doctrine that does not lead to remorse. Listen to that….
[as above]... (AN 10.185, PTS AN v 276)
And what, bhikkhus, is the burning dhamma?
Killing living beings ...
[and so on] ... wrong view.
This, monks, is called the burning quality. And what, monks, is the non-burning quality?
Abstinence from taking life... [and so on]... [up to] abstinence from false speech. This, monks, is called the non-burning quality.
“Right view— this,
monks, is called the state that does not cause remorse.
The eighth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.186 18.

Sādhuvagga Ācayagāmisutta (The Discourse on Leading to Accumulation) “Monks, there are these ten things that lead to accumulation. What ten? (1) One takes life; (2) one takes what is not given; (3) one engages in sexual misconduct; (4) one speaks falsely; (5) one speaks divisively; (6) one speaks harshly; (7) one indulges in idle chatter; (8) one is covetous; (9) one harbors ill will; (10) one holds wrong view. These, monks, are the ten things that lead to accumulation.”
“Monks, I will teach you the Dhamma that leads to accumulation and the Dhamma that leads to diminution.
Listen to that… [as before]….”
And what, bhikkhus, is the phenomenon that leads to accumulation?
Killing living beings ...
[and so on] ... wrong view.
This, monks, is called the phenomenon leading to accumulation.
And what, monks, is the phenomenon leading to diminution?
Abstinence from taking life... [and so forth]...
“Right view,
monks— this is called the Dhamma that leads to diminution.
Thus ends the ninth [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.187 18. Sādhuvagga Dukkhudrayasutta (The Discourse on the Source of Suffering) “Monks, there are these ten things that are the source of suffering. What ten? (1) Monks, for one who destroys life, with the destruction of life as the basis, there is the production of suffering in this very life, and there is the production of suffering in future lives. (2) For one who takes what is not given, with taking what is not given as the basis, there is the production of suffering in this very life, and there is the production of suffering in future lives. (3) For one who engages in sexual misconduct, with sexual misconduct as the basis, there is the production of suffering in this very life, and there is the production of suffering in future lives. (4) For one who speaks falsehood, with false speech as the basis, there is the production of suffering in this very life, and there is the production of suffering in future lives. (5) For one who speaks divisively, with divisive speech as the basis, there is the production of suffering in this very life, and there is the production of suffering in future lives. (6) For one who speaks harshly, with harsh speech as the basis, there is the production of suffering in this very life, and there is the production of suffering in future lives. (7) For one who indulges in idle chatter, with idle chatter as the basis, there is the production of suffering in this very life, and there is the production of suffering in future lives. (8) For one who is covetous, with covetousness as the basis, there is the production of suffering in this very life, and there is the production of suffering in future lives. (9) For one who harbors ill will, with ill will as the basis, there is the production of suffering in this very life, and there are the production of suffering in future lives. (10) For one who holds wrong view, with wrong view as the basis, there is the production of suffering in this very life, and there is the production of suffering in future lives. These, monks, are the ten things that are the source of suffering.”
“Monks, I will teach you the Dhamma that has suffering as its outcome and the Dhamma that has happiness as its outcome.
Listen to that…. [as above]”
And what, bhikkhus, is the state that has suffering as its outcome?
Killing living beings … [and so on] … wrong view.
This, monks, is called the teaching that has suffering as its outcome.
And what, monks, is the teaching that has happiness as its outcome?
Abstinence from taking life... [and so on].
“Right view— this,
monks, is called the Dhamma that has happiness as its fruit.
The tenth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.188 18.

Sādhuvagga Vipākasutta (The Discourse on Ripening) “Monks, there are these ten ripenings of merit, ripenings of the wholesome, which lead to what is beneficial, to happiness, and to the welfare and happiness for a long time. What ten? One acquires great wealth; one gains a good reputation; one is free from illness; one is well-favored by the deities; one has a pleasant appearance; one is well-spoken of among people; one enters a womb that is auspicious; one passes away with a mind free from remorse; one is reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world; and, having realized it for oneself with direct knowledge here and now, one attains final Nibbāna. These, monks, are the ten ripenings of merit, ripenings of the wholesome, which lead to what is beneficial, to happiness, and to the welfare and happiness for a long time.”
“Monks, I will teach you the Dhamma that has a painful result and the Dhamma that has a pleasant result.
Listen to that… [as above]….”
And what, monks, is the state that results in suffering?
Killing living beings … [as before] … wrong view.
This, monks, is called the phenomenon with a painful result.
And what, monks, is the phenomenon with a pleasant result?
Abstinence from taking life … [and so on] … [as above].
“Right view— this,
monks, is called the phenomenon with a pleasant ripening.
The eleventh.
The Third Chapter on the Virtuous.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.189.

The Noble Path Discourse (AN 10.189): “Monks,
I will teach you the noble path and the ignoble path.”
Listen to that … [as before] … And what,
bhikkhus, is the ignoble path? It is the destruction of life … [as before] …
Wrong view—
this, monks, is called the ignoble path.
And what, monks, is the noble path?
“Abstaining from taking life …pe… right view— this,
monks, is called the noble path.”
First.

Wrong view—
this, monks, is called the dark path.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.192.

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.193.

The Fifth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.194.

The Fourth Chapter on the Noble Path.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.199–210

20. Aparapuggalavagga Nasevitabbādisutta (AN 10.199–210, AN 10.199, PTS AN v 281) “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who should not be cultivated; the person who should be cultivated but not closely; the person who should be cultivated closely; and the person who is like a lotus leaf. And how, monks, is the person one who should not be cultivated? Here, monks, someone is unvirtuous, of bad character, impure, of evil conduct, secretive in his actions, and he does not associate with those who are virtuous. This, monks, is called the person who should not be cultivated. And how, monks, is the person one who should be cultivated but not closely? Here, monks, someone is virtuous, of good character, pure, of excellent conduct, not secretive in his actions, and he associates with those who are virtuous. However, he is not one who has abandoned the underlying tendencies, nor one who has fully understood them. This, monks, is called the person who should be cultivated but not closely. And how, monks, is the person one who should be cultivated closely? Here, monks, someone is virtuous, of good character, pure, of excellent conduct, not secretive in his actions, and he associates with those who are virtuous. Furthermore, he is one who has abandoned the underlying tendencies and has fully understood them. This, monks, is called the person who should be cultivated closely. And how, monks, is the person like a lotus leaf? Here, monks, someone is virtuous, of good character, pure, of excellent conduct, not secretive in his actions, and he associates with those who are virtuous. Furthermore, he is one who has abandoned the underlying tendencies and has fully understood them. Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, so too, monks, even if such a person is reviled, abused, threatened, or harassed by others, no resentment, anger, or ill will arises within him. This, monks, is called the person who is like a lotus leaf.”
“Bhikkhus, a person endowed with ten qualities should not be associated with. Which ten?
He is a destroyer of life, a taker of what is not given, one who engages in sexual misconduct, a speaker of falsehood, and a speaker of divisive speech...”
One is a speaker of falsehood, a speaker of harsh words, a frivolous talker, covetous, ill-willed,
and one of wrong view. Monks, a person endowed with these ten qualities should not be associated with.
“Bhikkhus, a person endowed with ten qualities should be associated with.
With which ten?

“Monks, a person endowed with these ten qualities should be cultivated.

Chapter on the Body Born of Karma (Karajakāyavagga).
Paṭhamanirayasaggasutta:
“Bhikkhus, one endowed with ten qualities is deposited in hell as if carried there. What ten? [The text continues with the ten unwholesome actions.]”
By which ten?
Here, monks, a certain person is a destroyer of life; he is cruel, bloody-handed, intent on killing and striking, and devoid of compassion toward all living beings.
He is a taker of what is not given; whatever belongs to another, whether it be the wealth or property of another in a village or in the wilderness, he takes it away ungiven, by means of theft.

He engages in sexual misconduct; he has intercourse with women who are protected by their mother, protected by their father, protected by both parents, protected by their brother, protected by their sister,
protected by their relatives, protected by their clan, protected by Dhamma, those who have a husband, those who are under threat of punishment,
and even those who are merely betrothed with a flower garland— such as these he approaches for sexual intercourse.

He is a speaker of falsehood. Having been summoned as a witness and questioned in an assembly, or in a gathering, or in the midst of kinsmen, or in the midst of a guild, or in the presence of the royal court, being told:
"Come, good man, speak what you know," he says, "I know," when he does not know;
or he says, "I do not know," when he knows; or he says, "I see," when he does not see; or he says, "I see," when he does see.
Or he says: ‘I do not see. Thus, for his own sake, or for the sake of another, or for the sake of some small material gain, he speaks a deliberate lie.
He is a slanderer: having heard something here, he reports it there for the purpose of dividing these people;

or having heard something there, he reports it here for the purpose of dividing those people. Thus, he is one who divides those who are united, or who incites those who are divided; he delights in factions.
He delights in factions, rejoices in factions, and utters speech that creates factions.
He is one of harsh speech; he utters such speech as is cutting, rough, bitter to others, abusive, provocative of anger, and conducive to lack of concentration.

He is a frivolous chatterer; he speaks at the wrong time, speaks what is untrue, speaks what is useless, speaks according to non-Dhamma, and speaks according to non-discipline; he utters speech that is worthless, untimely, groundless, indefinite, and unbeneficial.
He is covetous; he covets the wealth and possessions of others, thinking: "O, that what belongs to another were mine!
He has a mind of ill will and corrupt intentions, thinking: "May these beings be slain, or bound, or cut off, or destroyed, or may they not even exist!
He holds wrong view and possesses a perverted perspective:
‘There is no giving, there is no sacrifice, there is no offering; there is no fruit or result of deeds well done or ill done;
there is no this world, there is no other world; there is no mother, there is no father;

there are no beings who arise spontaneously; there are in the world no recluses or brahmins who have attained rightly and practice rightly, who have themselves realized this world and the other world and make them known to others.’
‘Having realized the world for themselves through direct higher knowledge, they make it known.
Monks, one who possesses these ten qualities is deposited in hell as if carried there.
Monks, one who possesses ten qualities is deposited in heaven as if carried there.
By which ten?

Here, monks, a certain person, having abandoned the taking of life, abstains from taking life; he lays aside the rod, lays aside the weapon, and dwells conscientious, compassionate, and sympathetic toward the welfare of all living beings.

Having abandoned taking what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given. Whatever belongs to another, whether it be in a village or in the forest—be it wealth or belongings—he does not take that which is not given, nor does he take it by means of theft.
Having abandoned sexual misconduct, he abstains from sexual misconduct. He does not engage in sexual intercourse with those women who are protected by their mother...
[and so on] ...or even those who are protected by a garland of flowers. Having abandoned false speech, he abstains from false speech.
Whether in an assembly, in a council, among his kinsmen, among a guild, or in the royal court, when summoned as a witness and asked: "Come now, good man, [speak the truth]."
"Tell me what you know. If he does not know, he says, "I do not know"; if he knows, he says, "I know";
if he has not seen, he says, "I have not seen"; if he has seen, he says, "I have seen.
Thus, whether for his own sake, for the sake of another, or for the sake of some small material gain, he does not speak a conscious lie.
Having abandoned malicious speech, he abstains from malicious speech.

He does not repeat elsewhere what he has heard here for the purpose of dividing those people, nor does he repeat to these people what he has heard elsewhere for the purpose of dividing them. Thus, he is a reconciler of those who are divided and a promoter of harmony among those who are united;
he delights in concord, rejoices in concord, and finds joy in concord; he speaks words that create concord.

Having abandoned harsh speech, he abstains from harsh speech. He speaks such words as are gentle, pleasing to the ear, lovable, heart-entrancing, urbane, agreeable to many people, and dear to many people.
Having abandoned idle chatter, he abstains from idle chatter; he speaks at the proper time, speaks what is true, speaks what is meaningful, speaks on the Dhamma, and speaks on the Vinaya.
He is one who speaks at the right time words that are well-founded, reasoned, measured, and beneficial.
He is free from covetousness; he does not covet the wealth and possessions of others, thinking: "O, that what belongs to another were mine!
He is of a mind without ill will and of pure intention, thinking: "May these beings be free from enmity, free from affliction, free from distress, and may they look after themselves with happiness!
He possesses right view and has an undistorted perspective:
‘There is what is given, there is what is sacrificed, there is what is offered; there is fruit and result of good and evil deeds;
there is this world and the other world; there is mother and father; there are beings of spontaneous birth;
there are in the world ascetics and brahmins who have fared rightly and practiced rightly, who have realized this world and the other world for themselves by direct knowledge.’
‘Having realized them for themselves through direct knowledge, they declare them.
Monks, one who possesses these ten qualities is deposited in heaven as if carried there. Thus was the first [discourse].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.212 21.

Karajakāyavagga Dutiyanirayasaggasutta (The Second Discourse on Hell and Heaven) “Monks, there are these ten qualities that lead to hell. What ten? Here, monks, a certain person destroys life, takes what is not given, engages in sexual misconduct, speaks falsely, speaks divisively, speaks harshly, indulges in idle chatter, is full of covetousness, has a mind of ill will, and holds wrong view. These, monks, are the ten qualities that lead to hell. Monks, there are these ten qualities that lead to heaven. What ten? Here, monks, a certain person abstains from destroying life, abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from false speech, abstains from divisive speech, abstains from harsh speech, abstains from idle chatter, is without covetousness, has a mind free from ill will, and holds right view. These, monks, are the ten qualities that lead to heaven.”
“Bhikkhus, one endowed with ten qualities is deposited in hell as if brought there. What are the ten? [The Buddha said:]”
In this case, monks, a certain person is a destroyer of life: he is cruel, his hands are stained with blood, intent on killing and striking, and devoid of compassion for all living beings.
He takes what is not given...
he engages in sexual misconduct...
He is a speaker of falsehood;
he is a speaker of malicious speech;
he is a speaker of harsh speech.
He is a speaker of idle chatter;
he is covetous;
he has a mind of ill will.
He holds wrong view and has a perverted perspective:
"There is no giving...
[as before] ...those who, having realized it for themselves through direct knowledge, make it known."
“Monks, one who possesses these ten qualities is deposited in hell as if carried there.
Monks, one who possesses ten qualities is deposited in heaven as if carried there.
What are the ten?”

In this case, monks, a certain person, having abandoned the taking of life, abstains from taking life; he lays aside the rod and the weapon, and being modest and compassionate, he dwells sympathetic toward the welfare of all living beings.
Having abandoned taking what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given...
Having abandoned sexual misconduct, he abstains from sexual misconduct...
Having abandoned false speech, he abstains from false speech;
having abandoned malicious speech, he abstains from malicious speech;
having abandoned harsh speech, he abstains from harsh speech.
Having abandoned idle chatter, he abstains from idle chatter; ...
he is free from covetousness; ...
he has a mind without ill will; ...
One possesses right view and has an undistorted perspective, thinking:
‘There is what is given... [and so on] ...there are those who, having realized for themselves through direct knowledge this world and the other world, make them known.
Monks, one who is endowed with these ten qualities is deposited in heaven as if carried there.”
The Second.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.213.

“Bhikkhus, possessed of ten qualities, a woman is deposited in hell as if carried there. [The Buddha then enumerates these ten qualities.]”
