21. Karajakāyavagga Visāradasutta (AN 10.215, AN 10.204, PTS AN v 288) “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is confident by birth; the person who is confident by learning; the person who is confident by both birth and learning; and the person who is confident by neither birth nor learning. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person confident by birth? Here, bhikkhus, a person is born into a high family—whether a khattiya family, a brahmin family, or a householder family—one that is rich, with great wealth and property, with abundant gold and silver, abundant treasures and commodities, abundant wealth and grain. This person, being thus born into a high family, is confident, fearless, and self-assured. This, bhikkhus, is called a person confident by birth. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person confident by learning? Here, bhikkhus, a person has learned much, remembered what he had learned, retained it in mind, and penetrated it well with his views. He is confident, fearless, and self-assured because of that learning. This, bhikkhus, is called a person confident by learning. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person confident by both birth and learning? Here, bhikkhus, a person is born into a high family—and has also learned much... [as above]... This, bhikkhus, is called a person confident by both birth and learning. And how, bhikkhus, is one a person confident by neither birth nor learning? Here, bhikkhus, a person is not born into a high family, and has not learned much... [as above]... Yet he is confident, fearless, and self-assured through his own bodily realization of the Dhamma. This, bhikkhus, is called a person confident by neither birth nor learning. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”
“Bhikkhus, possessed of ten qualities, a female lay follower dwells at home lacking confidence.
Which ten?
She is a destroyer of life …”
She takes what is not given;
she engages in sexual misconduct;
she speaks falsehoods.
She speaks maliciously;
she speaks harshly;
she indulges in idle chatter.
She is covetous… she has a mind of ill will… she holds wrong view….
“Monks, a female lay follower endowed with these ten qualities lives at home without confidence.
Monks, a female lay follower endowed with ten qualities lives at home with confidence.
With which ten? [The Buddha then recited:]”
She abstains from taking life...
she abstains from taking what is not given...
she abstains from sexual misconduct...
She abstains from false speech;
she abstains from malicious speech;
she abstains from harsh speech.
She abstains from idle chatter;
she is free from covetousness;
she is of a mind devoid of ill will.
She possesses right view...
It is, monks, by being endowed with these ten qualities that a female lay follower dwells confidently at home.
Thus ends the fifth [discourse].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.216 21. Karajakāyavagga Saṁsappanīyasutta (The Creeping Serpent) “Monks, there are these five kinds of creeping serpents found in the world. What five? The black snake, the brown snake, the red snake, the white snake, and the spotted snake. These are the five kinds of creeping serpents found in the world. In the same way, monks, there are these five kinds of creeping serpents found among human beings. What five? The one who creeps along with greed, the one who creeps along with hatred, the one who creeps along with delusion, the one who creeps along with views, and the one who creeps along with doubt. These, monks, are the five kinds of creeping serpents found among human beings. Just as, monks, a person might enter a dark house that has not been entered before, and having entered, would see a black snake, a brown snake, a red snake, a white snake, and a spotted snake; and he, being afraid and terrified, would run away from there. Why is that? Because of his fear of those creeping serpents. In the same way, monks, a noble disciple reflects thus: ‘I too have entered this dark house of the mind that has not been entered before, and I am beset by these five creeping serpents. Seeing this danger, he becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with volitional formations, and disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated. Through liberation, the knowledge arises: ‘It is liberated. He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’”
“Bhikkhus, I will teach you a discourse on the way of creeping.
Listen to it and attend closely; I shall speak.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“And what, bhikkhus, is the discourse on the Dhamma that is like a crawling snake?
“Bhikkhus, beings are owners of their actions, heirs of their actions; they originate from their actions, are bound to their actions, and have their actions as their refuge.
It is action that they do—whether good or evil—that they become the heirs of.
Here, bhikkhus, a certain person is a destroyer of life, cruel, bloody-handed, intent on injuring and killing, and devoid of compassion for all living beings.”
Thus he writhes with body, writhes with speech, and writhes with mind.
His bodily action is crooked, his verbal action is crooked, his mental action is crooked; his destination is crooked and his rebirth is crooked.
For one whose destination is crooked and whose rebirth is crooked, I say, monks, that there is one of two destinations: [either hell or the animal realm].
Either the hells, which are exclusively suffering, or the animal realm of crawling creatures.
And what, monks, is that animal realm of crawling creatures?
Snakes, scorpions, centipedes, mongooses, cats, mice, owls, or whatever other beings belonging to the animal realm crawl away when they see humans.
Thus, monks, there is the arising of a being from a being.
One is reborn according to what one has done.
Once reborn, contacts touch that person.
"In this way, monks, I say that beings are heirs to their own karma.
Furthermore, monks, here someone is a taker of what is not given...
[and] is one who engages in sexual misconduct."
He is a speaker of falsehood;
he is a speaker of malicious speech;
he is a speaker of harsh speech.
He is a speaker of idle chatter;
he is covetous;
he is ill-willed.
He holds wrong view and has a distorted perspective:
"There is no giving...
[as before] ...those who, having realized it for themselves through direct higher knowledge, make it known."
Thus one creeps along with the body, creeps along with speech, and creeps along with the mind.
One’s bodily action is crooked, one’s verbal action is crooked, and one’s mental action is crooked; one’s destination is crooked and one’s rebirth is crooked.
For one whose destination is crooked and whose rebirth is crooked, I say, monks, that there is one of two destinations: [either hell or the animal realm].
Either the hells, which are exclusively suffering, or the animal realm of crawling creatures.
And what, monks, is that animal realm of crawling creatures?
Snakes, scorpions, centipedes, mongooses, cats, rats, owls, or whatever other beings belonging to the animal realm crawl away when they see humans.
Thus, monks, there is the arising of a being from a being;
one is reborn according to what one has done.
Once reborn, contacts touch him.
"In this way, monks, I say that beings are heirs to their actions.
Beings, monks, own their actions; they are heirs to their actions, born of their actions, bound by their actions, and have their actions as their refuge.
Whatever action they perform—whether good or evil—they become the heirs of that."

In this case, monks, a certain person, having abandoned the taking of life, abstains from taking life; he lays aside the rod and the weapon, and dwells conscientious, compassionate, and sympathetic toward the welfare of all living beings.
He does not crawl along with body, speech, or mind.
His bodily action is straight, his verbal action is straight, his mental action is straight, his destination is straight, and his rebirth is straight.
But for one who is upright in conduct and upright in rebirth, monks, I declare two possible destinations:
either those heavens that are exclusively blissful, or those high-born families— whether among the great aristocratic clans of kshatriyas,
the great aristocratic clans of brahmins, or the great aristocratic clans of householders— who are wealthy, affluent, of great possessions, and abundant in gold and silver.
They possess abundant means of subsistence and abundant wealth and grain.
Thus, monks, the existence of a being arises from a being;
according to what one does, so one is reborn.
Contact touches him accordingly.
Thus, monks, I say that beings are heirs to their own kamma.
Furthermore, monks, here someone, having abandoned taking what is not given, abstains from taking what is not given... [and so on].
He abstains from sexual misconduct...
Having abandoned false speech, he abstains from false speech...
Having abandoned divisive speech, he abstains from divisive speech...
Having abandoned harsh speech, he abstains from harsh speech...
Having abandoned idle chatter, he abstains from idle chatter...
He is free from covetousness...
He is of a mind free from ill will;
he holds right view and possesses unperverted vision:
"There is what is given... [and so on]..."
‘Those who, having personally realized this world and the other world through direct higher knowledge, make them known.
He does not wriggle with body, he does not wriggle with speech, he does not wriggle with mind.
His bodily action is straight, his verbal action is straight, his mental action is straight; his destination is straight, his rebirth is straight.
“Monks, for one who is upright in conduct and upright in rebirth, I declare two possible destinies:
either those heavens that are exclusively blissful, or those high-born families— whether among the great khattiya clans,
the great brahmin clans, or the great householder clans— that are wealthy, affluent, of great possessions, and abundant in gold and silver.”
They possess abundant wealth and requisites, and abundant money and grain.
Thus, monks, the existence of one being arises from another being;
whatever one does, by that one is reborn.
“Contact touches him accordingly.
Thus, monks, I say that beings are heirs to their actions.
Beings, monks, are owners of their actions, heirs to their actions, born of their actions, bound by their actions, and have their actions as their refuge; it is the action they perform—”
Whether it be good or evil, they become its heirs.
This, monks, is that discourse on the Dhamma concerning the crawling snake.
The sixth.
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.217 21.
Karajakāyavagga First Discourse on Volitional Action (Paṭhamasañcetanikasutta)
“Monks, I do not say that there is an end to intentional kamma that has been performed and accumulated without its being experienced.
And that experience occurs either in this very life, or upon rebirth, or in some subsequent period.”
"But I do not say, bhikkhus, that there is an end to suffering without experiencing the results of intentional kamma that has been performed and accumulated.
In this regard, bhikkhus, there are three kinds of corruption and failure in bodily action that are unwholesome intentional kamma, having suffering as their outcome and suffering as their result;
and four kinds of corruption and failure in verbal action that are unwholesome intentional kamma, having suffering as their outcome and suffering as their result."
Threefold is the corruption and transgression of mental action consisting of unwholesome volition, which has suffering as its outcome and suffering as its result.
And how, monks, is the threefold corruption and transgression of bodily action consisting of unwholesome volition one that has suffering as its outcome and suffering as its result?
Here, monks, a certain person is a destroyer of life; he is cruel, bloody-handed, intent on killing and striking, and lacks compassion for all living beings.
He takes what is not given; he takes by way of theft what belongs to another, whether it be in a village or in the forest, whatever property of another’s that has not been given.
He engages in sexual misconduct; he has sexual relations with women who are protected by their mother... [and so on] ...even with those as far as those merely surrounded by a garland of flowers.
In this way, monks, there is a threefold corruption and failure of bodily action, consisting of unwholesome volition, which has suffering as its outcome and suffering as its result.
And how, monks, does the fourfold corruption and failure of verbal action, consisting of unwholesome volition, result in suffering as its outcome and suffering as its fruition?

Here, monks, someone is a speaker of falsehood. Whether in an assembly, in a gathering, in the midst of kinsmen, in the midst of a company, or in the presence of the royal court, when summoned and questioned as a witness—‘Come now, good man, speak what you know’—he says, ‘I know,’ though he does not know; or he says, ‘I do not know,’ though he knows.
He says, "I do not know," when he does not see; or he says, "I see," when he sees; or he says, "I do not see," when he does see.
Thus, for his own sake, or for the sake of another, or for the sake of some trifling material gain, he speaks a deliberate lie.
He is one of malicious speech: having heard something here, he reports it there for the purpose of dividing these people; or having heard something there, he reports it to these people...
He speaks for the sake of dividing those who are united. Thus, he is one who divides those who are united or who further incites those who are already divided;
he delights in factionalism, rejoices in factionalism, and finds pleasure in factionalism; he utters speech that causes division.
He is harsh of speech, uttering such words as are hurtful, rough, bitter, offensive to others, provocative of anger, and conducive to lack of concentration. He speaks such speech as this.

One is a frivolous talker; one speaks at the wrong time, speaks what is untrue, speaks what is useless, speaks according to what is not Dhamma, speaks according to what is not Vinaya; one utters speech that is worthless, untimely, groundless, indefinite, and unconnected with the goal.
In this way, monks, the fourfold corruption and transgression of verbal action, consisting of unwholesome volition, has suffering as its outcome and suffering as its result.
And how, monks, does the threefold corruption and transgression of mental action, consisting of unwholesome volition, have suffering as its outcome and suffering as its result?
“Here, monks, a certain person is covetous. He covets the wealth and possessions of others, thinking: ‘O, that what belongs to another were mine!
He is ill-willed, with a corrupt intention, thinking: ‘May these beings be slain, or bound, or cut off, or destroyed, or may they not even exist!
He holds wrong view, having a perverted perspective.”
‘There is no giving... [and so on] ...those who, having realized this world and the other world for themselves through direct knowledge, make it known.
In this way, monks, there is a threefold corruption and perversion of mental action consisting of unwholesome volition, which has suffering as its outcome and suffering as its result.
Or else, monks, it is because of a threefold corruption and perversion of bodily action consisting of unwholesome volition that beings [fall away] from the body.

Monks, it is because of the corruption and transgression of unwholesome volitional actions of fourfold verbal conduct, or because of the corruption and transgression of unwholesome volitional actions of threefold mental conduct, that beings, with the breakup of the body, after death, reappear in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or in hell.
“With the breakup of the body, after death, beings are reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.
Just as, monks, an unerring die, when thrown upward, settles wherever it lands, always settling firmly;
even so, monks, it is due to the cause of the threefold corruption and transgression of bodily action consisting in unwholesome volition.”

Or else, it is because of the unwholesome volitional actions consisting in the corruption and transgression of the fourfold verbal kamma that beings, with the breakup of the body after death, reappear in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell; or else,

it is because of the unwholesome volitional actions consisting in the corruption and transgression of the threefold mental kamma that beings, with the breakup of the body after death, reappear in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell.
Or else, with the breakup of the body, after death, they reappear in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, perdition, even in hell.
Monks, I do not say that intentional kamma which has been performed and accumulated comes to an end without being experienced;
rather, it must be experienced either in this very life, or in the next rebirth, or in some subsequent period.
"But I do not say, monks, that there is an end to suffering without experiencing the results of intentional deeds performed and accumulated.
In this regard, monks, threefold success in bodily action that is wholesome, intentional, and productive of happiness has a happy outcome;
fourfold success in verbal action that is wholesome, intentional, and productive of happiness has a happy outcome."
Threefold is the success of mental action consisting of wholesome volition that has happiness as its outcome and happiness as its result.
And how, bhikkhus, is the threefold success of bodily action consisting of wholesome volition that has happiness as its outcome and happiness as its result?

Here, bhikkhus, a certain person abstains from the destruction of life; he lays aside the rod and the weapon, dwells with a sense of shame and compassion, and abides sympathetic toward the welfare of all living beings... [as above].
He abstains from taking what is not given; he does not, with intent to steal, take what belongs to another, whether it be in a village or in the forest, that which has not been given.

Having abandoned sexual misconduct, he abstains from sexual misconduct; he does not engage in sexual intercourse with women who are protected by their mother... [and so on] ...or even those who are protected by a garland of flowers.
In this way, monks, there is a threefold success of bodily action consisting of wholesome volition, which has happiness as its outcome and happiness as its result.
And how, monks, does the fourfold success of verbal action—born of wholesome volition—result in happiness and have a happy outcome?
Here, monks, a certain person, having abandoned false speech, abstains from false speech.
Whether summoned to an assembly, to a council, to his own kin, to a guild, or to the royal court...
When questioned as a witness, saying, "Come now, good man, speak what you know," he says, "I do not know," if he does not know;
he says, "I know," if he knows; he says, "I do not see," if he does not see; he says, "I see," if he sees.
Thus, whether for his own sake, for the sake of another, or for the sake of some small material gain, he does not speak a conscious lie.
Having abandoned malicious speech, he abstains from malicious speech.
He does not repeat elsewhere what he has heard here for the purpose of dividing those people, nor does he repeat here what he has heard elsewhere for the purpose of dividing these people.

Thus, he is a reconciler of those who are divided and a promoter of harmony among those who are united; he delights in concord, rejoices in concord, and finds joy in concord; he speaks words that bring about concord.

Having abandoned harsh speech, he abstains from harsh speech. He speaks such words as are gentle, pleasing to the ear, endearing, heart-moving, urbane, agreeable to many people, and dear to many people.
Having abandoned idle chatter, he abstains from idle chatter; he speaks at the right time, speaks what is true, speaks what is beneficial, speaks on the Dhamma, and speaks on the Vinaya.
He speaks words that are worth treasuring, timely, reasoned, measured, and connected with the goal.
“Monks, in this way, fourfold success in verbal action, consisting of wholesome volition, has a pleasant outcome and a pleasant result.
And how, monks, does threefold success in mental action, consisting of wholesome volition, have a pleasant outcome and a pleasant result?
Here, monks, a certain person is not covetous. Regarding the wealth and possessions of others, he is not covetous, thinking: ‘Oh, that what belongs to another were mine!’”
He is of unmalicious mind and pure intention, thinking: “May these beings be free from enmity, free from affliction, free from distress; may they maintain themselves in happiness.
He possesses right view and undistorted vision, [thinking]:
“There is what is given, there is what is sacrificed... [as far as] those who, having realized this world and the other world for themselves through direct knowledge, make it known.”
"In this way, monks, the threefold success of mental action consisting of wholesome volition has happiness as its outcome and happiness as its result.

Or, monks, it is because of the cause of the threefold success of bodily action consisting of wholesome volition that beings, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world; and because of the cause of the fourfold success of verbal action consisting of wholesome volition..."
Or, monks, beings are reborn after death, upon the breakup of the body, in a happy destination, in a heavenly world,

because of the cause of wholesome volitional actions consisting in the threefold success of mental deeds. It is for this reason, monks, that beings are reborn after death, upon the breakup of the body,
in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
“Just as, monks, a die that has been thrown upwards lands firmly wherever it comes to rest, even so, monks,
through the cause of wholesome volitional actions consisting in the success of the threefold bodily conduct,

beings— upon the breakup of the body, after death— reappear in a happy destination, in a heavenly world; or [through the cause] of wholesome volitional actions consisting in the success of the fourfold verbal conduct.”

Or else, because of volitional actions consisting of the threefold success of mental deeds, beings, with the breakup of the body after death, reappear in a happy destination, in a heavenly world. Monks,
I do not say that there is the exhaustion of volitional actions performed and accumulated without experiencing their results.
"And that indeed, either in this very life, or upon rebirth, or in some subsequent period.
But I do not say, monks, that there is an end to suffering without experiencing the results of intentional kamma that has been performed and accumulated.
Thus ends the seventh [sutta].

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.218 21. Karajakāyavagga Dutiyasañcetanikasutta (The Second Discourse on Volitional Karma) “Monks, there are these three kinds of volitional karma. What three? There is volitional karma that is to be experienced in this very life; there is volitional karma that is to be experienced in the next rebirth; and there is volitional karma that is to be experienced in subsequent future lives. These, monks, are the three kinds of volitional karma. When this was said, a certain monk addressed the Blessed One: “But how, venerable sir, is volitional karma to be experienced in this very life? How is volitional karma to be experienced in the next rebirth? And how is volitional karma to be experienced in subsequent future lives? “Monk, here one performs and accumulates volitional karma that is to be experienced in this very life. That volitional karma of his is to be experienced in this very life. This, monk, is called volitional karma to be experienced in this very life. Furthermore, monk, here one performs and accumulates volitional karma that is to be experienced in the next rebirth. That volitional karma of his is to be experienced in the next rebirth. This, monk, is called volitional karma to be experienced in the next rebirth. Furthermore, monk, here one performs and accumulates volitional karma that is to be experienced in subsequent future lives. That volitional karma of his is to be experienced in subsequent future lives.

This, monk, is called volitional karma to be experienced in subsequent future lives. When this was said, that monk addressed the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘There are these three kinds of volitional karma. For, venerable sir, when one performs and accumulates volitional karma that is to be experienced in this very life, that volitional karma of his is to be experienced in this very life. When one performs and accumulates volitional karma that is to be experienced in the next rebirth, that volitional karma of his is to be experienced in the next rebirth. And when one performs and accumulates volitional karma that is to be experienced in subsequent future lives, that volitional karma of his is to be experienced in subsequent future lives. “It is so, monk; it is so, monk! There are these three kinds of volitional karma. What three? There is volitional karma that is to be experienced in this very life... [as above] ...This, monk, is called volitional karma to be experienced in subsequent future lives. When this was said, that monk addressed the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how does one know and see so that volitional karma to be experienced in this very life does not remain, and volitional karma to be experienced in the next rebirth does not remain, and volitional karma to be experienced in subsequent future lives does not remain, but rather all volitional karma is exhausted right here? “Monk, when one knows and sees the eye as it really is—with its origin, its passing away, its gratification, its danger, and the escape from it—then volitional karma to be experienced in this very life does not remain, and volitional karma to be experienced in the next rebirth does not remain, and volitional karma to be experienced in subsequent future lives does not remain, but rather all volitional karma is exhausted right here. One knows and sees the ear as it really is... the nose as it really is... the tongue as it really is... the body as it really is... the mind as it really is—with its origin, its passing away, its gratification, its danger, and the escape from it. Then volitional karma to be experienced in this very life does not remain, and volitional karma to be experienced in the next rebirth does not remain, and volitional karma to be experienced in subsequent future lives does not remain, but rather all volitional karma is exhausted right here. When this was said, that monk addressed the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘Monk, when one knows and sees the eye as it really is—with its origin, its passing away, its gratification, its danger, and the escape from it—then volitional karma to be experienced in this very life does not remain... but rather all volitional karma is exhausted right here. “It is so, monk; it is so, monk! When one knows and sees the eye as it really is—with its origin, its passing away, its gratification, its danger, and the escape from it—then volitional karma to be experienced in this very life does not remain... but rather all volitional karma is exhausted right here. One knows and sees the ear as it really is... the nose as it really is... the tongue as it really is... the body as it really is... the mind as it really is—with its origin, its passing away, its gratification, its danger, and the escape from it. Then volitional karma to be experienced in this very life does not remain, and volitional karma to be experienced in the next rebirth does not remain, and volitional karma to be experienced in subsequent future lives does not remain, but rather all volitional karma is exhausted right here. Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks! “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these three kinds of volitional karma. What three? There is volitional karma that is to be experienced in this very life; there is volitional karma that is to be experienced in the next rebirth; and there is volitional karma that is to be experienced in subsequent future lives. These, monks, are the three kinds of volitional karma. And what, monks, is volitional karma to be experienced in this very life? Here, monks, one performs and accumulates volitional karma that is to be experienced in this very life. That volitional karma of his is to be experienced in this very life. This, monks, is called volitional karma to be experienced in this very life. And what, monks, is volitional karma to be experienced in the next rebirth? Here, monks, one performs and accumulates volitional karma that is to be experienced in the next rebirth. That volitional karma of his is to be experienced in the next rebirth. This, monks, is called volitional karma to be experienced in the next rebirth. And what, monks, is volitional karma to be experienced in subsequent future lives? Here, monks, one performs and accumulates volitional karma that is to be experienced in subsequent future lives. That volitional karma of his is to be experienced in subsequent future lives. This, monks, is called volitional karma to be experienced in subsequent future lives. These, monks, are the three kinds of volitional karma. Monks, there are these three kinds of volitional karma. There is volitional karma that is to be experienced in this very life; there is volitional karma that is to be experienced in the next rebirth; and there is volitional karma that is to be experienced in subsequent future lives. “Monks, I do not say that there is an exhaustion of intentional kamma that has been done and accumulated without its being experienced; rather,
it is experienced either in this very life, or in the next rebirth, or in some subsequent period.”
"But I do not say, monks, that there is an end to suffering without experiencing the results of intentional kamma that has been performed and accumulated.

In this regard, monks, there are three kinds of corruption and failure in bodily action, consisting of unwholesome intentional kamma, which have suffering as their outcome and suffering as their result;
and four kinds of corruption and failure in verbal action, consisting of unwholesome intentional kamma, which have suffering as their outcome and suffering as their result."
In three ways, monks, there is corruption and transgression of mental action consisting of unwholesome volition that has suffering as its outcome and suffering as its result.
And how, monks, is there corruption and transgression of bodily action in three ways consisting of unwholesome volition that has suffering as its outcome and suffering as its result? ...

[as before] ... In this way, monks, there is corruption and transgression of bodily action in three ways consisting of unwholesome volition that has suffering as its outcome and suffering as its result.
And how, monks, does the fourfold corruption and transgression of verbal action, consisting of unwholesome volition, have suffering as its outcome and suffering as its result?
… [as before] … Thus, monks, the fourfold corruption and transgression of verbal action, consisting of unwholesome volition, has suffering as its outcome and suffering as its result.
And how, monks, does the threefold corruption and transgression of mental action, consisting of unwholesome volition, have suffering as its outcome and suffering as its result? … [as before] …
In this way, monks, there are three kinds of corruption and perversion of mental action consisting of unwholesome volition that have suffering as their outcome and suffering as their result.

Or, monks, it is because of the threefold corruption and perversion of bodily action consisting of unwholesome volition that, with the breakup of the body, after death, beings are reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower world, or hell; and [because of] the fourfold corruption of verbal action...

...pe... "Or, monks, it is due to the threefold corruption and transgression of unwholesome volitional actions of mind that beings, with the breakup of the body, after death, reappear in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, perdition, even in hell.
Monks, I do not say that there is an end to intentional kamma that has been done and accumulated without its being experienced."
And that occurs either in this very life, or upon rebirth, or in some subsequent period.
Yet, monks, I do not say that there is an end to suffering without experiencing the results of intentional kamma that has been performed and accumulated.
In this regard, monks, there is a threefold success in bodily action consisting of wholesome intentional kamma that has a pleasant outcome and a pleasant result.
Fourfold is the success of verbal action consisting of wholesome volition, which has happiness as its outcome and results in happiness;
threefold is the success of mental action consisting of wholesome volition, which has happiness as its outcome and results in happiness.
And how, bhikkhus, is the threefold success of bodily action consisting of wholesome volition, which has happiness as its outcome and results in happiness? ... [as above] ...
In this way, monks, threefold success in bodily action, consisting of wholesome volition, has a pleasant outcome and a pleasant result.
And how, monks, does fourfold success in verbal action, consisting of wholesome volition, have a pleasant outcome and a pleasant result? ...
[as before] ... In this way, monks, fourfold success in verbal action, consisting of wholesome volition, has a pleasant outcome and a pleasant result.
And how, monks, does the threefold success of mental action consisting of wholesome volition have a pleasant outcome and a pleasant result? ...
[as before] ... In this way, monks, the threefold success of mental action consisting of wholesome volition has a pleasant outcome and a pleasant result.
Or, monks, it is because of the threefold success of bodily action consisting of wholesome volition that, with the breakup of the body, beings—
After death, they reappear in a happy destination, in a heavenly world, because of their success in the fourfold verbal action ...

[and so on] ... or, monks, it is due to the cause of wholesome volitional intentions consisting in success in the threefold mental action that beings, with the breakup of the body, after death, reappear in a happy destination, in a heavenly world ... [and so on].
The Eighth. Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.219. Chapter 21:
On the Body Born of Karma (Karajakāyavagga).
The Discourse on the Body Born of Volition:
“Bhikkhus, I do not say that there is the exhaustion of volitional kamma that has been performed and accumulated without its being experienced;
rather, that occurs either in this very life, or upon rebirth, or in some subsequent period.”
"But I do not say, monks, that there is an end to suffering without experiencing the results of intentional kamma that has been performed and accumulated.

However, monks, that noble disciple—thus free from covetousness, free from ill will, undeluded, clearly comprehending, and mindful—abides pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with loving-kindness; likewise the second, likewise..."

The third [direction] likewise, and the fourth. Thus, above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—vast, exalted, measureless, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
He understands thus:
‘Formerly, indeed, this mind of mine was limited and undeveloped; but now this mind of mine is immeasurable and well-developed.
Whatever action is performed that is limited, it will not remain there, nor will it persist there.
What do you think, monks?
“If this prince had cultivated the liberation of mind through loving-kindness from his very childhood, would he have committed any evil deed?”—
“Certainly not, Bhante.”—
“And if he were not committing any evil deed, would suffering touch him?”
“Certainly not, Bhante.
For how, Bhante, could suffering touch one who does not perform evil karma?
“Furthermore, bhikkhus, this liberation of mind through loving-kindness should be developed by a woman or a man.”
"Monks, this body is not to be taken away by a woman or a man.
This mortal being, monks, has the mind within him.
He understands thus:"
‘Whatever evil deed I have previously done with this body born of karma, all of that is to be experienced right here;
it will not follow after me.
Bhikkhus, when the liberation of mind through loving-kindness is developed in this way, it leads to non-returning for a wise bhikkhu who has not yet penetrated a higher liberation in this very life.
With a mind imbued with compassion… with a mind imbued with sympathetic joy… with a mind imbued with equanimity,
he dwells pervading one quarter, likewise the second, likewise the third, and likewise the fourth.

Thus, above, below, across, and everywhere, to all as to himself, he dwells having pervaded the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
He understands thus:
"Formerly, indeed, this mind of mine was limited and undeveloped; but now this mind of mine is immeasurable."
“...well-developed. Furthermore, whatever limited karma has been performed, it will neither remain there nor persist there.
“What do you think, bhikkhus, if this boy were to develop the liberation of mind through equanimity from his very childhood, would he ever commit an evil deed?”
“No, venerable sir.
“But if one does not perform an evil deed, would suffering touch one?
“No, venerable sir.”
“Indeed, venerable sir, how could suffering touch one who does not perform evil deeds?
“Furthermore, bhikkhus, this liberation of mind through equanimity must be developed by a woman or a man.
For neither a woman nor a man can go taking this body with them.”
“Bhikkhus, this mortal being has consciousness as his innermost core.
He understands thus:
‘Whatever evil kamma I previously did with this body born of karma, all that is to be experienced here and now.’”
"It will not follow after him.
Thus, monks, when equanimity as liberation of mind is developed in this way, it leads to non-returning for a wise monk who has not yet penetrated further liberation.
Thus ends the ninth [sutta].
Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.220 21.

Karajakāyavagga Adhammacariyāsutta (The Discourse on Unrighteous Conduct) “Monks, there are these ten kinds of unrighteous conduct. What ten? (1) One destroys life; (2) one takes what is not given; (3) one engages in sexual misconduct; (4) one speaks falsehood; (5) one speaks divisively; (6) one speaks harshly; (7) one indulges in idle chatter; (8) one is covetous; (9) one harbors ill will; (10) one holds wrong view. These, monks, are the ten kinds of unrighteous conduct.”
(AN 10.220, AN 10.209, PTS AN v 301) Then a certain brahmin approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, that brahmin said this to the Blessed One:

“What, Master Gotama, is the cause, what is the reason why some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell?

“Brahmin, it is because of conduct contrary to the Dhamma and conduct that is unrighteous that some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, are reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell.”
“But what, Master Gotama, is the cause, what is the reason why some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, reappear in a happy destination, in a heavenly world?

“It is, brahmin, because of their practice of the Dhamma and practice of the way of peace that some beings here, with the breakup of the body, after death, reappear in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
“I do not understand in detail the meaning of this statement spoken in brief by Master Gotama.”
“It would be well, venerable Gotama, if you would teach me the Dhamma in such a way that I might understand in detail the meaning of what has been stated by the venerable Gotama in brief.
“In that case, brahmin, listen and pay close attention; I shall speak.
“Yes, sir,” that brahmin replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
"Brahmin, there are three kinds of unrighteous conduct and improper conduct by way of the body;
there are four kinds of unrighteous conduct and improper conduct by way of speech."
There are three kinds of unrighteous conduct and improper conduct by way of the mind.
And how, brahmin, are there three kinds of unrighteous conduct and improper conduct by way of the body? ... [as above] ...
In this way, brahmin, there are three kinds of unrighteous conduct and improper conduct by way of the body.
And how, brahmin, is there fourfold unrighteous conduct and uneven conduct by way of speech?
… [as above] … It is in this way, brahmin, that there is fourfold unrighteous conduct and uneven conduct by way of speech.
And how, brahmin, is there threefold unrighteous conduct and uneven conduct by way of mind? … [as above] …
In this way, brahmin, there are three kinds of unrighteous conduct and improper conduct by means of the mind.

It is because of such unrighteous and improper conduct, brahmin, that some beings here, with the breakup of the body after death, reappear in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell.
There are, brahmin, three kinds of righteous conduct and proper conduct by means of the body;

There are four kinds of righteous conduct and peaceful conduct by way of speech; there are three kinds of righteous conduct and peaceful conduct by way of mind. And how, brahmin, are there three kinds of righteous conduct and peaceful conduct by way of body? … [as above] … There are four kinds of righteous conduct and peaceful conduct by way of speech: abstaining from false speech, abstaining from malicious speech, abstaining from harsh speech, and abstaining from idle chatter. These are the four kinds of righteous conduct and peaceful conduct by way of speech. There are three kinds of righteous conduct and peaceful conduct by way of mind: abstaining from covetousness, abstaining from ill will, and abstaining from wrong view. These are the three kinds of righteous conduct and peaceful conduct by way of mind.
And how, brahmin, are there three kinds of righteous conduct and peaceful conduct by way of body? … [as above] …
"In this way, brahmin, there are three kinds of righteous conduct and peaceful conduct by way of the body.

[as before] ... In this way, brahmin, there is fourfold righteous conduct and peaceful conduct by way of speech."
"And how, brahmin, is there a threefold practice of the Dhamma and practice of equanimity by means of the mind? ...

Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.22 The Chapter on Asceticism (Sāmaññavagga) “Monks, there are these ten qualities of a true ascetic. What ten? (1) Here, monks, a bhikkhu is endowed with faith; he places faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgata thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. (2) He is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest fault; having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. (3) He has heard much, has retained what he has heard, accumulated what he has heard; those teachings that are lovely in the beginning, lovely in the middle, and lovely in the end, which in spirit and in letter proclaim the holy life that is utterly perfect and pure—such teachings as these he has heard much of, retained, and accumulated. (4) He is one who gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life. (5) He possesses the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human; he sees beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and understands how beings fare according to their kamma. (6) He possesses the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing the human; he hears both kinds of sounds, the divine and the human, whether far or near. (7) He recollects his manifold past lives, that is, one birth, two births, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand, many eons of cosmic contraction, many eons of cosmic expansion, many eons of cosmic contraction and expansion: ‘There I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, such a lifespan; passing away from there, I was reborn elsewhere, and there too I had such a name... Thus he recollects his manifold past lives in their modes and details. (8) With the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, he sees beings passing away and being reborn, inferior and superior, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate, and understands how beings fare according to their kamma. (9) By the destruction of the taints, he has realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, he dwells therein. These, monks, are the ten qualities of a true ascetic.”

and the perception of cessation— for the direct knowledge of lust, bhikkhus, these ten things are to be developed.”
